The hand is swollen, mottled, cooler and sweatier than the left, and the fingers are stiff. Radiographs show a healing fracture with patchy osteopenia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Graded physical and occupational therapy with adequate pain control

options.label: C
options.html: Observation without treatment, as symptoms always resolve

options.label: D
options.html: Reapplication of the cast for 4 more weeks

items.explanationHtml:
This is complex regional pain syndrome. Early, graded physical and occupational therapy to restore movement and use of the limb is the cornerstone, supported by pain control and psychological care. Glucocorticoids, bisphosphonates, neuropathic agents and sympathetic blocks are options for persistent cases.

Takeaway: CRPS: early graded rehabilitation is the cornerstone of treatment.

whyNot.D: Prolonged immobilisation worsens CRPS and delays recovery of the limb.
whyNot.B: Long-term opioids are not recommended and do not restore function.
whyNot.E: Sympathectomy is not an initial treatment and its benefit is unproven.
whyNot.C: Many cases improve, but untreated CRPS can lead to lasting stiffness and disability.

items.objective: Begin graded rehabilitation for complex regional pain syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has burning, electric pain in both feet that keeps her awake. She also has major depressive disorder that has not been treated. eGFR is 85 mL/min/1.73 m2. She takes metformin. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for her pain?
items.explanationHtml:
First-line drugs for painful diabetic neuropathy are SNRIs (duloxetine), gabapentinoids and tricyclics. Duloxetine also treats her depression and is suitable with normal kidney function (avoid with severe kidney impairment).

Takeaway: painful diabetic neuropathy + depression → duloxetine.

whyNot.E: Tramadol is not first-line and adds dependence, seizure and serotonin-syndrome risk.
whyNot.C: NSAIDs are ineffective for neuropathic pain and harm the kidneys over time.
whyNot.A: Carbamazepine has weaker evidence and more adverse effects in diabetic neuropathy.
whyNot.D: Opioids are not first-line for chronic neuropathic pain.

items.objective: Choose duloxetine for painful diabetic neuropathy with comorbid depression.

items.stemHtml:
A 76-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has burning pain in both feet that disturbs his sleep. His medical problems and medications are listed:

ProblemMedication
Type 2 diabetesMetformin
Benign prostatic hyperplasia with episodes of urinary retentionTamsulosin
First-degree atrioventricular block and a prolonged QTc on ECGNone
Orthostatic dizzinessNone

Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for his pain?
items.explanationHtml:
A gabapentinoid such as pregabalin is a first-line drug for painful diabetic neuropathy and avoids the anticholinergic, orthostatic and cardiac-conduction effects of tricyclics. Start low and titrate slowly in an older adult; adjust the dose if kidney function declines.

Takeaway: in older adults with urinary retention or conduction disease, prefer a gabapentinoid (or SNRI) over a tricyclic.

whyNot.A: Amitriptyline's anticholinergic effects worsen urinary retention, and it can slow cardiac conduction and cause orthostasis.
whyNot.D: Nortriptyline is better tolerated than amitriptyline but still carries anticholinergic and conduction risks.
whyNot.C: Opioids are not first-line for neuropathic pain and raise fall and dependence risks.
whyNot.B: Carbamazepine is not first-line for diabetic neuropathy and adds hyponatraemia and drug-interaction risks in older adults.

items.objective: Choose a neuropathic pain drug according to comorbidities in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman dies of pneumonia after 8 years of progressive memory loss. She first had trouble recalling recent conversations, later got lost in her own neighbourhood, and in her final years could not dress herself. At autopsy, silver staining of the hippocampus shows flame-shaped aggregates inside the cytoplasm of many pyramidal neurons. These intracellular aggregates are composed mainly of which of the following proteins?

options.label: C
options.html: Huntingtin with an expanded polyglutamine tract

items.explanationHtml:
The slow amnestic course with later disorientation and loss of self-care is typical of Alzheimer disease. The intracellular, flame-shaped aggregates are neurofibrillary tangles: hyperphosphorylated tau that has detached from microtubules. Tangle burden correlates with the degree of dementia better than plaque burden does.

Takeaway: Alzheimer disease has two lesions: extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intracellular tau tangles.

whyNot.B: Amyloid-beta forms the extracellular plaques of Alzheimer disease, not aggregates inside neurons.
whyNot.A: Alpha-synuclein forms Lewy bodies, which are round, not flame-shaped, and define Lewy body disease.
whyNot.E: Prion disease causes spongiform vacuolation over months, not a slow 8-year amnestic course with tangles.
whyNot.C: Huntingtin aggregates are intranuclear and occur in Huntington disease, which presents with chorea.

items.objective: Identify neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau as the intracellular lesion of Alzheimer disease.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with Down syndrome lives in a group home. Over the past 2 years staff have noticed that he forgets familiar routines, misplaces belongings and has become withdrawn. He was previously independent in self-care. Increased dosage of which of the following genes best explains the early onset of his cognitive decline?

options.label: A
options.html: Amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21

options.label: D
options.html: Microtubule-associated protein tau gene on chromosome 17

items.explanationHtml:
In trisomy 21 the extra copy of APP raises production of amyloid-beta throughout life. Most adults with Down syndrome have Alzheimer pathology by their 40s, and many develop clinical dementia in their 50s.

Takeaway: Three copies of APP (chromosome 21) explain early Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.

whyNot.E: Presenilin 1 mutations cause autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer disease, but chromosome 14 is not triplicated in Down syndrome.
whyNot.B: APOE e4 modifies risk of late-onset disease; trisomy 21 does not add copies of APOE.
whyNot.D: MAPT mutations cause frontotemporal dementia with tau pathology, unrelated to trisomy 21.
whyNot.C: Huntingtin repeat expansion causes Huntington disease, with chorea and psychiatric change.

items.objective: Relate APP gene dosage on chromosome 21 to early Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer disease starts a new medication for her memory. Four weeks later she has two brief episodes of lightheadedness, one of which leads to a fall. Her pulse is 46/min and regular. An ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a normal QRS duration. Which of the following best explains her new symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptors

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of cardiac fast sodium channels

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of NMDA receptors in the brainstem

options.label: D
options.html: Increased acetylcholine acting on cardiac muscarinic receptors

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulation of central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) raise acetylcholine at every cholinergic synapse, including vagal endings on the SA and AV nodes. The muscarinic (M2) effect slows the heart and can cause syncope and falls, especially with other rate-slowing drugs.

Takeaway: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia and syncope through increased vagal tone.

whyNot.A: Her memory drug is not a beta-blocker; the bradycardia here is cholinergic.
whyNot.B: Sodium channel blockade widens the QRS complex, which is normal here.
whyNot.C: Memantine blocks NMDA receptors and does not typically cause bradycardia.
whyNot.E: Central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine slow the heart, but they are not dementia drugs.

items.objective: Explain bradycardia and syncope caused by cholinesterase inhibitors used in dementia.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man with moderate Alzheimer disease takes donepezil. A second drug is added. It enters the ion channel of a glutamate-gated receptor only after the channel opens, and it leaves the channel quickly, so normal fast synaptic signals still pass while a constant low-level leak of calcium is reduced. Which of the following receptors does this drug act on?
items.explanationHtml:
The drug is memantine, an uncompetitive, low-affinity blocker of the open NMDA receptor channel. It is used in moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, alone or with a cholinesterase inhibitor, to limit excitotoxic calcium entry.

Takeaway: Memantine is an open-channel NMDA receptor blocker used in moderate to severe Alzheimer disease.

whyNot.A: AMPA receptors carry most fast sodium current; memantine does not act on them.
whyNot.B: GABA-A receptors are chloride channels enhanced by benzodiazepines, not glutamate-gated.
whyNot.D: Nicotinic receptors are gated by acetylcholine, not glutamate.
whyNot.C: Metabotropic glutamate receptors are G protein-coupled and have no ion pore to block.

items.objective: Identify the NMDA receptor as the target of memantine.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife because his behaviour has changed over 2 years. He tells crude jokes to strangers, has spent their savings on impulsive purchases, eats large amounts of sweets and no longer seems to care about his grandchildren. He scores almost normally on tests of recall and drawing. His father had a similar illness and later developed muscle wasting. Which of the following is most likely on brain MRI?

options.label: A
options.html: Atrophy of the frontal and anterior temporal lobes

options.label: B
options.html: Atrophy of the hippocampi and parietal lobes

options.label: C
options.html: Midbrain atrophy with a preserved pons

options.label: D
options.html: Multiple lacunes with confluent white matter change

options.label: E
options.html: Ventricles enlarged out of proportion to the sulci

items.explanationHtml:
Early disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and hyperorality with relatively preserved memory and visuospatial skills is behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia. The family history of dementia followed by muscle wasting suggests a C9orf72 repeat expansion, which links frontotemporal dementia with ALS.

Takeaway: Personality change before memory loss points to frontotemporal dementia and frontal and anterior temporal atrophy.

whyNot.B: Hippocampal and parietal atrophy fits Alzheimer disease, which starts with memory loss.
whyNot.E: Disproportionate ventricular enlargement suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus, with gait failure first.
whyNot.D: Small-vessel disease causes slowed thinking and focal signs rather than early disinhibition.
whyNot.C: Midbrain atrophy suggests progressive supranuclear palsy, with early falls and impaired downgaze.

items.objective: Recognise behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia and its imaging pattern.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old man has had 18 months of cognitive decline. On some days he is clear, and on others he is drowsy and confused. He describes seeing small children playing in the living room. His wife says he has shouted and punched in his sleep for years. He has mild symmetric rigidity. After a single dose of haloperidol for agitation in the emergency department, he becomes markedly rigid and stuporous. Which of the following is most likely found in his cortical neurons at autopsy?

options.label: E
options.html: Spongiform vacuoles with misfolded prion protein

items.explanationHtml:
Fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism define dementia with Lewy bodies. Cortical neurons contain Lewy bodies made of alpha-synuclein. Severe sensitivity to dopamine-blocking antipsychotics is a supportive feature and a real danger.

Takeaway: Fluctuations, visual hallucinations and dream enactment point to Lewy body dementia; avoid typical antipsychotics.

whyNot.C: Tau tangles mark Alzheimer disease, which rarely causes early hallucinations and dream enactment.
whyNot.E: Prion disease progresses over weeks to months with myoclonus, not over 18 months with fluctuations.
whyNot.B: TDP-43 inclusions occur in frontotemporal dementia and ALS, which present with behavioural change or weakness.
whyNot.A: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhages, not this clinical syndrome.

items.objective: Link the clinical features of dementia with Lewy bodies to cortical alpha-synuclein inclusions.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder lives in a shelter. He cannot remember what he ate for breakfast or the name of the nurse he met an hour ago, yet he talks fluently and gives detailed but false accounts of a business trip he says he took yesterday. Attention and language are otherwise normal. Brain MRI is most likely to show atrophy of which of the following structures?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation after thiamine deficiency is Korsakoff syndrome. The memory loop from the hippocampus through the fornix, mammillary bodies and medial thalamus is damaged; mammillary body atrophy is the classic imaging and autopsy finding.

Takeaway: Korsakoff syndrome is amnesia with confabulation from thiamine-related damage to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.

whyNot.B: Caudate atrophy is typical of Huntington disease, with chorea and psychiatric change.
whyNot.C: Alcohol-related vermian atrophy causes gait ataxia, not amnesia with confabulation.
whyNot.E: Occipital damage causes visual field or visual processing deficits, not anterograde amnesia.
whyNot.A: Damage to the basis pontis (for example, osmotic demyelination) causes quadriparesis and dysarthria.

items.objective: Localise Korsakoff amnesia to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day has had 3 months of difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs, a dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent at rest but become present after he contracts his quadriceps hard for 10 seconds. Refer to the figure.

Antibodies against which labelled site are most likely responsible for his weakness?
items.explanationHtml:
Proximal leg weakness, autonomic symptoms (dry mouth, erectile dysfunction) and reflexes that return after brief exercise are the signature of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Antibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels reduce calcium entry and therefore acetylcholine release; repeated activity builds up calcium and transiently improves release. Over half of cases are paraneoplastic, usually from small cell lung cancer.

Takeaway: Weakness that improves with effort plus dry mouth and absent reflexes means Lambert-Eaton syndrome and anti-VGCC antibodies.

whyNot.B: Site B is the SNARE fusion machinery, cleaved by botulinum toxin.
whyNot.C: Site C is acetylcholinesterase, which pyridostigmine and organophosphates inhibit; no antibody targets it in these diseases.
whyNot.D: Site D is the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, the target of antibodies in most myasthenia gravis.
whyNot.E: Site E is MuSK, targeted by antibodies in a minority of patients with myasthenia gravis who lack acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

items.objective: Localise Lambert-Eaton syndrome to the presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel.

items.stemHtml:
A 27-year-old woman has 2 months of drooping eyelids and double vision that are mild in the morning and worse by evening. After 2 minutes of sustained upgaze her left eyelid falls further. Pupils, sensation and reflexes are normal. Refer to the figure.

The autoantibodies most likely responsible bind which labelled site?
items.explanationHtml:
Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils and reflexes is myasthenia gravis. In most patients, antibodies bind the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, block it, cross-link it so it is internalised, and activate complement that damages the end plate. Fewer receptors mean the safety margin is lost with repeated firing.

Takeaway: Myasthenia gravis is antibody-mediated loss of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; weakness worsens with use.

whyNot.A: Site A is the presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel, the target of antibodies in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
whyNot.B: Site B is the SNARE fusion machinery, cleaved by botulinum toxin.
whyNot.C: Site C is acetylcholinesterase, which pyridostigmine and organophosphates inhibit; no antibody targets it in these diseases.
whyNot.E: Site E is MuSK, targeted by antibodies in a minority of patients with myasthenia gravis who lack acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

items.objective: Localise myasthenia gravis to the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.

items.stemHtml:
A 45-year-old man has blurred and double vision, difficulty swallowing and slurred speech that began 18 hours after he ate home-canned green beans. Over the next day his arms become weak, then his legs. He is alert and afebrile; his pupils are dilated and react poorly to light; sensation is normal. Refer to the figure.

The toxin responsible acts at which labelled site?
items.explanationHtml:
Descending, symmetric flaccid paralysis starting in the cranial nerves, with dilated pupils, a clear mind and no sensory loss after eating home-canned vegetables is foodborne botulism. Botulinum toxin enters the nerve terminal and its light chain, a zinc protease, cleaves SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin, SNAP-25 or syntaxin). Vesicles cannot fuse with the membrane, so acetylcholine is not released at neuromuscular and autonomic cholinergic synapses.

Takeaway: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and stops acetylcholine release; paralysis descends from the cranial nerves.

whyNot.A: Site A is the presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channel, the target of antibodies in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
whyNot.C: Site C is acetylcholinesterase, which pyridostigmine and organophosphates inhibit; no antibody targets it in these diseases.
whyNot.D: Site D is the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, the target of antibodies in most myasthenia gravis.
whyNot.E: Site E is MuSK, targeted by antibodies in a minority of patients with myasthenia gravis who lack acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

items.objective: Identify SNARE proteins as the site of action of botulinum toxin.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man has had 8 months of weakness in his right hand, which now cannot turn a key, followed by weakness of the left leg. His tongue and right hand muscles are wasted and show visible twitches. Reflexes are brisk in all limbs, and both plantar responses are extensor. Sensation and eye movements are normal, and bladder control is intact. Degeneration of which of the following best explains these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Anterior horn cells and lateral corticospinal tracts

options.label: C
options.html: Central gray matter near the spinal canal

options.label: D
options.html: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts

items.explanationHtml:
Lower motor neuron signs (atrophy, fasciculations) mixed with upper motor neuron signs (hyperreflexia, extensor plantars) in the same limbs, with normal sensation, eye movements and sphincters, define amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Anterior horn cells, brainstem motor nuclei and corticospinal neurons degenerate.

Takeaway: ALS combines upper and lower motor neuron signs with spared sensation, eye movements and sphincters.

whyNot.D: Dorsal column loss would remove vibration and position sense; it describes subacute combined degeneration.
whyNot.B: Pure lower motor neuron loss (as in spinal muscular atrophy) would not cause brisk reflexes or extensor plantars.
whyNot.E: Dorsal root ganglion loss causes sensory ataxia without weakness or fasciculations.
whyNot.C: A central cord cavity first interrupts crossing pain and temperature fibres in a cape distribution.

items.objective: Localise amyotrophic lateral sclerosis to upper and lower motor neurons.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman is diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Genetic testing shows no pathogenic variant. Her neurologist prescribes an oral drug that modestly prolongs survival and is thought to work by reducing excitotoxic injury to motor neurons. Which of the following is the main mechanism of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Riluzole reduces glutamate release (in part by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels on presynaptic terminals). Excess glutamate signalling is thought to contribute to motor neuron death in ALS. The survival gain is a few months. Liver enzymes should be monitored.

Takeaway: Riluzole limits glutamate excitotoxicity and modestly prolongs survival in ALS.

whyNot.A: Tofersen lowers SOD1 protein but is intrathecal and only for SOD1 variant carriers.
whyNot.D: Free-radical scavenging is the proposed mechanism of edaravone, which is given IV or as a suspension.
whyNot.B: Cholinesterase inhibition helps myasthenia gravis, not motor neuron death.
whyNot.E: SMN2 splicing modifiers treat spinal muscular atrophy.

items.objective: State the mechanism of riluzole in ALS.

items.stemHtml: A 4-month-old girl has had increasing floppiness and a weak cry. She is alert, follows faces and smiles. She lies with her legs frogged, cannot lift her arms against gravity, breathes mainly with her abdomen, and has fasciculations of the tongue. Reflexes are absent. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis, and she starts treatment with an antisense oligonucleotide given by lumbar puncture. Which of the following is the mechanism of this treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: It alters splicing of SMN2 pre-mRNA so that exon 7 is kept

options.label: B
options.html: It blocks the neonatal Fc receptor to lower IgG

options.label: C
options.html: It delivers a working SMN1 gene in a viral vector

options.label: D
options.html: It lowers production of mutant SOD1 protein

options.label: E
options.html: It skips a dystrophin exon to restore the reading frame

items.explanationHtml:
This is spinal muscular atrophy: loss of SMN1 causes anterior horn cell death, so the infant is weak, areflexic and hypotonic with tongue fasciculations but is cognitively normal. The back-up gene SMN2 mostly skips exon 7. Nusinersen binds SMN2 pre-mRNA and blocks a splicing silencer, so exon 7 is included and full-length SMN protein is made.

Takeaway: Nusinersen and risdiplam correct SMN2 splicing; onasemnogene replaces SMN1.

whyNot.C: Delivering SMN1 by an AAV9 vector describes onasemnogene abeparvovec, a one-time IV gene therapy.
whyNot.E: Exon skipping of dystrophin treats certain Duchenne muscular dystrophy deletions.
whyNot.D: Lowering SOD1 is the action of tofersen in SOD1-related ALS.
whyNot.B: FcRn blockade lowers pathogenic IgG in myasthenia gravis.

items.objective: Explain how nusinersen increases SMN protein in spinal muscular atrophy.

items.stemHtml: A 13-year-old boy has trouble running and climbing stairs. He walked at 14 months and kept up with friends until age 9. He has enlarged calves and uses his hands on his thighs to stand from the floor. Creatine kinase is markedly raised. Genetic testing shows a deletion of three whole exons in the dystrophin gene; the number of deleted bases is divisible by three. Which of the following best explains why his disease is milder than his cousin's Duchenne muscular dystrophy?

options.label: A
options.html: Dystrophin is made normally but is broken down faster

options.label: B
options.html: His mutation arose new rather than being inherited

options.label: C
options.html: Skewed X-inactivation leaves most of his muscle fibres normal

options.label: D
options.html: The deletion keeps the reading frame, so a shorter, partly working dystrophin is made

options.label: E
options.html: The deletion lies in an intron, so dystrophin protein is unchanged

items.explanationHtml:
In Becker muscular dystrophy the deletion is usually in frame: removing a multiple of three bases leaves the downstream code readable, so a truncated but partly functional dystrophin is made. In Duchenne dystrophy the deletion shifts the reading frame, a premature stop codon appears, and almost no dystrophin is produced.

Takeaway: In-frame dystrophin deletions give Becker; frameshift deletions give Duchenne.

whyNot.E: The deletion removes exons; an unchanged protein would cause no disease.
whyNot.A: Faster breakdown is not the mechanism of Becker dystrophy; protein structure is altered.
whyNot.C: X-inactivation occurs in females; a boy has one X chromosome.
whyNot.B: Whether a mutation is inherited or new does not change its effect on the protein.

items.objective: Explain the reading-frame rule that separates Becker from Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman has trouble letting go of objects after gripping them, and her handshake is slow to release. She has bilateral ptosis, wasting of the temporalis and sternocleidomastoid muscles, weak finger flexors and lens opacities. An ECG shows a PR interval of 240 ms. Her son was born very floppy and needed ventilation for several weeks. Which of the following mutations is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene

options.label: B
options.html: CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene

options.label: C
options.html: CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene

options.label: D
options.html: Frameshift deletion in the dystrophin gene

options.label: E
options.html: GAA repeat expansion in the FXN gene

items.explanationHtml:
Myotonia, facial and distal weakness, ptosis, cataracts and conduction disease are myotonic dystrophy type 1, an autosomal dominant CTG expansion in the 3' untranslated region of DMPK. The expanded RNA traps splicing regulators. Repeats tend to grow when passed on, and very large expansions transmitted by an affected mother cause the severe congenital form seen in her son.

Takeaway: Myotonia plus cataracts, ptosis and heart block means myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DMPK CTG repeat); congenital cases come from affected mothers.

whyNot.A: HTT CAG repeats cause Huntington disease, with chorea and dementia.
whyNot.B: FMR1 CGG repeats cause fragile X syndrome or premutation disorders, not myotonia.
whyNot.E: FXN GAA repeats cause Friedreich ataxia, with ataxia, areflexia and cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.D: Dystrophin frameshifts cause Duchenne dystrophy in boys, without myotonia or cataracts.

items.objective: Identify the repeat expansion that causes myotonic dystrophy type 1.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman develops tingling of both feet followed by weakness that climbs from her legs to her arms over 5 days. Three weeks earlier she had bloody diarrhea after a barbecue. Reflexes are absent. Nerve conduction studies show reduced motor amplitudes with normal conduction velocities. Antibodies against a nerve ganglioside are detected. Which of the following best explains how the infection led to her neuropathy?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibodies to bacterial lipooligosaccharide cross-react with axonal gangliosides

options.label: B
options.html: Bacteria invade peripheral nerves and multiply in Schwann cells

options.label: C
options.html: Bacterial toxin cleaves proteins needed for acetylcholine release

options.label: D
options.html: Circulating toxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels

options.label: E
options.html: Immune complexes deposit in the vasa nervorum

items.explanationHtml:
Campylobacter jejuni lipooligosaccharide resembles gangliosides such as GM1 on motor axons. Antibodies made against the bacterium cross-react with the nerve (molecular mimicry). The low amplitudes with preserved velocities point to the acute motor axonal form of Guillain-Barré syndrome, which is linked to anti-GM1 antibodies.

Takeaway: Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter is molecular mimicry against nerve gangliosides.

whyNot.C: Cleavage of SNARE proteins is the action of botulinum toxin, which causes descending paralysis.
whyNot.B: Invasion of Schwann cells is typical of leprosy, which causes patchy sensory loss.
whyNot.D: Sodium channel toxins such as tetrodotoxin act within hours of ingestion.
whyNot.E: Vasculitic neuropathy usually causes painful, asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex.

items.objective: Explain molecular mimicry as the mechanism of Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter infection.

items.stemHtml:
A 71-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension suddenly develops wild, flinging movements of his left arm and leg that stop only during sleep. He is alert, and strength is normal. Refer to the figure.

A small infarct in which labelled structure best explains these movements?
items.explanationHtml:
Large-amplitude, violent flinging of one side of the body is hemiballismus. It classically follows a small vessel infarct of the subthalamic nucleus on the opposite side. The subthalamic nucleus normally drives the internal pallidum, which brakes the thalamus. With it gone, the thalamus is released and unwanted movement appears.

Takeaway: Contralateral hemiballismus localises to the subthalamic nucleus.

whyNot.A: Structure A is the striatum; its loss of indirect-pathway neurons causes chorea, not unilateral flinging after a small stroke.
whyNot.B: Structure B is the external globus pallidus, which receives the indirect-pathway projection from the striatum.
whyNot.D: Structure D is the internal globus pallidus and substantia nigra pars reticulata, the output nuclei of the circuit.
whyNot.E: Structure E is the motor thalamus, which receives the pallidal output and projects to the cortex.

items.objective: Localise hemiballismus to the contralateral subthalamic nucleus using the basal ganglia circuit.

items.stemHtml:
A 41-year-old woman has 2 years of fidgety, flowing, involuntary movements of her face and limbs, irritability and depression. Her father had a similar illness. In early disease, the striatal GABAergic neurons that degenerate first are those that project to one particular structure. Refer to the figure.

Loss of the striatal projection to which labelled structure best explains her chorea?
items.explanationHtml:
This is Huntington disease. Early on, the striatal medium spiny neurons of the indirect pathway, which carry D2 receptors and project to the external globus pallidus, die first. The external pallidum is then overactive, inhibits the subthalamic nucleus, and the internal pallidum stops braking the thalamus, so excess movement (chorea) appears. Later, direct-pathway neurons are lost too and rigidity can develop.

Takeaway: Early loss of indirect-pathway striatal neurons (projecting to the external pallidum) causes chorea in Huntington disease.

whyNot.A: Structure A is the striatum itself, where the degenerating neurons sit; the question asks for their target.
whyNot.C: Structure C, the subthalamic nucleus, does not receive a direct projection from the striatum.
whyNot.D: Structure D receives the direct-pathway projection, which is relatively spared early in Huntington disease.
whyNot.E: Structure E is the motor thalamus, which receives the pallidal output and projects to the cortex.

items.objective: Explain chorea in Huntington disease by loss of indirect-pathway striatal neurons.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with Parkinson disease starts a combination tablet. One component crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine. The other component does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Which of the following is the action of the second component?

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of monoamine oxidase type B

items.explanationHtml:
Carbidopa inhibits aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylase outside the brain. Less levodopa is turned into dopamine in the blood and gut, so nausea and hypotension fall and more levodopa reaches the brain, where it is decarboxylated normally.

Takeaway: Carbidopa blocks peripheral decarboxylation of levodopa and does not enter the brain.

whyNot.C: COMT inhibition is the action of entacapone or opicapone, often added later for wearing off.
whyNot.D: MAO-B inhibition is the action of selegiline, rasagiline and safinamide.
whyNot.B: Direct D2 agonism describes pramipexole and ropinirole.
whyNot.A: Muscarinic blockade describes trihexyphenidyl and benztropine.

items.objective: State the mechanism and purpose of carbidopa in levodopa therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man has had 6 years of slow movements, a shuffling gait, a soft voice and a resting tremor of the right hand that disappears when he reaches for a cup. Before his motor symptoms began he had lost his sense of smell. At autopsy, the substantia nigra is pale, and surviving pigmented neurons contain round eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions with a pale halo. These inclusions are composed mainly of which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
The clinical picture is Parkinson disease. Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta are lost, and survivors carry Lewy bodies, made of aggregated alpha-synuclein. Loss of smell, constipation and REM sleep behaviour disorder often precede the motor signs.

Takeaway: Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease are alpha-synuclein inclusions in nigral neurons.

whyNot.C: Tau forms tangles in Alzheimer disease and progressive supranuclear palsy.
whyNot.B: Amyloid-beta forms extracellular plaques, not neuronal cytoplasmic inclusions.
whyNot.E: TDP-43 inclusions characterise ALS and many frontotemporal dementias.
whyNot.D: Huntingtin aggregates are intranuclear inclusions in Huntington disease.

items.objective: Identify alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies as the pathological hallmark of Parkinson disease.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with Parkinson disease starts a new medication. Three months later his wife finds that he has lost a large sum of money gambling online and has been buying expensive items he does not need. He had no such behaviour before. Which of the following medications was most likely added?
items.explanationHtml:
Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine) stimulate D3 and D2 receptors in the mesolimbic reward pathway. Impulse control disorders (gambling, shopping, binge eating, hypersexuality) occur in a substantial minority of patients. Ask about them at every visit; treatment is to taper the agonist.

Takeaway: Dopamine agonists can cause compulsive gambling and shopping; screen for it.

whyNot.B: Entacapone prolongs levodopa action; it may increase dyskinesia but is not a typical cause of compulsive gambling.
whyNot.E: Trihexyphenidyl causes dry mouth, constipation and confusion rather than impulse control disorders.
whyNot.A: Carbidopa alone has no central dopaminergic action.
whyNot.D: Propranolol is used for tremor and has no link to compulsive behaviour.

items.objective: Recognise impulse control disorders as an adverse effect of dopamine agonists.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man begins having involuntary jerky movements and mood changes. His father developed the same illness at age 58 and died at 70. Genetic testing of the son shows 49 CAG repeats in one HTT allele; his father's expanded allele had 42 repeats. Which of the following best explains the earlier onset in the son?

options.label: A
options.html: Expansion of the repeat during oogenesis

options.label: B
options.html: Expansion of the repeat during spermatogenesis

options.label: C
options.html: Imprinting of the maternal HTT allele

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of the normal allele by uniparental disomy

options.label: E
options.html: Mitochondrial heteroplasmy inherited from the mother

items.explanationHtml:
Anticipation in Huntington disease results from instability of the CAG repeat, which tends to expand during spermatogenesis. Longer repeats produce earlier onset, so juvenile cases usually inherit the gene from their father.

Takeaway: Huntington anticipation comes from CAG expansion in the male germline.

whyNot.A: Huntington repeats are most unstable in the male germline; the son inherited the allele from his father.
whyNot.D: Uniparental disomy is not a recognised cause of Huntington anticipation.
whyNot.C: HTT is not an imprinted gene.
whyNot.E: Heteroplasmy applies to mitochondrial DNA disorders, not a nuclear repeat disease.

items.objective: Explain paternal anticipation in Huntington disease.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman has 6 months of hand tremor, slurred speech, drooling and worsening school performance. Her mother says she has become irritable and tearful. Slit-lamp examination shows a golden-brown ring at the edge of each cornea. Serum ceruloplasmin is low. A defect in which of the following proteins is responsible?

options.label: A
options.html: Ceruloplasmin itself, with normal copper excretion

options.label: B
options.html: Hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase that moves copper into bile

options.label: C
options.html: Hepatocyte protein that regulates intestinal iron uptake

options.label: D
options.html: Intestinal copper-transporting ATPase that moves copper into blood

items.explanationHtml:
Tremor, dysarthria, drooling, psychiatric change and Kayser-Fleischer rings in a young person point to Wilson disease. Loss of ATP7B in hepatocytes stops copper being loaded onto ceruloplasmin and excreted in bile. Copper builds up in the liver, then spills into the basal ganglia (especially the putamen) and the cornea.

Takeaway: Wilson disease is loss of hepatocyte ATP7B: low ceruloplasmin, copper in liver, brain and cornea.

whyNot.D: Loss of the intestinal transporter (ATP7A) causes Menkes disease, a copper deficiency of infancy.
whyNot.C: HFE defects cause hereditary hemochromatosis, an iron overload disease.
whyNot.A: Primary ceruloplasmin deficiency causes iron accumulation, not copper toxicity with corneal rings.
whyNot.E: Metallothionein binds copper in enterocytes and is induced by zinc therapy; it is not the defect.

items.objective: Identify the ATP7B defect in Wilson disease presenting with neurological features.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with Huntington disease has disabling chorea. She starts a drug that blocks the transporter that packages monoamines into presynaptic vesicles, so less dopamine is released. Two months later she reports low mood and hopelessness. Which of the following drugs did she most likely receive?
items.explanationHtml:
Tetrabenazine (and the related deutetrabenazine and valbenazine) reversibly inhibits VMAT2, depleting presynaptic dopamine and reducing chorea. Depression and suicidality are important adverse effects, a concern in a disease that already carries a high suicide risk.

Takeaway: VMAT2 inhibitors treat Huntington chorea; watch for depression and suicidality.

whyNot.C: Haloperidol reduces chorea by blocking D2 receptors, not by emptying vesicles.
whyNot.B: Benztropine is an antimuscarinic used for dystonia and parkinsonism; it does not reduce chorea.
whyNot.A: Amantadine is an NMDA antagonist used for levodopa-induced dyskinesia.
whyNot.D: Riluzole reduces glutamate release and is used in ALS.

items.objective: Identify VMAT2 inhibition as the mechanism of tetrabenazine and its key adverse effect.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is brought in confused. He has horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus weakness and cannot walk without help. A blood test that measures the activity of a particular enzyme in his red blood cells before and after adding a cofactor shows a marked increase with the cofactor. Which enzyme was measured?
items.explanationHtml:
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in a patient with alcohol use disorder suggest Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency. Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway. Red-cell transketolase activity that rises sharply when thiamine pyrophosphate is added indicates deficiency.

Takeaway: Erythrocyte transketolase activity is a functional test of thiamine status.

whyNot.D: Pyruvate carboxylase needs biotin, not thiamine.
whyNot.C: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs vitamin B12 (adenosylcobalamin).
whyNot.B: G6PD uses NADP+ and is tested for hemolytic anemia, not vitamin deficiency.
whyNot.A: ALA synthase uses pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).

items.objective: Name the thiamine-dependent enzyme used to assess thiamine deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 7-month-old boy of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has lost the ability to sit and roll over, which he had learned at 5 months. He startles violently to ordinary sounds. Funduscopic examination shows a bright red spot at the centre of each macula. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Developmental regression, an exaggerated startle response and a macular cherry-red spot without organomegaly point to Tay-Sachs disease, autosomal recessive deficiency of hexosaminidase A. GM2 ganglioside accumulates in neuronal lysosomes. The cherry-red spot appears because lipid-laden ganglion cells whiten the retina around the fovea, which has no ganglion cells.

Takeaway: Cherry-red spot without hepatosplenomegaly means Tay-Sachs (hexosaminidase A).

whyNot.E: Sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick type A) also gives a cherry-red spot but with hepatosplenomegaly.
whyNot.B: Galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe disease) causes irritability, spasticity and neuropathy, without a cherry-red spot.
whyNot.A: Arylsulfatase A deficiency (metachromatic leukodystrophy) causes demyelination, usually starting after infancy.
whyNot.C: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher disease) causes hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease.

items.objective: Distinguish Tay-Sachs disease from Niemann-Pick disease by the presence of organomegaly.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy's teacher reports that his handwriting and schoolwork have declined over 6 months, and he has become hyperactive. His skin has darkened, and he has had two episodes of vomiting with low blood pressure during minor illnesses. Morning cortisol is low and ACTH is high. Brain MRI shows symmetric white matter lesions in the parieto-occipital regions. Accumulation of which of the following substances is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
A school-aged boy with behavioural and cognitive decline, posterior white matter disease and primary adrenal insufficiency has X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Mutations in ABCD1 disable a peroxisomal transporter, so very-long-chain fatty acids cannot be imported for beta-oxidation and accumulate in adrenal cortex, myelin and testis.

Takeaway: Adrenal insufficiency plus white matter disease in a boy means X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and VLCFA build-up.

whyNot.D: Sulfatides accumulate in metachromatic leukodystrophy, which does not cause adrenal failure.
whyNot.A: These accumulate in Krabbe disease, an infantile leukodystrophy without adrenal involvement.
whyNot.B: GM2 ganglioside accumulates in Tay-Sachs disease, affecting gray matter in infancy.
whyNot.C: Phytanic acid accumulates in Refsum disease, with neuropathy, ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.

items.objective: Identify very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man has 3 months of numb, tingling feet and an unsteady gait that is worse in the dark. He uses nitrous oxide cartridges recreationally several times a week. He cannot feel a vibrating tuning fork at his toes or knees, and he falls when he closes his eyes while standing. Knee reflexes are brisk and plantar responses are extensor. Hemoglobin is normal. Which of the following serum results is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt of cobalamin and inactivates it. Loss of vibration and position sense (dorsal columns) with upper motor neuron signs (lateral corticospinal tracts) is subacute combined degeneration. Cobalamin is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, so both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine rise. Anemia can be absent.

Takeaway: Functional B12 deficiency raises both methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; folate deficiency raises only homocysteine.

whyNot.D: A normal methylmalonic acid with high homocysteine suggests folate deficiency.
whyNot.B: Cobalamin deficiency blocks both pathways, so homocysteine should also rise.
whyNot.E: Normal values would argue against a functional cobalamin deficiency.
whyNot.C: Methylmalonic acid does not fall in any vitamin deficiency.

items.objective: Interpret methylmalonic acid and homocysteine in cobalamin deficiency myelopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder and malnutrition is admitted with a serum sodium of 106 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L). Over the first 24 hours her sodium rises to 124 mEq/L. She initially improves, but 4 days later she develops slurred speech, difficulty swallowing and weakness of all four limbs, and later can only blink and move her eyes vertically. Which of the following best describes the lesion responsible?

options.label: A
options.html: Diffuse cerebral edema with uncal herniation

options.label: B
options.html: Hemorrhagic necrosis of the mammillary bodies

options.label: C
options.html: Infarction of the pons from basilar artery occlusion

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of myelin in the central pons with relative sparing of neurons and axons

options.label: E
options.html: Perivenular inflammatory demyelination of the cerebral white matter

items.explanationHtml:
Her sodium rose by 18 mEq/L in 24 hours, far above the safe limit for a high-risk patient. Days later she developed dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis progressing to a locked-in state: osmotic demyelination syndrome. Shrinking, osmolyte-depleted cells injure oligodendrocytes, and myelin in the basis pontis is lost while neurons and axons are largely spared.

Takeaway: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too fast destroys pontine myelin days later.

whyNot.B: Mammillary body necrosis is the lesion of Wernicke encephalopathy, causing confusion and ophthalmoplegia.
whyNot.E: Perivenular inflammation describes MS or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, not an osmotic injury.
whyNot.C: A basilar infarct can cause a locked-in state, but the timing after rapid sodium correction points elsewhere.
whyNot.A: Cerebral edema occurs with untreated acute hyponatremia, not days after rapid correction.

items.objective: Describe the pathology and timing of osmotic demyelination syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis is confused and has a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. He is given an oral disaccharide that is not absorbed in the small intestine. Which of the following best describes how it lowers the absorption of the toxin responsible for his confusion?

options.label: A
options.html: Colonic bacteria ferment it to acids, which trap ammonia as ammonium

options.label: B
options.html: It binds ammonia directly in the bloodstream

options.label: C
options.html: It blocks benzodiazepine binding sites in the brain

options.label: D
options.html: It kills the gut bacteria that make urease

options.label: E
options.html: It stimulates urea cycle enzymes in the liver

items.explanationHtml:
In hepatic encephalopathy, ammonia from the gut is not cleared by the liver. Lactulose reaches the colon intact, where bacteria ferment it to lactic and acetic acid. The low pH converts NH3 into NH4+, which cannot cross the gut wall, and the osmotic laxative effect speeds its removal.

Takeaway: Lactulose acidifies the colon and traps ammonia as ammonium.

whyNot.D: Reducing ammonia-producing bacteria is the role of rifaximin, a poorly absorbed antibiotic.
whyNot.E: Lactulose does not act on hepatic urea cycle enzymes.
whyNot.B: Lactulose is not absorbed and does not bind ammonia in blood.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepine site antagonism is the action of flumazenil.

items.objective: Explain how lactulose lowers ammonia absorption in hepatic encephalopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis dies after several weeks of fluctuating confusion and asterixis. Brain histology shows many astrocytes with enlarged, pale, watery nuclei, while neurons appear largely normal. Which of the following processes best explains these astrocyte changes?

options.label: C
options.html: Osmotic injury after rapid sodium correction

options.label: E
options.html: Thiamine deficiency with mammillary body injury

items.explanationHtml:
Astrocytes are the brain's main ammonia sink: glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate. In hepatic encephalopathy glutamine builds up inside astrocytes, draws in water and causes swelling. The enlarged, pale nuclei are the characteristic reactive astrocytes of chronic liver failure.

Takeaway: In hepatic encephalopathy, astrocytes swell from glutamine made while detoxifying ammonia.

whyNot.C: Rapid sodium correction injures oligodendrocytes and myelin, not this astrocyte change.
whyNot.D: Prion disease causes spongiform vacuoles and neuronal loss.
whyNot.E: Thiamine deficiency damages mammillary bodies and medial thalamus.
whyNot.A: Copper deposition in the putamen occurs in Wilson disease; isolated cirrhosis with no copper overload does not explain it.

items.objective: Explain astrocyte swelling in hepatic encephalopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl has had three episodes of headache, vomiting and sudden loss of vision on one side, each followed by partial recovery. MRI during an episode shows cortical swelling in the occipital lobe that does not match an arterial territory. She is short, has sensorineural hearing loss and has an elevated blood lactate. Her mother has diabetes and hearing loss. A biopsy of her quadriceps muscle is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Atrophy of fibres at the edges of fascicles

options.label: C
options.html: Fat and fibrous replacement with absent dystrophin staining

options.label: D
options.html: Fibres with clumps of mitochondria under the sarcolemma on trichrome stain

options.label: E
options.html: Groups of small angular fibres of one fibre type

items.explanationHtml:
Stroke-like episodes outside vascular territories, lactic acidosis, short stature, hearing loss and maternal diabetes suggest MELAS, a mitochondrial DNA disorder (most often m.3243A>G). Abnormal mitochondria accumulate under the sarcolemma and appear as ragged red fibres on modified Gomori trichrome stain. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from the mother, and heteroplasmy explains her milder disease.

Takeaway: Ragged red fibres on muscle biopsy suggest a mitochondrial encephalomyopathy such as MELAS.

whyNot.A: Perifascicular atrophy is the biopsy finding of dermatomyositis.
whyNot.B: Rimmed vacuoles with inflammation describe inclusion body myositis in older adults.
whyNot.C: Absent dystrophin staining is diagnostic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
whyNot.E: Grouped atrophy reflects denervation and reinnervation, as in motor neuron disease.

items.objective: Recognise MELAS and its muscle biopsy hallmark.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman comes to the clinic with her son, who says she has repeated the same stories and missed bill payments over the past year. She lives alone and still cooks, drives locally and manages her medications with a pillbox. She takes amlodipine. Her MoCA score is 22 of 30, with errors mainly on delayed recall. Neurological examination is normal, and a depression screen is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the evaluation?

options.label: D
options.html: Lumbar puncture for CSF tau and amyloid

options.label: E
options.html: Serum vitamin B12 and TSH levels

items.explanationHtml:
Every patient with new cognitive decline needs a basic evaluation for treatable contributors: vitamin B12, TSH, a blood count and metabolic panel, a medication review, a mood screen and structural brain imaging. Biomarkers come later, and only when they change management.

Takeaway: Check B12 and TSH (and image the brain) before specialised biomarkers.

whyNot.A: Amyloid PET is reserved for selected cases where the result will change management, after the basic work-up.
whyNot.B: APOE genotype is a risk marker, not a diagnostic test for cognitive decline.
whyNot.D: CSF biomarkers are second-line tests used when they will guide treatment.
whyNot.C: An EEG is used for suspected seizures or prion disease, not routine evaluation of slow decline.

items.objective: Order the standard laboratory evaluation for reversible causes of cognitive decline.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man has had 10 months of slowly worsening walking. He takes short, wide-based steps and seems to have trouble lifting his feet off the floor. He has new urinary urgency with occasional incontinence, and his wife says he is slower to answer questions. He has no tremor and arm swing is normal. CT of the head shows enlarged lateral ventricles with only mild widening of the cortical sulci. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Large-volume lumbar tap test with gait assessment

options.label: B
options.html: Start acetazolamide to reduce CSF production

options.label: C
options.html: Start donepezil and reassess in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Gait failure first, then urinary urgency and cognitive slowing, with ventricles enlarged out of proportion to sulci, suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus. Removing 30–50 mL of CSF with a timed gait test before and after (the tap test) predicts improvement after a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.

Takeaway: Suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus: do a large-volume tap test to select patients for a shunt.

whyNot.D: His gait disorder lacks tremor, rigidity of the arms or reduced arm swing, and levodopa does not treat hydrocephalus.
whyNot.C: Treating cognition alone ignores a potentially reversible cause of all three symptoms.
whyNot.B: Acetazolamide is used for idiopathic intracranial hypertension, not to select patients for shunting.
whyNot.E: The urinary symptoms are part of the hydrocephalus syndrome; urodynamics will not guide its treatment.

items.objective: Use the lumbar tap test to evaluate suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man has dementia with Lewy bodies. His wife reports that he often sees strangers in the house and becomes frightened. He has mild parkinsonism and his attention fluctuates. He takes no medications. Basic laboratory tests are normal, and there is no infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Cholinesterase inhibitors such as rivastigmine improve cognition, attention and often visual hallucinations in dementia with Lewy bodies, where the cholinergic deficit is profound. Patients with Lewy body disease are highly sensitive to dopamine-blocking antipsychotics.

Takeaway: Treat hallucinations in Lewy body dementia with a cholinesterase inhibitor first; avoid typical antipsychotics.

whyNot.B: Haloperidol can cause severe, sometimes life-threatening rigidity and confusion in Lewy body disease.
whyNot.D: Risperidone blocks D2 receptors strongly and also risks severe sensitivity reactions.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines worsen confusion and falls in older adults with dementia.
whyNot.A: Anticholinergics worsen cognition and can trigger hallucinations.

items.objective: Choose a cholinesterase inhibitor for hallucinations in dementia with Lewy bodies.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman has mild cognitive impairment. Amyloid PET is positive, and she and her husband ask about starting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody given by infusion. She has hypertension and no history of stroke or bleeding, and she takes no anticoagulant. Before the first infusion, which of the following is needed to assess the risk of the most important adverse effect of this treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
The main risk of lecanemab and donanemab is amyloid-related imaging abnormalities: vasogenic edema (ARIA-E) and microhemorrhages or superficial siderosis (ARIA-H). A recent brain MRI is needed before starting to exclude patients with several microhemorrhages, prior intracerebral hemorrhage or siderosis, and scheduled MRIs follow during the first months. APOE e4 status (homozygotes have the highest risk) is discussed with the patient, and anticoagulant use is reviewed.

Takeaway: Anti-amyloid antibodies require a baseline MRI and MRI monitoring for ARIA.

whyNot.B: Anti-amyloid antibodies do not cause important conduction or rhythm problems.
whyNot.E: These antibodies do not cause myopathy.
whyNot.C: Hepatotoxicity is not a significant risk of these antibodies.
whyNot.A: Cytopenias are not an expected adverse effect of anti-amyloid antibodies.

items.objective: Identify baseline MRI as required safety screening before anti-amyloid antibody therapy.

items.stemHtml: An 85-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease lives in a nursing home. For the past week she has become restless and tearful every evening, pacing and pushing staff away. During the day she is calm. She has not had a bowel movement for 5 days. Vital signs are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Assess for triggers such as pain and constipation

options.label: B
options.html: Give diphenhydramine at bedtime each night

options.label: C
options.html: Give lorazepam when she becomes agitated

options.label: D
options.html: Start risperidone at bedtime each night

options.label: E
options.html: Use physical restraints during the evening

items.explanationHtml:
New behavioural symptoms in dementia often signal an unmet need or a medical problem. Five days without a bowel movement suggests constipation; pain, urinary retention, infection, noise and hunger are other common triggers. Treat the cause and use routines, daylight and calm caregiver approaches before considering any drug.

Takeaway: Agitation in dementia: search for triggers such as pain or constipation and use non-drug measures first.

whyNot.D: Antipsychotics raise mortality and stroke risk in dementia and are not first-line for agitation with a likely cause.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines increase confusion, falls and paradoxical agitation in older adults.
whyNot.B: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and worsens cognition.
whyNot.E: Restraints increase injury and distress and are a last resort.

items.objective: Manage behavioural symptoms of dementia by treating triggers and using non-drug measures first.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man is brought by his daughter because of poor memory and concentration for 3 months. His wife died 5 months ago. He sleeps poorly, has lost 5 kg (11 lb) and has stopped gardening. During cognitive testing he often says "I don't know" and gives up quickly. Physical examination and laboratory tests including B12 and TSH are normal. Brain MRI shows only age-appropriate changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Low mood after bereavement, insomnia, weight loss, loss of interest and poor effort on testing ("I don't know") suggest major depression with cognitive symptoms. An SSRI such as sertraline is first-line in older adults. Cognition often improves with treatment, but these patients have a higher later risk of dementia and should be followed.

Takeaway: Depression in older adults can mimic dementia; treat with an SSRI and reassess cognition.

whyNot.B: A cholinesterase inhibitor does not treat depression, which explains his symptoms.
whyNot.C: Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease, which is not the likely diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Zolpidem treats insomnia only and raises fall and confusion risk in older adults.
whyNot.A: Amitriptyline is strongly anticholinergic and can worsen cognition in older adults.

items.objective: Distinguish depression with cognitive symptoms from dementia and choose first-line treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband 2 hours after she came out of a cold sea swim and began asking where they were and what day it was, repeating the same questions every few minutes. She knows her name and recognises her husband. She can follow complex instructions, and the neurological examination is otherwise normal. Blood glucose is 104 mg/dL (5.8 mmol/L). Six hours later she is back to normal but cannot remember the afternoon. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden, isolated anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning, preserved identity and otherwise normal neurology, lasting hours and triggered by cold water immersion or exertion, is transient global amnesia. It needs reassurance; recurrence is uncommon and it does not predict stroke.

Takeaway: Hours of anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning and a normal exam: transient global amnesia.

whyNot.D: A TIA usually causes focal deficits such as vision loss, vertigo or ataxia, not isolated amnesia lasting hours.
whyNot.B: Focal seizures last minutes, often recur, and cause automatisms or reduced responsiveness.
whyNot.A: Dissociative amnesia often involves loss of personal identity and follows psychological trauma.
whyNot.C: Korsakoff amnesia is permanent and follows thiamine deficiency.

items.objective: Recognise transient global amnesia and distinguish it from TIA and seizure.

items.stemHtml:
A 38-year-old woman with generalized myasthenia gravis is admitted with pneumonia. She is treated with IV fluids and an antibiotic, and her pyridostigmine is continued. Over 24 hours her speech becomes nasal, she has trouble swallowing her saliva and her neck flexion is weak. Her cough is weak. Pulse oximetry shows 95% on room air. Bedside measurements:

TimeFVC (mL/kg)Negative inspiratory force (cm H2O)
Admission32−50
12 hours23−34
24 hours15−18

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain an arterial blood gas and repeat measurements in 6 hours

items.explanationHtml:
She is in myasthenic crisis, triggered by infection. Her FVC is below 20 mL/kg and falling, her NIF is weaker than −30 cm H2O, and she cannot clear secretions. A normal oxygen saturation is reassuring only falsely. Elective intubation in the ICU is needed, followed by IVIG or plasma exchange and a review of drugs that worsen myasthenia (several antibiotics do).

Takeaway: Intubate a myasthenic or Guillain-Barré patient when FVC falls below about 20 mL/kg, NIF weakens past −30, or secretions pool.

whyNot.A: More pyridostigmine increases secretions and can cause cholinergic weakness; it does not fix impending respiratory failure.
whyNot.E: High-dose steroids can transiently worsen weakness and act too slowly for an airway at risk.
whyNot.D: Hypercapnia is a late sign; the falling FVC and NIF already show she needs ventilatory support.
whyNot.C: Bronchospasm is not the problem; the weakness is neuromuscular.

items.objective: Recognise impending neuromuscular respiratory failure in myasthenic crisis and secure the airway.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has 3 months of double vision, drooping of the left eyelid late in the day and difficulty chewing tough meat. Examination shows fatigable ptosis and weakness of neck flexion. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Once myasthenia gravis is confirmed, image the anterior mediastinum (CT or MRI) for a thymoma, found in about 10–15% of patients. Any thymoma is removed. Thymectomy also benefits many younger adults with generalized acetylcholine-receptor-positive disease without a thymoma.

Takeaway: Every new diagnosis of myasthenia gravis needs chest imaging for thymoma.

whyNot.C: Brain imaging is not needed when the clinical and serological picture confirms myasthenia gravis.
whyNot.B: CSF studies do not help diagnose or stage myasthenia gravis.
whyNot.D: Muscle biopsy is used for myopathies, not neuromuscular junction disease.
whyNot.E: Creatine kinase is normal in myasthenia gravis and does not alter management.

items.objective: Order chest imaging for thymoma after diagnosing myasthenia gravis.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with well-controlled myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine and azathioprine comes to the emergency department with fever, flank pain and pyuria. Urine culture is pending. He is admitted for IV antibiotics. Which of the following antibiotics is most likely to worsen his myasthenic weakness?
items.explanationHtml:
Aminoglycosides reduce acetylcholine release and blunt postsynaptic sensitivity, and can precipitate a myasthenic crisis. Fluoroquinolones, macrolides, IV magnesium and beta-blockers carry similar risks. A beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone is a safer choice for pyelonephritis in this patient.

Takeaway: Avoid aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and macrolides in myasthenia gravis when an alternative exists.

whyNot.B: Third-generation cephalosporins are not associated with worsening myasthenia gravis.
whyNot.E: Penicillins are not a recognised trigger of myasthenic weakness.
whyNot.D: Carbapenems are not known to impair neuromuscular transmission.
whyNot.A: Aztreonam is not linked to myasthenic exacerbation.

items.objective: Identify antibiotics that can worsen myasthenia gravis.

items.stemHtml:
A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 4 days of tingling in his feet and hands and weakness that began in his legs and now affects his arms. Two weeks ago he had diarrhea. He cannot rise from a chair without help. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent. Sensation to pinprick is mildly reduced in the feet. His heart rate varies between 58/min and 124/min, and blood pressure swings between 98/60 and 168/96 mm Hg.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ice pack test of the eyelids

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
Ascending weakness with areflexia, distal sensory symptoms and autonomic instability after a diarrheal illness strongly suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome. A lumbar puncture supports the diagnosis (high protein with a normal cell count) and excludes infectious or malignant mimics. Nerve conduction studies are also useful.

Takeaway: Suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome: do a lumbar puncture looking for albuminocytologic dissociation.

whyNot.C: Brain MRI does not assess a peripheral nerve disorder.
whyNot.D: Creatine kinase helps in myopathy, but areflexia and paresthesias point to a neuropathy.
whyNot.E: Botulism causes descending paralysis starting with cranial nerves and no sensory symptoms.
whyNot.A: The ice pack test is used for ptosis in suspected myasthenia gravis.

items.objective: Choose lumbar puncture to support a diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

items.stemHtml:
The lumbar puncture shows a CSF protein of 180 mg/dL (15–45 mg/dL), 2 leukocytes/mm3 (0–5/mm3) and a normal glucose. His forced vital capacity is 30 mL/kg. He is admitted to a monitored bed.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
High CSF protein with a normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation) confirms the picture. A patient who cannot walk unaided should receive IVIG or plasma exchange (equally effective) within about 2 weeks of onset. Corticosteroids do not help.

Takeaway: Treat Guillain-Barré syndrome with IVIG or plasma exchange, not steroids.

whyNot.C: Corticosteroids, alone or added to IVIG, do not improve outcome in Guillain-Barré syndrome.
whyNot.D: Oral corticosteroids are ineffective in Guillain-Barré syndrome, unlike in CIDP.
whyNot.B: There is no evidence of herpes virus infection; the CSF shows no pleocytosis.
whyNot.E: Pyridostigmine treats myasthenia gravis, not a demyelinating neuropathy.

items.objective: Select immunotherapy for Guillain-Barré syndrome.

items.stemHtml:
Over the next 48 hours, despite treatment, his FVC falls from 30 to 17 mL/kg and his negative inspiratory force from −45 to −22 cm H2O. He speaks in short phrases and his cough is weak. Oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, and PaCO2 is 42 mm Hg (33–45 mm Hg).

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: A second full course of IVIG

options.label: B
options.html: Continue ward monitoring with FVC every 12 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Plasma exchange added to the IVIG

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer to the ICU for elective intubation

items.explanationHtml:
A falling FVC below about 20 mL/kg and an NIF weaker than −30 cm H2O signal impending neuromuscular respiratory failure, even with normal saturation and PaCO2. Controlled, elective intubation in the ICU is safer than an emergency intubation in a patient with autonomic instability.

Takeaway: In Guillain-Barré syndrome, intubate on falling FVC and NIF, not on desaturation.

whyNot.A: A second IVIG course has not been shown to help and does not address the immediate airway risk.
whyNot.D: Plasma exchange after IVIG removes the infused antibody and adds no benefit.
whyNot.C: Steroids are ineffective in Guillain-Barré syndrome and would not prevent respiratory failure.
whyNot.B: His FVC and NIF are below safe thresholds and falling; waiting risks a crash intubation.

items.objective: Decide on elective intubation in Guillain-Barré syndrome using FVC and NIF.

items.stemHtml: A 3-month-old boy has had 4 days of constipation, poor feeding and a weak cry. Today he cannot hold his head up. He is afebrile. He has bilateral ptosis, sluggish pupils, a poor suck and generalized hypotonia with reduced reflexes. His family lives near a construction site; he has not been given honey. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Constipation followed by a weak cry, poor suck, ptosis, sluggish pupils and descending hypotonia in a young infant is infant botulism: spores swallowed from dust or soil (or honey) colonise the immature gut and produce toxin. Give human botulism immune globulin as early as possible without waiting for stool testing; it shortens ventilation and hospital stay. Provide supportive care.

Takeaway: Treat suspected infant botulism with human botulism immune globulin; avoid aminoglycosides.

whyNot.B: Antibiotics are not used for infant botulism; aminoglycosides can worsen neuromuscular blockade.
whyNot.E: Cholinesterase inhibitors do not reverse a presynaptic release failure caused by botulinum toxin.
whyNot.D: Standard IVIG lacks a reliable titre against botulinum toxin; the specific human immune globulin is used.
whyNot.C: Plasma exchange is used for Guillain-Barré syndrome and myasthenia gravis, not for infant botulism.

items.objective: Manage suspected infant botulism.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis diagnosed 14 months ago reports waking with headaches, poor sleep, and breathlessness when he lies flat. He still eats by mouth without choking. His forced vital capacity is 45% of predicted. He wants to remain at home and has not decided about long-term invasive ventilation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula at night

items.explanationHtml:
Orthopnea, morning headaches and an FVC below about 50% predicted indicate hypoventilation from respiratory muscle weakness. Noninvasive ventilation improves symptoms, quality of life and survival in ALS. Continue advance care planning about gastrostomy and invasive ventilation.

Takeaway: Start noninvasive ventilation in ALS when FVC falls below about 50% or orthopnea appears.

whyNot.D: Oxygen alone can worsen hypercapnia in neuromuscular hypoventilation.
whyNot.E: Tracheostomy is a later, values-based choice; he has not chosen it and NIV is the indicated first step.
whyNot.C: Cholinesterase inhibitors do not treat motor neuron loss.
whyNot.A: There is no airway obstruction; the cause is respiratory muscle weakness.

items.objective: Start noninvasive ventilation for respiratory insufficiency in ALS.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because he falls often and has trouble climbing stairs. He walked at 18 months. He has a waddling gait, uses his hands to push on his thighs to stand from the floor, and has large, firm calves. Serum creatine kinase is 14,500 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A toddler with proximal weakness, a Gowers manoeuvre, calf pseudohypertrophy and a very high creatine kinase most likely has Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Most cases are deletions or duplications in the dystrophin gene, detected by deletion/duplication analysis; sequencing follows if that is negative. Genetic confirmation also guides exon-skipping therapy and carrier testing of the mother.

Takeaway: Confirm suspected Duchenne muscular dystrophy with dystrophin gene testing, not biopsy.

whyNot.E: Biopsy is reserved for cases where genetic testing is negative or unclear.
whyNot.C: EMG shows a myopathic pattern but cannot identify the specific disease.
whyNot.D: Muscle MRI can show fatty replacement but is not diagnostic.
whyNot.B: Cardiac evaluation is needed after diagnosis, but it does not confirm it.

items.objective: Choose genetic testing to confirm Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman who smokes has 4 months of difficulty rising from a low chair and climbing stairs, a dry mouth and constipation. Her leg strength improves for a few seconds after she pushes hard against resistance. Ankle reflexes are absent. Antibodies to P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
This is Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Over half of cases are paraneoplastic, usually from small cell lung cancer, which may not yet be visible. Image the chest with CT (and PET-CT if negative), and repeat screening for at least 2 years in high-risk patients. Treating the cancer often improves the weakness; amifampridine treats symptoms.

Takeaway: Lambert-Eaton syndrome in a smoker: search for small cell lung cancer.

whyNot.E: Thymectomy is a treatment for myasthenia gravis, not Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
whyNot.D: Symptomatic drugs do not replace the urgent search for an underlying cancer.
whyNot.C: Biopsy does not help in a neuromuscular junction disorder confirmed by antibodies.
whyNot.A: The disorder is at the neuromuscular junction; the priority is a cancer search.

items.objective: Search for small cell lung cancer in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman has had a year of slowness, a shuffling gait and a resting tremor of her left hand that now make it hard for her to dress and cook. She has mild memory complaints and her MoCA score is 24 of 30. Examination shows left-sided rigidity and bradykinesia with reduced arm swing. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Her Parkinson disease now limits daily function. Carbidopa-levodopa is the most effective drug and the preferred first choice in older adults, especially those with cognitive complaints, who tolerate dopamine agonists and anticholinergics poorly.

Takeaway: Carbidopa-levodopa is first choice for Parkinson disease that impairs function, especially in older adults.

whyNot.B: Anticholinergics cause confusion, constipation and urinary retention in older adults and do not treat bradykinesia well.
whyNot.D: Dopamine agonists are less effective and cause hallucinations, sleepiness and impulse control problems, especially in older patients with cognitive complaints.
whyNot.E: MAO-B inhibitors have a modest effect, too small for symptoms that already limit daily function.
whyNot.A: Amantadine has a small effect on parkinsonism and causes confusion in older adults.

items.objective: Select initial therapy for Parkinson disease in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease for 5 years takes carbidopa-levodopa and, for the past month, trihexyphenidyl for tremor. His wife reports that he now sees insects on the walls and is confused at night. Urinalysis, blood count and metabolic panel are normal, and he has no fever. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
New hallucinations and confusion soon after starting an anticholinergic in an older adult with Parkinson disease point to drug toxicity. After excluding infection and metabolic causes, withdraw the least essential drugs first: anticholinergics, then amantadine, MAO-B inhibitors, dopamine agonists and COMT inhibitors. If psychosis persists, pimavanserin, low-dose quetiapine or clozapine are options.

Takeaway: Parkinson disease psychosis: stop anticholinergics first; keep levodopa; avoid typical antipsychotics.

whyNot.B: Haloperidol worsens parkinsonism and should be avoided in Parkinson disease.
whyNot.D: Levodopa is the most essential drug and is reduced last; stopping it abruptly can cause a dangerous hyperthermic rigid state.
whyNot.C: Risperidone blocks D2 receptors strongly and worsens motor symptoms.
whyNot.A: A cholinesterase inhibitor may help later, but first remove the drug most likely to be causing his hallucinations.

items.objective: Manage drug-induced psychosis in Parkinson disease.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman has had Parkinson disease for 7 years and takes carbidopa-levodopa four times a day. For the past few months her stiffness and slowness return about an hour before each next dose and improve 30 minutes after it. She has no dyskinesia, hallucinations or cognitive problems. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Symptoms that return before the next dose are end-of-dose wearing off. A COMT inhibitor such as entacapone slows peripheral breakdown of levodopa and lengthens each dose. Alternatives are more frequent levodopa doses, an MAO-B inhibitor or a dopamine agonist.

Takeaway: Wearing off: shorten the dosing interval or add a COMT inhibitor, MAO-B inhibitor or dopamine agonist.

whyNot.B: Haloperidol blocks dopamine receptors and worsens parkinsonism.
whyNot.E: Anticholinergics help tremor in younger patients but do not treat wearing off and cause confusion in older adults.
whyNot.C: Metoclopramide is a dopamine blocker that worsens parkinsonism.
whyNot.D: Propranolol treats essential tremor, not end-of-dose bradykinesia.

items.objective: Treat end-of-dose wearing off in Parkinson disease.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man has a tremor of both hands that makes it hard to drink from a cup or sign his name. He also has a slight side-to-side head tremor. The tremor improves for an hour after a glass of wine. His father had a similar tremor. He has moderate persistent asthma. There is no rigidity or bradykinesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
