Bilateral action tremor with head involvement, a family history and improvement with alcohol is essential tremor. First-line drugs are propranolol and primidone; with asthma, primidone is preferred. Thalamic deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound is considered for disabling, drug-resistant tremor.

Takeaway: Essential tremor: propranolol or primidone; choose primidone in asthma.

whyNot.E: Propranolol is first-line for essential tremor, but a nonselective beta-blocker can provoke bronchospasm in asthma.
whyNot.B: Levodopa treats Parkinson disease, not essential tremor.
whyNot.A: Anticholinergics are not effective for essential tremor.
whyNot.C: Haloperidol does not treat essential tremor and causes parkinsonism.

items.objective: Treat essential tremor in a patient with a contraindication to propranolol.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman with schizophrenia has taken haloperidol for 12 years. Her psychotic symptoms are well controlled. Her daughter has noticed that she constantly smacks her lips, pushes her tongue against her cheek and makes writhing finger movements. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for these movements?
items.explanationHtml:
Repetitive orofacial and limb movements after years of dopamine-blocker treatment are tardive dyskinesia. A VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) reduces the movements. Review whether the antipsychotic is still needed or whether a lower-risk agent such as clozapine is appropriate.

Takeaway: Treat tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor; anticholinergics make it worse.

whyNot.A: Anticholinergics treat acute dystonia and parkinsonism but can worsen tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.C: A higher dose may mask the movements briefly while worsening the underlying problem.
whyNot.B: Diphenhydramine treats acute dystonia, not tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.D: Propranolol treats akathisia, not tardive dyskinesia.

items.objective: Select treatment for tardive dyskinesia.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after receiving intramuscular haloperidol for acute agitation. His neck is twisted to the right, his eyes are fixed in upward gaze and he is distressed. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and he is alert. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Sustained twisting of the neck (torticollis) and fixed upward gaze (oculogyric crisis) within hours of a high-potency antipsychotic is an acute dystonic reaction. An IV or IM anticholinergic, such as diphenhydramine or benztropine, relieves it within minutes. Continue an oral anticholinergic for a few days if the antipsychotic is continued.

Takeaway: Acute dystonia after an antipsychotic: give IV or IM diphenhydramine or benztropine.

whyNot.B: Dantrolene is used for malignant hyperthermia and sometimes severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not acute dystonia.
whyNot.A: Bromocriptine is used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which causes fever and generalized rigidity.
whyNot.D: Propranolol treats akathisia, a feeling of restlessness.
whyNot.E: VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia, which develops over months to years.

items.objective: Treat an acute dystonic reaction to an antipsychotic.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has had frequent eye blinking, shoulder shrugging and throat clearing for 18 months. The tics wax and wane, worsen with stress and embarrass him at school. He can briefly suppress them. He has no attention or obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and the neurological examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple motor tics plus a vocal tic for over a year beginning in childhood is Tourette syndrome. Education and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics (habit-reversal training) are first-line when tics cause distress. Alpha-2 agonists or antipsychotics are added if needed.

Takeaway: Behavioural therapy is first-line for tics that cause distress in Tourette syndrome.

whyNot.D: Antipsychotics are effective but reserved for severe tics after behavioural therapy, because of adverse effects.
whyNot.E: Stimulants treat ADHD, which he does not have.
whyNot.C: SSRIs treat associated OCD or anxiety, not the tics themselves.
whyNot.B: Surgery is reserved for severe, refractory adult cases.

items.objective: Choose first-line treatment for Tourette syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman whose mother has Huntington disease asks to be tested for the gene. She has no symptoms and is planning a family. She says the uncertainty is making her anxious. Her examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Order brain MRI to look for caudate atrophy

options.label: E
options.html: Tell her predictive testing is not offered to asymptomatic adults

items.explanationHtml:
Predictive testing for Huntington disease is offered to adults at risk, but only after pre-test genetic counseling that covers the meaning of results, psychological impact, insurance and family implications, and reproductive options such as preimplantation testing. Results are given in person with support.

Takeaway: Predictive Huntington testing in adults requires pre-test genetic counseling.

whyNot.B: Predictive testing for an untreatable adult-onset disease should follow structured counseling, not be ordered immediately.
whyNot.A: Imaging cannot predict whether an asymptomatic person carries the gene.
whyNot.E: Competent adults may choose predictive testing after counseling.
whyNot.D: No drug delays the onset of Huntington disease.

items.objective: Arrange appropriate counseling before predictive testing for Huntington disease.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man has had 18 months of frequent falls, mostly backward. He has trouble looking down at his food and walking down stairs. Examination shows impaired voluntary downgaze that improves when his head is passively tilted, a stiff upright posture with more rigidity in the neck than the limbs, and a slowed, monotonous voice. A trial of carbidopa-levodopa gave no benefit. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Early backward falls, a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy (voluntary downgaze is lost but reflex eye movements are kept), axial rigidity and poor levodopa response point to progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy with midbrain atrophy.

Takeaway: Early falls plus impaired downgaze and a poor levodopa response suggests progressive supranuclear palsy.

whyNot.D: Parkinson disease responds to levodopa and rarely causes early falls or vertical gaze palsy.
whyNot.B: Multiple system atrophy features early autonomic failure or cerebellar signs.
whyNot.A: Lewy body dementia presents with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations.
whyNot.C: Normal pressure hydrocephalus causes a magnetic gait and urinary incontinence, without gaze palsy.

items.objective: Distinguish progressive supranuclear palsy from Parkinson disease.

items.stemHtml:
A 70-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a generalized seizure at home. She has been drinking large amounts of water and started a thiazide diuretic 3 weeks ago. She is drowsy and vomits twice. There are no focal deficits. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference range
Sodium112 mEq/L136–145 mEq/L
Potassium3.3 mEq/L3.5–5.0 mEq/L
Glucose, fasting96 mg/dL70–100 mg/dL
Osmolality, serum236 mOsm/kg275–295 mOsm/kg

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Fluid restriction to 1 L per day

options.label: D
options.html: Lorazepam alone and repeat sodium in 6 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Seizure and vomiting with a sodium of 112 mEq/L is severe symptomatic hyponatremia. Give a 100 mL bolus of 3% saline, repeated up to twice if symptoms continue, aiming for a rise of about 4–6 mEq/L, which relieves cerebral edema. Then stop the thiazide, correct potassium and limit the 24-hour rise to about 8 mEq/L, because she is at risk of overcorrection.

Takeaway: Seizures from hyponatremia: give 3% saline boluses for a quick 4–6 mEq/L rise, then cap the daily rise.

whyNot.C: Fluid restriction acts over days and is inadequate for hyponatremia causing seizures.
whyNot.A: Isotonic saline raises sodium slowly and unpredictably and is not the treatment for severe symptoms.
whyNot.E: Tolvaptan is not used for severe symptomatic hyponatremia and can cause overcorrection.
whyNot.D: A benzodiazepine may be needed for an ongoing seizure, but the cause, brain swelling, must be treated now.

items.objective: Treat severe symptomatic hyponatremia with hypertonic saline.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and poor oral intake is admitted with confusion and a serum sodium of 110 mEq/L. Potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. He receives 1 L of 0.9% saline and potassium chloride. Over the next 8 hours he passes 3 L of dilute urine, and his sodium is now 120 mEq/L. He is more alert. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: 5% dextrose in water and IV desmopressin

options.label: B
options.html: Continue 0.9% saline at the current rate

items.explanationHtml:
His sodium rose 10 mEq/L in 8 hours, already beyond the 8 mEq/L limit for 24 hours in a high-risk patient (alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalemia). Once volume was replaced, ADH release fell and a water diuresis began. To prevent osmotic demyelination, stop the saline, give free water (5% dextrose) and desmopressin to halt the diuresis and bring sodium back toward the target.

Takeaway: If sodium overshoots in a high-risk patient, re-lower it with dextrose water and desmopressin.

whyNot.B: Continuing saline during a water diuresis will push sodium higher still.
whyNot.E: Hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms; he is improving and already rising too fast.
whyNot.D: Tolvaptan causes free water loss and would raise sodium further.
whyNot.C: Loop diuretics with fluid restriction would also raise sodium further.

items.objective: Manage overcorrection of chronic hyponatremia to prevent osmotic demyelination.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is brought in by his wife because he has been sleepy during the day and awake at night, and is now disoriented. He has ascites and asterixis. Temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). He has no GI bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment in addition to treating the precipitating cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Confusion, sleep-wake reversal and asterixis in cirrhosis is hepatic encephalopathy. Treat with lactulose, titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day, and find the trigger. Here the low-grade fever and ascites call for a diagnostic paracentesis to look for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Takeaway: Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose plus a search for the trigger (infection, bleeding, drugs, dehydration).

whyNot.E: Ammonia levels do not correlate well with severity and are not needed to guide treatment.
whyNot.A: Flumazenil has only a brief, inconsistent effect and is not standard treatment.
whyNot.D: Protein restriction worsens malnutrition and is not recommended.
whyNot.B: Diuresis can cause dehydration and hypokalemia, which worsen encephalopathy.

items.objective: Begin treatment of hepatic encephalopathy and identify its precipitant.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman with cirrhosis is admitted for the second time in 4 months with overt hepatic encephalopathy. She has taken lactulose daily as prescribed, with 2–3 soft stools a day. No infection, bleeding or electrolyte problem is found this time. She recovers with lactulose. Which of the following is the most appropriate addition to her maintenance therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
After a recurrence despite adherence to lactulose, adding rifaximin, a poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria, lowers the risk of further episodes and hospital admissions. She should also be assessed for liver transplant.

Takeaway: Recurrent hepatic encephalopathy on lactulose: add rifaximin.

whyNot.A: Protein restriction worsens sarcopenia and is not recommended in cirrhosis.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines can precipitate encephalopathy.
whyNot.B: Diuretics can cause dehydration and hypokalemia, both triggers of encephalopathy.
whyNot.D: Oral vancomycin is not a standard treatment for hepatic encephalopathy.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent hepatic encephalopathy with rifaximin.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 6 years ago and stopped taking her supplements. She has 4 months of numb feet, poor balance in the dark and memory lapses. Vibration sense is absent at the toes, Romberg sign is positive, and plantar responses are extensor. Hemoglobin is 12.6 g/dL (12.0–16.0 g/dL). Serum vitamin B12 is low and methylmalonic acid is elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Dorsal column loss (absent vibration, positive Romberg) with corticospinal signs and cognitive change, a low B12 and a high methylmalonic acid after gastric bypass is subacute combined degeneration. Anemia is often absent. Neurological involvement calls for prompt parenteral cobalamin, followed by lifelong replacement. Early treatment gives the best chance of recovery.

Takeaway: B12 deficiency with neurological signs: give intramuscular cobalamin promptly, even if the hemoglobin is normal.

whyNot.E: Folate alone can improve blood counts but does not treat, and may unmask, the neurological damage.
whyNot.D: Her B12 and methylmalonic acid results already explain the myelopathy.
whyNot.C: Thiamine treats Wernicke encephalopathy, not dorsal column and corticospinal damage.
whyNot.B: IVIG treats immune neuropathies, not a vitamin deficiency.

items.objective: Treat B12-deficiency myelopathy after bariatric surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman has 6 months of progressive numbness of the feet, an unsteady gait and leg stiffness. She uses large amounts of zinc-containing denture adhesive every day. Vibration and joint position sense are reduced in the feet, and she has a spastic gait with brisk knee reflexes. Hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL (12.0–16.0 g/dL) and the leukocyte count is 3,100/mm3 (4,500–11,000/mm3). Vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Excess zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, which traps copper and blocks its absorption. Copper deficiency produces a myeloneuropathy that mimics B12 deficiency, together with anemia and neutropenia. Check serum copper and ceruloplasmin, stop the zinc source and replace copper.

Takeaway: A B12-like myeloneuropathy with normal B12 and cytopenias: check copper (zinc excess, bariatric surgery).

whyNot.B: Her normal B12 and methylmalonic acid argue against pernicious anemia.
whyNot.D: Folate deficiency does not cause a myeloneuropathy like this.
whyNot.A: The findings point to a spinal cord and nerve problem with a likely nutritional cause.
whyNot.E: Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary before checking a simple, likely cause.

items.objective: Recognise copper deficiency myelopathy from zinc excess.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy is referred after his newborn screen showed elevated very-long-chain fatty acids. Confirmatory testing shows a pathogenic ABCD1 variant. He is developing normally and the neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Brain biopsy to stage white matter disease

options.label: B
options.html: Dietary restriction of very-long-chain fatty acids alone

options.label: E
options.html: Regular adrenal function tests and serial brain MRI

items.explanationHtml:
Boys with X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy found by newborn screening need surveillance: periodic adrenal testing (morning cortisol and ACTH), because adrenal insufficiency can be life-threatening, and serial brain MRI in childhood, because transplant or gene therapy only helps when started at the first sign of cerebral disease. Offer cascade testing to the family.

Takeaway: Asymptomatic X-ALD: monitor adrenals and brain MRI so transplant can be offered at the first MRI change.

whyNot.C: Transplant carries significant risk and is offered when early cerebral disease appears on MRI, not to every boy.
whyNot.B: Diet does not prevent cerebral disease or adrenal failure.
whyNot.D: By the time symptoms appear, cerebral disease is often too advanced for transplant to help.
whyNot.A: MRI, not biopsy, detects and stages cerebral involvement.

items.objective: Plan surveillance for asymptomatic X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department confused and unable to walk steadily. He has nystagmus on lateral gaze and cannot fully abduct either eye. Fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL (3.2 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: IV thiamine given with IV dextrose

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the brain before any treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in a patient with alcohol use disorder is Wernicke encephalopathy. Give high-dose IV thiamine immediately, together with or before glucose. Hypoglycemia must still be corrected, but not with glucose alone. Check and correct magnesium, which thiamine-dependent enzymes also need.

Takeaway: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine before or with glucose, without waiting for tests.

whyNot.A: Glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.
whyNot.E: Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol use disorder and too slow for an acute encephalopathy.
whyNot.D: Treatment must not wait for imaging, which can be normal.
whyNot.B: There are no features of opioid toxicity such as miosis or respiratory depression.

items.objective: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy safely in a hypoglycemic patient.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease missed his last three hemodialysis sessions. He is confused and has myoclonic jerks and a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. A pericardial friction rub is heard. Blood urea nitrogen is 148 mg/dL (7–18 mg/dL) and potassium is 5.4 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Confusion, asterixis and myoclonus with uremic pericarditis in a patient who has missed dialysis are uremic emergencies. Urgent hemodialysis is indicated; both encephalopathy and pericarditis are accepted indications.

Takeaway: Uremic encephalopathy or pericarditis is an indication for urgent dialysis.

whyNot.C: Lactulose treats hepatic, not uremic, encephalopathy.
whyNot.D: Bicarbonate treats metabolic acidosis but not the uremic encephalopathy or pericarditis.
whyNot.A: Furosemide has little effect in end-stage kidney disease and does not remove uremic toxins.
whyNot.B: Sedation does not treat the cause and can worsen the encephalopathy.

items.objective: Identify uremic encephalopathy as an indication for urgent dialysis.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician because her teacher has noticed that she stops talking in mid-sentence and stares blankly several times a day. Each episode lasts about 10 seconds, after which she resumes what she was doing as if nothing had happened. Asking her to breathe deeply and quickly for 2 minutes in the office brings on a typical episode. Her EEG shows generalized 3-per-second spike-and-wave discharges. The most appropriate drug for her blocks which of the following?

options.label: D
options.html: T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons

options.label: E
options.html: Voltage-gated sodium channels in cortical neurons

items.explanationHtml:
Typical absence seizures arise from rhythmic burst firing in thalamocortical circuits driven by low-threshold T-type calcium currents in thalamic relay neurons. Ethosuximide blocks these channels and is the first-line drug for childhood absence epilepsy.

Takeaway: absence seizures (3-per-second spike-and-wave, provoked by hyperventilation) respond to ethosuximide, a thalamic T-type calcium channel blocker.

whyNot.E: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine treat focal seizures and can worsen absence seizures.
whyNot.C: That is levetiracetam's target; it is not the first-line drug for childhood absence epilepsy.
whyNot.A: Vigabatrin inhibits GABA transaminase and is used mainly for infantile spasms, not absence.
whyNot.B: NMDA antagonism is not the mechanism of any first-line absence drug.

items.objective: Relate the thalamic T-type calcium current to absence seizures and to the mechanism of ethosuximide.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred the morning after an all-night party. For a year he has had brief jerks of both arms shortly after waking, which make him spill his drinks. He is otherwise well, and neurological examination is normal. Which of the following EEG findings is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges at 4–6 per second

options.label: C
options.html: Generalized spike-and-wave discharges at 3 per second

options.label: E
options.html: Periodic sharp-wave complexes at 1 per second

items.explanationHtml:
Morning myoclonic jerks in an adolescent, with tonic-clonic seizures provoked by sleep deprivation, define juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, a genetic generalized epilepsy. The EEG shows generalized polyspike-and-wave discharges, often faster than 3 per second and sometimes triggered by flashing lights.

Takeaway: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy pairs morning myoclonus with generalized polyspike-and-wave on EEG.

whyNot.C: This is the typical pattern of childhood absence epilepsy, not the morning myoclonus of this syndrome.
whyNot.D: Chaotic high-voltage slowing with multifocal spikes is the pattern of infantile spasms.
whyNot.A: This is self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes, which causes nocturnal focal seizures in younger children.
whyNot.E: Periodic sharp waves suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rapidly progressive dementia.

items.objective: Identify the EEG pattern of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with episodic migraine has had two coronary stents placed for angina. His sumatriptan is stopped because of his coronary disease. His physician prescribes a different acute migraine drug that is a serotonin receptor agonist but does not constrict blood vessels. The patient is warned not to drive for 8 hours after each dose. This drug most likely acts at which receptor?
items.explanationHtml:
Lasmiditan is a selective 5-HT1F agonist. It blocks neuropeptide release from trigeminal endings without the vasoconstriction caused by 5-HT1B agonism. Its central side effects (dizziness, sedation) lead to the 8-hour driving restriction.

Takeaway: lasmiditan (5-HT1F) and the gepants (CGRP receptor antagonists) are acute options when triptans are contraindicated by vascular disease.

whyNot.B: 5-HT<sub>1B</sub> agonism constricts cranial and coronary arteries, which is why triptans are avoided in coronary disease.
whyNot.C: 5-HT<sub>2A</sub> agonism causes hallucinations and is overstimulated in serotonin syndrome; it is not a migraine drug target.
whyNot.D: 5-HT<sub>3</sub> is a ligand-gated ion channel targeted by antiemetics such as ondansetron, as an antagonist.
whyNot.E: 5-HT<sub>4</sub> agonists act on gut motility, not migraine.

items.objective: Identify the receptor target of lasmiditan and why it is safe in vascular disease.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman describes episodes that begin with a shimmering zigzag line near the centre of her vision. Over 20 minutes it expands toward the edge of her left visual field, leaving a blind patch behind it, and then fades. A throbbing headache with nausea follows and lasts most of the day. Neurological examination between episodes is normal. Which of the following best explains the visual symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: A focal seizure starting in the right occipital lobe

options.label: B
options.html: A slowly spreading wave of cortical depolarization followed by suppressed activity

options.label: C
options.html: Compression of the optic chiasm by a pituitary adenoma

options.label: D
options.html: Transient occlusion of the right posterior cerebral artery

options.label: E
options.html: Vasospasm of the central retinal artery

items.explanationHtml:
A migraine aura that builds over 5–20 minutes with positive (zigzag) features followed by a blind patch matches cortical spreading depolarization crossing the occipital cortex at a few millimetres per minute. The wave also activates trigeminovascular pain pathways.

Takeaway: a gradually spreading visual aura with positive then negative symptoms is migraine aura from cortical spreading depolarization.

whyNot.D: Ischemia causes sudden, negative symptoms that do not march across the visual field over many minutes.
whyNot.A: Occipital seizures usually cause brief, coloured, circular images that spread within seconds to a few minutes, not zigzag lines over 20 minutes.
whyNot.E: Retinal ischemia causes loss of vision in one eye, not a homonymous field disturbance.
whyNot.C: Chiasmal compression causes fixed, slowly progressive bitemporal field loss, not episodic aura.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of migraine aura.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with focal epilepsy is started on a drug whose antiseizure effect comes from binding a synaptic vesicle glycoprotein and modulating neurotransmitter release. It is excreted mainly unchanged by the kidneys and has few drug interactions. Two months later his wife reports that he has become irritable and short-tempered. Which drug was most likely started?
items.explanationHtml:
Levetiracetam binds synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A). It is renally cleared with minimal interactions. Behavioural effects (irritability, low mood, aggression) are its main adverse effects.

Takeaway: levetiracetam = SV2A binding, renal clearance, few interactions, mood and behaviour side effects.

whyNot.A: Carbamazepine blocks sodium channels, is metabolized by CYP3A4 and induces many drug interactions.
whyNot.E: Phenytoin blocks sodium channels, has saturable hepatic metabolism and many interactions.
whyNot.B: Gabapentin binds the α2δ subunit of calcium channels, not a vesicle protein.
whyNot.D: Phenobarbital prolongs GABA<sub>A</sub> channel opening and is a strong enzyme inducer.

items.objective: Match levetiracetam to its mechanism and characteristic adverse effect.

items.stemHtml: Investigators record chloride currents from single GABAA receptor channels in cultured neurons. Adding drug X to a fixed concentration of GABA increases how often the channel opens but does not change how long each opening lasts. Drug X does not open the channel in the absence of GABA. Drug X is most likely which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam are positive allosteric modulators that increase the frequency of GABAA channel opening and need GABA to be present. This ceiling on their effect makes them safer in overdose than barbiturates.

Takeaway: benzodiazepines increase opening frequency; barbiturates increase opening duration.

whyNot.D: Barbiturates mainly prolong each channel opening and can open the channel directly at high doses.
whyNot.B: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels; it does not act on GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors.
whyNot.A: Baclofen is a GABA<sub>B</sub> agonist acting on a G-protein-coupled receptor, not the chloride channel.
whyNot.E: Vigabatrin raises GABA levels by inhibiting GABA transaminase; it does not change single-channel kinetics directly.

items.objective: Distinguish benzodiazepine and barbiturate actions on the GABA<sub>A</sub> receptor.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man has attacks of severe pain behind his right eye that wake him at about 2 AM most nights for the past 3 weeks. Each attack lasts about 45 minutes, and he paces the room. During attacks his right eye waters and his right nostril runs. Which of the following pathways carries the efferent signal responsible for the tearing?

options.label: A
options.html: Edinger-Westphal nucleus, oculomotor nerve, ciliary ganglion

options.label: B
options.html: Hypothalamus, intermediolateral cell column, superior cervical ganglion

options.label: C
options.html: Inferior salivatory nucleus, glossopharyngeal nerve, otic ganglion

options.label: D
options.html: Superior salivatory nucleus, facial nerve, pterygopalatine ganglion

options.label: E
options.html: Superior salivatory nucleus, facial nerve, submandibular ganglion

items.explanationHtml:
This is cluster headache, a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia. Trigeminal pain afferents trigger a reflex parasympathetic outflow: superior salivatory nucleus → facial nerve (greater petrosal nerve) → pterygopalatine ganglion → lacrimal gland and nasal mucosa. This produces same-side tearing and rhinorrhea.

Takeaway: the autonomic signs of cluster headache are a trigeminal-parasympathetic reflex through the facial nerve and the pterygopalatine ganglion.

whyNot.A: This parasympathetic pathway constricts the pupil and drives accommodation; it does not supply the lacrimal gland.
whyNot.C: This pathway supplies the parotid gland.
whyNot.B: This is the sympathetic pathway; its disruption causes ptosis and miosis, not tearing.
whyNot.E: The chorda tympani route reaches the submandibular ganglion, which supplies the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.

items.objective: Trace the parasympathetic pathway that causes tearing in cluster headache.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has migraine on 10 days a month despite trials of propranolol and topiramate. She starts a monthly subcutaneous injection of a fully human monoclonal antibody for prevention. Unlike the other antibodies in its class, this drug binds the receptor rather than the ligand. Which of the following does this antibody bind?
items.explanationHtml:
Erenumab is the CGRP-pathway antibody that blocks the CGRP receptor. The others in the class neutralize the CGRP ligand. All reduce trigeminovascular signalling and monthly migraine days.

Takeaway: erenumab blocks the CGRP receptor; the other CGRP antibodies bind the peptide.

whyNot.C: This is the target of triptans, which are small molecules used for acute attacks.
whyNot.A: Fremanezumab, galcanezumab and eptinezumab bind the ligand; this antibody binds the receptor.
whyNot.E: No migraine preventive antibody targets NMDA receptors.
whyNot.B: Neurokinin-1 antagonists are antiemetics and were not effective for migraine.

items.objective: Distinguish receptor-targeting from ligand-targeting CGRP monoclonal antibodies.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had seizures since a prolonged febrile seizure at age 2. Her current episodes begin with a rising feeling in her stomach, followed by staring, lip smacking and fumbling with her clothes for about a minute, after which she is confused. Several drugs have failed, and she undergoes surgical resection of the right anterior temporal lobe. Microscopy of the resected tissue is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaques in the entorhinal cortex

options.label: C
options.html: Neuron loss and gliosis in the hippocampus, most marked in the CA1 sector

options.label: D
options.html: Perivascular lymphocytic cuffing with microglial nodules

options.label: E
options.html: Spongiform vacuolation of the cortical neuropil

items.explanationHtml:
Epigastric aura, staring and oral automatisms are typical of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy. The usual lesion is hippocampal sclerosis: neuron loss and gliosis that are most severe in CA1, often after prolonged febrile seizures in early childhood. Surgery is effective when drugs fail.

Takeaway: drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy is most often due to hippocampal sclerosis (CA1 neuron loss and gliosis).

whyNot.B: These are features of Alzheimer disease, not a cause of drug-resistant focal epilepsy in a young adult.
whyNot.E: Spongiform change is the hallmark of prion disease.
whyNot.D: These suggest viral encephalitis, an acute illness.
whyNot.A: Lewy bodies characterize Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, not epilepsy.

items.objective: Recognize the pathology of mesial temporal sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with known epilepsy is brought to the emergency department by ambulance because of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that began 8 minutes ago and is still continuing. Paramedics could not place an IV line. His airway is being supported with a jaw thrust and oxygen by mask. Fingerstick glucose is 112 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous fosphenytoin through a newly placed line

options.label: E
options.html: Rapid sequence intubation and propofol infusion

items.explanationHtml:
He is in convulsive status epilepticus. A benzodiazepine is first. Without IV access, IM midazolam works at least as fast as IV lorazepam once the time to place a line is counted.

Takeaway: status epilepticus is treated first with a benzodiazepine: IV lorazepam, or IM midazolam if there is no IV access.

whyNot.B: A second-line drug is given after a benzodiazepine; starting it first delays the most effective treatment.
whyNot.C: Imaging can wait until the seizure is controlled.
whyNot.D: A convulsing patient cannot take oral drugs safely, and oral absorption is too slow.
whyNot.E: Anaesthetic infusion is for refractory status after a benzodiazepine and a second-line drug have failed.

items.objective: Give a benzodiazepine first in status epilepticus, choosing the route by IV access.

items.stemHtml: The patient receives intramuscular midazolam and, after IV access is obtained, a dose of IV lorazepam. Twelve minutes later he is still having rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. Blood pressure is 152/88 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 95% on a non-rebreather mask. Sodium is 138 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L) and calcium is 9.1 mg/dL (8.4–10.2 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: A third dose of a benzodiazepine

options.label: E
options.html: Oral carbamazepine through a nasogastric tube

items.explanationHtml:
Seizures persisting after adequate benzodiazepines need an IV second-line drug: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate. These were similarly effective in a large randomized trial, so levetiracetam is a reasonable choice with few interactions and no cardiac monitoring requirement.

Takeaway: benzodiazepine-resistant status epilepticus needs IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.

whyNot.A: After two adequate benzodiazepine doses, more benzodiazepine adds respiratory depression with little extra benefit.
whyNot.C: Magnesium is the anticonvulsant for eclampsia, not for status epilepticus in general.
whyNot.D: There is no sign of infection, and a lumbar puncture does not stop the seizure.
whyNot.E: Enteral loading is too slow and unreliable in status epilepticus.

items.objective: Choose an IV second-line drug when status epilepticus continues after benzodiazepines.

items.stemHtml: The convulsive movements stop 5 minutes after the levetiracetam infusion. Forty minutes later the patient remains unresponsive to voice and pain, and has occasional subtle twitching of the eyelids. Pupils are equal and reactive. He is breathing adequately. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain before any further treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Observation in the ward for return of consciousness

items.explanationHtml:
A patient who does not wake after convulsive status, especially with subtle eye or face twitches, may be in nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Continuous EEG confirms it and guides further treatment, which often includes intubation and an anaesthetic infusion.

Takeaway: if consciousness does not return after convulsive status, get an EEG to look for nonconvulsive status.

whyNot.D: Failure to wake after 40 minutes with eyelid twitching suggests ongoing seizures, which need confirmation and treatment.
whyNot.B: Flumazenil can provoke seizures and would not treat ongoing electrical seizure activity.
whyNot.E: Prolactin does not guide management of a patient who may still be seizing.
whyNot.C: Imaging can follow, but the urgent question is whether seizures continue, which only an EEG answers.

items.objective: Recognize when to evaluate for nonconvulsive status epilepticus after convulsions stop.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized convulsion at work that lasted about 1 minute. He was confused for 20 minutes afterward and is now back to normal. He has no history of seizures, head injury or substance use, and takes no medications. Neurological examination is normal. Glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium and a urine drug screen are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: CT angiography of the head and neck

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain and an EEG

options.label: E
options.html: Video-EEG monitoring in a specialised unit

items.explanationHtml:
After an unprovoked first seizure with normal labs, an EEG and brain MRI are the standard evaluation. Epileptiform discharges or a relevant lesion raise the recurrence risk and may justify starting a drug after one seizure.

Takeaway: unprovoked first seizure: labs, then brain MRI and EEG.

whyNot.B: He has no fever, headache or meningeal signs to suggest infection or hemorrhage.
whyNot.D: An unprovoked first seizure in an adult needs imaging and an EEG to estimate recurrence risk and find a cause.
whyNot.E: Long-term video-EEG is for diagnosing frequent unexplained events or surgical planning, not a single first seizure.
whyNot.A: Vascular imaging is not part of the standard first-seizure work-up without stroke features.

items.objective: Choose the standard evaluation of a first unprovoked seizure.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy has been seizure-free for 3 years on valproate. She tells her physician that she and her partner would like to have a baby within the next year. She uses condoms for contraception. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue valproate and add high-dose folic acid

options.label: B
options.html: Continue valproate and advise against pregnancy

options.label: C
options.html: Stop all antiseizure drugs before conception

options.label: D
options.html: Switch gradually to levetiracetam and start folic acid now

items.explanationHtml:
Valproate carries the highest fetal risk of any antiseizure drug (neural tube defects and other malformations, lower IQ, autism). For someone planning pregnancy, switch to a lower-risk drug that controls generalized epilepsy, such as levetiracetam (or lamotrigine), well before conception, and start folic acid.

Takeaway: avoid valproate in anyone who could become pregnant; switch before conception.

whyNot.A: Folic acid does not remove valproate's risk of malformations and of lower IQ and autism in the child.
whyNot.C: Stopping risks seizures, including during pregnancy, which can harm both her and the fetus.
whyNot.E: Carbamazepine can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures in generalized epilepsy and is also teratogenic.
whyNot.B: Her goal is pregnancy; a safer drug lets her pursue it with less fetal risk.

items.objective: Manage antiseizure therapy in a woman planning pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with migraine asks about contraception. Several times a year, a flickering zigzag line spreads across her vision for 20 minutes before the headache starts. She is a nonsmoker with a blood pressure of 122/78 mm Hg, and she would like a highly effective method. Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive?
items.explanationHtml:
She has migraine with aura. Estrogen-containing contraceptives (pill, patch or ring) are contraindicated since estrogen added to migraine with aura raises ischemic stroke risk. A levonorgestrel or copper IUD, an implant or a progestin-only pill avoids that risk.

Takeaway: migraine with aura is a contraindication to estrogen-containing contraception.

whyNot.A: Estrogen-containing methods are contraindicated in migraine with aura because they raise ischemic stroke risk.
whyNot.B: The ring contains estrogen and has the same contraindication as combined pills.
whyNot.E: The patch delivers estrogen and is contraindicated in migraine with aura.
whyNot.C: It is far less effective than an IUD for someone who wants a reliable method.

items.objective: Select contraception for a woman with migraine with aura.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has had attacks of excruciating pain around his left eye for the past 2 weeks. They occur once or twice a night, last about an hour, and make him rock back and forth. During attacks his left eye is red and watery and his left eyelid droops. He had a similar 6-week period 2 years ago. He is in the emergency department now during an attack. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this attack?
items.explanationHtml:
This is cluster headache. High-flow 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min by non-rebreather mask for about 15 minutes) or subcutaneous sumatriptan aborts attacks. Verapamil is started for prevention during the cluster.

Takeaway: acute cluster headache: high-flow oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan; prevention with verapamil.

whyNot.C: Oral analgesics act too slowly and are ineffective for cluster attacks.
whyNot.E: Verapamil prevents attacks during a cluster period but does not abort the current attack.
whyNot.B: Opioids are ineffective for cluster headache and should be avoided.
whyNot.D: Topiramate is a migraine preventive and does not treat an acute cluster attack.

items.objective: Treat an acute cluster headache attack.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman has had headaches for 20 years. Over the past year they have become almost daily: a dull bilateral ache on waking that eases after her medication. She takes a tablet containing acetaminophen, aspirin and caffeine on about 25 days each month. She has occasional severe throbbing headaches with nausea, as she has had since her twenties. Neurological examination, including fundoscopy, is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add a triptan for the daily headaches

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain with contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Replace the combination analgesic with an opioid

options.label: E
options.html: Stop the combination analgesic and start a migraine preventive

items.explanationHtml:
Migraine has become daily headache because of medication overuse: combination analgesics on 10 or more days a month. Management is to withdraw the overused drug (simple and combination analgesics can usually be stopped at once; opioids and butalbital need a taper), with a preventive drug and patient education.

Takeaway: near-daily headache with frequent analgesic use is medication-overuse headache: withdraw and start prevention.

whyNot.C: The long history, normal examination and medication pattern point to a benign cause; imaging is not needed.
whyNot.A: Triptans used on 10 or more days a month also cause medication-overuse headache.
whyNot.D: Opioids are an even stronger cause of medication-overuse headache and dependence.
whyNot.B: There is no papilledema or other sign of raised intracranial pressure.

items.objective: Diagnose and manage medication-overuse headache.

items.stemHtml:
An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a seizure at home. He had a runny nose and cough for 2 days and felt hot this morning. His mother saw him stiffen and then jerk all four limbs for about 2 minutes. Forty-five minutes later he is alert, playful and drinking. Vaccinations are up to date. Findings are shown:

MeasureResult
Temperature39.3°C (102.7°F)
Pulse138/min
NeckSupple
Fontanelle and skinFontanelle closed; no rash
Neurological examinationNormal for age; moves all limbs equally
Glucose (fingerstick)96 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the brain without contrast

items.explanationHtml:
A generalized seizure under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, in a feverish child aged 6 months to 5 years is a simple febrile seizure. When the child is well and vaccinated with a normal examination, no tests are needed. Treat the illness, explain the benign prognosis (about a third recur) and teach seizure first aid. Antipyretics are for comfort; they do not prevent recurrence.

Takeaway: simple febrile seizure in a well, vaccinated child: reassurance and education, no routine tests.

whyNot.C: A well-appearing, fully vaccinated child with a normal examination and no meningeal signs does not need a lumbar puncture.
whyNot.B: An EEG does not change management after a simple febrile seizure.
whyNot.D: Neuroimaging is not indicated after a simple febrile seizure.
whyNot.A: Daily antiseizure drugs are not recommended; their harms outweigh the small benefit.

items.objective: Manage a simple febrile seizure without unnecessary investigation.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman has had 15 episodes in 3 months, each lasting 5–20 minutes. Witnesses describe her eyes clenched shut, side-to-side head shaking, and arm and leg movements that stop and start. She cries during some episodes and afterwards remembers people talking to her. Two antiseizure drugs have had no effect. MRI of the brain and a routine EEG are normal. Which of the following is the best way to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat routine EEG with sleep deprivation

options.label: D
options.html: Serum prolactin measured 6 hours after an event

options.label: E
options.html: Video-EEG monitoring to capture a typical event

items.explanationHtml:
Long events with eyes closed, waxing and waning asynchronous movements, side-to-side head shaking, crying and preserved recall suggest functional (psychogenic nonepileptic) seizures. The standard for diagnosis is video-EEG that records a typical event with no epileptic EEG change. Treatment is clear explanation and cognitive behavioural therapy.

Takeaway: suspected functional seizures are confirmed by capturing a typical event on video-EEG.

whyNot.D: Prolactin, if used at all, must be drawn within about 20 minutes and is not reliable enough to confirm the diagnosis.
whyNot.A: Further drug trials expose her to side effects without clarifying the diagnosis.
whyNot.B: PET helps localize foci for epilepsy surgery but cannot characterize these events.
whyNot.C: A routine EEG is often normal between events and cannot show what happens during one.

items.objective: Choose video-EEG to diagnose psychogenic nonepileptic seizures.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has episodes about an hour after falling asleep in which he sits up screaming, sweating, with a fast heart rate and dilated pupils. He cannot be comforted, does not respond to his parents and goes back to sleep after a few minutes. In the morning he remembers nothing. The figure shows a normal adult night of sleep. At which labelled point are these episodes most likely to begin?
items.explanationHtml:
These are sleep terrors, a disorder of arousal from N3 (slow-wave) sleep. N3 is concentrated in the first third of the night, so episodes typically start 1–2 hours after sleep onset, with autonomic arousal, inconsolability and amnesia.

Takeaway: sleep terrors and sleepwalking arise from N3 early in the night with no recall.

whyNot.B: Point B is in a long REM period near morning, when nightmares and REM sleep behavior disorder occur, with vivid recall.
whyNot.C: Point C is in N1 at sleep onset, where hypnic jerks occur.
whyNot.D: Point D is a brief normal awakening; the child would be oriented and responsive.
whyNot.E: Point E is in N2 late in the night, which is not when arousal disorders typically arise.

items.objective: Place NREM arousal parasomnias in early-night N3 sleep on a hypnogram.

items.stemHtml: In a sleep laboratory, a healthy 22-year-old volunteer is recorded overnight. The figure shows a normal night of sleep. At which labelled point would the EEG most likely show sleep spindles and K complexes?
items.explanationHtml:
Sleep spindles (brief 11–16 Hz bursts) and K complexes (large biphasic waves) define N2, which takes up about half of a normal night and fills much of the later cycles.

Takeaway: spindles and K complexes = N2; delta waves = N3; sawtooth waves = REM.

whyNot.A: Point A is N3, where high-amplitude delta waves dominate.
whyNot.B: Point B is REM sleep, with low-voltage mixed-frequency activity and sawtooth waves.
whyNot.C: Point C is N1, with theta activity and vertex waves but not yet spindles or K complexes.
whyNot.D: Point D is a brief awakening, with alpha or beta activity.

items.objective: Match EEG features to sleep stages on a hypnogram.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student falls asleep in lectures and while eating, despite 8 hours of sleep at night. When she laughs hard, her knees buckle and her jaw sags for a few seconds while she stays fully aware. She sometimes cannot move for a minute on waking. She carries the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele. Loss of which of the following neuron populations is the most likely cause of her disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta

options.label: B
options.html: GABA neurons of the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus

options.label: C
options.html: Melatonin-secreting cells of the pineal gland

options.label: E
options.html: Orexin (hypocretin) neurons of the lateral hypothalamus

items.explanationHtml:
Sleep attacks with cataplexy, sleep paralysis and HLA-DQB1*06:02 point to narcolepsy type 1. It is caused by selective, probably autoimmune, loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Without orexin, wakefulness is unstable and REM features (atonia, dreaming) intrude into wakefulness.

Takeaway: narcolepsy type 1 = loss of lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons, low CSF orexin, cataplexy.

whyNot.C: Pineal melatonin conveys circadian timing; its loss does not cause cataplexy.
whyNot.B: Loss of these sleep-promoting neurons causes insomnia, not sleep attacks.
whyNot.A: Their loss causes Parkinson disease.
whyNot.D: Damage to the circadian pacemaker disorganizes the timing of sleep but does not cause cataplexy.

items.objective: Identify orexin neuron loss as the cause of narcolepsy with cataplexy.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man's wife reports that for 3 years he has shouted, punched and kicked during sleep in the early morning hours, once striking her. When woken, he describes being chased in his dream. Polysomnography shows loss of the expected muscle atonia during REM sleep. He is at greatest long-term risk for a neurodegenerative disease characterized by abnormal aggregation of which protein?
items.explanationHtml:
REM sleep behavior disorder (dream enactment with REM sleep without atonia) is often the first sign of an α-synucleinopathy: Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies or multiple system atrophy. Most patients with the isolated disorder develop one of these over long follow-up.

Takeaway: REM sleep behavior disorder is a prodrome of α-synucleinopathies.

whyNot.E: β-Amyloid plaques characterize Alzheimer disease, which is not specifically linked to this sleep disorder.
whyNot.B: Tau aggregates define frontotemporal lobar degenerations and progressive supranuclear palsy, which are not strongly linked to it.
whyNot.C: TDP-43 is the main aggregate in ALS and most frontotemporal dementia.
whyNot.A: Misfolded prion protein causes Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rapidly progressive dementia.

items.objective: Link REM sleep behavior disorder to α-synuclein neurodegeneration.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman cannot fall asleep until 2 AM. Her physician prescribes a drug that acts as an agonist at receptors normally stimulated by a hormone released by the pineal gland at night. It has little risk of dependence. The release of this hormone is controlled by a pathway that includes which of the following structures?

options.label: A
options.html: Lateral geniculate nucleus and primary visual cortex

options.label: C
options.html: Suprachiasmatic nucleus and superior cervical ganglion

options.label: E
options.html: Ventral tegmental area and nucleus accumbens

items.explanationHtml:
The drug is ramelteon, an MT1/MT2 melatonin receptor agonist. Light acts on melanopsin retinal ganglion cells, which signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus via the retinohypothalamic tract. The SCN controls a sympathetic relay through the spinal intermediolateral column and the superior cervical ganglion to the pineal gland, which releases melatonin in darkness.

Takeaway: melatonin release is set by retina → SCN → sympathetic chain (superior cervical ganglion) → pineal.

whyNot.D: This pathway releases vasopressin, not the pineal hormone.
whyNot.A: This is the image-forming visual pathway, not the circadian pathway.
whyNot.B: These nuclei are not part of the pineal control pathway.
whyNot.E: This is the mesolimbic dopamine reward pathway.

items.objective: Describe the neural pathway controlling melatonin secretion and the action of ramelteon.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with chronic insomnia is prescribed a drug that blocks the receptors for a lateral hypothalamic neuropeptide that stabilizes wakefulness. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
items.explanationHtml:
Suvorexant (and lemborexant, daridorexant) are orexin receptor antagonists. Blocking orexin's wake-stabilizing signal helps people fall and stay asleep. Their effect mirrors narcolepsy, so they are contraindicated in narcolepsy.

Takeaway: orexin antagonists (-orexants) treat insomnia; they are contraindicated in narcolepsy.

whyNot.E: Zolpidem binds the benzodiazepine site of GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors.
whyNot.B: Ramelteon is a melatonin receptor agonist.
whyNot.D: Trazodone blocks 5-HT<sub>2A</sub>, H<sub>1</sub> and α<sub>1</sub> receptors.
whyNot.A: Pitolisant blocks H<sub>3</sub> autoreceptors to increase histamine and promote wakefulness; it treats narcolepsy.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of orexin receptor antagonists.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25% has disturbed sleep. Polysomnography shows cycles in which breathing gradually waxes to deep, rapid breaths and then wanes to a pause of about 20 seconds without respiratory effort, repeating every minute or so. Which of the following best explains this breathing pattern?

options.label: A
options.html: Collapse of the upper airway from loss of pharyngeal muscle tone

options.label: B
options.html: Damage to the medullary respiratory centre from hypoxia

options.label: C
options.html: Delayed chemoreceptor feedback with high CO<sub>2</sub> sensitivity

options.label: E
options.html: Opioid suppression of the respiratory drive

items.explanationHtml:
This is Cheyne-Stokes breathing, a form of central sleep apnea in heart failure. A long circulation time delays the arrival of blood gas changes at the chemoreceptors, and the chemoreceptors overreact to CO2. Ventilation overshoots, drives CO2 below the apnea threshold and stops, then restarts: a high-gain, delayed control loop.

Takeaway: Cheyne-Stokes breathing in heart failure comes from delayed, overly sensitive ventilatory control (high loop gain).

whyNot.A: Upper airway collapse causes obstructive apneas with continued respiratory effort.
whyNot.B: Medullary damage tends to cause ataxic or absent breathing, not smooth crescendo-decrescendo cycles.
whyNot.D: Weakness causes shallow breathing and hypercapnia, especially in REM, not periodic apneas.
whyNot.E: Opioids cause ataxic breathing and central apneas, but this patient has no opioid exposure.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of Cheyne-Stokes respiration in heart failure.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with narcolepsy has frequent episodes of sudden knee weakness when she laughs. She starts a drug taken at bedtime and again during the night, which consolidates nighttime sleep and reduces these episodes. The drug is the sodium salt of an endogenous metabolite of GABA and is subject to strict distribution controls because of misuse. This drug acts mainly as an agonist at which receptor?
items.explanationHtml:
Sodium oxybate is the sodium salt of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB). It acts mainly as a GABAB agonist, deepens and consolidates night sleep, and reduces cataplexy and daytime sleepiness. It causes respiratory depression with alcohol or sedatives and is a drug of misuse.

Takeaway: sodium oxybate (GHB) is a GABAB agonist that treats cataplexy.

whyNot.B: This is where benzodiazepines and Z-drugs act; they do not treat cataplexy.
whyNot.E: Orexin agonists would mimic the missing peptide, but this drug is not one.
whyNot.D: Pitolisant blocks H<sub>3</sub> receptors; it is not a GABA metabolite.
whyNot.A: Modafinil and stimulants act here; they treat sleepiness but not cataplexy well.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of sodium oxybate in narcolepsy.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old accountant has had trouble falling asleep and staying asleep on most nights for 8 months, since a stressful audit. She lies awake worrying about not sleeping and feels tired and irritable during the day. She drinks one cup of coffee in the morning and no alcohol. She does not snore, and her partner has not seen pauses in her breathing. Depression and anxiety screening are negative. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
She has chronic insomnia disorder. CBT-I (sleep restriction, stimulus control, a fixed wake time and work on sleep-related worry) is first-line, works as well as drugs in the short term and lasts longer.

Takeaway: CBT-I is first-line treatment for chronic insomnia.

whyNot.E: Hypnotics may be added short term but are not first line and lose benefit when stopped.
whyNot.B: Sedating antihistamines have poor evidence, cause tolerance and have anticholinergic effects.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines cause dependence, falls and cognitive effects and are not first-line treatment.
whyNot.D: Polysomnography is not needed for insomnia without features of sleep apnea or another sleep disorder.

items.objective: Choose cognitive behavioural therapy as first-line treatment of chronic insomnia.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old man has fallen asleep in class and while driving over the past year, even though he sleeps 8–9 hours a night. When friends make him laugh, his head drops and his knees give way for a few seconds. He takes no medications and uses no drugs. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?

options.label: A
options.html: Home sleep apnea test on two nights

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with and without contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Polysomnography, then a multiple sleep latency test the next day

options.label: D
options.html: Routine EEG recorded while awake and drowsy

options.label: E
options.html: Two-week sleep diary with no further testing

items.explanationHtml:
Sleepiness with cataplexy suggests narcolepsy type 1. Polysomnography confirms adequate sleep and excludes other causes. The next-day MSLT supports narcolepsy with a mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less and 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods. He should not drive until treated and alert.

Takeaway: narcolepsy is confirmed by polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test.

whyNot.A: A home test detects sleep apnea but cannot measure sleep latency or sleep-onset REM periods.
whyNot.B: Imaging is not needed in a typical presentation with a normal examination.
whyNot.E: A diary helps exclude insufficient sleep but cannot confirm narcolepsy.
whyNot.D: A routine EEG cannot measure sleep tendency or REM onset.

items.objective: Order the correct test sequence for suspected narcolepsy.

items.stemHtml:
A 54-year-old woman has an uncomfortable creeping feeling in her legs every evening when she sits or lies down, with an irresistible urge to move them. Walking relieves it. It delays her sleep by an hour most nights. She has heavy menstrual periods. Neurological examination is normal. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Hemoglobin12.4 g/dL (12.0–16.0 g/dL)
Ferritin28 ng/mL
Transferrin saturation16%
Creatinine0.8 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL)

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
She has restless legs syndrome with low iron stores (ferritin 75 ng/mL or less, transferrin saturation under 20%). Brain iron deficiency drives the disorder, so iron replacement (oral, or IV for faster effect) comes first, and the cause of iron loss should be addressed. If symptoms persist, an α2δ ligand is the drug of choice.

Takeaway: check iron in restless legs syndrome and replace it when ferritin is 75 ng/mL or less.

whyNot.E: Dopamine agonists are no longer preferred for routine use because of augmentation, and correcting iron comes first.
whyNot.A: Benzodiazepines do not treat the underlying cause and add sedation and fall risk.
whyNot.B: Sedating antihistamines worsen restless legs syndrome.
whyNot.D: Levodopa carries the highest augmentation risk and is not first-line.

items.objective: Treat iron deficiency first in restless legs syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has restless legs syndrome that disturbs his sleep most nights. Ferritin is 180 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 32%. He has no kidney disease. He took ropinirole for 2 years, but his symptoms now start in the early afternoon, are more intense and have spread to his arms, despite dose increases. Which of the following is the most appropriate change in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Symptoms starting earlier in the day, getting stronger and spreading to the arms on a dopamine agonist are augmentation. Manage it by tapering the dopamine agonist and switching to an α2δ ligand (pregabalin, gabapentin or gabapentin enacarbil), now the preferred first-line drugs.

Takeaway: augmentation on a dopamine agonist: taper it and switch to an α2δ ligand.

whyNot.C: These features are augmentation, which higher doses make worse.
whyNot.D: Levodopa causes augmentation even more often than dopamine agonists.
whyNot.A: His iron stores are already adequate.
whyNot.B: A hypnotic does not address augmentation or the restless legs symptoms.

items.objective: Recognize and manage augmentation in restless legs syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician with his wife, who says that he has been talking, shouting and flailing his arms during sleep for 2 years, mostly in the early morning. Last week he fell out of bed and bruised his face. When she wakes him he quickly becomes alert and describes being attacked in a dream. He has a reduced sense of smell and chronic constipation. Neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Polysomnography with video and limb EMG

items.explanationHtml:
Dream enactment in the second half of the night, rapid return to alertness and recall of the dream suggest REM sleep behavior disorder. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia and excludes mimics such as sleep apnea arousals and nocturnal seizures. His smell loss and constipation also suggest prodromal synucleinopathy. Treatment is bedroom safety plus melatonin or clonazepam.

Takeaway: REM sleep behavior disorder is confirmed by polysomnography showing REM sleep without atonia.

whyNot.B: Imaging does not show the defining feature, which is loss of muscle atonia during REM.
whyNot.A: This scan can show a dopamine deficit but does not diagnose the sleep disorder itself.
whyNot.E: A daytime EEG does not record REM sleep or muscle tone during it.
whyNot.C: The MSLT measures sleepiness for narcolepsy, not dream enactment.

items.objective: Confirm suspected REM sleep behavior disorder with polysomnography.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she is late for school most days and falls asleep in morning classes. She cannot fall asleep before 2 AM, however early she goes to bed. On weekends she sleeps from 2 AM until 11 AM and wakes refreshed. She does not snore and uses no drugs. Mood screening is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Bright light exposure late each evening

options.label: C
options.html: Morning light, fixed wake time, early-evening melatonin

options.label: E
options.html: Zolpidem at 10 PM on school nights

items.explanationHtml:
This is delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, common in adolescents. Shift the clock earlier with a fixed wake time, bright light in the morning and a small dose of melatonin several hours before the desired bedtime, with good sleep habits (screens off in the evening).

Takeaway: delayed sleep phase: morning light and early-evening melatonin; advanced phase: evening light.

whyNot.E: A hypnotic does not shift the circadian clock and is inappropriate for a teenager.
whyNot.B: A wake-promoting drug treats the symptom, not the shifted clock.
whyNot.A: Evening light delays the clock further; light is needed in the morning.
whyNot.D: The history is typical; polysomnography is not needed.

items.objective: Manage delayed sleep-wake phase disorder in an adolescent.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing and daytime sleepiness. He nearly fell asleep while driving last month. BMI is 36 kg/m2, neck circumference is 46 cm and blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg. A home sleep apnea test shows an apnea-hypopnea index of 34 events per hour, with oxygen saturation falling to 82%. In addition to advice on weight loss, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
An AHI of 30 or more events per hour is severe obstructive sleep apnea, and he is symptomatic with a near miss while driving. CPAP is first-line therapy. It improves sleepiness and lowers blood pressure. Weight loss, including with drugs such as tirzepatide, is added.

Takeaway: symptomatic moderate-severe OSA is treated with CPAP plus weight loss.

whyNot.C: Modafinil can help residual sleepiness after effective CPAP, but it does not treat the apneas.
whyNot.D: Oxygen raises saturation but does not prevent the airway from collapsing or the arousals.
whyNot.E: Pharyngeal surgery is less effective and is not first-line therapy for severe OSA.
whyNot.B: This is for selected patients who cannot use CPAP, usually with a lower BMI.

items.objective: Choose CPAP as first-line treatment for symptomatic severe obstructive sleep apnea.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman was diagnosed with narcolepsy type 1. Modafinil has improved her daytime sleepiness, but she still has several episodes a day of sudden weakness of her knees and neck when she laughs. She has fallen twice. She does not drink alcohol and takes no sedatives. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate to add for these episodes?
items.explanationHtml:
Sodium oxybate reduces cataplexy and also improves daytime sleepiness and night sleep. It must not be combined with alcohol or other sedatives because of respiratory depression. REM-suppressing antidepressants are alternatives for cataplexy.

Takeaway: for cataplexy, use sodium oxybate (or a REM-suppressing antidepressant); modafinil treats sleepiness only.

whyNot.A: Armodafinil is closely related to modafinil and treats sleepiness, not cataplexy.
whyNot.B: Stimulants treat sleepiness and have little effect on cataplexy.
whyNot.E: A hypnotic does not prevent cataplexy and adds daytime sedation.
whyNot.C: A melatonin agonist does not reduce cataplexy.

items.objective: Select a treatment for cataplexy in narcolepsy.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with epilepsy has a phenytoin level of 9 µg/mL (therapeutic 10–20 µg/mL) on 300 mg/day. His dose is increased to 400 mg/day. Two weeks later he has nystagmus, unsteady gait and slurred speech, and his level is 32 µg/mL. Which of the following best explains the disproportionate rise in his drug level?

options.label: A
options.html: Displacement of phenytoin from albumin by the higher dose

options.label: B
options.html: First-order elimination at the new dose

options.label: C
options.html: Induction of CYP enzymes by phenytoin

options.label: D
options.html: Reduced renal excretion of unchanged phenytoin

options.label: E
options.html: Saturation of the hepatic enzymes that metabolize phenytoin

items.explanationHtml:
At usual doses phenytoin's hepatic metabolism (mainly CYP2C9) saturates, so elimination shifts from first-order to zero-order: a fixed amount is removed per unit time. A modest dose increase therefore causes a steep rise in level and toxicity (nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria).

Takeaway: phenytoin has saturable (zero-order) kinetics: small dose changes can cause large level changes.

whyNot.C: Enzyme induction would lower, not raise, drug levels.
whyNot.D: Phenytoin is eliminated mainly by hepatic metabolism, not renal excretion.
whyNot.A: Higher doses do not displace the drug from albumin; displacement changes the free fraction, not the total level.
whyNot.B: First-order elimination would make levels rise in proportion to the dose.

items.objective: Explain the disproportionate rise in phenytoin levels with dose increases.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man of Han Chinese ancestry is started on an antiseizure drug for focal seizures. Three weeks later he develops fever, painful oral ulcers, conjunctivitis and a dusky rash with blistering and skin peeling over 10% of his body surface area. Which of the following tests would most likely have identified his risk before treatment began?
items.explanationHtml:
Carbamazepine (and related drugs such as oxcarbazepine and phenytoin) can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. The risk is much higher in carriers of HLA-B*15:02, common in people of Southeast and East Asian ancestry, who should be tested before starting.

Takeaway: screen for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in patients of Asian ancestry.

whyNot.A: CYP2D6 variants affect codeine and many antidepressants, not this reaction.
whyNot.E: TPMT deficiency predicts myelosuppression with thiopurines.
whyNot.D: HLA-B*57:01 predicts abacavir hypersensitivity.
whyNot.B: G6PD deficiency predicts hemolysis with oxidant drugs.

items.objective: Identify the pharmacogenetic marker for carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receives induction chemotherapy. After 3 weeks he has tingling in his feet, absent ankle reflexes, jaw pain, constipation and difficulty climbing stairs. The drug most likely responsible exerts its anticancer effect by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Binding tubulin and preventing microtubule assembly

options.label: E
options.html: Stabilizing microtubules and preventing their disassembly

items.explanationHtml:
Vincristine binds β-tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, arresting cells in metaphase. In neurons this disrupts axonal transport and causes a length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy, jaw pain, and autonomic neuropathy with constipation and ileus. It spares the bone marrow relatively.

Takeaway: vincristine blocks microtubule assembly: neuropathy and constipation, little marrow suppression.

whyNot.E: This is the mechanism of taxanes such as paclitaxel, not the usual drug in this regimen.
whyNot.B: This describes platinum compounds and alkylating agents.
whyNot.D: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR; its toxicity is mucositis and myelosuppression, not neuropathy.
whyNot.C: Asparaginase causes pancreatitis, thrombosis and hypersensitivity rather than neuropathy.

items.objective: Relate vincristine's mechanism to its neurotoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after taking a large number of her roommate's tuberculosis tablets. She has had three generalized seizures. Two doses of IV lorazepam have not stopped them. Arterial blood gas shows a severe metabolic acidosis. Which of the following best explains why her seizures are resistant to benzodiazepines?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors by the drug

options.label: B
options.html: Excess glutamate release from direct NMDA receptor activation

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced GABA synthesis due to pyridoxal phosphate depletion

items.explanationHtml:
Isoniazid depletes active pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, the cofactor for glutamate decarboxylase, which makes GABA. With little GABA available, benzodiazepines (which only enhance GABA's effect) work poorly. The antidote is IV pyridoxine, given with a benzodiazepine.

Takeaway: isoniazid seizures resist benzodiazepines because GABA synthesis falls; give IV pyridoxine.

whyNot.A: The drug does not block GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors; the problem is too little GABA.
whyNot.B: The drug does not directly activate NMDA receptors.
whyNot.D: Inhibiting reuptake would raise synaptic GABA and reduce seizures.
whyNot.C: Hypoglycemia is not the main mechanism; benzodiazepines fail because GABA is lacking.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of isoniazid-induced seizures and their treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl with generalized epilepsy is taking valproate. Lamotrigine is added at the usual starting dose and increased quickly over 2 weeks. She then develops fever, a widespread rash and erosions of the lips and mouth. Which of the following interactions most likely contributed to this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Lamotrigine displaced valproate from plasma proteins

options.label: B
options.html: Lamotrigine inhibited valproate clearance, causing valproate toxicity

options.label: C
options.html: Valproate increased the renal excretion of lamotrigine

options.label: D
options.html: Valproate induced CYP3A4 and produced a toxic lamotrigine metabolite

options.label: E
options.html: Valproate inhibited the glucuronidation of lamotrigine

items.explanationHtml:
Valproate inhibits glucuronidation, roughly doubling lamotrigine levels. Lamotrigine's risk of serious rash (including SJS/TEN) rises with high levels, fast titration and co-treatment with valproate. When combining them, lamotrigine is started at a lower dose and titrated slowly.

Takeaway: valproate raises lamotrigine levels; start lamotrigine low and slow to avoid serious rash.

whyNot.D: Valproate inhibits rather than induces drug metabolism.
whyNot.A: This would raise free valproate, which does not explain a severe rash.
whyNot.B: Valproate toxicity causes sedation, tremor or hepatotoxicity, not a mucocutaneous rash.
whyNot.C: Increased excretion would lower lamotrigine levels and reduce risk.

items.objective: Explain the valproate-lamotrigine interaction and its link to rash.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman taking a drug to prevent migraine has lost 6 kg in 4 months. She now has right flank pain and blood in her urine, and CT shows a radiopaque stone in the right ureter. Serum bicarbonate is 18 mEq/L (22–28 mEq/L) with a normal anion gap, and her urine pH is 6.8. Her symptoms are best explained by which action of the drug?

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of the angiotensin II type 1 receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake

items.explanationHtml:
Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase. This causes a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, alkaline urine, low urinary citrate and calcium phosphate stones. Other effects include weight loss, paresthesias, word-finding difficulty and, rarely, acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Takeaway: topiramate: carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes acidosis and calcium phosphate stones; also weight loss and word-finding difficulty.

whyNot.C: β-blockers do not cause metabolic acidosis or kidney stones.
whyNot.A: CGRP antagonists do not affect renal acid handling.
whyNot.E: Tricyclic-like reuptake inhibition causes weight gain and anticholinergic effects, not stones.
whyNot.B: Candesartan can raise potassium, but it does not cause stones or this acidosis.

items.objective: Link topiramate's carbonic anhydrase inhibition to its adverse effects.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has taken haloperidol for schizophrenia for 12 years. Over the past year she has developed constant chewing and lip-smacking movements and writhing movements of her fingers. Her psychiatrist adds a drug that reversibly inhibits the vesicular monoamine transporter 2. Which of the following is the main effect of this drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of muscarinic receptors in the striatum

items.explanationHtml:
Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine inhibit VMAT2, which packages monoamines into synaptic vesicles. Unpackaged dopamine is degraded in the cytoplasm, so less dopamine is released onto supersensitive postsynaptic receptors. This reduces tardive dyskinesia.

Takeaway: VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia by depleting presynaptic dopamine.

whyNot.B: Increasing D<sub>2</sub> blockade can mask tardive dyskinesia briefly but worsens it over time; it is not how VMAT2 inhibitors act.
whyNot.A: Antimuscarinic drugs worsen tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.D: Reuptake inhibition would increase synaptic dopamine and worsen the movements.
whyNot.E: Baclofen acts here; it is not a VMAT2 inhibitor.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of VMAT2 inhibitors in tardive dyskinesia.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy is given IV prochlorperazine for vomiting in the emergency department. Four hours later his neck twists painfully to the left and his eyes are fixed in an upward gaze. He is fully alert. His temperature is normal. An injection of benztropine relieves the symptoms within minutes. Benztropine works in this condition mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of hypothalamic histamine H<sub>1</sub> receptors

options.label: B
options.html: Direct stimulation of striatal D<sub>2</sub> receptors

options.label: E
options.html: Muscarinic receptor blockade in the striatum

items.explanationHtml:
Blocking D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway leaves striatal cholinergic interneurons relatively unopposed, which produces acute dystonia (torticollis, oculogyric crisis). Benztropine, a muscarinic antagonist, restores the balance and relieves dystonia within minutes.

Takeaway: acute dystonia from D2 blockers responds to antimuscarinic drugs (benztropine or diphenhydramine).

whyNot.B: Benztropine is not a dopamine agonist.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines work this way; benztropine does not.
