Biopsy shows small lymphocytes with plasmacytic differentiation and a clonal B-cell population. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Cavernous venous malformation of the orbit

items.explanationHtml:
A painless, slowly growing orbital mass with a salmon-pink conjunctival component in an older adult, and a clonal B-cell infiltrate of small lymphocytes with plasmacytic differentiation, is extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma, the most common lymphoma of the ocular adnexa. After systemic staging, localised disease responds well to low-dose radiotherapy.

Takeaway: a salmon-patch orbital or conjunctival mass in an older adult is lymphoma until proven otherwise.

whyNot.E: Thyroid eye disease swells the muscles and causes lid retraction, and biopsy would not show a clonal B-cell population.
whyNot.C: Orbital cellulitis is acute, painful and febrile.
whyNot.D: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a rapidly growing tumour of children.
whyNot.A: This benign vascular lesion causes slow proptosis but has no lymphoid infiltrate.

items.objective: Recognise ocular adnexal marginal zone lymphoma.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 2 hours after severe pain in her left eye began while she was watching a film in a cinema. She has a frontal headache, has vomited twice, and sees coloured halos around lights. She wears glasses for long sight. Her left eye is red, the cornea is cloudy, and the pupil is fixed and mid-dilated. Visual acuity is counting fingers in the left eye. The left eye is rock-hard to gentle palpation, and the intraocular pressure is 58 mm Hg (normal 10–21). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Topical timolol and apraclonidine plus acetazolamide

items.explanationHtml:
Severe eye pain, headache, vomiting, halos, a cloudy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and a very high pressure in a hyperopic woman after time in the dark are acute angle-closure glaucoma. Lower the pressure at once: topical β-blocker and α2-agonist, systemic acetazolamide, then pilocarpine once the pressure begins to fall, and IV mannitol if needed. Arrange emergency ophthalmology.

Takeaway: angle closure: drops plus acetazolamide immediately, then laser iridotomy.

whyNot.C: Atropine dilates the pupil further and worsens angle closure.
whyNot.B: This is not a migraine; the eye findings show acute angle closure.
whyNot.A: The diagnosis is clear from the eye; imaging delays pressure-lowering treatment.
whyNot.D: Steroid and antibiotic drops do not lower the pressure.

items.objective: Start immediate pressure-lowering treatment for acute angle-closure glaucoma.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item received topical timolol, apraclonidine and pilocarpine, and intravenous acetazolamide. Two hours later the pressure in her left eye is 22 mm Hg, the cornea has cleared and her pain has resolved. Gonioscopy shows that the drainage angle of her right eye is also very narrow. In addition to laser peripheral iridotomy of the left eye, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for her right eye?

options.label: B
options.html: No intervention, as the other eye is rarely affected

items.explanationHtml:
Once the attack is broken, laser peripheral iridotomy treats the affected eye by letting aqueous bypass the pupil and flattening the iris away from the angle. The fellow eye usually shares the same anatomy, and many untreated fellow eyes later have an attack, so it receives a prophylactic iridotomy.

Takeaway: after angle closure, treat the other eye with a prophylactic iridotomy.

whyNot.A: Lifelong miotic drops are a poor substitute for a definitive laser procedure and cause dim vision and brow ache.
whyNot.E: Observation leaves a high risk of an attack in the narrow-angled fellow eye.
whyNot.D: Filtering surgery is not the first choice for a narrow angle that has not yet closed.
whyNot.B: The fellow eye has a high risk of an acute attack, so it is treated.

items.objective: Recommend prophylactic laser iridotomy of the fellow eye after acute angle closure.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man is referred after a routine eye examination. He has no symptoms. His father went blind from glaucoma. Intraocular pressure is 28 mm Hg in both eyes (normal 10–21), the angles are open on gonioscopy, the optic cups are enlarged with a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8, and visual field testing shows early arcuate defects in both eyes. He has mild asthma. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Raised pressure, open angles, optic cupping and arcuate field defects confirm primary open-angle glaucoma. First-line treatment is a prostaglandin analogue such as latanoprost once at night (selective laser trabeculoplasty is an equal first-line alternative). Timolol is also effective but is avoided here because of his asthma.

Takeaway: open-angle glaucoma: prostaglandin analogue first; avoid topical β-blockers in asthma.

whyNot.D: Topical β-blockers are absorbed systemically and can provoke bronchospasm in a patient with asthma.
whyNot.C: Oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause paraesthesia, acidosis and kidney stones and are not first-line long-term therapy.
whyNot.E: Steroids can raise intraocular pressure.
whyNot.A: Atropine dilates the pupil and does not lower pressure.

items.objective: Choose first-line treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma and recognise β-blocker contraindications.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old woman has had gradually worsening blurred vision in both eyes over 2 years. She has trouble driving at night because of glare from headlights and can no longer read the newspaper comfortably. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/60 in both eyes. Both lenses have yellow-brown central opacities, and the red reflex is dimmed. The retinas and optic nerves look normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Gradual painless blurring, glare at night and nuclear lens opacities that limit driving and reading are age-related cataract. There is no medical treatment. Surgery (phacoemulsification with an intraocular lens) is offered when the cataract impairs function, usually one eye at a time.

Takeaway: cataract that limits daily activities is treated surgically.

whyNot.A: No drops reverse or slow cataract.
whyNot.D: New spectacles cannot overcome a dense cataract that already limits daily life.
whyNot.E: YAG capsulotomy treats clouding of the capsule after cataract surgery, not a native cataract.
whyNot.B: Supplements do not treat cataract.

items.objective: Refer for cataract surgery when cataract impairs function.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had a painless lump in her right upper eyelid for 3 weeks. It began as a tender swelling that settled. Examination shows a firm, nontender, 5-mm nodule within the lid, away from the lid margin, with normal overlying skin and normal lashes. Vision is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
items.explanationHtml:
A firm, painless nodule in the lid after an earlier tender phase is a chalazion: a blocked meibomian gland with lipogranulomatous inflammation. Most resolve with warm compresses and gentle massage several times a day for a few weeks. Persistent lesions can be injected with a steroid or removed by incision and curettage. Recurrent lesions in older adults need a biopsy.

Takeaway: treat a typical chalazion with warm compresses first.

whyNot.C: There is no cellulitis, and a chalazion is a sterile lipogranuloma.
whyNot.A: A first, typical chalazion in a young adult does not need a biopsy.
whyNot.D: Steroid drops do not treat a chalazion and carry eye risks.
whyNot.B: Most chalazia resolve with conservative care; procedures are for persistent lesions.

items.objective: Manage a typical chalazion conservatively.

items.stemHtml:
A 44-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of blurred vision and aching pain in both eyes that started yesterday. Distant objects look much blurrier than usual. Both eyes are red, both corneas are mildly hazy, and the anterior chambers are very shallow. Intraocular pressure is 42 mm Hg in the right eye and 40 mm Hg in the left (normal 10–21). Her medication list is shown.

MedicationIndicationStarted
TopiramateMigraine prevention10 days ago
LisinoprilHypertension4 years ago
SertralineDepression5 years ago
AtorvastatinHyperlipidaemia3 years ago
MetforminType 2 diabetes2 years ago

Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of her eye findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral acute angle closure with a sudden myopic shift, starting within the first weeks of a new drug, is the classic adverse effect of topiramate. The drug causes swelling of the ciliary body and fluid around the choroid, which rotates the lens–iris diaphragm forward. Stop topiramate and lower the pressure with aqueous suppressants and cycloplegia; pilocarpine and iridotomy do not help because the mechanism is not pupillary block.

Takeaway: new bilateral angle closure with myopia in the first weeks of topiramate is a drug reaction.

whyNot.B: ACE inhibitors are not linked to angle closure.
whyNot.D: SSRIs have been linked rarely to angle closure, but she has taken sertraline for 5 years without problems; the new drug is the likely cause.
whyNot.A: Statins do not cause angle closure.
whyNot.C: Metformin does not affect the anterior chamber.

items.objective: Recognise topiramate-induced bilateral angle closure.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has had gritty, burning eyes for 6 months, worse after working at a computer. She also needs to sip water to swallow dry food and has had several new dental cavities. A Schirmer test shows 3 mm of wetting in 5 minutes in both eyes (normal ≥10 mm). Fluorescein shows fine punctate staining of both corneas. In addition to artificial tears, which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic test?
items.explanationHtml:
Dry eyes with reduced tear production (low Schirmer test), a dry mouth and new dental caries suggest Sjögren syndrome. Test for anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies; a labial salivary gland biopsy helps when serology is negative. Manage dry eye with artificial tears and, if needed, anti-inflammatory drops, and watch for systemic features and lymphoma.

Takeaway: dry eyes plus dry mouth: check anti-Ro and anti-La.

whyNot.B: Anti-CCP antibodies support rheumatoid arthritis, which may coexist but is not suggested by these symptoms.
whyNot.C: Anti-dsDNA supports systemic lupus erythematosus, and she has no features of it.
whyNot.A: Anti-centromere antibodies are linked to limited systemic sclerosis.
whyNot.D: Anti-Jo-1 is linked to inflammatory myopathy with interstitial lung disease.

items.objective: Evaluate dry eye with dry mouth for Sjögren syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a severe headache behind her left eye and drooping of her left eyelid that began this morning. She has hypertension. The left upper eyelid covers the pupil. When the lid is lifted, the left eye rests down and out, and the left pupil is 6 mm and unreactive to light. The right pupil is 3 mm and reactive. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: E
options.html: MRI of the orbits within 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
An acute, painful oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil is a compressive lesion until proven otherwise, classically an expanding posterior communicating artery aneurysm that may be about to rupture. Obtain emergency CT angiography (or MR angiography); if it is negative and suspicion remains high, catheter angiography follows.

Takeaway: painful oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil: emergency vascular imaging.

whyNot.D: A pupil-involving oculomotor palsy with headache is not presumed ischaemic.
whyNot.A: Myasthenia never affects the pupil.
whyNot.E: A possible expanding aneurysm needs emergency vascular imaging, not delayed orbital imaging.
whyNot.C: Myasthenia does not cause a dilated pupil, and this test is rarely used now.

items.objective: Order emergency vascular imaging for a pupil-involving oculomotor palsy.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has had pain on the left side of his neck and a left-sided headache for 2 days, beginning shortly after a chiropractic neck manipulation. His wife says his left eyelid droops. Examination shows 2 mm of left ptosis and a left pupil that is 2 mm smaller than the right, with the difference greater in dim light. Facial sweating is normal. Strength and sensation are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: CT angiography of the head and neck

items.explanationHtml:
Acute, painful Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis greater in the dark) after neck manipulation means internal carotid artery dissection until proven otherwise. The sympathetic fibres run on the wall of the internal carotid, and facial sweating is spared because its fibres follow the external carotid. Obtain urgent CT angiography or MR angiography of the head and neck; antithrombotic therapy is started to prevent stroke.

Takeaway: painful Horner syndrome is carotid dissection until proven otherwise.

whyNot.A: A chest radiograph would look for an apical tumour, which does not fit acute painful Horner syndrome after neck manipulation.
whyNot.C: There are no features of meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage that need a lumbar puncture.
whyNot.D: Plain radiographs show bone, not the carotid artery.
whyNot.E: Untreated carotid dissection carries a risk of stroke.

items.objective: Investigate acute painful Horner syndrome for carotid artery dissection.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with Graves disease diagnosed 4 months ago is now euthyroid on methimazole. Over 6 weeks her eyes have become painful and swollen. She has double vision when looking up and her eyes look increasingly prominent. She smokes 10 cigarettes a day. Examination shows red, swollen eyelids, conjunctival redness, 23 mm of proptosis in both eyes, restricted upgaze and lid retraction. Visual acuity, colour vision and pupils are normal. She has agreed to stop smoking. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her eye disease?
items.explanationHtml:
Painful, red, swollen lids, progressive proptosis and double vision indicate moderate-to-severe, active thyroid eye disease without optic neuropathy. A standard first-line treatment is intravenous methylprednisolone pulses over about 12 weeks; teprotumumab and other immunotherapies are alternatives. Smoking cessation, a steady euthyroid state and lubrication are essential for everyone. Surgery waits until the disease is inactive.

Takeaway: active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease is treated with IV glucocorticoid pulses.

whyNot.D: Radioactive iodine can worsen active orbitopathy and is not a treatment for the eye disease.
whyNot.A: Decompression is reserved for compressive optic neuropathy that does not respond to steroids, or for stable, inactive disease.
whyNot.C: Propranolol controls adrenergic symptoms of hyperthyroidism; she is euthyroid and it does not treat orbitopathy.
whyNot.E: Selenium may help mild disease, but this is moderate-to-severe active disease.

items.objective: Treat active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl fails vision screening at preschool. Examination shows significant long-sightedness in the right eye and a normal refraction in the left. Her eyes are straight. After 3 months of full-time wear of correct spectacles, visual acuity is 20/80 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Media, fundi and alignment are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Atropine drops in the right eye

options.label: B
options.html: Observation until she is 8 years old

options.label: C
options.html: Patching of the left eye for part of each day

items.explanationHtml:
Reduced vision in one eye from anisometropia that persists after the refractive error is corrected is amblyopia. The next step is to penalise the stronger eye so that the brain uses the weaker one: patching the good eye for a few hours a day, or atropine drops in the good eye. Treatment works best in young children.

Takeaway: treat amblyopia by correcting the refraction and then patching or blurring the good eye.

whyNot.D: Patching the weaker eye would deepen its amblyopia.
whyNot.B: Amblyopia responds best when treated young; waiting loses the window of plasticity.
whyNot.E: Refractive surgery is not standard treatment for amblyopia in young children.
whyNot.A: Atropine penalisation is placed in the stronger (left) eye, not the amblyopic eye.

items.objective: Treat anisometropic amblyopia by occluding the stronger eye.

items.stemHtml: The parents of a 7-month-old boy are worried that his eyes look crossed, especially when he looks to the side. He was born at term and is developing normally. He has a broad, flat nasal bridge and prominent epicanthal folds. The light reflex from a penlight falls in the centre of both pupils, and on cover testing neither eye moves to take up fixation. Red reflexes are normal and equal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A symmetric corneal light reflex and a normal cover test show that the eyes are aligned. The appearance of crossing comes from a broad nasal bridge and epicanthal folds that hide the white of the eye on the nasal side: pseudostrabismus. Reassure the parents and continue routine vision screening.

Takeaway: symmetric light reflexes and a normal cover test mean pseudostrabismus.

whyNot.C: There is no amblyopia or squint to treat.
whyNot.E: There is no true misalignment.
whyNot.B: There are no neurological signs or true misalignment.
whyNot.A: This treats some true squints, not pseudostrabismus.

items.objective: Distinguish pseudostrabismus from true strabismus in an infant.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had horizontal double vision for 1 week. Eighteen months ago she had numbness and tingling of both legs that resolved over 6 weeks. On gaze to either side, the adducting eye moves slowly and stops short of the midline, and the abducting eye shows nystagmus. Convergence is normal. Pupils and fundi are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Lumbar puncture as the first test

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the brain and spine with gadolinium

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult, with a previous episode of sensory symptoms, strongly suggests multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium shows lesions disseminated in space and time; CSF oligoclonal bands can add support.

Takeaway: an INO in a young adult calls for MRI looking for demyelination.

whyNot.E: CT is insensitive for demyelinating lesions in the brainstem.
whyNot.A: Myasthenia can mimic an INO, but her earlier sensory episode and preserved convergence point to demyelination.
whyNot.B: Carotid disease does not cause an INO in a young adult.
whyNot.C: CSF testing can support the diagnosis, but MRI is the first and most informative test.

items.objective: Investigate internuclear ophthalmoplegia in a young adult with MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is referred because his right eyelid has drooped slightly for several months. The right pupil is smaller, and the asymmetry increases when the room lights are turned down. He sweats normally on both sides of the face. Apraclonidine 0.5% drops make the right pupil larger than the left. Two days later, hydroxyamphetamine 1% drops dilate the left pupil but not the right. Which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
Reversal of anisocoria with apraclonidine confirms Horner syndrome: the denervated dilator muscle has upregulated α1 receptors. Hydroxyamphetamine releases noradrenaline from intact third-order nerve endings; failure to dilate shows the third-order (postganglionic) neuron is damaged, beyond the superior cervical ganglion along the internal carotid artery. Normal facial sweating fits, because those fibres follow the external carotid. Imaging should target the carotid artery and skull base.

Takeaway: a Horner pupil that will not dilate with hydroxyamphetamine has a postganglionic lesion.

whyNot.C: A first-order lesion leaves the third-order neuron intact, so hydroxyamphetamine would dilate the pupil, and facial sweating would usually be reduced.
whyNot.D: A second-order lesion also leaves the third-order neuron intact, so the pupil would dilate with hydroxyamphetamine.
whyNot.A: The ciliary ganglion is parasympathetic; damage causes a large tonic pupil.
whyNot.E: Oculomotor nerve damage causes a large pupil and severe ptosis with eye movement problems.

items.objective: Use pharmacological testing to localise Horner syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped his anticoagulant 2 months ago has sudden, painless loss of vision in the right eye. Fundus examination shows a whitened, opaque posterior retina with a bright red spot at the centre of the macula. Which of the following best explains why the centre of the macula looks red?

options.label: A
options.html: Blood has leaked from occluded vessels into the foveal pit

options.label: B
options.html: The fovea has extra retinal capillaries that stay perfused by collaterals

options.label: C
options.html: The optic disc is swollen and displaces the macula

options.label: D
options.html: The retinal pigment epithelium at the fovea has been lost

options.label: E
options.html: The thin fovea lacks ischaemic inner layers, so the normal choroid shows through

items.explanationHtml:
Central retinal artery occlusion makes the inner retina ischaemic, oedematous and opaque white. The fovea has no ganglion-cell or inner nuclear layers and no retinal capillaries, so there is nothing at the fovea to whiten. The intact, red choroidal circulation shows through and contrasts with the pale surroundings.

Takeaway: the cherry-red spot is normal choroid seen through the thin fovea, surrounded by whitened inner retina.

whyNot.B: The fovea has no retinal capillaries at all (the foveal avascular zone).
whyNot.A: There is no haemorrhage in arterial occlusion; the spot is the normal choroid seen through thin retina.
whyNot.C: Disc swelling does not produce a red fovea; arterial occlusion leaves the disc pale or normal.
whyNot.D: Loss of pigment epithelium causes pale atrophy, not a red spot.

items.objective: Explain the cherry-red spot of central retinal artery occlusion from the dual blood supply of the retina.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes diagnosed 9 years ago has a routine dilated eye examination. Her hemoglobin A1c is 9.4%. Scattered microaneurysms and a few dot-blot haemorrhages are seen in both eyes. Which of the following cellular changes in the retinal capillaries is the earliest to contribute to these findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Deposition of amyloid in capillary walls

options.label: D
options.html: Lymphocytic infiltration of the capillary walls

options.label: E
options.html: Proliferation of endothelial cells into the vitreous

items.explanationHtml:
Pericytes support retinal capillaries and regulate their tone. Their early loss weakens the capillary wall, which bulges into microaneurysms and leaks. Basement-membrane thickening and capillary closure follow, leading to ischaemia and later VEGF-driven new vessels.

Takeaway: pericyte loss is the earliest histological change in diabetic retinopathy, and microaneurysms are the earliest clinical sign.

whyNot.E: Endothelial proliferation into the vitreous defines proliferative disease, which comes much later.
whyNot.A: Amyloid is not part of diabetic microangiopathy.
whyNot.B: Fibrinoid necrosis is a lesion of malignant hypertension, not early diabetic retinopathy.
whyNot.D: Diabetic retinopathy is not a lymphocytic vasculitis.

items.objective: Identify pericyte loss as the earliest microvascular lesion of diabetic retinopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 1 diabetes has new vessels growing on the optic disc and along the retinal arcades of both eyes. His ophthalmologist recommends a series of injections into the vitreous of a monoclonal antibody fragment. The drug most likely binds which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
Ischaemic retina releases VEGF-A, which drives new vessel growth and capillary leakage. Ranibizumab is an antibody fragment against VEGF-A; bevacizumab is a full antibody, and aflibercept is a decoy receptor. Faricimab blocks both VEGF-A and angiopoietin-2.

Takeaway: intravitreal anti-VEGF agents treat proliferative diabetic retinopathy and macular oedema by blocking the hypoxia-driven growth signal.

whyNot.D: Anti-TNF agents treat uveitis in some diseases but are not used for retinal neovascularization.
whyNot.C: PDGF inhibition is not an approved intraocular treatment for proliferative retinopathy.
whyNot.A: EGFR antagonists are anticancer drugs without a role in retinal neovascularization.
whyNot.B: IL-6 receptor blockade (tocilizumab) treats giant cell arteritis, not diabetic new vessels.

items.objective: Relate retinal neovascularization to VEGF and identify the target of intravitreal anti-VEGF drugs.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension and open-angle glaucoma wakes with blurred vision in the left eye. Visual acuity is 20/200 in that eye. Her fundus resembles panel 3 of the figure. Which of the following is the most likely underlying event?

options.label: A
options.html: A tear in the peripheral retina allowing fluid under it

options.label: B
options.html: Cholesterol embolus lodged in the central retinal artery

options.label: C
options.html: Inflammation of the short posterior ciliary arteries

options.label: D
options.html: Raised intracranial pressure transmitted to the optic nerve sheath

options.label: E
options.html: Thrombosis of the central retinal vein at the lamina cribrosa

items.explanationHtml:
Dilated, tortuous veins, haemorrhages in all four quadrants, cotton-wool spots and disc swelling are the picture of central retinal vein occlusion. Thrombosis happens where the central retinal artery and vein share a sheath at the lamina cribrosa; a stiff arteriole compresses the vein. Hypertension, age, diabetes and glaucoma (raised pressure at the disc) are the main risk factors.

Takeaway: haemorrhages in every quadrant with dilated veins point to central retinal vein occlusion.

whyNot.B: Arterial occlusion gives a pale retina with a cherry-red spot (panel 2), not diffuse haemorrhages and dilated veins.
whyNot.D: Raised intracranial pressure causes bilateral disc swelling without haemorrhages throughout the retina (panel 4).
whyNot.C: Arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy causes a pale swollen disc, not haemorrhages in every quadrant.
whyNot.A: Rhegmatogenous detachment causes flashes, floaters and a curtain, with a grey elevated retina.

items.objective: Recognize central retinal vein occlusion on fundus appearance and relate it to its risk factors.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man says he has always had trouble walking in dim light and now keeps bumping into objects at his sides. His maternal uncle had similar problems. Fundus examination shows dark, branching pigment clumps in the mid-periphery of both retinas, narrowed arterioles and a pale disc. Which of the following cells is affected first in this condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Bipolar cells of the inner nuclear layer

items.explanationHtml:
Night blindness, shrinking peripheral fields and bone-spicule pigment are typical of retinitis pigmentosa, an inherited rod-cone dystrophy. Rods, which dominate the peripheral retina and work in dim light, degenerate first. Inheritance can be autosomal dominant, recessive or X-linked, as in this family.

Takeaway: retinitis pigmentosa starts in the rods, so night blindness and peripheral field loss come before central loss.

whyNot.D: Ganglion cell loss (as in glaucoma) causes disc cupping, not night blindness and peripheral pigment.
whyNot.B: Cones are affected later; central vision is preserved until late in the disease.
whyNot.A: Bipolar cells are not the primary target.
whyNot.C: Müller cells are not the primary target; their disease (for example, retinoschisis) looks different.

items.objective: Identify rod photoreceptors as the primary target in retinitis pigmentosa from its presentation.

items.stemHtml: A boy born at 26 weeks' gestation needed several weeks of supplemental oxygen. At 35 weeks' postmenstrual age, retinal examination shows a ridge of abnormal fibrovascular tissue at the border between vascularized and avascular retina. Which of the following sequences best explains this finding?

options.label: A
options.html: Congenital infection inflames the retina and causes scarring

options.label: B
options.html: Excess VEGF from the placenta speeds retinal vascularization

options.label: C
options.html: Low oxygen during ventilation directly causes endothelial necrosis and scarring

options.label: D
options.html: Maternal antibodies cross the placenta and attack retinal endothelium

options.label: E
options.html: Oxygen-induced arrest of vessel growth, then hypoxia-driven VEGF

items.explanationHtml:
In a preterm infant the retina is incompletely vascularized. Supplemental oxygen suppresses VEGF and stops vessel growth. As the avascular retina grows and its metabolic demand rises, it becomes hypoxic and releases VEGF, which drives disorganized growth at the vascular border. This can progress to fibrovascular traction and detachment.

Takeaway: retinopathy of prematurity is a two-phase disease: oxygen-induced arrest of vessel growth, then hypoxia-driven VEGF-mediated proliferation.

whyNot.C: The initial injury comes from hyperoxia suppressing vessel growth, not from direct hypoxic necrosis.
whyNot.D: Retinopathy of prematurity is not an immune-mediated disease.
whyNot.A: Congenital infections (toxoplasmosis, CMV) cause chorioretinitis, not a vascular ridge.
whyNot.B: The VEGF that matters comes from the hypoxic avascular retina after birth, not the placenta.

items.objective: Describe the two-phase pathogenesis of retinopathy of prematurity.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old woman who smoked for 40 years notices that the lines of her bathroom tiles look wavy in her right eye and that a grey patch blocks the centre of her vision. The change developed over 10 days. Fundus examination shows a grey-green lesion with haemorrhage beneath the macula and several yellow subretinal deposits in both eyes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of her sudden symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium

options.label: B
options.html: Deposition of drug crystals in the macula

options.label: C
options.html: New choroidal vessels growing through Bruch membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Occlusion of a branch retinal artery

options.label: E
options.html: Traction from the vitreous tearing the macula

items.explanationHtml:
Yellow deposits (drusen) in both eyes show underlying age-related macular degeneration. Rapid distortion (metamorphopsia), a central scotoma and a grey-green lesion with subretinal blood mean conversion to neovascular (wet) disease: VEGF-driven choroidal vessels break through Bruch membrane and leak or bleed. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor.

Takeaway: sudden metamorphopsia in an older patient with drusen means choroidal neovascularization until proved otherwise.

whyNot.A: Atrophy (geographic atrophy, the end of dry AMD) causes slow loss, not sudden distortion with haemorrhage.
whyNot.D: Branch artery occlusion causes a sudden sectoral field defect with a pale, whitened retina, not distortion and subretinal blood.
whyNot.E: A macular hole causes central distortion and a scotoma but no haemorrhage or grey-green membrane.
whyNot.B: Drug crystal deposition is not suggested; she takes no implicated drug.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of visual distortion in neovascular age-related macular degeneration.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman has had a new headache over the temples and pain in her jaw when chewing for 3 weeks. This morning she lost vision in the lower half of the left visual field. The left optic disc is pale and swollen. ESR is 96 mm/h. Occlusion of which of the following vessels most directly caused her visual loss?
items.explanationHtml:
This is giant cell arteritis with arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Granulomatous inflammation of branches of the ophthalmic artery occludes the short posterior ciliary arteries, which supply the optic nerve head. The disc infarcts and swells, often with chalky pallor, and the field loss is typically altitudinal.

Takeaway: in giant cell arteritis, blindness usually results from occlusion of the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the optic nerve head.

whyNot.B: Vein occlusion causes haemorrhages throughout the retina, not a pale swollen disc.
whyNot.E: This artery is inflamed and causes headache, but it does not supply the eye.
whyNot.C: Occipital infarction gives a homonymous field defect in both eyes with a normal disc.
whyNot.A: These supply the anterior segment and rectus muscles, not the optic nerve head.

items.objective: Identify the vascular basis of arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has floaters and a patchy blind area in the right eye. His CD4 count is 24/mm3. Fundus examination shows a white granular area of retinal necrosis with haemorrhage along the vessels. Treatment begins with a drug that must first be phosphorylated by a virus-encoded kinase. Which of the following resistance mechanisms is most likely if the infection later stops responding to this drug?

options.label: A
options.html: Alteration of the neuraminidase active site

options.label: D
options.html: Mutation in the viral UL97 kinase

items.explanationHtml:
Necrotizing retinitis along the vessels at a CD4 count below 50 is cytomegalovirus retinitis. Ganciclovir (and its oral prodrug valganciclovir) is first monophosphorylated by the CMV-encoded UL97 kinase and then by host kinases; the triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase. UL97 mutations are the commonest cause of resistance; UL54 (polymerase) mutations can also cause it. Foscarnet does not need activation and is used for resistant virus.

Takeaway: ganciclovir needs the CMV UL97 kinase for activation, so UL97 mutations cause resistance.

whyNot.B: Thymidine kinase mutations cause acyclovir resistance in herpes simplex virus, not resistance of this virus.
whyNot.E: Efflux pumps are a bacterial and fungal resistance mechanism.
whyNot.C: Reverse transcriptase mutations affect HIV drugs, not treatment of this retinitis.
whyNot.A: Neuraminidase changes cause resistance of influenza to oseltamivir.

items.objective: Recognize CMV retinitis and explain ganciclovir activation and resistance.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 kg/m2 has had daily headaches for 2 months and brief greying-out of vision when she stands up. Both optic discs are swollen with blurred margins. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Which of the following best explains the disc swelling?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct compression of the optic chiasm

options.label: B
options.html: Inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerves

options.label: C
options.html: Ischaemia of the optic nerve heads from low perfusion pressure

options.label: D
options.html: Leakage of plasma from inflamed retinal vessels

options.label: E
options.html: Obstructed axoplasmic flow in nerve fibres at the disc

items.explanationHtml:
Raised intracranial pressure is transmitted through the subarachnoid space around the optic nerves. Pressure at the lamina cribrosa slows axoplasmic transport in ganglion cell axons, so axons swell at the disc. This is papilloedema; in this patient the likely cause is idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Acuity stays normal until late, but the blind spot enlarges and transient obscurations occur.

Takeaway: papilloedema is axonal swelling from stasis of axoplasmic flow caused by raised intracranial pressure, usually bilateral with preserved acuity.

whyNot.B: Optic neuritis is usually unilateral and reduces acuity and colour vision early.
whyNot.C: Ischaemic optic neuropathy is unilateral, painless and causes field loss in older patients.
whyNot.D: Retinal vasculitis causes sheathing and haemorrhages, not isolated bilateral disc swelling.
whyNot.A: Chiasmal compression causes bitemporal field loss and eventually optic atrophy, not disc swelling.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of papilloedema.

items.stemHtml: Two workers are splashed in the eyes on the same day: one with drain cleaner containing sodium hydroxide and one with a dilute sulfuric acid solution. The worker exposed to sodium hydroxide develops much deeper corneal and intraocular injury. Which of the following best explains the difference?

options.label: A
options.html: Acid is cleared faster through the nasolacrimal duct

options.label: B
options.html: Acids are neutralized instantly by the tear film

options.label: C
options.html: Alkali causes coagulative necrosis that seals the surface

options.label: D
options.html: Alkali triggers a type I hypersensitivity reaction in the cornea

items.explanationHtml:
Alkalis are lipophilic: they saponify fatty acids in cell membranes, cause liquefactive necrosis and continue into the stroma and anterior chamber. Acids precipitate surface proteins (coagulative necrosis), which acts as a barrier. Hydrofluoric acid is an exception that penetrates deeply.

Takeaway: alkali burns of the eye are usually worse than acid burns because liquefactive necrosis lets the chemical keep penetrating.

whyNot.C: Coagulative necrosis is what acids cause, and it limits penetration.
whyNot.B: Tears buffer only small amounts; acids cause injury, but their coagulated proteins form a barrier.
whyNot.D: Chemical injury is direct tissue destruction, not an allergic reaction.
whyNot.A: Drainage rates do not explain the difference in depth.

items.objective: Contrast the tissue injury mechanisms of alkali and acid burns of the eye.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is struck in the right eye by a softball. He has double vision when he looks up. The right eye cannot move upward past the midline, and the skin of the right cheek, side of the nose and upper lip is numb. CT shows a fracture of the orbital floor. Which of the following structures is trapped in the fracture?
items.explanationHtml:
The thin orbital floor, the roof of the maxillary sinus, gives way under a sudden rise in orbital pressure. The inferior rectus and surrounding fat herniate and become trapped, so the eye cannot be pulled upward against the tethered muscle. The infraorbital nerve (from V2) runs in the floor; its injury numbs the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip.

Takeaway: limited upgaze plus cheek numbness after blunt orbital trauma means an orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment.

whyNot.E: The superior oblique lies along the medial roof and is not involved in floor fractures.
whyNot.B: Lateral rectus entrapment would limit abduction, and it lies along the lateral wall.
whyNot.C: The levator lies under the orbital roof and elevates the eyelid, not the globe.
whyNot.D: Medial rectus entrapment occurs with medial wall fractures and limits horizontal movement.

items.objective: Identify the muscle and nerve involved in an orbital floor fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy is hit in the left eye by an elbow during basketball. The eye looks almost normal, but he is nauseated and vomits twice. Pulse is 44/min. When he tries to look up, the pulse falls further. Which of the following nerves carries the efferent limb of the reflex responsible for his bradycardia?
items.explanationHtml:
Traction on an extraocular muscle trapped in an orbital floor fracture triggers the oculocardiac reflex. Stretch is sensed by trigeminal (ophthalmic division) afferents, which synapse in the brainstem with vagal neurons; the vagus slows the heart and causes nausea and vomiting. A child with this "white-eyed" fracture needs urgent surgical release.

Takeaway: the oculocardiac reflex is trigeminal in and vagal out.

whyNot.C: The oculomotor nerve moves the eye and constricts the pupil; it is not part of this reflex.
whyNot.D: The trigeminal nerve (ophthalmic division) carries the afferent limb, not the efferent.
whyNot.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries afferents of the carotid sinus reflex, not this reflex.
whyNot.A: The facial nerve is not part of the oculocardiac reflex.

items.objective: Describe the afferent and efferent limbs of the oculocardiac reflex.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman scratches her right cornea with a fingernail while removing a contact lens. She has severe pain, tearing and difficulty opening the eye. A single drop of topical anaesthetic relieves the pain within seconds. The sensory fibres responsible for her pain travel to the brainstem in which of the following nerves?

options.label: A
options.html: Greater petrosal branch of the facial nerve

options.label: B
options.html: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve

options.label: D
options.html: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Parasympathetic root of the ciliary ganglion

items.explanationHtml:
The cornea is one of the most densely innervated tissues in the body. Its sensory fibres run in the long ciliary nerves to the nasociliary branch of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve. The same fibres form the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

Takeaway: corneal pain and the afferent limb of the corneal reflex travel in V1.

whyNot.E: This root comes from the oculomotor nerve and carries pupilloconstrictor fibres, not corneal sensation.
whyNot.C: The maxillary division supplies the cheek and lower lid, not the cornea.
whyNot.A: This branch carries parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland; the facial nerve closes the eye but does not carry corneal pain.
whyNot.B: The mandibular division supplies the lower face and jaw, not the eye.

items.objective: Identify the sensory innervation of the cornea.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy is hit in the eye by a paintball. A 2-mm layer of blood is present in the inferior anterior chamber. He has sickle cell trait. Two days later his intraocular pressure is 38 mm Hg, much higher than expected for the size of the bleed. Which of the following best explains the greater pressure rise?

options.label: A
options.html: Free hemoglobin stimulates aqueous production by the ciliary body

options.label: B
options.html: Red cells induce angle-closure by pushing the iris forward

options.label: C
options.html: Red cells sickle in the aqueous and obstruct the trabecular meshwork

options.label: D
options.html: Sickle hemoglobin causes vasospasm of the ciliary arteries

options.label: E
options.html: Sickle trait causes congenital narrowing of Schlemm canal

items.explanationHtml:
Aqueous humour has low oxygen tension and becomes acidic after bleeding. Red cells carrying hemoglobin S sickle there, become rigid and plug the trabecular meshwork, so pressure rises even with a small hyphema. The optic nerve in these patients also tolerates raised pressure poorly. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors promote acidosis and sickling and are avoided.

Takeaway: in sickle cell disease or trait, rigid sickled red cells block aqueous outflow and make a hyphema more dangerous.

whyNot.D: Ciliary vasospasm would not raise pressure; the problem is outflow.
whyNot.A: Haemoglobin does not increase aqueous secretion.
whyNot.B: A small hyphema does not cause pupillary block or angle closure.
whyNot.E: Sickle trait does not alter the anatomy of the outflow pathway.

items.objective: Explain why hyphema is more dangerous in sickle cell disease or trait.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is punched in the right eye. One hour later the eye is protruding and hard to the touch, the eyelids are tense, eye movements are restricted, and visual acuity has fallen to counting fingers. A relative afferent pupillary defect is present. The emergency physician incises at the lateral corner of the eye and cuts the inferior part of a ligament to decompress the orbit. Which of the following structures is cut?
items.explanationHtml:
Retrobulbar haemorrhage raises pressure in a closed compartment bounded by the orbital bones and the septum, which is anchored by the canthal tendons. Lateral canthotomy followed by inferior cantholysis (cutting the inferior limb of the lateral canthal tendon) frees the lower lid, lets the globe move forward and lowers orbital pressure, restoring blood flow to the optic nerve.

Takeaway: orbital compartment syndrome is relieved by releasing the lateral canthal tendon.

whyNot.C: Cutting the lateral rectus would not decompress the orbit and would cause strabismus.
whyNot.E: The periosteum is not incised in an emergency canthotomy.
whyNot.A: The lacrimal ducts open into the superolateral fornix and have nothing to do with decompression.
whyNot.D: The medial ligament is at the inner corner; the procedure is performed laterally.

items.objective: Identify the structure released in lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man falls against the corner of a table and strikes his left eye. Vision is reduced to hand motions. The pupil is irregular and points toward the 3 o'clock position, and there is a large circumferential subconjunctival haemorrhage. Where does the globe most commonly rupture after blunt trauma?

options.label: A
options.html: Anterior lens capsule behind the pupil

options.label: B
options.html: Central cornea within the visual axis

options.label: C
options.html: Iris root at the ciliary body

options.label: D
options.html: Posterior sclera near the optic nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Sclera just behind the rectus muscle insertions

items.explanationHtml:
Blunt force compresses the globe and raises its pressure; the wall gives way where the sclera is thinnest: just behind the rectus muscle insertions and at the limbus. A peaked pupil pointing toward the wound, severe subconjunctival haemorrhage and very poor vision are signs of an open globe.

Takeaway: blunt globe rupture occurs at the thinnest sclera, behind the rectus insertions or at the limbus.

whyNot.B: The central cornea is relatively strong; lacerations occur here, but blunt ruptures occur where the sclera is thin.
whyNot.D: The posterior sclera is thick and shielded by orbital fat.
whyNot.A: The lens capsule is inside the globe; it can tear but is not where the globe ruptures.
whyNot.C: Iris root tears cause hyphema but are not a full-thickness rupture of the globe wall.

items.objective: Identify the usual sites of globe rupture after blunt trauma.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman started a new drug for migraine prevention 10 days ago. She now has blurred distance vision and aching pain in both eyes. Both anterior chambers are shallow, and intraocular pressure is 44 mm Hg on the right and 41 mm Hg on the left. Ultrasound shows fluid in the suprachoroidal space of both eyes. Which of the following is the mechanism of her eye findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Antimuscarinic dilation of the pupil causing pupillary block

options.label: B
options.html: Blood in the trabecular meshwork after a vessel rupture

options.label: C
options.html: Ciliochoroidal effusion rotating the lens-iris diaphragm forward

options.label: E
options.html: Increased aqueous production by the ciliary epithelium

items.explanationHtml:
Topiramate, a sulfonamide derivative, can cause an idiosyncratic ciliochoroidal effusion. The ciliary body swells and rotates forward, pushing the lens and iris anteriorly, which closes the angle in both eyes and causes a myopic shift. Because there is no pupillary block, iridotomy does not help; stopping the drug does.

Takeaway: topiramate causes bilateral angle closure through ciliochoroidal effusion, not pupillary block.

whyNot.A: Pupillary block is unilateral or asymmetric and is not caused by choroidal fluid.
whyNot.E: Increased production is not the mechanism and would not shallow the chamber.
whyNot.D: Steroid-induced glaucoma is open-angle, develops over weeks, and the chamber stays deep.
whyNot.B: There is no haemorrhage or trauma.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of topiramate-induced angle closure.

items.stemHtml: During cataract surgery in a 74-year-old man, the iris billows with the irrigation flow, prolapses toward the incisions and the pupil keeps constricting despite dilating drops. He takes a drug for urinary hesitancy from benign prostatic hyperplasia. Blockade of which receptor most likely explains this complication?

options.label: B
options.html: Alpha-1A adrenergic receptors in the iris dilator

options.label: C
options.html: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors in the ciliary body

options.label: D
options.html: Muscarinic M3 receptors in the iris sphincter

items.explanationHtml:
Tamsulosin is selective for alpha-1A receptors, which mediate contraction of both prostatic smooth muscle and the iris dilator muscle. Chronic blockade leaves the dilator weak and atrophic, causing intraoperative floppy iris syndrome. The effect can persist for a long time after stopping.

Takeaway: alpha-1A blockade by tamsulosin weakens the iris dilator and causes floppy iris during cataract surgery.

whyNot.D: Muscarinic blockade would dilate the pupil, not make it constrict.
whyNot.A: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate and do not affect the iris dilator.
whyNot.C: Beta-2 receptors affect aqueous production, not iris tone.
whyNot.E: PDE5 inhibition does not cause floppy iris.

items.objective: Relate tamsulosin's receptor selectivity to intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man reports that, for a few hours after taking a medication, everything looks tinged with blue and lights seem too bright. He started the drug for erectile dysfunction last month. Inhibition of which enzyme in the retina explains these symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Sildenafil and similar drugs inhibit PDE5 but also weakly inhibit PDE6, the enzyme in rods and cones that hydrolyses cGMP during phototransduction. The effect is dose-related and reversible: a blue tint (cyanopsia) and light sensitivity.

Takeaway: PDE5 inhibitors cross-inhibit retinal PDE6 and tint vision blue.

whyNot.D: PDE3 inhibitors (milrinone, cilostazol) do not affect photoreceptors.
whyNot.A: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors lower intraocular pressure and do not tint vision.
whyNot.B: Guanylyl cyclase is stimulated, not inhibited, by drugs such as riociguat; it is not the target here.
whyNot.C: MAO-B inhibitors treat Parkinson disease and do not affect colour vision.

items.objective: Explain the visual side effect of PDE5 inhibitors.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman has taken hydroxychloroquine for systemic lupus erythematosus for 12 years. Her dose is 400 mg daily, and she weighs 54 kg. Screening shows parafoveal loss of the photoreceptor layer and matching ring-shaped field defects in both eyes. Which of the following factors most increased her risk of this complication?

options.label: A
options.html: A daily dose above 5 mg per kilogram of actual body weight

options.label: B
options.html: A diagnosis of lupus rather than rheumatoid arthritis

items.explanationHtml:
Hydroxychloroquine binds melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium and damages photoreceptors around the fovea, eventually producing a bull's-eye maculopathy. Risk rises with daily dose relative to actual body weight (here about 7.4 mg/kg, above the 5 mg/kg limit), duration beyond 5 years, renal impairment, tamoxifen use and pre-existing macular disease. The damage is irreversible.

Takeaway: keep hydroxychloroquine at 5 mg/kg/day of actual body weight or less to limit retinal toxicity.

whyNot.C: Aspirin is not a risk factor for antimalarial retinopathy.
whyNot.B: The indication does not change the risk; dose, duration and renal function do.
whyNot.D: Sex is not an independent risk factor.
whyNot.E: Taking the drug with food does not affect toxicity.

items.objective: Identify the main risk factors for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with mild asthma starts eye drops for open-angle glaucoma. Two weeks later she has her first asthma attack in years. Her heart rate is 52/min. Which of the following eye drops was most likely prescribed?
items.explanationHtml:
Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker. Drops drain through the nasolacrimal duct and are absorbed through the nasal mucosa straight into the circulation, avoiding first-pass hepatic metabolism. Beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm, and beta-1 blockade causes bradycardia. Pressing on the inner corner of the eye after each drop reduces absorption.

Takeaway: topical timolol can cause systemic beta-blockade, so avoid it in asthma and bradycardia.

whyNot.C: Latanoprost darkens the iris and lengthens lashes; it does not cause bronchospasm or bradycardia.
whyNot.A: Brimonidine causes allergy, dry mouth and fatigue but not bronchospasm.
whyNot.B: Dorzolamide causes a bitter taste and stinging, not bronchospasm.
whyNot.D: Netarsudil (a rho kinase inhibitor) causes conjunctival redness, not bronchospasm.

items.objective: Recognize systemic adverse effects of topical timolol.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis with four drugs. At 3 months he says that colours look washed out and red objects look brownish. Visual acuity has fallen from 20/20 to 20/60 in both eyes, and he has central scotomas. Which drug is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Ethambutol causes a dose-related optic neuropathy with falling acuity, loss of red-green colour discrimination and central or centrocaecal scotomas. Renal impairment raises drug levels and risk. Isoniazid can rarely cause optic neuropathy, but ethambutol is the classic cause.

Takeaway: new red-green colour loss in a patient on tuberculosis treatment means ethambutol optic neuropathy.

whyNot.D: Rifampin causes orange body fluids and hepatitis, not optic neuropathy.
whyNot.B: Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia and hepatitis, not optic neuropathy.
whyNot.C: Pyridoxine is a supplement given with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy; it is not toxic to the optic nerve at usual doses.
whyNot.E: Streptomycin causes ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity, not optic neuropathy.

items.objective: Recognize ethambutol optic neuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl with drug-resistant focal epilepsy and tuberous sclerosis is started on an antiseizure drug that irreversibly inhibits the enzyme that degrades the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain. Her ophthalmologist plans regular eye examinations while she takes it. Which of the following ocular effects is the main concern with this drug?

options.label: D
options.html: Posterior subcapsular cataract of both lenses

items.explanationHtml:
Vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase and raises brain GABA. It is used for infantile spasms (particularly in tuberous sclerosis) and refractory focal seizures. It can cause irreversible bilateral concentric visual field loss from retinal toxicity, so fields are tested before and during treatment.

Takeaway: vigabatrin can cause permanent peripheral field loss; monitor visual fields.

whyNot.D: Cataract is linked with glucocorticoids, not this drug.
whyNot.B: Bull's-eye maculopathy is linked with chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine.
whyNot.A: Acute angle closure is linked with topiramate, a different antiseizure drug.
whyNot.E: Corneal deposits are linked with amiodarone.

items.objective: Recognize the visual field toxicity of vigabatrin.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman has taken oral prednisone for 4 years for autoimmune hepatitis. She now has glare when driving at night and difficulty reading. Oncoming headlights dazzle her, and near vision is worse than distance vision. On retroillumination, a small central lens opacity blocks the red reflex. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-term glucocorticoids by any route cause posterior subcapsular cataract. Because it lies near the nodal point of the eye, even a small opacity causes glare and reduced near vision. Steroids can also raise intraocular pressure (steroid-induced open-angle glaucoma).

Takeaway: glucocorticoids cause posterior subcapsular cataract and can raise eye pressure.

whyNot.C: Nuclear cataract is the usual age-related type, with a yellow central lens; it is not the steroid pattern.
whyNot.B: Cortical spokes are typical of ageing and diabetes.
whyNot.A: Anterior polar cataract is usually congenital.
whyNot.D: Oil-droplet cataract is the classic lens finding in galactosaemia.

items.objective: Identify the cataract type caused by glucocorticoids.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man has sudden, painless loss of vision in the left eye that began 90 minutes ago. He has hypertension and smokes. He has no headache, jaw pain or scalp tenderness. Visual acuity is counting fingers in the left eye; there is a left relative afferent pupillary defect. The left retina is pale with a red fovea and thin, segmented arteries. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Firm ocular massage and recheck of the fundus

options.label: B
options.html: Immediate transfer to an emergency stroke centre

options.label: C
options.html: Outpatient carotid duplex ultrasound within 2 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Routine ophthalmology clinic appointment this week

items.explanationHtml:
This is central retinal artery occlusion, a form of ischaemic stroke. He should go straight to a stroke centre, as for a cerebral stroke: a rapid assessment for any reperfusion protocol, then an urgent search for the embolic source (carotid imaging, cardiac rhythm monitoring, echocardiography) and secondary prevention. In patients over 50, ESR and CRP are checked to exclude giant cell arteritis.

Takeaway: treat central retinal artery occlusion as a stroke: immediate referral to a stroke centre.

whyNot.A: Ocular massage has no proven benefit and must not delay emergency care.
whyNot.E: Lowering eye pressure has no proven benefit in arterial occlusion.
whyNot.D: This is an ocular stroke: delay loses the chance of any acute treatment and of preventing a cerebral stroke.
whyNot.C: Carotid imaging is part of the work-up but should be done urgently within the stroke pathway, not as an outpatient.

items.objective: Manage acute central retinal artery occlusion as a stroke equivalent.

items.stemHtml: An 80-year-old woman has lost vision in the right eye since waking this morning. For a month she has had a temporal headache, pain in her jaw when chewing and aching in both shoulders. The right optic disc is pale and swollen; acuity is hand motions. ESR is 104 mm/h, and CRP is markedly raised. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the orbits before any treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Temporal artery biopsy, then glucocorticoids once the result is known

items.explanationHtml:
Jaw claudication, temporal headache, polymyalgia symptoms, very high inflammatory markers and a pale swollen disc mean giant cell arteritis with arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy. With visual loss, give high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone immediately to protect the other eye, then confirm by temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound. Tocilizumab can later be added to spare steroids.

Takeaway: in giant cell arteritis with visual loss, give high-dose glucocorticoids immediately and confirm the diagnosis afterward.

whyNot.E: Waiting for biopsy risks loss of the other eye; the biopsy remains informative for up to about 2 weeks after starting steroids.
whyNot.C: Low doses are for polymyalgia rheumatica alone; visual loss needs high-dose glucocorticoid.
whyNot.A: Aspirin is not a substitute for glucocorticoids.
whyNot.D: Imaging must not delay treatment of a sight-threatening vasculitis.

items.objective: Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately for giant cell arteritis with visual loss.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes after a routine hemoglobin A1c of 7.6%. He has no visual symptoms. He is started on metformin. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for eye screening?

options.label: A
options.html: Dilated eye examination 5 years after diagnosis

options.label: C
options.html: Dilated eye examination once A1c is below 7%

options.label: D
options.html: Eye examination only if visual symptoms develop

items.explanationHtml:
Type 2 diabetes may have been present for years before diagnosis, so retinopathy can already exist. A dilated eye examination (or retinal photography) at diagnosis is recommended, then yearly; the interval can be extended to every 1–2 years if there is no retinopathy and glucose is well controlled. In type 1 diabetes, screening starts within 5 years of onset.

Takeaway: screen for retinopathy at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and within 5 years of type 1.

whyNot.A: The 5-year delay applies to type 1 diabetes, where retinopathy takes years to develop.
whyNot.D: Retinopathy is often asymptomatic until advanced, so screening is needed.
whyNot.C: Screening is not postponed until glycaemic targets are met.
whyNot.E: Angiography is a diagnostic test for known disease, not a screening test.

items.objective: Apply retinopathy screening timing in type 2 diabetes.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has had gradually blurred central vision in the right eye for 2 months. Acuity is 20/70 on the right. Optical coherence tomography shows thickening of the central macula with intraretinal fluid. There are no new vessels. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the right eye?

options.label: B
options.html: Observation with repeat imaging in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with reduced vision is treated first with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections, which reduce leakage and improve acuity. Intravitreal steroids and focal laser are alternatives or additions. Better control of glucose, blood pressure and lipids helps every patient.

Takeaway: centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with visual loss: intravitreal anti-VEGF first.

whyNot.D: Panretinal laser treats proliferative disease and does not treat central macular oedema.
whyNot.C: Acetazolamide has no established role in diabetic macular oedema.
whyNot.E: Vitrectomy is for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage or traction, not first-line for macular oedema.
whyNot.B: Observation is reasonable only when vision is good; this patient has reduced acuity.

items.objective: Choose anti-VEGF therapy for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with reduced vision.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old woman with known dry age-related macular degeneration says that, over the last week, door frames look bent and a smudge has appeared in the centre of vision in her left eye. Examination shows subretinal fluid and a small haemorrhage at the left macula. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: Photodynamic therapy as the first-line treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Start an AREDS2-type supplement and review in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
New distortion with subretinal fluid and blood means conversion to neovascular (wet) AMD. Prompt, repeated intravitreal anti-VEGF injections preserve vision in most patients and improve it in many. Delay allows scarring of the macula.

Takeaway: wet AMD is treated urgently with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.

whyNot.E: Supplements slow progression of intermediate disease but do not treat active neovascularization.
whyNot.D: Photodynamic therapy has largely been replaced by anti-VEGF therapy as first line.
whyNot.C: Panretinal laser is for proliferative diabetic retinopathy, not choroidal neovascularization.
whyNot.B: Steroids do not treat neovascular macular degeneration.

items.objective: Treat neovascular age-related macular degeneration with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day has many large drusen in both eyes and no neovascularization. Acuity is 20/25 in both eyes. He asks what he can do to protect his sight. In addition to stopping smoking, which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: A supplement of high-dose beta-carotene and vitamin A

options.label: B
options.html: An omega-3 fatty acid supplement taken on its own

options.label: C
options.html: Daily low-dose aspirin to improve choroidal flow

options.label: D
options.html: Monthly intravitreal anti-VEGF injections in both eyes

options.label: E
options.html: Vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein and zeaxanthin

items.explanationHtml:
Large drusen without new vessels is intermediate AMD. An AREDS2-type supplement (vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein and zeaxanthin) reduces the risk of progression to advanced disease. Beta-carotene is avoided in current and former smokers because of lung cancer risk. Smoking cessation is the most important change he can make.

Takeaway: intermediate AMD: stop smoking and take an AREDS2-type supplement without beta-carotene.

whyNot.A: Beta-carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers and was removed from the newer formula.
whyNot.D: Anti-VEGF treats neovascular disease; it is not given for dry AMD.
whyNot.C: Aspirin does not slow macular degeneration.
whyNot.B: Adding omega-3 fatty acids gave no benefit in the large trial of supplements.

items.objective: Recommend the AREDS2-type supplement for intermediate age-related macular degeneration in a smoker.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with high myopia had uncomplicated cataract surgery on his right eye 4 months ago. Since this morning he has seen flashes of light and a shower of black dots in that eye. In the last hour, a grey shadow has spread from the lower part of his vision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the head without contrast

options.label: B
options.html: Reassure him that new floaters are common after cataract surgery

options.label: D
options.html: Same-day ophthalmology evaluation for retinal repair

options.label: E
options.html: Topical corticosteroid drops for postoperative inflammation

items.explanationHtml:
Flashes, a burst of floaters and a spreading shadow in a highly myopic, pseudophakic eye mean rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. He needs same-day ophthalmology for repair (pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle or vitrectomy). The best visual outcome comes from repairing it before the macula detaches; a shadow from below threatens the macula less quickly than one from above, but it still needs same-day assessment.

Takeaway: flashes, floaters and a curtain mean retinal detachment and same-day ophthalmology.

whyNot.B: Floaters with flashes and a field shadow are a red flag for detachment.
whyNot.A: This is a retinal problem; head imaging is not indicated.
whyNot.E: Inflammation does not cause flashes and a spreading shadow.
whyNot.C: Delay risks detachment of the macula and permanent loss of central vision.

items.objective: Recognize retinal detachment and arrange same-day ophthalmology.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman has had worsening daily headaches for 6 weeks, worse lying down, with episodes of brief dimming of vision and a whooshing noise in her ears. She has gained 12 kg in the last year. She takes no medications. Both fundi look like panel 4 of the figure. Neurological examination is otherwise normal, and acuity is 20/20 in each eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain with MR venography

options.label: D
options.html: Start acetazolamide and review in 1 month

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral optic disc swelling with headache means papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure. Brain imaging with venography comes first, to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; it also makes lumbar puncture safe. If imaging is normal, a raised opening pressure with normal CSF confirms idiopathic intracranial hypertension, treated with weight loss and acetazolamide.

Takeaway: bilateral disc swelling means imaging (MRI with venography) before lumbar puncture.

whyNot.B: LP comes after imaging, which must exclude a mass or venous sinus thrombosis first.
whyNot.D: Treatment for idiopathic intracranial hypertension is started only after secondary causes are excluded.
whyNot.E: Giant cell arteritis is very unlikely at 25 and does not cause bilateral disc swelling.
whyNot.A: IV steroids treat optic neuritis, which is usually unilateral and painful with reduced acuity.

items.objective: Order neuroimaging with venography before lumbar puncture in papilloedema.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection has had floaters in the left eye for 2 weeks. His CD4 count is 18/mm3, and he is not on treatment. Dilated examination shows a peripheral area of white retinal necrosis with haemorrhage, well away from the fovea and optic disc. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravitreal amphotericin B, and antiretroviral therapy at 8 weeks

options.label: B
options.html: Oral acyclovir, and start antiretroviral therapy within about 2 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Oral prednisone, then antiretroviral therapy once inflammation settles

options.label: D
options.html: Oral valganciclovir, and start antiretroviral therapy within about 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Start antiretroviral therapy now and delay antiviral therapy for the eye until immune recovery

items.explanationHtml:
This is CMV retinitis. Peripheral disease that does not threaten the fovea or disc can be treated with oral valganciclovir induction then maintenance; sight-threatening lesions also get intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet. Antiretroviral therapy should start soon (within about 2 weeks) to restore immunity; watch for immune recovery uveitis.

Takeaway: CMV retinitis is treated with valganciclovir (plus intravitreal therapy if sight-threatening) and prompt antiretroviral therapy.

whyNot.E: Waiting for immune recovery lets the retinitis spread; anti-CMV treatment starts now.
whyNot.B: Acyclovir is not reliably active against cytomegalovirus.
whyNot.A: Amphotericin treats fungal endophthalmitis, not viral retinitis.
whyNot.C: Steroids would worsen a viral retinitis and leave it untreated.

items.objective: Treat CMV retinitis in advanced HIV.

items.stemHtml: The neonatal intensive care unit reviews which infants need screening for retinopathy of prematurity. All are clinically stable, and none needed prolonged oxygen. Which of the following infants meets standard screening criteria?

options.label: A
options.html: Born at 29 weeks' gestation, birth weight 1,350 g

options.label: B
options.html: Born at 32 weeks' gestation, birth weight 1,750 g

options.label: C
options.html: Born at 33 weeks' gestation, birth weight 1,600 g

options.label: D
options.html: Born at 34 weeks' gestation, birth weight 2,100 g

options.label: E
options.html: Born at 36 weeks' gestation, birth weight 1,900 g (small for gestational age)

items.explanationHtml:
US guidance screens infants born at 30 weeks' gestation or earlier, or weighing 1,500 g or less, plus selected infants of 1,500–2,000 g or more than 30 weeks who had an unstable clinical course. The infant born at 29 weeks and 1,350 g meets both criteria. Severe disease is treated with laser to the avascular retina or intravitreal anti-VEGF.

Takeaway: screen for retinopathy of prematurity at 30 weeks or less or 1,500 g or less.

whyNot.D: Above both cut-offs and clinically stable: screening is not needed.
whyNot.E: Above both cut-offs; being small for gestational age alone does not meet criteria.
whyNot.B: Above both cut-offs and stable; screening would be needed only with an unstable course.
whyNot.C: Above both cut-offs and stable.

items.objective: Apply screening criteria for retinopathy of prematurity.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman has had blurred vision in the right eye for 3 days, with pain when she moves the eye. Acuity is 20/80 on the right, red objects look faded, and there is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. The right optic disc looks normal. She had numbness of the left leg for 2 weeks a year ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the orbits without contrast

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the brain and orbits with gadolinium

items.explanationHtml:
Painful monocular visual loss with colour desaturation and an afferent pupillary defect in a young woman is optic neuritis; the disc is normal when the inflammation is behind it. An earlier episode of leg numbness suggests multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain and orbits with gadolinium confirms optic nerve enhancement and shows white-matter lesions that predict MS. Intravenous methylprednisolone may be given to speed recovery.

Takeaway: optic neuritis needs gadolinium MRI of the brain and orbits to assess for multiple sclerosis.

whyNot.C: CSF can support multiple sclerosis but is not the first test; she has no signs of raised pressure.
whyNot.E: Giant cell arteritis does not occur at this age and is painless.
whyNot.A: This is not a vascular event; pain on eye movement and her age point to optic neuritis.
whyNot.B: CT does not show demyelinating lesions well.

items.objective: Evaluate optic neuritis with MRI of the brain and orbits.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old construction worker arrives at the emergency department 15 minutes after wet cement splashed into his left eye. He has severe pain and cannot keep the eye open. He rinsed it briefly with a water bottle at the site. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?

options.label: C
options.html: Measure visual acuity in both eyes

options.label: D
options.html: Neutralize with a weak acid solution

options.label: E
options.html: Patch the eye and arrange urgent ophthalmology

items.explanationHtml:
Cement contains calcium hydroxide, an alkali. The first step is immediate, copious irrigation, before acuity or any other examination. A topical anaesthetic and a lid speculum or irrigating lens make it possible.

Takeaway: in a chemical eye injury, irrigate first and examine later.

whyNot.C: Acuity is important but is measured after irrigation; every minute of contact deepens an alkali burn.
whyNot.B: Fluorescein examination comes after irrigation.
whyNot.D: Neutralizing agents produce heat and further injury; plain irrigation is used.
whyNot.E: Patching traps the chemical against the eye.

items.objective: Irrigate immediately as the first step in chemical eye injury.

items.stemHtml: The patient's left eye is irrigated with 2 L of normal saline. Five minutes after stopping, the pH of the tear film is 8.5. Gritty grey particles are seen in the lower fornix. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge with erythromycin ointment and review tomorrow

options.label: B
options.html: Instil a topical glucocorticoid and recheck pH in 1 hour

options.label: D
options.html: Measure intraocular pressure before further irrigation

options.label: E
options.html: Sweep the fornices and keep irrigating to a neutral pH

items.explanationHtml:
A pH of 8.5 means alkali is still present. Retained cement particles keep releasing it, so sweep the fornices (evert the lids) and continue irrigating until the pH is about 7.0–7.5, rechecking a few minutes after each stop. Then examine and refer urgently to ophthalmology.

Takeaway: irrigate a chemical injury until the tear pH is neutral, and remove retained particles.

whyNot.A: The eye is still alkaline and particles remain, so the injury is ongoing.
whyNot.B: Steroids may be used later by ophthalmology; they do not remove the chemical.
whyNot.D: Pressure measurement can wait until the chemical is removed.
whyNot.C: A buffer is not used; irrigation with saline or lactated Ringer is continued.

items.objective: Use tear-film pH to guide the endpoint of irrigation after a chemical injury.

items.stemHtml: Once the pH is 7.2, examination shows a large corneal epithelial defect and whitening of the conjunctiva and limbal vessels over about half of the corneal circumference. Which of the following findings most strongly predicts a poor long-term outcome for this eye?

options.label: A
options.html: Conjunctival redness away from the limbus

items.explanationHtml:
The limbus holds the stem cells that renew the corneal epithelium. Limbal ischaemia (white, bloodless vessels) shows stem-cell loss: the surface may fail to heal, the cornea becomes vascularized and opaque, and perforation can follow. The extent of limbal ischaemia is central to grading severity.

Takeaway: the extent of limbal whitening is the key prognostic sign after a chemical burn.

whyNot.D: Photophobia is common after any surface injury and does not predict outcome.
whyNot.A: Hyperaemia shows the vessels are perfused, which is less worrying than whitening.
whyNot.E: Tearing is a normal response.
whyNot.C: Lid swelling does not predict corneal outcome.

items.objective: Identify limbal ischaemia as the main prognostic sign in chemical eye injury.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman who wears soft contact lenses for up to 16 hours a day has had right eye pain and photophobia since removing her lenses last night. Acuity is 20/25. Fluorescein shows a 2-mm epithelial defect outside the visual axis with clear stroma underneath and no infiltrate. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: A bottle of topical anaesthetic drops to use as needed

options.label: B
options.html: Erythromycin ointment and a pressure patch for 24 hours

options.label: C
options.html: Fluoroquinolone drops, no patch, no lens wear

options.label: D
options.html: Resume lens wear with artificial tears

items.explanationHtml:
Contact lens wearers with an abrasion are at risk of Pseudomonas keratitis. Treat with an anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone drop, give oral analgesia, stop lens wear and do not patch. Review in 24 hours.

Takeaway: a lens-related corneal abrasion needs anti-pseudomonal drops and no patch.

whyNot.B: Patching a lens-related abrasion raises the risk of Pseudomonas keratitis.
whyNot.A: Repeated anaesthetic use delays healing and can cause corneal melt.
whyNot.E: Steroids slow epithelial healing and promote infection.
whyNot.D: Lens wear must stop until the defect heals and the infection risk passes.

items.objective: Treat a contact lens-related corneal abrasion with anti-pseudomonal cover and no patching.
