items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man is struck in the right eye by a metal fragment when a lawnmower blade hits a rock. Acuity is hand motions. The pupil is peaked toward a small corneal wound, and fluorescein flowing from the wound is diluted by clear fluid. He is nauseated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: A rigid shield, antiemetic, IV antibiotics and orbital CT

options.label: B
options.html: Antibiotic ointment and a firm pressure patch over the eye

options.label: C
options.html: Irrigation of the eye with saline, then a shield

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the orbits to locate the metal fragment

options.label: E
options.html: Tonometry to measure intraocular pressure, then CT

items.explanationHtml:
A peaked pupil and a positive Seidel sign mean an open globe. Protect it with a rigid shield, avoid any pressure or drops, keep him nil by mouth, give an antiemetic and analgesia, start systemic antibiotics against endophthalmitis, update tetanus and obtain CT of the orbits to look for an intraocular foreign body. Emergency surgical repair follows.

Takeaway: open globe: shield, antiemetic, antibiotics, CT, and nothing that touches or presses the eye.

whyNot.E: Pressing on an open globe can extrude its contents.
whyNot.B: Ointment can enter the eye and a pressure patch squeezes it.
whyNot.D: MRI is contraindicated while a metallic foreign body may be present; CT is used.
whyNot.C: Irrigation is for chemical injury; it can push contents out of an open globe.

items.objective: Manage a suspected open globe injury.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy has a 3-mm layer of blood in the anterior chamber of the left eye after being hit by a lacrosse ball. Acuity is 20/50 and intraocular pressure is 30 mm Hg. His sickle cell screening test is positive, and hemoglobin electrophoresis shows sickle cell trait. Which of the following should be avoided in his management?

options.label: D
options.html: Raising the head of the bed

items.explanationHtml:
In sickle cell disease or trait, systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide cause metabolic acidosis, which increases sickling in the aqueous and blocks outflow further. Osmotic agents are also used cautiously. Topical beta-blockers and alpha agonists are preferred, and pressure that stays high may need anterior chamber washout.

Takeaway: avoid systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors in hyphema with sickle cell disease or trait.

whyNot.D: Head elevation helps blood settle and clear; it is recommended.
whyNot.B: A shield protects the eye and is recommended.
whyNot.E: A topical beta-blocker is an acceptable first pressure-lowering drug.
whyNot.A: Cycloplegics reduce pain and are used by ophthalmology.

items.objective: Avoid acetazolamide in hyphema with sickle cell disease or trait.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl is kicked in the right eye during a soccer game. She has vomited three times and feels faint. Her pulse is 46/min. The right eye looks only mildly bruised, but it cannot move upward, and attempts to look up worsen the nausea. CT shows a small linear fracture of the right orbital floor with soft tissue held in the fracture line. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Atropine and discharge when the heart rate normalizes

options.label: C
options.html: Observation until the swelling settles, then reassess eye movements

options.label: D
options.html: Oral antibiotics and outpatient review in 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent surgical release of the trapped muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Children have elastic bone: the floor can crack, trap the inferior rectus and spring back, so the eye looks quiet (a "white-eyed" blow-out fracture). Entrapment with an oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia, nausea, syncope) needs urgent surgical repair to prevent muscle necrosis and permanent restriction, and to stop the reflex.

Takeaway: a child with an orbital floor fracture, entrapment and oculocardiac reflex needs urgent surgery.

whyNot.D: Delayed elective repair suits fractures without entrapment, not this one.
whyNot.C: Waiting risks permanent muscle ischaemia and ongoing reflex bradycardia.
whyNot.A: Atropine treats the bradycardia but not the cause; the entrapped muscle remains ischaemic.
whyNot.B: Steroids may reduce swelling but do not free a trapped muscle.

items.objective: Recognize the trapdoor orbital floor fracture with oculocardiac reflex as a surgical emergency.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman taking warfarin falls and strikes her face. Forty minutes later her right eye is protruding and the lids are tense. She cannot move the eye in any direction. Acuity has fallen to counting fingers, there is a right relative afferent pupillary defect, and intraocular pressure is 52 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the orbits, then decide on treatment

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma alone

options.label: C
options.html: Lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis at the bedside

items.explanationHtml:
Proptosis, a tense orbit, ophthalmoplegia, an afferent pupillary defect and very high pressure after trauma mean retrobulbar haemorrhage with orbital compartment syndrome. Perform lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis immediately, before imaging; the optic nerve tolerates ischaemia poorly. Reverse anticoagulation alongside.

Takeaway: orbital compartment syndrome needs bedside canthotomy and cantholysis before imaging.

whyNot.A: This is a clinical diagnosis; imaging delays a procedure needed within about 90–120 minutes.
whyNot.B: Reversing anticoagulation is part of care but does not relieve the pressure now compressing the optic nerve.
whyNot.E: Drops cannot relieve orbital compartment syndrome.
whyNot.D: A patch adds pressure to an already tense orbit.

items.objective: Perform emergency lateral canthotomy for orbital compartment syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man was hammering a steel chisel when he felt something strike his left eye. He has mild discomfort. Acuity is 20/30. There is a tiny self-sealing wound at the edge of the cornea and a small hole in the iris; the eye is otherwise quiet. Which of the following is the most appropriate imaging study?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the orbits with thin slices

options.label: D
options.html: No imaging, because the wound has sealed

items.explanationHtml:
Hammering metal on metal can drive a tiny, hot, sterile fragment through the eye wall with few symptoms. A corneal wound and an iris hole mark its path. CT of the orbits with thin slices finds and localizes metal; MRI is contraindicated until a metallic foreign body is excluded. An unrecognized iron fragment can later cause siderosis and blindness.

Takeaway: suspected metallic intraocular foreign body: CT, not MRI.

whyNot.C: MRI can move a metallic fragment and injure the eye.
whyNot.E: Radiographs are less sensitive and do not localize a fragment as well as CT.
whyNot.D: A small self-sealing wound can hide an intraocular foreign body.
whyNot.B: Angiography studies retinal circulation and does not detect a foreign body.

items.objective: Choose CT to look for a metallic intraocular foreign body.

items.stemHtml:
A 38-year-old woman has had blurred distance vision and aching in both eyes for 1 day. Both eyes are red, the anterior chambers are shallow, and intraocular pressure is 46 mm Hg on the right and 43 mm Hg on the left. Her medication list is shown.

MedicationIndicationStarted
Levonorgestrel intrauterine deviceContraception3 years ago
Sertraline 100 mg dailyDepression2 years ago
Topiramate 50 mg twice dailyMigraine prevention12 days ago
Ibuprofen as neededHeadacheSeveral years
Cetirizine as neededAllergic rhinitisSeveral years

Which of the following is the most appropriate management, in addition to drops to lower the pressure?

options.label: A
options.html: Laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral angle closure with a myopic shift starting within weeks of a new drug is typical of topiramate, which causes ciliochoroidal effusion. Stop it at once, and treat with aqueous suppressants (topical beta-blocker, alpha-2 agonist, carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) and cycloplegic drops, which pull the lens-iris diaphragm back. Pilocarpine and iridotomy do not help.

Takeaway: bilateral angle closure soon after starting topiramate: stop the drug and use aqueous suppressants and cycloplegics.

whyNot.A: Iridotomy treats pupillary block; topiramate angle closure is caused by ciliochoroidal effusion and does not respond.
whyNot.B: Miotics can worsen this type of angle closure by moving the lens further forward.
whyNot.D: Sertraline is a rare cause of angle closure and has been taken for 2 years without trouble; the timing points to topiramate.
whyNot.C: Second-generation antihistamines have little antimuscarinic action, and she has taken it for years.

items.objective: Identify topiramate as the cause of bilateral angle closure and stop it.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is starting hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily. She weighs 70 kg, has normal kidney function and takes no other drugs. She has no eye disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for eye screening?

options.label: A
options.html: An eye examination only when the dose is increased

options.label: B
options.html: Baseline examination now, then yearly from 5 years of use

options.label: C
options.html: Monthly visual acuity checks by her primary care physician

options.label: D
options.html: No eye examinations unless she develops visual symptoms

options.label: E
options.html: Yearly screening starting in the first year of treatment

items.explanationHtml:
Her dose is about 4.3 mg/kg/day, within the recommended 5 mg/kg of actual body weight. Guidance calls for a baseline examination early in treatment (to exclude macular disease) and annual screening after 5 years, sooner if there are risk factors such as kidney disease, tamoxifen or high doses. Screening uses optical coherence tomography and automated visual fields.

Takeaway: hydroxychloroquine: baseline eye examination, then yearly screening from 5 years (earlier with risk factors).

whyNot.D: Toxicity is silent until advanced, so screening is needed.
whyNot.C: Acuity falls late; screening uses OCT and automated visual fields.
whyNot.E: With no extra risk factors, yearly screening can start after 5 years.
whyNot.A: Screening is based on duration and risk factors, not dose changes alone.

items.objective: Plan retinal screening for a low-risk patient starting hydroxychloroquine.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is in the second month of treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis with rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. He says reading has become harder and colours look dull. Acuity has dropped from 20/20 to 20/40 in both eyes, and he misses several colour plates. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Increase the pyridoxine dose and continue all drugs

options.label: B
options.html: Reassure him and recheck vision in 3 months

options.label: C
options.html: Stop ethambutol and refer to ophthalmology

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral loss of acuity and colour vision on four-drug therapy, with kidney disease raising drug levels, indicates ethambutol optic neuropathy. Stop ethambutol at once and refer; vision often recovers partly or fully over months if the drug is stopped early. Adjust the regimen with the tuberculosis team.

Takeaway: visual change on ethambutol means stop the drug now.

whyNot.A: Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy but does not treat ethambutol optic neuropathy.
whyNot.D: Isoniazid is a much rarer cause; ethambutol is the likely culprit, especially with kidney disease.
whyNot.B: Optic neuropathy can become permanent if the drug is continued.
whyNot.E: Rifampin does not cause optic neuropathy.

items.objective: Stop ethambutol when optic neuropathy develops.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man is scheduled for cataract surgery in 3 weeks. He has taken tamsulosin for benign prostatic hyperplasia for 4 years. He asks whether he should do anything about this medication before surgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue tamsulosin and make sure the surgeon knows he takes it

options.label: B
options.html: Postpone surgery until he has been off tamsulosin for 6 months

options.label: C
options.html: Stop tamsulosin 2 weeks before surgery to prevent complications

options.label: D
options.html: Switch to finasteride the day before surgery

options.label: E
options.html: Take an extra dose of tamsulosin on the morning of surgery

items.explanationHtml:
Tamsulosin causes intraoperative floppy iris syndrome. Stopping it before surgery does not reliably prevent the problem, because the dilator muscle stays weak. The key step is to tell the surgeon, who can plan (iris hooks or rings, intracameral drugs). He can usually continue the drug.

Takeaway: before cataract surgery, patients taking tamsulosin should tell the surgeon; stopping it is not needed.

whyNot.C: Stopping does not reliably reverse the iris effect and may worsen urinary symptoms.
whyNot.D: Switching the day before does nothing for the iris and is not needed.
whyNot.B: The effect can persist for years; postponing is not recommended.
whyNot.E: Extra alpha-1A blockade would worsen floppy iris.

items.objective: Advise patients on tamsulosin before cataract surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman applied a scopolamine patch for nausea on a cruise. Six hours later she has severe pain in the right eye, blurred vision with haloes around lights, headache and vomiting. The right eye is red with a hazy cornea and a fixed, mid-dilated pupil; intraocular pressure is 58 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Atropine drops to relax the ciliary muscle and pupil

options.label: C
options.html: Remove the patch, give an antiemetic and observe

options.label: D
options.html: Remove the patch; lower pressure with drops and IV acetazolamide

options.label: E
options.html: Topical glucocorticoid drops alone, then review tomorrow

items.explanationHtml:
An antimuscarinic patch dilated the pupil and precipitated acute pupillary-block angle closure. Remove the cause and lower pressure at once: topical beta-blocker, alpha-2 agonist and, once pressure starts to fall, pilocarpine, plus systemic acetazolamide (or mannitol). Laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes follows to prevent recurrence.

Takeaway: drug-induced pupillary-block angle closure: stop the drug, lower pressure medically, then iridotomy.

whyNot.A: Further antimuscarinic action dilates the pupil more and worsens pupillary block.
whyNot.E: Steroids reduce inflammation but do not lower pressure in acute angle closure.
whyNot.B: Filtration surgery is not the first step; pressure is lowered medically, then laser iridotomy is done.
whyNot.C: The effect lasts long enough to harm the eye: very high pressure can damage the optic nerve within hours.

items.objective: Treat acute angle closure precipitated by an antimuscarinic drug.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old man with open-angle glaucoma has had episodes of light-headedness for 2 months. Pulse is 46/min and regular; an ECG shows sinus bradycardia. He takes amlodipine, atorvastatin and timolol eye drops twice daily. Which of the following is the most appropriate change?

options.label: B
options.html: Double the timolol dose to once-daily gel for convenience

options.label: D
options.html: Replace timolol with a prostaglandin analogue eye drop

items.explanationHtml:
Topical timolol is absorbed through the nasal mucosa and can cause symptomatic bradycardia and heart block, especially in older adults. Replacing it with a prostaglandin analogue (such as latanoprost), which has no systemic cardiac effect, removes the cause while keeping glaucoma control. Teaching punctal occlusion helps if a beta-blocker must continue.

Takeaway: consider timolol eye drops as a cause of unexplained bradycardia.

whyNot.E: Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine and does not slow the heart rate.
whyNot.C: A reversible drug cause should be removed first.
whyNot.A: Atropine would risk angle closure and does not fix the cause.
whyNot.B: This continues the systemic beta-blockade causing the bradycardia.

items.objective: Recognize and correct bradycardia caused by topical timolol.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old welder was treated for a corneal abrasion 3 weeks ago. The eye has become more painful, and vision is worse. He admits he took a bottle of numbing drops from the clinic and uses them many times a day. The cornea shows a large non-healing epithelial defect with a grey ring-shaped stromal infiltrate; cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue the drops at a lower frequency and add artificial tears

options.label: B
options.html: Patch the eye firmly for 48 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Stop the anaesthetic drops and refer urgently to ophthalmology

options.label: E
options.html: Switch to a different topical anaesthetic

items.explanationHtml:
Repeated topical anaesthetic use causes toxic keratopathy: the epithelium cannot heal, the blink reflex is blunted, and a ring infiltrate and stromal melting can follow, mimicking or complicating infectious keratitis. Stop the drops, refer urgently, and treat for infection until cultures return. Topical anaesthetics should never be given to patients for home use.

Takeaway: a non-healing corneal defect in someone using "numbing drops" is anaesthetic toxicity: stop them and refer urgently.

whyNot.A: Any continued use keeps the epithelium from healing.
whyNot.B: Patching does not address the toxic cause and risks infection.
whyNot.C: Steroids are not started before infection is excluded and would slow healing.
whyNot.E: All topical anaesthetics are toxic to the epithelium with repeated use.

items.objective: Recognize topical anaesthetic abuse keratopathy and manage it.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has had nausea, poor appetite and confusion for 4 days. She says that lights have yellow-green rings around them. Her medications include digoxin, furosemide and apixaban. Serum creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL (0.6–1.2) [168 µmol/L (53–106)]. Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?

options.label: A
options.html: Dilated fundus examination by an ophthalmologist

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with and without contrast

options.label: C
options.html: Serum ammonia and liver function tests

items.explanationHtml:
Nausea, confusion and yellow-green haloes (xanthopsia) in an older woman with reduced kidney function and on furosemide suggest digoxin toxicity. Check the digoxin level, potassium and magnesium (low levels worsen toxicity) and an ECG. Severe toxicity is treated with digoxin-specific antibody fragments.

Takeaway: coloured haloes or yellow vision in a patient on digoxin suggests toxicity: check the level and electrolytes.

whyNot.A: The visual symptom is a drug effect, not a retinal disease to be examined first.
whyNot.B: Imaging is not the first step when a drug toxicity explains the picture.
whyNot.E: Thyroid disease does not explain coloured haloes.
whyNot.C: Ammonia is checked for hepatic encephalopathy, which does not cause coloured vision.

items.objective: Recognize the visual symptoms of digoxin toxicity and test for it.

items.stemHtml: A 20-month-old boy is brought to the clinic because of fever and fussiness for 2 days. He has been rubbing his left ear, and both eyes have had thick yellow discharge since yesterday. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). The left tympanic membrane is red and bulging, and both conjunctivae are injected with purulent discharge. Which of the following organisms most likely explains both the ear and eye findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Otitis media together with purulent conjunctivitis (otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome) is typical of nontypeable H. influenzae. These unencapsulated strains are not covered by the Hib vaccine and often make beta-lactamase, which is why amoxicillin-clavulanate is chosen in this situation.

Takeaway: otitis media plus purulent conjunctivitis suggests beta-lactamase-producing nontypeable H. influenzae.

whyNot.E: Pneumococcus is a leading cause of otitis media but is not the organism classically linked with the combination of otitis and purulent conjunctivitis.
whyNot.A: Moraxella causes otitis media but is rarely the cause of the otitis-conjunctivitis combination.
whyNot.D: S. aureus is an uncommon cause of acute otitis media in toddlers and is more typical of otitis externa.
whyNot.C: Pseudomonas causes otitis externa and chronic draining ears, not acute otitis media with conjunctivitis in a toddler.

items.objective: Identify nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae as the usual cause of otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 14-month-old girl has had 3 episodes of acute otitis media in the past 6 months, each following a cold. Her parents ask why ear infections are so common at her age. Which of the following anatomic features best explains the higher risk in young children?

options.label: A
options.html: A larger and more pneumatized mastoid air cell system

options.label: B
options.html: A narrower and more curved external auditory canal

options.label: C
options.html: A shorter stapedius tendon with a weaker acoustic reflex

options.label: D
options.html: A shorter, more horizontal and less rigid eustachian tube

options.label: E
options.html: A thinner and more transparent tympanic membrane

items.explanationHtml:
The infant eustachian tube is shorter, more horizontal and floppier. It ventilates and drains the middle ear poorly and lets nasopharyngeal fluid and bacteria reflux into it, especially when a viral infection swells the mucosa.

Takeaway: eustachian tube anatomy explains why acute otitis media peaks between 6 and 24 months.

whyNot.E: The thickness of the eardrum does not determine whether nasopharyngeal secretions reach the middle ear.
whyNot.B: The external canal is separated from the middle ear by the drum and is not the route of infection in otitis media.
whyNot.A: The mastoid is less pneumatized in infants, and pneumatization does not cause middle-ear infection.
whyNot.C: The acoustic reflex protects against loud sound and has no role in middle-ear ventilation.

items.objective: Explain the anatomic basis for the high incidence of otitis media in young children.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus has had worsening right ear pain and discharge for 4 weeks despite ear drops. The pain wakes him at night. Examination shows granulation tissue on the floor of the right external canal and weakness of the entire right side of his face. His erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 92 mm/h (0-15 mm/h). Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe night pain, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal floor, a facial nerve palsy and a high ESR in an older patient with diabetes are typical of necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa. This is osteomyelitis of the temporal bone and skull base, almost always caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Takeaway: necrotizing otitis externa is invasive Pseudomonas skull-base osteomyelitis in older people with diabetes.

whyNot.E: Group A streptococci cause cellulitis of the auricle but rarely invade the skull base from the ear canal.
whyNot.A: Aspergillus causes fungal otitis externa with visible debris and occasionally invasive disease, but Pseudomonas is by far the usual cause of this syndrome.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcus causes acute otitis media and mastoiditis, not invasive external canal infection in older adults with diabetes.
whyNot.B: Tuberculous otitis is rare and causes painless discharge with multiple perforations, not this acute skull-base infection.

items.objective: Recognize Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the cause of necrotizing otitis externa.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has had painless, foul-smelling discharge from his left ear on and off for 2 years, and his hearing on that side has slowly worsened. Otoscopy shows a deep retraction pocket in the upper part of the tympanic membrane filled with white, flaky material. CT shows erosion of the ossicles. The lesion is removed surgically. Microscopic examination of the specimen will most likely show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Atypical squamous cells invading bone with keratin pearls

options.label: B
options.html: Cholesterol clefts surrounded by foreign-body giant cells

options.label: C
options.html: Keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium with layers of keratin

options.label: D
options.html: Nests of chromogranin-positive cells in a vascular stroma

options.label: E
options.html: Spindle cells with nuclear palisading around pink fibrillar zones

items.explanationHtml:
A cholesteatoma is a sac of keratinizing squamous epithelium that keeps shedding keratin into the middle ear. It forms from a retraction pocket in a poorly ventilated ear and erodes bone through pressure and enzyme release. That explains the ossicular erosion and the conductive loss.

Takeaway: a cholesteatoma is skin (keratin) in the middle ear; it contains no cholesterol.

whyNot.B: This describes a cholesterol granuloma, a reaction to old blood in the middle ear or petrous apex, not a cholesteatoma.
whyNot.E: Palisading spindle cells (Verocay bodies) are typical of a schwannoma.
whyNot.D: Nests of neuroendocrine chief cells describe a paraganglioma (glomus tumor).
whyNot.A: Invasive squamous cell carcinoma is malignant; a cholesteatoma is benign squamous epithelium in the wrong place.

items.objective: Describe the histology of cholesteatoma and distinguish it from cholesterol granuloma.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman has severe right ear pain and, 2 days later, cannot close her right eye or raise her right eyebrow. Examination shows clustered vesicles in the right external canal and on the concha. Her hearing on the right is reduced. The causative virus was most likely latent in which of the following structures?
items.explanationHtml:
Ear pain, vesicles in the ear and a lower motor neuron facial palsy make up Ramsay Hunt syndrome: varicella-zoster virus reactivating in the sensory geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. Spread to the nearby vestibulocochlear nerve explains the hearing loss.

Takeaway: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is varicella-zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of cranial nerve VII.

whyNot.E: Reactivation in the trigeminal ganglion causes zoster in a trigeminal dermatome, such as herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
whyNot.C: The spiral ganglion holds cochlear neurons; hearing loss here comes from spread to cranial nerve VIII, not from the primary site of latency.
whyNot.D: The superior cervical ganglion is a sympathetic ganglion and is not a site of varicella-zoster latency.
whyNot.B: The pterygopalatine ganglion is a parasympathetic relay for lacrimation and is not the source of this syndrome.

items.objective: Identify the geniculate ganglion as the site of viral reactivation in herpes zoster oticus.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had left ear pain and fever for 10 days. For the past 2 days he has had a worsening headache and vomiting. His left auricle is pushed forwards, and the skin behind it is red and tender. Funduscopy shows bilateral papilledema. Contrast-enhanced CT shows opacified left mastoid air cells and a filling defect in the venous structure that lies directly against the inner surface of the mastoid. Which of the following structures is most likely thrombosed?
items.explanationHtml:
Acute mastoiditis can spread inwards through the thin bone between the mastoid and the posterior fossa. The sigmoid sinus lies directly behind and against the mastoid, so septic thrombosis there (otitic hydrocephalus, with raised intracranial pressure and papilledema) is a recognized complication.

Takeaway: mastoid infection can thrombose the adjacent sigmoid sinus and raise intracranial pressure.

whyNot.A: Cavernous sinus thrombosis usually follows facial or sphenoid sinus infection and causes ophthalmoplegia and proptosis.
whyNot.E: The superior sagittal sinus runs in the midline at the vertex, far from the mastoid.
whyNot.D: The straight sinus lies in the junction of the falx and tentorium, away from the temporal bone.
whyNot.B: The great cerebral vein drains deep brain structures and is not next to the mastoid.

items.objective: Relate the anatomy of the mastoid to sigmoid sinus thrombosis as a complication of mastoiditis.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl with acute otitis media is treated with high-dose amoxicillin rather than the standard dose. The higher dose is chosen to overcome the most common mechanism by which Streptococcus pneumoniae loses susceptibility to penicillins. Which of the following best describes that mechanism?

options.label: A
options.html: Active efflux of the drug from the cytoplasm

options.label: B
options.html: Altered penicillin-binding proteins with lower affinity for the drug

options.label: C
options.html: Methylation of the 23S ribosomal RNA binding site

items.explanationHtml:
Pneumococcal resistance to penicillins comes from mosaic penicillin-binding proteins that bind beta-lactams less tightly. Raising the drug concentration (amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day) restores binding for most strains. A beta-lactamase inhibitor adds nothing against this mechanism.

Takeaway: pneumococci resist penicillins through altered PBPs, which high-dose amoxicillin overcomes.

whyNot.D: Pneumococcus does not rely on beta-lactamase; that mechanism is typical of H. influenzae and Moraxella, and it is overcome by clavulanate, not by a higher dose.
whyNot.E: Pneumococcus is gram-positive and has no outer membrane or porins.
whyNot.A: Efflux pumps cause macrolide resistance in pneumococci, not penicillin resistance.
whyNot.C: Ribosomal methylation causes macrolide and lincosamide resistance; beta-lactams act on the cell wall.

items.objective: Explain why high-dose amoxicillin is used for otitis media in terms of pneumococcal resistance.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman has had slowly progressive hearing loss and ringing in her left ear for 2 years. MRI shows an enhancing mass in the left internal auditory canal extending into the cerebellopontine angle. After resection, microscopy shows densely cellular areas with nuclear palisading alternating with loose myxoid areas, and the cells stain strongly for S-100. From which of the following cells did this tumor arise?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a vestibular schwannoma: a benign tumor of Schwann cells on the vestibular part of cranial nerve VIII. Antoni A (cellular, palisading) and Antoni B (loose) areas with S-100 positivity are typical. Slowly progressive one-sided sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are the usual first symptoms.

Takeaway: one-sided sensorineural loss plus an internal auditory canal mass is a schwannoma until proven otherwise.

whyNot.A: Arachnoid cells give rise to meningiomas, which show whorls and psammoma bodies, not palisading Antoni A areas.
whyNot.B: Ependymomas arise in the ventricles and central canal and show perivascular pseudorosettes.
whyNot.D: Chief cells form paragangliomas (glomus tumors), which grow in nests and stain for chromogranin.
whyNot.C: Astrocytes form gliomas inside the brain parenchyma, not tumors of the cranial nerve sheath.

items.objective: Identify the cell of origin and histology of vestibular schwannoma.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man has hearing loss in both ears. MRI shows enhancing masses in both internal auditory canals and a small mass attached to the dura over the right convexity. He had cataract surgery at age 15. His father had similar tumors. A germline loss-of-function variant in the gene encoding which of the following proteins is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: Menin, a nuclear protein that regulates transcription

options.label: C
options.html: Merlin, which links the cytoskeleton to the cell membrane

options.label: D
options.html: Neurofibromin, a GTPase-activating protein for Ras

options.label: E
options.html: pVHL, which targets hypoxia-inducible factor for breakdown

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, a meningioma, juvenile cataract and an affected parent indicate NF2-related schwannomatosis. It is autosomal dominant, caused by variants in NF2 on chromosome 22, which encodes the tumor suppressor merlin.

Takeaway: bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the defining feature of NF2 (merlin, chromosome 22).

whyNot.D: Neurofibromin loss causes NF1: café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas and optic gliomas, not bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
whyNot.A: Hamartin and tuberin loss causes tuberous sclerosis, with cortical tubers, angiofibromas and renal angiomyolipomas.
whyNot.E: Von Hippel-Lindau disease causes hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.
whyNot.B: Menin loss causes MEN1, with parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumors.

items.objective: Link bilateral vestibular schwannomas to NF2 and the protein merlin.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man with a known left vestibular schwannoma declined treatment 5 years ago. The tumor has grown and now extends well into the cerebellopontine angle. Besides worse left-sided hearing, which of the following new findings is most likely on examination?

options.label: B
options.html: Deviation of the tongue to the left

options.label: C
options.html: Left ptosis with a dilated pupil

items.explanationHtml:
As a vestibular schwannoma grows out of the internal auditory canal, it compresses the trigeminal nerve above it, causing facial numbness and a reduced corneal reflex. It also compresses the cerebellum, causing ipsilateral ataxia. The facial nerve tolerates slow stretching, so clinical facial weakness usually appears late.

Takeaway: a growing cerebellopontine angle tumor affects CN V (corneal reflex) before CN VII weakness becomes obvious.

whyNot.E: The corticospinal tracts are deep in the brainstem and are compressed only by very large tumors, after the cranial nerve signs.
whyNot.B: The hypoglossal nerve leaves the medulla far below the cerebellopontine angle.
whyNot.C: This is an oculomotor palsy, from compression near the midbrain or posterior communicating artery, not the cerebellopontine angle.
whyNot.D: Vertical gaze palsy comes from a dorsal midbrain (pineal region) lesion.

items.objective: Predict the cranial nerve findings of an enlarging cerebellopontine angle tumor.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman hears a whooshing sound in her right ear in time with her pulse. Otoscopy shows a reddish mass behind the lower half of an intact right tympanic membrane. Imaging shows an enhancing mass on the cochlear promontory. After removal, the tumor consists of nests of chromogranin-positive cells surrounded by S-100-positive sustentacular cells. These tumor cells are derived from which of the following embryologic tissues?

options.label: A
options.html: Endoderm of the first pharyngeal pouch

items.explanationHtml:
Pulsatile tinnitus with a red mass behind an intact drum is a paraganglioma (glomus tympanicum). Paraganglion chief cells come from the neural crest, like adrenal medullary cells. They are neuroendocrine (chromogranin positive) and sit in nests surrounded by sustentacular cells.

Takeaway: glomus tumors are neural crest-derived paragangliomas; pulsatile tinnitus is the clue.

whyNot.E: Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis, the lens and the anterior pituitary, not paraganglia.
whyNot.A: The first pouch forms the lining of the middle ear and eustachian tube, not the paraganglion cells.
whyNot.D: Paraxial mesoderm forms bone, skeletal muscle and dermis.
whyNot.C: The neural tube forms central neurons and glia, not peripheral paraganglia.

items.objective: State the neural crest origin of head and neck paragangliomas.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man is found to have a paraganglioma of the left jugular foramen and a second paraganglioma at the right carotid bifurcation. His father had a similar neck tumor. Genetic testing is most likely to show a germline variant in a gene encoding a subunit of which of the following enzymes?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple or familial head and neck paragangliomas most often come from germline variants in a succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) subunit gene. SDH is both a citric acid cycle enzyme and complex II of the electron transport chain. When it is lost, succinate builds up and stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor, a pseudohypoxic signal that drives tumor growth.

Takeaway: hereditary head and neck paragangliomas usually reflect SDH (complex II) variants.

whyNot.D: Pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency causes lactic acidosis and neurologic disease, not hereditary paragangliomas.
whyNot.A: This citric acid cycle enzyme is not a recognized hereditary paraganglioma gene.
whyNot.C: Cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) deficiency causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies.
whyNot.B: ATP synthase (complex V) variants cause mitochondrial diseases such as NARP, not paragangliomas.

items.objective: Associate hereditary paraganglioma with succinate dehydrogenase gene variants.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man who moved from southern China 10 years ago has had a blocked feeling in his right ear for 3 months. Otoscopy shows fluid behind the right tympanic membrane. A firm, painless lymph node is palpable high in the right neck. Biopsy of a nasopharyngeal mass shows sheets of undifferentiated carcinoma cells with many lymphocytes. Infection with which of the following viruses is most closely associated with this tumor?
items.explanationHtml:
Non-keratinizing, undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma is strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus and is common in southern China. A tumor in the lateral nasopharynx blocks the eustachian tube, so a one-sided effusion in an adult, often with a neck node, is a classic presentation.

Takeaway: an adult with a one-sided middle-ear effusion and a neck node may have EBV-related nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

whyNot.D: HPV-16 drives oropharyngeal (tonsil and tongue base) squamous cell carcinoma, not the endemic undifferentiated nasopharyngeal type.
whyNot.C: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma.
whyNot.A: Cytomegalovirus is not an oncogenic virus in head and neck cancer.
whyNot.E: HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and tropical spastic paraparesis.

items.objective: Associate nasopharyngeal carcinoma with Epstein-Barr virus and one-sided effusion.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old retired farmer has a crusted, bleeding nodule on the rim of his left ear that has grown over 4 months. Biopsy shows atypical squamous cells invading the dermis, with keratin pearls. The DNA damage that most likely started this tumor is normally repaired by which of the following processes?
items.explanationHtml:
Ultraviolet B light makes pyrimidine (thymine) dimers that distort the DNA helix. Nucleotide excision repair cuts out the damaged stretch and fills the gap. The helix of the ear is heavily sun-exposed, so squamous and basal cell carcinomas are common there. Defective excision repair (xeroderma pigmentosum) causes these cancers in childhood.

Takeaway: ultraviolet damage (pyrimidine dimers) is fixed by nucleotide excision repair; the auricle is a common skin cancer site.

whyNot.C: Mismatch repair fixes replication errors; its loss causes Lynch syndrome and microsatellite instability, not ultraviolet-induced lesions.
whyNot.A: Base excision repair removes single damaged bases, such as deaminated or oxidized bases, not bulky dimers.
whyNot.B: Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks (BRCA1 and BRCA2), not ultraviolet dimers.
whyNot.D: Nonhomologous end joining rejoins double-strand breaks, such as those from ionizing radiation.

items.objective: Connect ultraviolet-induced pyrimidine dimers on the auricle to nucleotide excision repair.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man has had gradual difficulty understanding speech in restaurants. An audiogram shows symmetric sensorineural loss that is worst at 4000 and 8000 Hz. In the schematic of the inner ear shown, which labeled site would show the earliest loss of hair cells responsible for his findings?
items.explanationHtml:
The basilar membrane is narrow and stiff at the base of the cochlea, where high-frequency sound produces its peak displacement. Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) and noise damage begin with the hair cells of the basal turn (site D), so the high frequencies, which carry consonant sounds, go first.

Takeaway: high frequencies are coded at the cochlear base, where age- and noise-related damage begins.

whyNot.A: Site A is the stapes footplate; fixation there (otosclerosis) causes conductive, not sensorineural, loss.
whyNot.B: Site B is a semicircular canal; it senses rotation and plays no role in hearing.
whyNot.C: Site C is the endolymphatic sac; poor resorption there is linked to Ménière disease, with fluctuating low-frequency loss.
whyNot.E: Site E is the vestibular part of cranial nerve VIII, which carries balance, not hearing, signals.

items.objective: Apply cochlear tonotopy to localize high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman has had muffled hearing in her left ear since a cold 1 week ago. A 512-Hz tuning fork placed on her forehead is heard louder in the left ear. On the left side, the fork is heard longer when held on the mastoid than in front of the ear canal. On the right, air conduction is louder than bone conduction. Which of the following best describes her hearing loss?
items.explanationHtml:
The Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne is negative (bone louder than air): a left conductive hearing loss, here most likely middle-ear fluid after a cold. In conductive loss the affected ear hears bone-conducted sound better, because ambient noise is masked out.

Takeaway: Weber to the bad ear plus a negative Rinne on that ear means conductive loss.

whyNot.C: With left sensorineural loss, the Weber lateralizes to the right (better) ear, and the left Rinne stays positive.
whyNot.D: Right conductive loss would send the Weber to the right ear and make the right Rinne negative.
whyNot.E: Right sensorineural loss sends the Weber to the left ear, but the left Rinne would then be normal (air louder than bone).
whyNot.A: Symmetric loss keeps the Weber in the midline, and both Rinne tests stay positive.

items.objective: Interpret the Weber and Rinne tests to classify hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 9-month-old boy who failed newborn hearing screening is confirmed to have profound sensorineural hearing loss in both ears. Pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated, and his growth and development are otherwise normal. Both parents hear normally and are not related. Examination of the eyes, skin, thyroid and kidneys is normal. A defect in which of the following proteins is the most likely cause?

options.label: B
options.html: A gap junction protein that recycles potassium in the cochlea

options.label: C
options.html: A transcription factor for melanocyte development

options.label: E
options.html: The alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen

items.explanationHtml:
Non-syndromic, autosomal recessive congenital deafness in a child of hearing parents is most often caused by variants in GJB2, which encodes connexin 26. This gap junction protein lets supporting cells recycle K+ back to the stria vascularis after hair cells fire.

Takeaway: GJB2 (connexin 26) is the most common genetic cause of non-syndromic congenital hearing loss.

whyNot.E: Type IV collagen variants cause Alport syndrome, with hematuria and later-onset hearing loss, not isolated congenital deafness.
whyNot.D: Pendrin defects cause Pendred syndrome, with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct and goiter, usually later in childhood.
whyNot.A: Potassium channel variants with deafness cause Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, which also prolongs the QT interval.
whyNot.C: PAX3 and related defects cause Waardenburg syndrome, with pigment changes such as a white forelock.

items.objective: Identify connexin 26 defects as the leading genetic cause of non-syndromic congenital deafness.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old girl has had progressive sensorineural hearing loss since early childhood. She now has a diffusely enlarged thyroid. TSH and free thyroxine are within the reference ranges. CT of the temporal bones shows enlarged vestibular aqueducts in both ears. Her thyroid disorder is most likely due to impaired function of which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Deiodination of thyroxine in peripheral tissues

options.label: C
options.html: Iodide transport across the apical membrane into the follicular lumen

options.label: D
options.html: Sodium-iodide symporter uptake across the basolateral membrane

items.explanationHtml:
Pendred syndrome (autosomal recessive, SLC26A4) combines sensorineural hearing loss and enlarged vestibular aqueducts with goiter. Pendrin is an anion exchanger that moves iodide across the apical membrane of thyroid cells into the colloid, where it is organified. Its loss impairs organification. Many patients stay euthyroid but develop goiter, and the inner-ear defect reflects pendrin's role in endolymph ion balance.

Takeaway: hearing loss plus goiter plus an enlarged vestibular aqueduct points to pendrin (Pendred syndrome).

whyNot.D: Defects in the sodium-iodide symporter reduce iodide trapping without hearing loss or vestibular aqueduct changes.
whyNot.E: Thyroid peroxidase deficiency impairs organification but is not linked to inner-ear malformation.
whyNot.A: TSH-receptor problems cause congenital hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism, not goiter with an enlarged vestibular aqueduct.
whyNot.B: Deiodinase defects alter T3 production but do not cause goiter with deafness.

items.objective: Explain the thyroid defect in Pendred syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has had gradually worsening hearing in both ears for 3 years, with a clear decline during her recent pregnancy. Her mother wore hearing aids from age 40. Both tympanic membranes look normal and move normally. Audiometry shows a conductive hearing loss in both ears. In the schematic of the ear shown, which labeled site is most likely affected?
items.explanationHtml:
Progressive conductive loss with a normal eardrum in a young woman, worse in pregnancy and with a family history, is otosclerosis. Abnormal remodeling of the otic capsule fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window (site A), so sound is no longer transmitted into the inner ear. Treatment is a hearing aid or stapes surgery.

Takeaway: conductive loss with a normal drum in a young adult suggests otosclerosis, with the stapes fixed in the oval window.

whyNot.B: Site B is a semicircular canal; disease there causes vertigo, not conductive hearing loss.
whyNot.C: Site C is the endolymphatic sac; it is linked to Ménière disease, which causes sensorineural loss.
whyNot.D: Site D is the basal cochlea; damage there causes high-frequency sensorineural, not conductive, loss.
whyNot.E: Site E is the vestibular nerve; it carries balance signals, and lesions there do not cause conductive loss.

items.objective: Localize otosclerosis to the stapes footplate and recognize its typical presentation.

items.stemHtml: Deflecting the stereocilia of cochlear inner hair cells towards the tallest stereocilium opens mechanotransduction channels at their tips. The cell depolarizes even though the channel is nonselective for cations. Influx of which of the following ions mainly carries this depolarizing current?
items.explanationHtml:
Stereocilia project into endolymph, which is rich in K+ and held at about +80 mV by the stria vascularis. When the transduction channels open, the large electrical and chemical gradient drives K+ into the hair cell and depolarizes it. This is unusual, because elsewhere in the body K+ entry is not depolarizing. The K+ then leaves the cell base into perilymph and is recycled.

Takeaway: hair cells depolarize by K+ influx from potassium-rich endolymph.

whyNot.E: Endolymph has a very low sodium concentration, so little sodium is available to enter through the channels.
whyNot.A: Calcium enters too and helps adaptation, but its concentration in endolymph is low, so it carries only a small share of the current.
whyNot.B: Chloride is an anion; its influx would hyperpolarize the cell, and the transduction channels are cation channels.
whyNot.C: Magnesium does not carry meaningful current through the transduction channels.

items.objective: Describe ionic transduction in cochlear hair cells.

items.stemHtml: A 2-day-old girl fails her newborn hearing screen in both ears. She was born at term and is small for gestational age, with microcephaly, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly. Cranial ultrasound shows calcifications lining the lateral ventricles. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hearing loss?
items.explanationHtml:
Congenital cytomegalovirus is the most common non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children. Periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly are typical of symptomatic infection. The hearing loss can be delayed or can progress over early childhood.

Takeaway: congenital CMV is the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural deafness.

whyNot.D: Congenital rubella causes deafness, cataracts and patent ductus arteriosus; it is now rare where vaccination is routine, and its calcifications are not typically periventricular.
whyNot.E: Congenital toxoplasmosis causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, and hearing loss is less typical.
whyNot.B: Neonatal herpes usually appears with skin, eye or mouth lesions, encephalitis or sepsis, not congenital deafness at birth.
whyNot.C: Parvovirus B19 causes fetal anemia and hydrops, not deafness with periventricular calcifications.

items.objective: Recognize congenital cytomegalovirus infection as a cause of neonatal hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman has brief spells of spinning when she rolls over in bed or looks up to a high shelf. Each spell lasts about 20 seconds. When her head is turned to the right and she is quickly laid back with the head hanging below the table, torsional upbeating nystagmus begins after a few seconds and fades within 30 seconds. In the schematic of the ear shown, the displaced particles causing her symptoms are most likely located at which labeled site?
items.explanationHtml:
Brief positional vertigo with delayed, fatiguing torsional upbeat nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike test is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Otoconia loosened from the utricle settle in a semicircular canal, usually the posterior canal (site B). They move with gravity when the head moves and deflect the cupula.

Takeaway: BPPV is otoconia loose in a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal.

whyNot.A: Site A is the stapes footplate in the middle ear; otoconia cannot reach it.
whyNot.C: Site C is the endolymphatic sac; its disorders are linked to Ménière disease, which causes spontaneous attacks lasting hours.
whyNot.D: Site D is the cochlea, which senses sound, not head position.
whyNot.E: Site E is the vestibular nerve; inflammation there (vestibular neuritis) causes continuous vertigo for days.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of BPPV and localize it to a semicircular canal.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has had 4 attacks of spinning vertigo in 6 months, each lasting 2 to 4 hours, with nausea, roaring tinnitus and fullness in his right ear. Audiometry between attacks shows low-frequency sensorineural loss on the right that varies from test to test. Which of the following best describes the underlying abnormality?

options.label: A
options.html: Bony fixation of the stapes footplate

options.label: B
options.html: Compression of cranial nerve VIII by a schwannoma

options.label: C
options.html: Distension of the endolymphatic space by excess endolymph

options.label: D
options.html: Loose otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal

options.label: E
options.html: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting hours, with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, are Ménière disease. Its pathologic correlate is endolymphatic hydrops: an enlarged endolymphatic space, linked to impaired resorption of endolymph by the endolymphatic sac.

Takeaway: Ménière disease = endolymphatic hydrops: episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-tone loss, tinnitus, fullness.

whyNot.D: Loose otoconia (BPPV) cause seconds-long positional vertigo without hearing loss.
whyNot.E: Vestibular neuritis causes a single episode of continuous vertigo for days without hearing loss.
whyNot.A: Otosclerosis causes conductive hearing loss without attacks of vertigo.
whyNot.B: A schwannoma causes slowly progressive loss and mild imbalance, not discrete attacks of vertigo lasting hours.

items.objective: Relate the clinical features of Ménière disease to endolymphatic hydrops.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has had constant spinning vertigo, nausea and vomiting since waking yesterday, 1 week after a cold. Her hearing is normal. Imaging later confirms that she has acute inflammation of the right vestibular nerve and no central lesion. Which of the following is most likely to be seen when she looks straight ahead?

options.label: A
options.html: Horizontal-torsional nystagmus with the fast phase beating to the left

options.label: B
options.html: Horizontal-torsional nystagmus with the fast phase beating to the right

options.label: C
options.html: No nystagmus until the head is tilted back

options.label: D
options.html: Nystagmus that reverses direction with each change in gaze

items.explanationHtml:
When the right vestibular nerve stops working, the left nerve's normal tonic firing is unopposed. The brain interprets this as rotation to the left, so the eyes drift slowly to the right and corrective fast phases beat to the left, away from the lesion. Peripheral nystagmus is horizontal-torsional, keeps the same direction in every gaze, and is damped by visual fixation.

Takeaway: in peripheral vestibular loss, the fast phase of nystagmus beats away from the bad ear.

whyNot.B: The fast phase beats away from the damaged side; with right-sided loss it beats to the left.
whyNot.E: Vertical (downbeat) nystagmus suggests a central lesion, such as at the craniocervical junction or in the cerebellum.
whyNot.D: Direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus is a central sign.
whyNot.C: Nystagmus only on positional testing suggests BPPV, not acute vestibular neuritis.

items.objective: Predict the direction of nystagmus in unilateral peripheral vestibular loss.

items.stemHtml: A pilot in a cloudless night sky accelerates forward steadily and wrongly feels that the aircraft's nose is pitching up. This illusion arises because a single receptor cannot tell linear acceleration apart from tilt of the head relative to gravity. Which of the following structures generates this sensation?

options.label: B
options.html: Maculae of the utricle and saccule

items.explanationHtml:
The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) have maculae topped by otoconia. Both linear acceleration and gravitational tilt shift the otoconial membrane and bend the hair cells in the same way. Without visual cues, forward acceleration is felt as backward tilt (nose-up). This is called the somatogravic illusion.

Takeaway: otolith organs sense linear acceleration and tilt; semicircular canals sense rotation.

whyNot.A: The cristae sense angular (rotational) acceleration, not linear acceleration or static tilt.
whyNot.D: The organ of Corti transduces sound, not head acceleration.
whyNot.C: Neck proprioceptors contribute to position sense but do not respond to whole-body linear acceleration.
whyNot.E: The stria vascularis produces endolymph and the endocochlear potential; it is not a sensory organ.

items.objective: Distinguish otolith function from semicircular canal function.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with complete loss of function of his left vestibular nerve after surgery fixes his eyes on the examiner's nose while the examiner turns his head quickly by about 15 degrees. Which of the following is most likely to be observed?

options.label: A
options.html: With a quick turn to the left, the eyes move with the head and then make a saccade to the right back to the target

options.label: B
options.html: With a quick turn to the left, the eyes overshoot the target and then drift back slowly

options.label: C
options.html: With a quick turn to the right, the eyes move with the head and then make a saccade to the left back to the target

options.label: D
options.html: With quick turns in either direction, the eyes move with the head and then make corrective saccades

options.label: E
options.html: With quick turns in either direction, the eyes stay on the target without saccades

items.explanationHtml:
A quick head turn to the left mainly excites the left horizontal canal. With the left nerve cut, the vestibulo-ocular reflex fails for leftward turns. The eyes are carried with the head and must make a catch-up saccade back to the right to refixate. Rightward turns are sensed by the intact right side, so they are normal.

Takeaway: the head impulse test is abnormal (catch-up saccade) when the head is turned towards the damaged side.

whyNot.C: A turn to the right is sensed by the intact right horizontal canal, so the reflex works and the eyes stay on target.
whyNot.E: This normal response would be expected only if both labyrinths and vestibular nerves worked.
whyNot.D: Bilateral abnormal impulses occur with bilateral vestibular loss, such as gentamicin toxicity.
whyNot.B: An overshoot followed by slow drift is not the pattern of vestibular loss.

items.objective: Interpret the head impulse test in unilateral vestibular loss.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman applies a scopolamine patch behind her ear the evening before a cruise. The next morning she has blurred vision, a red painful right eye, headache and nausea. Her right pupil is mid-dilated and does not react to light. Which of the following best explains how the drug caused this complication?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of H1 receptors in the vestibular nuclei

options.label: D
options.html: Blockade of muscarinic receptors on the iris sphincter

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulation of alpha-1 receptors on the iris dilator

items.explanationHtml:
Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist. Blocking muscarinic receptors on the iris sphincter dilates the pupil, and blocking them on the ciliary muscle paralyzes accommodation. In an eye with a narrow angle, the dilated iris crowds the angle and blocks aqueous outflow, causing acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Takeaway: anticholinergic motion-sickness drugs can precipitate angle-closure glaucoma by causing mydriasis.

whyNot.E: Scopolamine has no alpha-adrenergic agonist action; dilation results from unopposed sympathetic tone after cholinergic blockade.
whyNot.C: H1 blockade is how antihistamines treat motion sickness; it does not explain pupil dilation.
whyNot.B: D2 antagonists are antiemetics but do not dilate the pupil.
whyNot.A: 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron cause constipation and QT prolongation, not mydriasis.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of scopolamine-induced angle closure.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes suddenly develops severe vertigo, vomiting and complete hearing loss in his left ear. Examination shows weakness of the entire left side of his face, decreased pain and temperature sensation over the left face, and left arm and leg ataxia. Occlusion of which of the following arteries is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral caudal pons and the middle cerebellar peduncle, and in most people gives off the labyrinthine artery. Occlusion causes vertigo with sudden ipsilateral deafness, ipsilateral facial weakness (facial nucleus), ipsilateral facial sensory loss and ipsilateral ataxia. Sudden one-sided hearing loss with vertigo in a patient with vascular risk factors must raise concern for this stroke.

Takeaway: vertigo plus sudden one-sided deafness and facial palsy suggests an AICA (lateral pontine) infarct.

whyNot.D: PICA infarction (lateral medullary syndrome) causes vertigo and ataxia, but with hoarseness and dysphagia and without facial weakness or deafness.
whyNot.E: Superior cerebellar artery infarction causes limb ataxia and dysarthria without hearing loss or facial palsy.
whyNot.C: Posterior cerebral artery infarction causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
whyNot.B: Anterior spinal artery occlusion affects the medial medulla or cord, causing contralateral weakness and tongue deviation.

items.objective: Localize vertigo with ipsilateral hearing loss and facial palsy to the AICA territory.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college wrestler has a tense, fluctuant swelling on the front of his left auricle 2 days after a match. He did not seek care, and over the next months the ear becomes thickened, firm and misshapen. Which of the following best explains the permanent deformity?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacterial infection destroyed the elastic fibers of the cartilage

options.label: B
options.html: Blood clotted inside the cartilage matrix and calcified

options.label: C
options.html: Blood separated the cartilage from its nourishing perichondrium

options.label: D
options.html: The skin of the auricle healed with a keloid scar

options.label: E
options.html: The underlying temporal bone fractured and healed with callus

items.explanationHtml:
Auricular cartilage is avascular and depends on diffusion from the overlying perichondrium. A hematoma lifts the perichondrium off the cartilage, which then necroses. The perichondrium lays down new, disorganized fibrocartilage, producing cauliflower ear. Prompt drainage and a compressive dressing prevent it.

Takeaway: cauliflower ear results from undrained blood cutting cartilage off from its perichondrial blood supply.

whyNot.A: The hematoma was not infected; the deformity follows loss of blood supply, not infection.
whyNot.B: Blood collects between perichondrium and cartilage, not inside the matrix.
whyNot.D: A keloid forms in the dermis after skin injury; it does not cause cartilage necrosis and crumpling.
whyNot.E: The auricle has no bony support; the deformity arises in its cartilage.

items.objective: Explain the pathogenesis of cauliflower ear after auricular hematoma.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man is struck on the back of the head in an assault. CT shows a fracture line that crosses the left petrous temporal bone at right angles to its long axis and passes through the otic capsule. Which combination of findings on the left is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Conductive hearing loss with a cholesteatoma

options.label: B
options.html: Conductive hearing loss, hemotympanum and a normal facial nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Normal hearing, anosmia and clear rhinorrhea

options.label: D
options.html: Pulsatile tinnitus and a red mass behind the drum

options.label: E
options.html: Sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo and facial weakness

items.explanationHtml:
A fracture that runs across the petrous bone (older term: transverse) usually violates the otic capsule, destroying the cochlea and vestibule. It causes sensorineural loss and vertigo, and it is more often associated with facial nerve injury. Longitudinal fractures, which spare the capsule, cause conductive loss with a torn drum and hemotympanum.

Takeaway: otic capsule-violating (transverse) fractures cause sensorineural loss, vertigo and facial palsy.

whyNot.B: This pattern fits a fracture that spares the otic capsule (the usual longitudinal type), not one through it.
whyNot.C: Anosmia and rhinorrhea point to an anterior cranial fossa (cribriform plate) fracture.
whyNot.A: Cholesteatoma is a late, rare complication of trauma and does not appear acutely.
whyNot.D: This describes a glomus tumor, not an acute fracture.

items.objective: Distinguish the consequences of otic capsule-sparing and otic capsule-violating temporal bone fractures.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman involved in a motor vehicle collision has bruising behind her right ear. Clear, watery fluid drips from her right ear canal. Which test on the fluid would best confirm that it is cerebrospinal fluid?
items.explanationHtml:
Beta-2 transferrin is a desialylated form of transferrin made in the central nervous system. It is found in CSF and perilymph but not in serum or ordinary secretions, so it is the specific test for a CSF leak.

Takeaway: confirm CSF otorrhea or rhinorrhea with beta-2 transferrin.

whyNot.B: Glucose dipsticks give false positives because mucus and blood also contain glucose; this is unreliable.
whyNot.E: Protein content overlaps with other secretions and is not specific for CSF.
whyNot.D: LDH is not a marker for CSF.
whyNot.C: A blood-stained fluid ring on paper is nonspecific and does not confirm CSF.

items.objective: Select beta-2 transferrin to confirm cerebrospinal fluid leakage.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with a cold has severe left ear pain as her airplane descends. Swallowing and yawning do not help. Normally, contraction of which of the following muscles opens the eustachian tube during swallowing and equalizes middle-ear pressure?
items.explanationHtml:
The tensor veli palatini, supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, pulls open the cartilaginous eustachian tube during swallowing and yawning. During descent, the cabin pressure rises. If inflamed mucosa keeps the tube shut, the relatively low middle-ear pressure pulls the eardrum inwards and causes pain, effusion and bleeding (barotrauma).

Takeaway: the tensor veli palatini (CN V3) opens the eustachian tube; a blocked tube causes barotrauma on descent.

whyNot.D: The tensor tympani tenses the eardrum to dampen sound; it does not open the eustachian tube.
whyNot.B: The stapedius dampens stapes movement in loud sound.
whyNot.A: The palatoglossus elevates the tongue and narrows the oropharyngeal isthmus.
whyNot.C: The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing and does not open the tube.

items.objective: Identify the muscle that opens the eustachian tube and relate it to barotrauma.

items.stemHtml: Several people are injured when a gas cylinder explodes in a closed workshop. None were hit by debris. Which of the following organs is most commonly injured by the primary blast wave?
items.explanationHtml:
Primary blast injury results from the pressure wave and mainly affects air-filled organs. The tympanic membrane ruptures at the lowest pressures, so it is the most frequent primary blast injury. An intact drum does not exclude lung or bowel injury.

Takeaway: the eardrum is the organ most often injured by a primary blast wave.

whyNot.D: Blast lung is the most common fatal primary blast injury but is less common than eardrum rupture.
whyNot.A: Gas-containing bowel can be injured, but less often than the eardrum.
whyNot.B: Brain injury from the pressure wave alone is less frequent than eardrum injury.
whyNot.C: Eye injuries in explosions are mostly from fragments, a secondary mechanism.

items.objective: Identify the tympanic membrane as the organ most susceptible to primary blast injury.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy pushes a small coin-shaped lithium button battery into his right ear canal. Within hours the canal skin is ulcerated and the tympanic membrane is perforated. Which of the following best explains the rapid tissue injury?

options.label: A
options.html: A thermal burn from the battery overheating

options.label: B
options.html: Acid coagulative necrosis from the battery electrolyte

options.label: C
options.html: Alkaline liquefactive necrosis from hydroxide generated by the current

options.label: E
options.html: Pressure necrosis from the weight of the battery

items.explanationHtml:
Current flowing through moist tissue causes electrolysis, which makes hydroxide ions at the negative pole. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis that penetrates deeply, and this starts within hours, even when the battery seems "dead". That is why button batteries in the ear, nose or esophagus need immediate removal.

Takeaway: button batteries cause rapid alkaline liquefactive necrosis: remove them immediately.

whyNot.B: Acids cause coagulative necrosis, but the main injury from button batteries is alkaline, from hydroxide made at the negative pole.
whyNot.E: Pressure contributes little; the battery is light and the injury begins within hours.
whyNot.D: Systemic lithium absorption is not the cause of the local burn.
whyNot.A: Batteries do not get hot enough to cause the injury; electrolysis does.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of tissue injury from button batteries.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old diver has trouble equalizing her ears during descent and performs a very forceful Valsalva maneuver. She immediately hears a pop in her right ear, followed by roaring tinnitus, hearing loss and vertigo that worsen when she strains. Otoscopy shows a normal right tympanic membrane. Weber lateralizes to the left. Which of the following has most likely ruptured?
items.explanationHtml:
A sudden surge in CSF and perilymph pressure from forceful Valsalva, or an implosive middle-ear pressure change, can rupture the round (or oval) window membrane. Perilymph leaks into the middle ear, a perilymph fistula, causing sensorineural loss (Weber to the good ear), tinnitus and vertigo that get worse with straining.

Takeaway: sudden sensorineural loss and vertigo after forceful Valsalva suggests a round window perilymph fistula.

whyNot.D: The drum looks normal, and a drum perforation would cause conductive, not sensorineural, loss.
whyNot.A: The basilar membrane is inside the cochlea and is not ruptured by middle-ear pressure changes.
whyNot.B: Reissner membrane rupture has been proposed in Ménière disease, not in Valsalva-induced barotrauma.
whyNot.E: The utricular macula is a sensory epithelium and is not torn by pressure surges.

items.objective: Recognize perilymph fistula as a mechanism of inner-ear barotrauma.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman becomes profoundly deaf in both ears after a single dose of gentamicin given for suspected sepsis. Her serum gentamicin level was within the target range. Her mother's brother and her maternal grandmother also became deaf after antibiotic treatment. Her father's relatives have normal hearing. Which of the following best explains her susceptibility?

options.label: A
options.html: A maternally inherited mitochondrial ribosomal RNA variant

options.label: B
options.html: A nuclear variant that slows renal aminoglycoside clearance

options.label: C
options.html: An autosomal dominant defect in drug-metabolizing enzymes

options.label: D
options.html: An X-linked defect in the cochlear gap junction protein

options.label: E
options.html: Antibodies against inner-ear antigens triggered by the drug

items.explanationHtml:
The maternal pattern of aminoglycoside-induced deafness points to the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant in the 12S ribosomal RNA. It changes the mitochondrial ribosome so that aminoglycosides bind it as they bind bacterial ribosomes. This disrupts mitochondrial protein synthesis in hair cells, and even a single standard dose can cause permanent deafness.

Takeaway: maternally inherited aminoglycoside deafness = mitochondrial 12S rRNA (MT-RNR1) variant.

whyNot.B: Her drug level was normal, and the family pattern is maternal, which points to mitochondrial inheritance.
whyNot.D: Connexin 26 (GJB2) is autosomal recessive and causes congenital, not drug-triggered, deafness.
whyNot.C: Aminoglycosides are excreted unchanged by the kidney and are not metabolized by hepatic enzymes.
whyNot.E: Autoimmune inner-ear disease causes progressive loss over weeks to months, not deafness after a single dose.

items.objective: Explain mitochondrial susceptibility to aminoglycoside ototoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man with acute kidney injury and pulmonary edema receives a large dose of furosemide as a rapid intravenous push. An hour later he reports ringing in both ears and muffled hearing, which resolve over the next day. Inhibition of which of the following transporters best explains his symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule

options.label: B
options.html: Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct

options.label: C
options.html: Na<sup>+</sup>-Cl<sup>−</sup> cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule

items.explanationHtml:
Loop diuretics block the Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter (NKCC1) in the stria vascularis. This cotransporter helps secrete K+ into endolymph and maintain the endocochlear potential. When the potential falls, hearing falls. The effect is usually reversible and depends on the dose. It is greatest after rapid high-dose IV doses in kidney failure, and it adds to aminoglycoside toxicity.

Takeaway: loop diuretic ototoxicity comes from NKCC1 blockade in the stria vascularis and is usually reversible.

whyNot.C: This is the thiazide target in the kidney; thiazides are not ototoxic.
whyNot.B: This is the target of amiloride, which does not affect the endocochlear potential.
whyNot.A: Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase and is not typically ototoxic.
whyNot.E: This is the digoxin target and is unrelated to loop diuretic ototoxicity.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of loop diuretic ototoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman with osteoarthritis has been taking high-dose aspirin daily for 3 weeks. She now has ringing in both ears and mildly reduced hearing. Audiometry shows a mild, flat sensorineural loss in both ears. Which of the following best describes the expected course if the aspirin is stopped?

options.label: A
options.html: Improvement only after treatment with systemic corticosteroids

options.label: B
options.html: Permanent high-frequency loss that progresses for months

options.label: C
options.html: Permanent loss limited to low frequencies

options.label: D
options.html: Recovery of hearing and resolution of tinnitus within days

options.label: E
options.html: Recovery of hearing but permanent bilateral vestibular loss

items.explanationHtml:
High-dose salicylates cause tinnitus and a mild, flat sensorineural loss by interfering with outer hair cell electromotility. Unlike aminoglycosides or cisplatin, the effect is reversible and usually resolves within a few days of lowering or stopping the dose.

Takeaway: salicylate tinnitus and hearing loss are reversible after stopping the drug.

whyNot.B: Progressive, permanent loss is typical of aminoglycosides and cisplatin, not salicylates.
whyNot.C: Salicylate ototoxicity does not leave a permanent low-frequency loss.
whyNot.E: Salicylates do not cause permanent vestibular damage.
whyNot.A: No specific treatment is needed; stopping the drug is enough.

items.objective: Describe the reversible nature of salicylate ototoxicity.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl is receiving cisplatin-based chemotherapy for a solid tumor. She has no hearing complaints. Which of the following audiometric findings is most likely to appear first if she develops cisplatin ototoxicity?

options.label: A
options.html: A mixed loss with an air-bone gap at all frequencies

options.label: B
options.html: A notch at 4000 Hz with recovery at 8000 Hz

options.label: C
options.html: Bilateral low-frequency sensorineural loss that fluctuates

options.label: D
options.html: Bilateral sensorineural loss beginning at the highest frequencies

options.label: E
options.html: Unilateral conductive loss at low frequencies

items.explanationHtml:
Cisplatin damages the outer hair cells of the basal turn first, producing a bilateral, symmetric, high-frequency sensorineural loss. It can be detected by high-frequency audiometry before the child notices. It is dose-related and usually permanent, and children are especially vulnerable.

Takeaway: cisplatin ototoxicity is bilateral, high-frequency first, sensorineural and usually permanent.

whyNot.E: Cisplatin damages cochlear hair cells, causing sensorineural, not conductive, loss, and it affects both ears.
whyNot.C: Fluctuating low-frequency loss suggests Ménière disease.
whyNot.B: A notch at 4 kHz is the pattern of noise exposure.
whyNot.A: An air-bone gap means a conductive component, which cisplatin does not cause.

items.objective: Recognize the audiometric pattern of cisplatin ototoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has received intravenous gentamicin for 3 weeks for endocarditis. He now says that when he walks, the world seems to bounce, and he feels very unsteady in the dark. He has no spinning sensation and hears normally. Which of the following findings on examination is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: A negative Romberg test with a wide-based gait

options.label: B
options.html: Catch-up saccades on quick head turns to both sides

options.label: C
options.html: Spontaneous horizontal nystagmus beating to one side

options.label: D
options.html: Torsional nystagmus on the Dix-Hallpike test

items.explanationHtml:
Gentamicin is mainly vestibulotoxic and damages both labyrinths symmetrically. With no difference between the sides, there is no vertigo or spontaneous nystagmus. Instead, the vestibulo-ocular reflex fails in both directions, causing oscillopsia during head movement, and balance depends on vision (positive Romberg, unsteady in the dark). Head impulse testing shows bilateral catch-up saccades.

Takeaway: gentamicin causes bilateral vestibular loss: oscillopsia and imbalance in the dark, not vertigo.

whyNot.C: Spontaneous nystagmus suggests an asymmetric (unilateral) loss; aminoglycoside damage is symmetric.
whyNot.D: Positional torsional nystagmus is the sign of BPPV.
whyNot.A: Bilateral vestibular loss makes the Romberg test positive, because vision becomes essential for balance.
whyNot.E: Vertical gaze-evoked nystagmus suggests a central lesion.

items.objective: Recognize the clinical findings of bilateral aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with heart failure and a gram-negative bloodstream infection is being treated in hospital. Which of the following drug combinations given together would carry the greatest risk of permanent hearing loss?
items.explanationHtml:
Aminoglycosides and loop diuretics are synergistically ototoxic. The loop diuretic disrupts the stria vascularis and lets more aminoglycoside into the endolymph and hair cells, which raises the risk of permanent loss. Avoid giving them together where possible, or monitor closely.
