Takeaway: an aminoglycoside plus a loop diuretic is the classic synergistic ototoxic combination.

whyNot.A: Ceftriaxone is not ototoxic, so this pair carries little added risk.
whyNot.C: Thiazides are not ototoxic; the dangerous interaction is with loop diuretics.
whyNot.E: Neither drug is meaningfully ototoxic.
whyNot.D: Neither drug causes ototoxicity.

items.objective: Identify drug combinations that increase ototoxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has had tinnitus, mildly reduced hearing, headache, blurred vision and nausea for 5 days. A friend recently gave her tablets to take each night for painful leg cramps. Her platelet count is 82,000/mm3 (150,000-400,000/mm3). Which of the following drugs is she most likely taking?
items.explanationHtml:
Tinnitus, hearing loss, headache, visual disturbance and nausea make up cinchonism, typical of quinine. Quinine can also cause immune thrombocytopenia and other serious blood reactions. It is not recommended for leg cramps for this reason.

Takeaway: cinchonism (tinnitus, hearing loss, visual blurring) plus thrombocytopenia suggests quinine.

whyNot.A: Baclofen causes drowsiness and weakness, not tinnitus with thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.C: Gabapentin causes dizziness and sedation but not cinchonism.
whyNot.D: Magnesium causes diarrhea and, in kidney failure, hypermagnesemia, not tinnitus and thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.B: Cyclobenzaprine has anticholinergic effects but does not cause tinnitus with low platelets.

items.objective: Recognize quinine toxicity (cinchonism) and its hematologic risks.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl has had left ear pain for 1 day after 3 days of a runny nose. She is eating and playing between doses of ibuprofen. Temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F). The left tympanic membrane is mildly bulging and red with reduced mobility; the right is normal. Her parents would prefer to avoid antibiotics if possible. They have a car and a phone and can return at any time. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: A single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone

options.label: B
options.html: Analgesia and observation with recheck in 48 to 72 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Oral azithromycin once daily for 5 days

options.label: E
options.html: Referral to ENT for tympanostomy tube placement

items.explanationHtml:
She is 2 years or older with non-severe, one-sided AOM: mild pain for less than 48 hours and a temperature below 39°C. In this group, either antibiotics or observation with reliable follow-up is appropriate, and the family's preference decides. Pain relief is given in all cases, and antibiotics start if she does not improve within 48 to 72 hours.

Takeaway: non-severe AOM at age 2 or older (or one-sided at 6-23 months) may be observed with a 48-72 hour safety net.

whyNot.C: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is reserved for recent amoxicillin use, conjunctivitis or treatment failure; antibiotics are not required here.
whyNot.D: Macrolides are poor choices for AOM because of pneumococcal resistance, and observation is acceptable here.
whyNot.A: Ceftriaxone is for children who cannot take or have failed oral therapy.
whyNot.E: Tubes are considered for recurrent AOM, not a first episode.

items.objective: Apply criteria for initial observation versus antibiotics in acute otitis media.

items.stemHtml: A 13-month-old boy has had fever and irritability for 2 days and is pulling at both ears. He has had no antibiotics this year and has no allergies. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). Both tympanic membranes are bulging, opaque and immobile. There is no conjunctivitis. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral AOM in a child younger than 2 years, with a temperature of 39°C or higher, needs antibiotics. The first-line drug is high-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses). It covers most pneumococci, including those with altered penicillin-binding proteins. A 10-day course is used under age 2.

Takeaway: high-dose amoxicillin is first line for AOM when antibiotics are indicated.

whyNot.B: Observation is not appropriate with severe signs (temperature 39°C or higher) or with bilateral AOM under age 2.
whyNot.C: This is for children with recent amoxicillin use, purulent conjunctivitis or amoxicillin failure.
whyNot.E: Oral cephalosporins are alternatives for penicillin allergy that is not immediate-type.
whyNot.D: Azithromycin has poor activity against many otitis pathogens and is not recommended.

items.objective: Choose first-line antibiotic therapy for acute otitis media.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl has had right ear pain and fever for 2 days. She finished a 10-day course of amoxicillin for streptococcal pharyngitis 2 weeks ago. She has no drug allergies. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). The right tympanic membrane is bulging and yellow. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
When a child has received amoxicillin in the past 30 days, the infection is more likely to involve beta-lactamase-producing H. influenzae or M. catarrhalis. The choice is amoxicillin-clavulanate (high-dose amoxicillin component). The same applies when purulent conjunctivitis accompanies AOM.

Takeaway: recent amoxicillin use or otitis-conjunctivitis calls for amoxicillin-clavulanate.

whyNot.E: After amoxicillin in the past 30 days, beta-lactamase-producing organisms are more likely, so amoxicillin alone is not preferred.
whyNot.B: Macrolides have poor coverage of otitis pathogens.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcal resistance makes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole unreliable for AOM.
whyNot.C: Clindamycin does not cover H. influenzae or Moraxella.

items.objective: Recognize indications for amoxicillin-clavulanate in acute otitis media.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus has had severe left ear pain for 6 weeks that has not improved with antibiotic ear drops. Examination shows purulent discharge and granulation tissue on the floor of the left ear canal. Facial nerve function is normal. ESR is 88 mm/h (0-15 mm/h). CT shows erosion of the bony canal floor. Swabs are sent for culture. In addition to glucose control, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is necrotizing otitis externa: osteomyelitis of the temporal bone, usually from Pseudomonas aeruginosa. It needs prolonged systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics, typically several weeks of an IV agent such as cefepime, ceftazidime or piperacillin-tazobactam, or a fluoroquinolone. Treatment is adjusted to culture results and combined with glucose control and ENT debridement as needed. ESR and imaging help track the response.

Takeaway: necrotizing otitis externa needs weeks of systemic antipseudomonal therapy, not drops.

whyNot.C: Amoxicillin-clavulanate does not cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
whyNot.E: Drops alone cannot treat skull-base osteomyelitis.
whyNot.B: Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms only, not Pseudomonas.
whyNot.D: Antifungal treatment is for proven fungal infection; the usual cause is Pseudomonas.

items.objective: Treat necrotizing otitis externa with prolonged systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old swimmer has had right ear pain and itching for 3 days. Pulling on the auricle and pressing the tragus are very painful. The ear canal is red and swollen with moist debris, but the tympanic membrane is visible and intact. He is afebrile, with no swelling beyond the ear canal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Irrigation of the ear canal with tap water

items.explanationHtml:
Uncomplicated acute otitis externa is treated with topical antibiotic drops, often with a corticosteroid, plus pain relief and keeping the ear dry. Drops reach far higher concentrations at the site than oral drugs. A wick is placed if swelling blocks the canal.

Takeaway: uncomplicated otitis externa: topical drops, not oral antibiotics.

whyNot.C: Oral amoxicillin treats otitis media and does not cover Pseudomonas; oral antibiotics are unnecessary for uncomplicated otitis externa.
whyNot.D: Systemic antibiotics are reserved for spread beyond the canal or immunocompromise.
whyNot.B: Water irrigation worsens maceration and is not treatment.
whyNot.E: There is no evidence of fungal infection, and oral antifungals are not first line.

items.objective: Manage uncomplicated acute otitis externa with topical therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has had left ear pain and fever for 6 days despite oral amoxicillin. His left auricle sticks out forwards and downwards, and the skin behind it is red, swollen, fluctuant and tender. The left tympanic membrane bulges. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). Intravenous antibiotics are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Contrast-enhanced CT of the temporal bones

options.label: C
options.html: Observation for 48 hours before any imaging

options.label: E
options.html: Switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and discharge

items.explanationHtml:
This is acute mastoiditis with a likely subperiosteal abscess. Besides IV antibiotics, contrast CT of the temporal bones (with MRI if intracranial spread is suspected) shows the abscess, bone erosion and complications such as sigmoid sinus thrombosis. It guides drainage: myringotomy, with or without a tube, and mastoidectomy or abscess drainage when needed.

Takeaway: mastoiditis with a fluctuant swelling needs IV antibiotics plus contrast CT to plan drainage.

whyNot.E: Mastoiditis with a probable abscess needs inpatient care and imaging, not outpatient oral therapy.
whyNot.B: He has no meningeal signs; imaging should come first to look for abscess or venous sinus thrombosis.
whyNot.D: Plain films are insensitive and do not show abscess or intracranial spread.
whyNot.C: A fluctuant postauricular swelling suggests a subperiosteal abscess that needs prompt imaging and drainage.

items.objective: Evaluate suspected complicated acute mastoiditis with contrast CT.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has had foul-smelling discharge from her right ear on and off for 18 months. It improves with antibiotic drops but always returns. She has no ear pain. Otoscopy shows a retraction pocket in the upper (pars flaccida) part of the right drum filled with white, flaky debris. Audiometry shows a 30-dB conductive loss on the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Continuous antibiotic ear drops for 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent, painless, foul discharge with keratin debris in a retraction pocket is a cholesteatoma. It keeps growing and destroys bone, and complications include facial palsy, a labyrinthine fistula and intracranial infection. Treatment is surgical removal (tympanomastoid surgery), with long-term follow-up for recurrence.

Takeaway: cholesteatoma is treated surgically; drops only suppress the discharge.

whyNot.B: Drops only calm the surface infection; the keratin sac keeps growing and eroding bone.
whyNot.A: Oral antibiotics do not remove a cholesteatoma.
whyNot.E: A tube does not remove the keratin sac and is not treatment.
whyNot.C: Untreated cholesteatoma can erode the ossicles, labyrinth, facial canal and skull base.

items.objective: Refer cholesteatoma for surgical management.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy is seen for follow-up 3 weeks after treatment of acute otitis media. He is well, without fever or ear pain, and his parents think he hears normally. Speech is normal for age. The left tympanic membrane is not bulging, but there is an amber air-fluid level behind it with reduced mobility. The right ear is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: A second 10-day course of high-dose amoxicillin

options.label: B
options.html: A short course of oral prednisolone

options.label: D
options.html: Oral antihistamine and decongestant for 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Watchful waiting with re-examination in about 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Fluid without signs of acute inflammation is otitis media with effusion, which commonly follows AOM. Most effusions clear within 3 months. A child without risk factors is managed by watchful waiting, with hearing tests if the fluid lasts 3 months or longer. Medicines have no role.

Takeaway: post-AOM effusion in a well child is watched for 3 months; no antibiotics, steroids or decongestants.

whyNot.A: Antibiotics do not speed resolution of effusion without acute infection.
whyNot.B: Corticosteroids are not recommended for otitis media with effusion.
whyNot.D: Antihistamines and decongestants do not help effusion and have side effects.
whyNot.C: Tubes are considered for effusion lasting 3 months or more with hearing loss, or in at-risk children.

items.objective: Manage otitis media with effusion with watchful waiting.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man has had severe burning pain in his left ear for 3 days. Today he cannot close his left eye and his mouth droops on the left. There are clustered vesicles on the left concha and in the ear canal. He reports mild left hearing loss. He has no other neurologic deficits. In addition to eye protection, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent surgical decompression of the facial nerve

items.explanationHtml:
Ear pain, vesicles in the ear and a lower motor neuron facial palsy make up Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Early treatment with a corticosteroid plus an antiviral (valacyclovir, famciclovir or acyclovir) is recommended, ideally within 72 hours, along with eye care. The facial prognosis is worse than in Bell palsy.

Takeaway: Ramsay Hunt syndrome: steroid plus antiviral early, and protect the eye.

whyNot.B: A corticosteroid alone is appropriate for Bell palsy, but zoster oticus also warrants an antiviral.
whyNot.D: Combined antiviral and corticosteroid therapy is preferred for Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
whyNot.A: This is a viral, not bacterial, infection.
whyNot.E: Surgery is not a first-line treatment for Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

items.objective: Treat herpes zoster oticus with combined antiviral and corticosteroid therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has noticed reduced hearing in her right ear over the past year, with a constant high-pitched ringing on that side. She has no vertigo, ear pain or discharge. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows a moderate sensorineural loss on the right, a normal left ear, and poor right-sided speech discrimination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium

items.explanationHtml:
Asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or one-sided tinnitus, especially with speech discrimination that is worse than the tone thresholds predict, suggests a retrocochlear lesion such as a vestibular schwannoma. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals is the test of choice.

Takeaway: asymmetric sensorineural loss or one-sided tinnitus is investigated with gadolinium MRI of the internal auditory canals.

whyNot.B: CT can miss small tumors inside the internal auditory canal.
whyNot.C: Asymmetric sensorineural loss needs investigation now, not later.
whyNot.D: Autoimmune inner-ear disease is usually bilateral and rapidly progressive; laboratory screening is not the first step.
whyNot.E: Tympanometry assesses middle-ear function, which is normal in sensorineural loss.

items.objective: Order MRI of the internal auditory canals for asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man has had a blocked feeling and muffled hearing in his left ear for 2 months. He has had no recent cold or flight. He smokes and sometimes has bloody nasal discharge. Otoscopy shows an amber effusion behind the left tympanic membrane; the right ear is normal. There is a firm 2-cm node in the upper left neck. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Fine-needle aspiration of the left parotid gland

options.label: D
options.html: Intranasal corticosteroid spray and review in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
New one-sided middle-ear effusion in an adult is unusual. With a neck node and bloody nasal discharge, it strongly suggests a nasopharyngeal tumor blocking the eustachian tube. Endoscopic examination of the nasopharynx, with biopsy of any mass, is the next step.

Takeaway: one-sided effusion in an adult: look in the nasopharynx before treating the ear.

whyNot.A: Antibiotics do not treat effusion and would delay diagnosis of a possible tumor.
whyNot.E: A tube relieves the effusion but misses the likely cause in the nasopharynx.
whyNot.D: Waiting is inappropriate with red flags such as a neck node and blood-stained discharge.
whyNot.C: The node is in the neck, and the effusion points to the nasopharynx, not the parotid.

items.objective: Evaluate unilateral adult middle-ear effusion for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old woman hears a whooshing noise in her left ear that keeps time with her heartbeat. Otoscopy shows a red mass behind the lower half of an intact left tympanic membrane; the mass blanches when positive pressure is applied with the pneumatic otoscope. Audiometry shows a mild conductive loss on the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: A course of oral antibiotics and re-examination

options.label: B
options.html: Biopsy of the mass through the tympanic membrane

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the temporal bone and MRI

options.label: D
options.html: Myringotomy to drain the middle ear

items.explanationHtml:
Pulsatile tinnitus and a red, blanching retrotympanic mass suggest a paraganglioma (glomus tympanicum or jugulare). Evaluate with CT of the temporal bone (bone involvement) and MRI (soft-tissue and intracranial extent), not biopsy. Treatment options include surgery, radiotherapy or observation.

Takeaway: a red pulsatile retrotympanic mass needs imaging, never biopsy through the drum.

whyNot.B: Biopsy of a vascular tumor through the drum can cause severe bleeding and is avoided.
whyNot.D: This is not an effusion; incising it risks hemorrhage.
whyNot.A: This is not an infection.
whyNot.E: A middle-ear mass needs imaging to define its extent and plan treatment.

items.objective: Evaluate a suspected middle-ear paraganglioma with imaging rather than biopsy.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had hearing loss in both ears that has worsened over 2 years, along with unsteadiness. She had cataract surgery at age 16. She has no café-au-lait macules or axillary freckling. MRI shows bilateral enhancing masses in the cerebellopontine angles and a small intradural extramedullary mass in the thoracic spine. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are diagnostic of NF2-related schwannomatosis. Juvenile cataract and spinal tumors (schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas) are typical associated findings. Management involves a specialist multidisciplinary team, genetic counseling and screening of relatives.

Takeaway: bilateral vestibular schwannomas = NF2-related schwannomatosis.

whyNot.A: NF1 causes café-au-lait macules, freckling, neurofibromas and optic gliomas, not bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
whyNot.D: Tuberous sclerosis causes cortical tubers, seizures, facial angiofibromas and renal angiomyolipomas.
whyNot.E: VHL causes cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, not schwannomas.
whyNot.C: Sturge-Weber causes a facial port-wine stain with leptomeningeal angiomatosis.

items.objective: Diagnose NF2-related schwannomatosis from bilateral vestibular schwannomas.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old man with heart failure and chronic kidney disease has mild hearing loss in his left ear. MRI shows a 7-mm enhancing mass confined to the left internal auditory canal, consistent with a vestibular schwannoma. He has no imbalance, facial numbness or facial weakness. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Small vestibular schwannomas often grow slowly or not at all. For a small intracanalicular tumor in an older patient with other illnesses, observation with serial MRI ("wait and scan") is appropriate. Stereotactic radiosurgery or surgery is offered if the tumor grows or causes symptoms.

Takeaway: small, stable vestibular schwannomas, especially in older patients, are watched with serial MRI.

whyNot.D: Surgery has real risks and little benefit for a small, asymptomatic tumor in an older man with other illnesses.
whyNot.E: Whole-brain radiation is not used for vestibular schwannoma.
whyNot.C: Chemotherapy has no role in sporadic vestibular schwannoma.
whyNot.A: Corticosteroids do not shrink schwannomas.

items.objective: Select observation for small vestibular schwannomas in appropriate patients.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man who worked outdoors for 40 years has a crusted, ulcerated nodule on the helix of his right ear that has grown over 3 months and bleeds when touched. There is no palpable lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A growing, ulcerated, bleeding lesion on the sun-exposed helix is suspicious for squamous or basal cell carcinoma. A biopsy establishes the diagnosis and depth before definitive excision (often Mohs surgery to spare cartilage) and staging of the parotid and neck nodes.

Takeaway: biopsy any non-healing, growing lesion on the auricle before treating it.

whyNot.D: This is not an infection; delaying diagnosis allows a possible cancer to grow.
whyNot.B: Destroying the lesion without a biopsy loses the diagnosis and margin information.
whyNot.E: Topical fluorouracil is for actinic keratoses and some superficial lesions, not an ulcerated nodule.
whyNot.C: A growing, bleeding nodule needs prompt tissue diagnosis.

items.objective: Biopsy suspicious auricular skin lesions before treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has a jugular foramen paraganglioma causing pulsatile tinnitus and mild hoarseness. Surgical resection is planned. He has episodic headaches and palpitations, and his blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg. Which of the following tests is most important before surgery?
items.explanationHtml:
Head and neck paragangliomas only occasionally secrete catecholamines. Headaches, palpitations and hypertension raise that possibility here. Plasma free (or urine fractionated) metanephrines should be measured before surgery. A secreting tumor needs alpha-blockade first to prevent a hypertensive crisis during the operation.

Takeaway: check metanephrines before operating on any paraganglioma; treat secreting tumors with alpha-blockade first.

whyNot.D: Calcitonin screens for medullary thyroid carcinoma, not catecholamine secretion.
whyNot.A: 5-HIAA screens for carcinoid tumors that secrete serotonin.
whyNot.B: Cortisol tests adrenal cortical function, not catecholamine excess.
whyNot.E: TSH does not detect catecholamine excess.

items.objective: Screen paragangliomas for catecholamine secretion before surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man woke this morning with muffled hearing and ringing in his left ear. He had no ear pain, discharge, trauma or recent flight. Both ear canals and tympanic membranes look normal. A 512-Hz tuning fork on the forehead is heard louder in the right ear. On both sides, air conduction is louder than bone conduction. Which of the following best describes his hearing loss?
items.explanationHtml:
The Weber lateralizes away from the symptomatic left ear, and the Rinne is positive on both sides: a left sensorineural loss. With a sudden onset and a normal ear examination, this suggests sudden sensorineural hearing loss, an urgent condition.

Takeaway: a sudden one-sided loss with Weber to the good ear and a positive Rinne is sensorineural until audiometry says otherwise.

whyNot.A: With left conductive loss, the Weber would go to the left ear and the left Rinne would be negative.
whyNot.E: With right sensorineural loss, the Weber would go to the left ear.
whyNot.D: Right conductive loss would send the Weber right, but the right Rinne would be negative.
whyNot.C: Lateralization of the Weber indicates an asymmetric loss.

items.objective: Use tuning-fork tests to recognize sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: Audiometry the same day confirms a 55-dB sensorineural loss across 4 neighboring frequencies in the left ear, with a normal right ear. He has no vertigo or other neurologic symptoms, and he has no contraindications to any of the treatments listed. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.label: C
options.html: Observation with repeat audiometry in 4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
For idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss, offer a corticosteroid, oral or intratympanic, as early as possible and ideally within 2 weeks of onset. Intratympanic steroid is also used as salvage when recovery is incomplete. Antivirals, vasodilators and antibiotics are not recommended.

Takeaway: sudden sensorineural loss: confirm with audiometry and start a corticosteroid early.

whyNot.E: Antivirals have not been shown to help sudden sensorineural loss and are not recommended.
whyNot.D: There is no bacterial infection.
whyNot.C: Delaying treatment lowers the chance of recovery; steroids work best when started early.
whyNot.B: Amplification may be needed later, but early steroid treatment is the priority.

items.objective: Treat sudden sensorineural hearing loss with early corticosteroids.

items.stemHtml: He starts oral prednisone. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to look for an underlying cause of his hearing loss?

options.label: B
options.html: Comprehensive serologic and autoimmune blood panel

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium

items.explanationHtml:
A small proportion of sudden sensorineural losses are caused by a retrocochlear lesion, most importantly vestibular schwannoma. Evaluate with gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the internal auditory canals, or ABR if MRI is not possible. Routine CT and broad laboratory panels are not recommended.

Takeaway: every sudden sensorineural loss needs a retrocochlear workup, usually MRI of the internal auditory canals.

whyNot.E: Routine CT is not recommended; it misses small retrocochlear lesions.
whyNot.B: Routine laboratory panels have low yield and are not recommended without specific clinical features.
whyNot.A: Carotid disease does not cause isolated sudden hearing loss.
whyNot.C: EEG has no role in evaluating hearing loss.

items.objective: Evaluate sudden sensorineural hearing loss for retrocochlear pathology.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman says she can hear people talking but cannot make out their words, especially in restaurants and on the telephone. Her family says she turns the television up loud. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows symmetric sensorineural loss in both ears, mild at low frequencies and moderate at high frequencies. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals

items.explanationHtml:
Gradual, symmetric, high-frequency sensorineural loss with poor understanding of speech in noise is presbycusis. Treatment is amplification: hearing aids (including over-the-counter devices for mild to moderate loss), assistive listening devices and communication strategies. Treating hearing loss may also help reduce social isolation and cognitive decline.

Takeaway: presbycusis is treated with hearing aids; it does not need imaging or steroids.

whyNot.C: Symmetric, gradual, age-related loss does not need imaging.
whyNot.D: Steroids are for sudden sensorineural loss, not gradual presbycusis.
whyNot.B: Cochlear implants are for severe to profound loss that no longer benefits from hearing aids.
whyNot.A: Tubes treat middle-ear effusion, not sensorineural loss.

items.objective: Manage presbycusis with amplification.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has had slowly worsening hearing in her left ear for 2 years, noticeably worse since her pregnancy last year. Her father had similar hearing loss that improved after an operation. Both tympanic membranes are normal and mobile. The Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne shows bone conduction louder than air conduction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Conductive loss with a normal tympanic membrane in a young adult, worse during pregnancy and with a family history, is typical of otosclerosis (stapes fixation). Management is a hearing aid or stapes surgery (stapedotomy).

Takeaway: conductive loss with a normal drum in a young woman suggests otosclerosis.

whyNot.A: Cholesteatoma shows an abnormal drum with debris and usually causes discharge.
whyNot.C: An effusion would make the drum look abnormal and move poorly.
whyNot.B: Ménière disease causes episodic vertigo and fluctuating sensorineural loss.
whyNot.E: Presbycusis is a sensorineural loss in older adults.

items.objective: Diagnose otosclerosis from its typical presentation.

items.stemHtml: A healthy term boy fails the otoacoustic emission hearing screen in his right ear in the newborn nursery, and again on a repeat screen at 2 weeks of age. His parents are relieved that he startles to loud sounds at home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Diagnostic auditory brainstem response testing before 3 months of age

options.label: C
options.html: Re-evaluate only if speech is delayed at 2 years

options.label: D
options.html: Reassurance because he startles to loud sounds

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat otoacoustic emission testing at 12 months of age

items.explanationHtml:
Newborn hearing programs follow the 1-3-6 goals: screen by 1 month, confirm with a full diagnostic audiological evaluation (diagnostic ABR) by 3 months, and begin intervention by 6 months. A failed screen always needs diagnostic testing, and parents' impressions are not reliable.

Takeaway: a failed newborn hearing screen means diagnostic ABR by 3 months of age.

whyNot.E: Waiting a year misses the window for early intervention.
whyNot.D: Startling does not exclude a significant hearing loss, especially a one-sided one.
whyNot.B: Imaging may follow once a hearing loss is confirmed, but the first step is diagnostic audiology.
whyNot.C: Waiting for speech delay forfeits the benefit of early amplification.

items.objective: Follow up a failed newborn hearing screen within the 1-3-6 timeline.

items.stemHtml: An 80-year-old man noticed muffled hearing in his left ear after a shower 2 days ago. He often cleans his ears with cotton swabs. The left ear canal is completely blocked by hard brown wax; the right canal is clear. The Weber lateralizes to the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Hearing aid fitting for the left ear

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals

items.explanationHtml:
Cerumen impaction is a common cause of acute conductive loss, especially in older adults and cotton-swab users. Treat with softening drops and removal by irrigation (if the drum is known to be intact) or by instruments. Recheck hearing afterwards.

Takeaway: impacted cerumen causing conductive loss: soften and remove, then recheck hearing.

whyNot.B: The loss is conductive with an obvious cause; imaging is not needed.
whyNot.D: Steroids treat sudden sensorineural loss, not cerumen impaction.
whyNot.A: Removing the wax will likely restore hearing.
whyNot.C: There is no infection, so antibiotics have no role.

items.objective: Manage cerumen impaction as a cause of conductive hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has worked for 20 years in a metal-stamping plant and rarely wore ear protection. He has trouble hearing his grandchildren and has a constant high-pitched ringing in both ears. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows a symmetric sensorineural loss with its greatest dip at 4000 Hz and partial recovery at 8000 Hz. Which of the following is the most important recommendation?

options.label: B
options.html: Consistent hearing protection and reduced noise exposure

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals

items.explanationHtml:
A bilateral sensorineural loss with a notch near 4 kHz after years of noise exposure is noise-induced hearing loss. The damage is permanent, so the priority is preventing further loss with hearing protection and less exposure. Workplace programs are triggered by an average exposure of 85 dBA over 8 hours. Amplification and tinnitus management help with the existing loss.

Takeaway: noise-induced loss (4 kHz notch) is permanent; prevent progression with hearing protection.

whyNot.A: Steroids are not effective for chronic noise-induced loss.
whyNot.D: Symmetric loss with a noise notch and a clear exposure history does not need imaging.
whyNot.E: This is a sensorineural, not a conductive, loss.
whyNot.C: High-dose salicylates cause tinnitus rather than relieving it.

items.objective: Recommend prevention for noise-induced hearing loss.

items.stemHtml:
A 19-year-old man is referred because of hearing loss in both ears, first noticed at age 12. His maternal uncle needed dialysis in his 30s. Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. Audiometry shows symmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss. Laboratory studies show:

TestResultReference range
Creatinine1.4 mg/dL (124 µmol/L)0.6-1.2 mg/dL (53-106 µmol/L)
Urea nitrogen (BUN)22 mg/dL7-18 mg/dL
Urinalysis: blood3+, with dysmorphic red cells and red cell castsnegative
Urinalysis: protein2+negative
Complement C3normalnormal

Slit-lamp examination shows a conical bulge of the anterior lens surface in both eyes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Hematuria with red cell casts progressing to kidney failure, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and anterior lenticonus, with affected males on the mother's side, indicate X-linked Alport syndrome. It is caused by a defect in the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen, which is present in the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea and lens capsule. ACE inhibitors slow progression of the kidney disease.

Takeaway: hematuria plus sensorineural hearing loss plus lens changes = Alport syndrome (type IV collagen).

whyNot.D: IgA nephropathy causes episodic hematuria after infections, without deafness or lens changes.
whyNot.C: This vasculitis causes sinus, lung and kidney disease, sometimes with conductive loss from middle-ear involvement, but not lenticonus.
whyNot.E: This follows a streptococcal infection with low C3 and does not cause deafness.
whyNot.B: Fabry disease causes neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas and corneal opacities, not anterior lenticonus with hematuria from childhood.

items.objective: Diagnose Alport syndrome from renal, auditory and ocular findings.

items.stemHtml: A 10-day-old boy failed his newborn hearing screen, and diagnostic ABR shows moderate sensorineural loss in both ears. He was small for gestational age, with microcephaly, petechiae and a platelet count of 62,000/mm3 (150,000-400,000/mm3) at birth. Cytomegalovirus PCR on a saliva sample collected on day 5 is positive and is confirmed in urine. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Newborns with symptomatic congenital CMV, here with microcephaly, thrombocytopenia and hearing loss, are treated with oral valganciclovir for 6 months, started within the first month of life. This improves hearing and developmental outcomes. Neutropenia is the main adverse effect, so blood counts are monitored. Hearing must be checked repeatedly, because the loss can progress.

Takeaway: symptomatic congenital CMV: 6 months of oral valganciclovir, plus serial hearing tests.

whyNot.B: Acyclovir treats neonatal herpes simplex and has poor activity against cytomegalovirus.
whyNot.D: Symptomatic congenital CMV with hearing loss benefits from antiviral treatment started in the first month.
whyNot.A: CMV immune globulin is not an established treatment for congenital infection.
whyNot.C: Foscarnet is a second-line drug for resistant CMV in immunocompromised patients and is toxic.

items.objective: Treat symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection to protect hearing.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman has had brief episodes of intense spinning for 1 week. They occur when she lies down, rolls to the right in bed or bends over, and each lasts less than a minute. Her hearing is normal. With the head turned to the right during the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, upbeating torsional nystagmus starts after a few seconds and stops within 30 seconds. The rest of the neurologic examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Brief positional vertigo with a positive right Dix-Hallpike test is right posterior canal BPPV. The treatment is a canalith repositioning maneuver (Epley), which moves the otoconia back into the utricle. No imaging or medicines are needed.

Takeaway: positive Dix-Hallpike: do the Epley maneuver; no imaging or drugs.

whyNot.D: Typical BPPV with a normal neurologic exam does not need imaging.
whyNot.B: Vestibular suppressants do not treat the cause and slow compensation.
whyNot.E: Steroids have no role in BPPV.
whyNot.C: This is maintenance treatment for Ménière disease.

items.objective: Treat posterior canal BPPV with canalith repositioning.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes and atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) has had continuous vertigo, nausea and unsteadiness for 5 hours. He cannot walk without support. His hearing is unchanged. Examination shows left-beating nystagmus on left gaze and right-beating nystagmus on right gaze. A rapid head impulse test is normal in both directions. Alternate cover testing shows a small vertical misalignment of the eyes. A noncontrast CT of the head is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge with oral meclizine and follow-up

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted imaging

items.explanationHtml:
In an acute vestibular syndrome, a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation point to a central cause, most often a posterior circulation stroke. Inability to walk and vascular risk factors add to the concern. CT misses most posterior fossa infarcts. Obtain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging, which may need repeating if done very early.

Takeaway: acute vertigo with a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew = stroke until MRI proves otherwise.

whyNot.A: His findings are central; discharging him risks missing a cerebellar or brainstem stroke.
whyNot.B: The vertigo is continuous, not positional, so BPPV is not the diagnosis.
whyNot.D: A normal head impulse test with direction-changing nystagmus and skew does not fit vestibular neuritis.
whyNot.E: CT is insensitive for posterior fossa infarcts; MRI is needed now.

items.objective: Use bedside oculomotor findings to identify central vertigo and order MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had constant spinning vertigo with vomiting since she woke yesterday, 10 days after a viral upper respiratory infection. Her hearing is normal and she has no headache. Examination shows left-beating horizontal-torsional nystagmus that does not change direction with gaze and is reduced when she fixes on a target. A rapid head turn to the right produces a catch-up saccade. There is no skew deviation. She can walk with support. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Acute, continuous vertigo with one-direction nystagmus beating away from the lesion (left-beating), an abnormal head impulse to the right, no skew and normal hearing indicates right vestibular neuritis. Management is a short course of a vestibular suppressant and antiemetic for the first days, then early mobilization and vestibular rehabilitation.

Takeaway: vestibular neuritis: continuous vertigo, normal hearing and a peripheral pattern on bedside testing.

whyNot.D: Labyrinthitis also causes hearing loss, and her hearing is normal.
whyNot.A: BPPV causes brief positional spells, not continuous vertigo for a day.
whyNot.C: Ménière attacks last hours and come with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness.
whyNot.B: Her findings are all peripheral: an abnormal head impulse, one-direction nystagmus and no skew.

items.objective: Diagnose vestibular neuritis from bedside findings.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has had 5 episodes of vertigo in 4 months. Each lasts 2 to 3 hours and comes with roaring tinnitus and fullness in his left ear. Audiometry shows a low-frequency sensorineural loss on the left that improves between attacks. MRI of the internal auditory canals is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line measure to reduce the frequency of attacks?
items.explanationHtml:
This is Ménière disease. First-line measures to reduce attacks are education, salt restriction and limiting caffeine and alcohol, with diuretics or betahistine as options. Vestibular suppressants are used only during attacks. Intratympanic steroids, then ablative options, are kept for refractory disease.

Takeaway: Ménière maintenance starts with a low-salt diet; suppressants are for attacks only.

whyNot.A: Vestibular suppressants are for acute attacks only; daily use slows central compensation.
whyNot.D: Gentamicin ablation is reserved for disabling vertigo that does not respond to conservative and medical measures.
whyNot.E: Labyrinthectomy destroys hearing and is a last resort.
whyNot.C: Repositioning treats BPPV, not endolymphatic hydrops.

items.objective: Select first-line maintenance therapy for Ménière disease.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has had recurrent spells of vertigo for 2 years, each lasting 30 minutes to several hours. During most spells she also has a throbbing headache with sensitivity to light. She has had migraine headaches since adolescence. Between spells, her neurologic examination, Dix-Hallpike test and audiogram are all normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent vestibular episodes lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours, with migraine features (headache, photophobia) during many of them, in a person with migraine and a normal audiogram, fit vestibular migraine. Treat as migraine: avoid triggers, use acute migraine treatment, and add preventive drugs for frequent attacks.

Takeaway: episodic vertigo with migraine features and normal hearing suggests vestibular migraine.

whyNot.B: Ménière disease requires documented low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss, which she does not have.
whyNot.A: BPPV causes brief positional spells with a positive Dix-Hallpike test.
whyNot.E: A schwannoma causes progressive one-sided hearing loss, not episodic vertigo with migraine.
whyNot.C: Recurrent posterior circulation ischemia is unlikely in a young woman with typical migraine features and a normal exam.

items.objective: Diagnose vestibular migraine.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 28-year-old woman is going on a 7-day cruise and asks for something to prevent the severe seasickness she had on a previous boat trip. She takes no medicines and has no glaucoma or urinary symptoms. Which of the following is the most effective preventive option?

options.label: B
options.html: Oral haloperidol each night at bedtime

options.label: D
options.html: Oral ondansetron as needed once symptoms start

options.label: E
options.html: Scopolamine patch applied hours before departure

items.explanationHtml:
Transdermal scopolamine, applied behind the ear several hours before travel and replaced every 3 days, is among the most effective preventive drugs for motion sickness. First-generation antihistamines (meclizine, dimenhydrinate) are alternatives. Anticholinergic side effects include dry mouth, drowsiness, blurred vision and, rarely, angle closure or confusion. Patients should wash their hands after handling the patch, because touching the eye with residue dilates the pupil.

Takeaway: scopolamine patch before travel is first-line prophylaxis for motion sickness.

whyNot.D: Ondansetron is less effective for motion sickness, and waiting until symptoms start reduces any benefit.
whyNot.C: Metoclopramide is not first line for motion sickness and can cause dystonic reactions.
whyNot.B: Antipsychotics are not used for motion sickness.
whyNot.A: Benzodiazepines sedate and are not the preferred prophylaxis.

items.objective: Choose prophylaxis for motion sickness.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man had vestibular neuritis 3 months ago. His vertigo resolved within a week, but he still feels unsteady and briefly off balance whenever he turns his head quickly, especially in crowded places. He has taken meclizine 3 times daily since the illness began. Examination shows a catch-up saccade on quick head turns to the left and is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat MRI of the brain with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
Ongoing imbalance with head movement after vestibular neuritis reflects incomplete central compensation, which long-term meclizine can make worse. Vestibular rehabilitation uses gaze-stabilization, balance and habituation exercises to speed recovery. Vestibular suppressants should be stopped.

Takeaway: persistent imbalance after vestibular loss: vestibular rehabilitation, and stop suppressants.

whyNot.B: Long-term vestibular suppressants slow the brain's compensation.
whyNot.D: Imaging adds nothing when the findings fit incomplete compensation after neuritis.
whyNot.C: Ablation would worsen vestibular function.
whyNot.A: Steroids months after the event do not help compensation.

items.objective: Use vestibular rehabilitation for chronic imbalance after vestibular injury.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old wrestler has had a painful swelling of his right ear since a match yesterday. The front of the right auricle is tense, purple and fluctuant, and its contours are lost. The skin is intact, and there is no fever. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Elective plastic surgery once the swelling settles

options.label: B
options.html: Ice packs and review in 2 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: Incision and drainage followed by a compressive bolster dressing

items.explanationHtml:
An auricular hematoma must be drained promptly, by incision or aspiration, and followed by a compressive bolster to prevent reaccumulation. Review within a day or so. Untreated, blood cuts the cartilage off from its perichondrial blood supply, causing necrosis and a permanent cauliflower ear.

Takeaway: auricular hematoma: drain early and compress to prevent cauliflower ear.

whyNot.B: Delay allows the cartilage to necrose and fibrose into a cauliflower ear.
whyNot.E: There is no infection; the problem is a collection of blood.
whyNot.D: Without compression, the hematoma usually reaccumulates.
whyNot.A: Reconstruction after deformity is a poor substitute for prompt drainage.

items.objective: Manage auricular hematoma with drainage and compression.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man felt sharp pain in his left ear while cleaning it with a cotton swab 1 day ago. There was a small amount of blood. He has mildly muffled hearing, but no vertigo, tinnitus or facial weakness. Otoscopy shows a small slit-like perforation in the posterior-inferior part of the left drum, with no discharge. Weber lateralizes to the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Irrigation of the canal to remove blood

options.label: B
options.html: Keep the ear dry and arrange follow-up with audiometry

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent surgical repair of the drum

items.explanationHtml:
Small traumatic perforations without inner-ear symptoms usually heal spontaneously within weeks. Keep water out of the ear, avoid ototoxic drops, and arrange follow-up with audiometry. Refer for repair if it has not healed after about 2 to 3 months. Vertigo, sensorineural loss or facial weakness would need urgent ENT referral.

Takeaway: most small traumatic eardrum perforations heal: keep dry, avoid ototoxic drops, follow up.

whyNot.E: Small traumatic perforations usually heal on their own; repair is for failure to heal.
whyNot.C: Aminoglycoside drops are avoided with a perforation because of the risk of ototoxicity.
whyNot.A: Irrigation through a perforation can introduce infection and should be avoided.
whyNot.D: Steroids are not indicated for a traumatic perforation with conductive loss.

items.objective: Manage an uncomplicated traumatic tympanic membrane perforation.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after her brother saw her put a small round button battery from a toy into her left ear. She is crying and pulling at the ear. Otoscopy shows a shiny metallic disc deep in the left canal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the temporal bone before any removal attempt

options.label: D
options.html: Irrigation of the canal with warm water

options.label: E
options.html: Mineral oil drops and removal at a clinic visit in 2 days

items.explanationHtml:
A button battery in the ear (or nose, or esophagus) is an emergency. Electrolysis produces hydroxide and causes alkaline liquefactive necrosis within hours, which can perforate the drum and damage the middle ear and facial nerve. Remove it immediately under direct vision, under sedation if needed, without irrigation. Then inspect for burns and arrange follow-up.

Takeaway: a button battery in the ear needs immediate removal, without irrigation.

whyNot.D: Irrigation of a button battery adds an electrolyte solution that speeds tissue injury.
whyNot.E: A delay of even hours allows alkaline liquefactive necrosis.
whyNot.A: Drops do not address the battery and can worsen the injury.
whyNot.B: Imaging should not delay removal of a visible battery.

items.objective: Manage an aural button battery foreign body as an emergency.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man woke at night with a loud buzzing and scratching in his right ear. Otoscopy shows a live moth moving in the ear canal; the drum looks intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?

options.label: A
options.html: Attempt immediate removal with forceps while the insect moves

options.label: B
options.html: Instill mineral oil or lidocaine into the canal

options.label: C
options.html: Irrigate the canal with cold water

options.label: D
options.html: Refer for removal under general anesthesia

items.explanationHtml:
A live insect in the ear should be killed first by filling the canal with mineral oil or lidocaine. Once it is still, it can be removed with forceps, suction or irrigation (if the drum is intact). This reduces pain and the risk of injury to the canal and drum.

Takeaway: kill a live insect in the ear with oil or lidocaine before removing it.

whyNot.A: A moving insect is hard to grasp and may be pushed deeper, damaging the canal or drum.
whyNot.C: Cold water can cause vertigo and does not kill the insect quickly; it is not the first step.
whyNot.E: There is no infection to treat.
whyNot.D: Most insects can be removed in the emergency department once immobilized.

items.objective: Manage a live insect in the external ear canal.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man was hit by a car 2 days ago. He has a right temporal bone fracture and a small subdural hematoma that does not need surgery. He is alert. Clear fluid continues to drain from his right ear, and beta-2 transferrin testing confirms cerebrospinal fluid. He has no fever or meningeal signs, and his facial nerve function is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the leak at this time?

options.label: A
options.html: Antibiotic ear drops four times daily

options.label: B
options.html: Head elevation, avoid straining and nose-blowing, and observe

options.label: C
options.html: Immediate surgical repair of the dural tear

options.label: D
options.html: Pack the ear canal tightly with gauze

items.explanationHtml:
Most traumatic CSF otorrhea stops within days with conservative care: head of bed up, bed rest, stool softeners, and no straining or nose-blowing. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended. A lumbar drain or surgical repair is considered if the leak persists, and meningitis is treated if it develops.

Takeaway: traumatic CSF otorrhea: conservative care first, without prophylactic antibiotics.

whyNot.E: Prophylactic antibiotics for traumatic CSF leaks are not recommended; watch for infection instead.
whyNot.D: Packing may trap fluid and raise the risk of infection; leave the canal open.
whyNot.C: Most traumatic leaks stop within about a week with conservative care.
whyNot.A: Drops do not treat the leak, and instilling them into a CSF-leaking ear is avoided.

items.objective: Manage traumatic cerebrospinal fluid otorrhea conservatively.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with a left temporal bone fracture from a fall had normal facial movement in the emergency department. On the second hospital day she develops incomplete weakness of the left side of her face. She can still close the left eye with effort. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Botulinum toxin injection to the right face

options.label: C
options.html: Emergency surgical decompression of the facial nerve

items.explanationHtml:
After a temporal bone fracture, delayed-onset or incomplete facial weakness usually reflects swelling within the facial canal and has an excellent prognosis. It is managed with observation and corticosteroids, plus eye care. Immediate, complete paralysis suggests transection or a bone fragment and leads to electrodiagnostic testing and consideration of surgery.

Takeaway: delayed or incomplete traumatic facial palsy recovers well with conservative care; immediate complete palsy may need surgery.

whyNot.C: Surgery is considered for immediate, complete paralysis with poor electrical findings, not delayed incomplete weakness.
whyNot.E: This is traumatic swelling of the nerve, not viral reactivation.
whyNot.A: Botulinum toxin is used much later for asymmetry or synkinesis, not acute palsy.
whyNot.D: Nerve transfer is for permanent nerve loss with no chance of recovery.

items.objective: Use the timing and completeness of traumatic facial palsy to guide management.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman has had a painful, blocked left ear since a flight yesterday. She had a cold during the trip. Her hearing is mildly muffled, but she has no vertigo or tinnitus. The left drum is retracted with a small area of bleeding in it and an amber effusion behind it. The Weber lateralizes to the left, and the left Rinne is negative. She plans to scuba dive next week. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

options.label: A
options.html: Analgesia, decongestant and no diving until healed

options.label: B
options.html: Dive as planned, equalizing every few meters

options.label: C
options.html: Myringotomy today to drain the effusion

options.label: D
options.html: Oral prednisone and urgent audiometry for inner-ear injury

items.explanationHtml:
This is middle-ear barotrauma: pain, a retracted bruised drum and conductive loss after descent with a blocked eustachian tube. It is self-limited, so give pain relief and decongestants, and advise no flying or diving until symptoms and the examination are normal. Vertigo or sensorineural loss would need urgent evaluation for inner-ear injury.

Takeaway: middle-ear barotrauma: symptomatic care and no diving until healed; inner-ear symptoms need urgent evaluation.

whyNot.C: Middle-ear barotrauma usually resolves on its own; procedures are for severe or persistent cases.
whyNot.D: She has no vertigo or sensorineural loss, so there is no sign of inner-ear barotrauma.
whyNot.E: Hyperbaric oxygen treats decompression sickness, not middle-ear barotrauma after a flight.
whyNot.B: Diving with a damaged ear and a blocked eustachian tube risks worse barotrauma.

items.objective: Manage middle-ear barotrauma.

items.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old man has been receiving intravenous gentamicin and ampicillin for 12 days for enterococcal endocarditis of a native valve. Today he says the hallway seems to jump when he walks, and he feels unsteady in the dark. His hearing is unchanged. Results:

TestDay 1Day 12Reference range
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL (88 µmol/L)1.9 mg/dL (168 µmol/L)0.6-1.2 mg/dL (53-106 µmol/L)
Urea nitrogen (BUN)14 mg/dL31 mg/dL7-18 mg/dL
Gentamicin troughbelow 1 µg/mL2.6 µg/mLtarget below 1 µg/mL

A quick head turn to either side produces a catch-up saccade. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add furosemide to improve gentamicin clearance

options.label: B
options.html: Continue gentamicin at the same dose and start meclizine

options.label: C
options.html: Lower the gentamicin dose by half and recheck the level in 1 week

options.label: D
options.html: Order MRI of the brain before changing therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Stop gentamicin and continue ampicillin with ceftriaxone

items.explanationHtml:
Oscillopsia, unsteadiness in the dark and bilateral abnormal head impulses on gentamicin, with rising creatinine and a high trough, indicate aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity together with nephrotoxicity. Stop the aminoglycoside. For Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis, ampicillin plus ceftriaxone is an effective regimen without aminoglycoside toxicity. Arrange vestibular and hearing testing, and vestibular rehabilitation.

Takeaway: new ototoxicity on an aminoglycoside: stop it and switch to an effective alternative.

whyNot.B: Continuing the drug risks more permanent vestibular and cochlear damage, and meclizine slows compensation.
whyNot.C: Ototoxicity has already appeared; an effective non-aminoglycoside alternative exists.
whyNot.A: Loop diuretics add to ototoxicity and do not meaningfully increase aminoglycoside clearance.
whyNot.D: The findings fit bilateral aminoglycoside vestibulotoxicity; changing the drug should not wait for imaging.

items.objective: Recognize aminoglycoside ototoxicity and change therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman is about to start a regimen that includes intravenous amikacin for several months for a drug-resistant mycobacterial lung infection. She has normal hearing and kidney function. Which of the following should be done before the first dose?

options.label: C
options.html: Electronystagmography only if she becomes dizzy

options.label: E
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals

items.explanationHtml:
Long courses of aminoglycosides, especially the mainly cochleotoxic amikacin, need baseline audiometry (including high frequencies) and repeat testing during treatment. This detects high-frequency loss before it reaches speech frequencies. Also monitor drug levels and kidney function, and ask about tinnitus, fullness and imbalance at each visit.

Takeaway: get a baseline high-frequency audiogram before prolonged aminoglycoside therapy, then monitor.

whyNot.E: Imaging has no role in screening for drug ototoxicity.
whyNot.C: Baseline hearing testing is needed before treatment to detect early cochlear loss.
whyNot.D: Testing family members is not part of routine pretreatment workup.
whyNot.B: Calcium monitoring does not detect aminoglycoside ototoxicity.

items.objective: Monitor hearing during prolonged aminoglycoside therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy with localized, non-metastatic hepatoblastoma is starting cisplatin-based chemotherapy. His parents are worried about hearing loss. Which of the following measures has been shown to reduce the risk of cisplatin-induced hearing loss in this setting?

options.label: A
options.html: Amifostine given before each cisplatin dose

options.label: B
options.html: Furosemide given with each cisplatin dose

options.label: C
options.html: Gentamicin prophylaxis during periods of neutropenia

options.label: E
options.html: Sodium thiosulfate given about 6 hours after each cisplatin dose

items.explanationHtml:
Sodium thiosulfate, given about 6 hours after cisplatin, binds platinum in the circulation and reduces cisplatin-induced hearing loss in children with localized, non-metastatic solid tumors. The delay is chosen to protect the cochlea without compromising tumor control. Children on cisplatin also need audiological monitoring at each cycle.

Takeaway: in children with localized solid tumors, delayed sodium thiosulfate reduces cisplatin hearing loss.

whyNot.B: Loop diuretics add to cochlear injury and do not protect hearing.
whyNot.A: Amifostine has not been shown to reliably prevent cisplatin ototoxicity and is not recommended for this purpose.
whyNot.C: Aminoglycosides are themselves ototoxic and would increase the risk.
whyNot.D: Salicylates are ototoxic and increase bleeding risk with chemotherapy.

items.objective: Identify an otoprotective strategy for pediatric cisplatin therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis increased his aspirin intake on his own to control joint pain. Over 2 weeks he has developed ringing in both ears and mildly muffled hearing. He has no vertigo. Otoscopy is normal, and audiometry shows a mild, symmetric sensorineural loss. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Add furosemide to speed salicylate excretion

options.label: C
options.html: Measure a serum salicylate level and reduce or stop the aspirin

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the internal auditory canals

options.label: E
options.html: Oral prednisone for sudden hearing loss

items.explanationHtml:
Tinnitus and a mild, symmetric sensorineural loss on high-dose aspirin suggest salicylate ototoxicity. Check the serum salicylate level, watching also for systemic toxicity, and lower or stop the dose. Hearing typically recovers within days. A different approach to his arthritis pain is needed.

Takeaway: salicylate ototoxicity is reversible: check the level and reduce the dose.

whyNot.D: Symmetric loss with a clear drug cause does not need imaging.
whyNot.E: This is a gradual, drug-related, reversible loss, not idiopathic sudden sensorineural loss.
whyNot.B: The loss is expected to recover once the salicylate is reduced.
whyNot.A: Loop diuretics are ototoxic and do not treat salicylate toxicity.

items.objective: Manage salicylate-induced tinnitus and hearing loss.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman has acute pyelonephritis and needs intravenous antibiotics. She is hemodynamically stable. Two years ago genetic testing showed that she carries the mitochondrial MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant, after her brother became deaf following a course of gentamicin. Local resistance data show that the organism is likely to be susceptible to third-generation cephalosporins. Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic?

options.label: D
options.html: Intravenous gentamicin with daily trough levels

items.explanationHtml:
Carriers of the MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant have a very high risk of permanent hearing loss after any aminoglycoside, even a single dose at therapeutic levels. Aminoglycosides should be avoided unless no effective alternative exists for a life-threatening infection. Ceftriaxone is an appropriate choice here. The variant should be recorded as a drug alert for her and her maternal relatives.

Takeaway: known MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G carriers should avoid aminoglycosides whenever an alternative exists.

whyNot.D: Carriers can lose hearing after a single dose even at normal levels; aminoglycosides should be avoided when alternatives exist.
whyNot.E: All aminoglycosides carry the same risk in carriers of this variant.
whyNot.B: Monitoring does not prevent the abrupt, permanent loss seen in carriers.
whyNot.A: Inhaled tobramycin does not treat pyelonephritis and is still an aminoglycoside.

items.objective: Avoid aminoglycosides in carriers of mitochondrial ototoxicity susceptibility variants.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman takes quinine tablets each night, bought abroad, for nocturnal leg cramps. She reports ringing in her ears and blurred vision for a week. Her platelet count is 54,000/mm3 (150,000-400,000/mm3), with no bleeding. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add oral prednisone and continue quinine

options.label: B
options.html: Reduce quinine to every other night

options.label: C
options.html: Stop quinine and recheck her platelet count

options.label: D
options.html: Switch to hydroxychloroquine for the cramps

items.explanationHtml:
Tinnitus and visual blurring (cinchonism) with thrombocytopenia in a patient taking quinine indicate quinine toxicity, with possible quinine-induced immune thrombocytopenia. Stop quinine and monitor platelets, which recover over days. Quinine is not recommended for leg cramps; stretching is the first measure.

Takeaway: quinine for leg cramps is unsafe; stop it if tinnitus or thrombocytopenia develop.

whyNot.B: Any quinine can provoke drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia; it should be stopped.
whyNot.A: Continuing the cause of drug-induced thrombocytopenia is unsafe.
whyNot.D: Hydroxychloroquine has no role in leg cramps and is related to quinine.
whyNot.E: Platelet transfusion is not needed without bleeding, and quinine must be stopped.

items.objective: Recognize and manage quinine toxicity.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease and acute decompensated heart failure received a large intravenous push of furosemide. Within an hour he reported bilateral tinnitus and muffled hearing, which resolved by the next day. He still needs high-dose loop diuretic therapy. Which of the following changes is most likely to prevent recurrence while keeping diuresis?

options.label: A
options.html: Add gentamicin to treat possible infection

options.label: B
options.html: Give the furosemide as a slow intravenous infusion

options.label: C
options.html: Give the same dose as a faster push

items.explanationHtml:
Loop diuretic ototoxicity depends on the peak concentration and is more likely in kidney failure and with large, rapid IV doses. Giving high doses as a slow infusion (often cited as no faster than about 4 mg/min for furosemide) maintains diuresis while lowering peak levels. Avoid other ototoxic drugs at the same time.

Takeaway: prevent loop diuretic ototoxicity by avoiding rapid high-dose IV pushes, especially in kidney failure.

whyNot.E: A thiazide alone is usually insufficient in advanced kidney disease and decompensated heart failure.
whyNot.A: Aminoglycosides add to ototoxicity and are not indicated.
whyNot.C: Higher peak concentrations increase ototoxicity.
whyNot.D: Salicylates are ototoxic and can blunt diuretic response.

items.objective: Reduce the risk of loop diuretic ototoxicity by changing administration.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for 5 months. Her hallucinations have resolved, but she has had no menstrual period for 3 months and notices milky fluid from both nipples. A pregnancy test is negative. Refer to the midsagittal schematic of dopaminergic pathways and sites. Dopamine D2 blockade at which labelled site best explains her new symptoms?
items.explanationHtml:
Dopamine released from hypothalamic neurons into the portal vessels of the pituitary stalk (the tuberoinfundibular pathway, site D) tonically inhibits lactotrophs. Risperidone blocks D2 receptors there, so prolactin rises, causing galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Risperidone and paliperidone raise prolactin more than most antipsychotics.

Takeaway: antipsychotic-induced galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea come from D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway.

whyNot.A: Site A is the mesocortical pathway to the prefrontal cortex; reduced signalling there is linked to negative and cognitive symptoms, not to prolactin.
whyNot.B: Site B is the nigrostriatal pathway; blockade there causes parkinsonism and dystonia.
whyNot.C: Site C is the mesolimbic pathway to the nucleus accumbens, where blockade relieves positive symptoms; it does not control prolactin.
whyNot.E: Site E is the area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone) in the medulla; blockade there suppresses nausea.

items.objective: Link antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia to D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is given intramuscular haloperidol in the emergency department for agitation and paranoid delusions. Eighteen hours later his neck twists painfully to the right and his eyes are fixed upward. He is afebrile and alert. Refer to the midsagittal schematic of dopaminergic pathways and sites. D2 blockade at which labelled site is chiefly responsible for this reaction?
items.explanationHtml:
This is acute dystonia (torticollis and an oculogyric crisis) within a day of a high-potency D2 blocker. Blocking D2 receptors in the striatum, the target of the nigrostriatal pathway (site B), unbalances dopamine and acetylcholine in the basal ganglia. It responds within minutes to an anticholinergic such as benztropine or to diphenhydramine.

Takeaway: extrapyramidal effects of antipsychotics come from nigrostriatal D2 blockade.

whyNot.A: Mesocortical blockade (site A) is linked to blunted motivation and cognition, not to sudden muscle spasm.
whyNot.C: Mesolimbic blockade (site C) gives the antipsychotic effect, not abnormal postures.
whyNot.D: Tuberoinfundibular blockade (site D) raises prolactin.
whyNot.E: Area postrema blockade (site E) is antiemetic and does not cause dystonia.

items.objective: Attribute acute dystonia to antipsychotic blockade of nigrostriatal D2 receptors.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy is given prochlorperazine, a phenothiazine that blocks dopamine D2 receptors, for persistent nausea, and her nausea improves. Refer to the midsagittal schematic of dopaminergic pathways and sites. Blockade at which labelled site most directly accounts for the antiemetic effect?
items.explanationHtml:
The area postrema (site E) lies in the floor of the fourth ventricle, outside the blood-brain barrier. Its chemoreceptor trigger zone carries D2 receptors (and 5-HT3 and NK1 receptors) and relays emetic signals to the vomiting centre. D2 blockers such as prochlorperazine, metoclopramide and haloperidol act here, which is also why they can cause extrapyramidal effects.

Takeaway: D2 antagonists are antiemetic through the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema.

whyNot.A: Site A, the mesocortical projection, has no role in vomiting.
whyNot.B: Site B, the nigrostriatal pathway, controls movement; blocking it causes extrapyramidal effects.
whyNot.C: Site C, the mesolimbic pathway, is the target for the antipsychotic effect, not nausea.
whyNot.D: Site D, the tuberoinfundibular pathway, controls prolactin release.

items.objective: Identify the area postrema as the site of the antiemetic action of D2 antagonists.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has taken haloperidol for schizophrenia for 9 years. His family notices continuous lip smacking, tongue thrusting and writhing movements of his fingers. His psychiatrist starts valbenazine. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
The movements are tardive dyskinesia, a late effect of long-term D2 blockade thought to involve supersensitive striatal dopamine receptors. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine inhibit VMAT2, which packages dopamine into presynaptic vesicles, so less dopamine is released onto the supersensitive receptors.

Takeaway: tardive dyskinesia is treated with VMAT2 inhibitors, which deplete presynaptic dopamine stores.

whyNot.B: This is how benztropine works; anticholinergics tend to worsen tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.A: Dopamine agonists would worsen psychosis and are not used for tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.D: COMT inhibitors (entacapone) prolong levodopa action in Parkinson disease.
whyNot.C: This describes amantadine or memantine, not valbenazine.

items.objective: State the mechanism of VMAT2 inhibitors used for tardive dyskinesia.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after taking an illicit drug at a party. He is agitated and violent, believes the staff are plotting against him, and has vertical and horizontal nystagmus, hypertension and a blunted response to pain. Over the following day he becomes withdrawn, with flat affect and very little speech. Blockade of which of the following receptors best explains how this drug reproduces both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia?
items.explanationHtml:
Nystagmus, hypertension, analgesia and violent psychosis point to phencyclidine. PCP and ketamine are noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonists. Unlike stimulants, which mostly mimic positive symptoms by releasing dopamine, NMDA antagonists also produce negative and cognitive symptoms. This supports the hypothesis that hypofunction of NMDA receptors on inhibitory interneurons contributes to schizophrenia.

Takeaway: NMDA antagonists reproduce the full schizophrenia picture, supporting the glutamate hypothesis.

whyNot.A: D2 blockade relieves rather than produces positive symptoms.
whyNot.E: 5-HT2A agonists (LSD, psilocybin) cause perceptual distortion; blockade is part of second-generation antipsychotic action.
whyNot.B: Blocking GABA-A receptors causes seizures, not a schizophrenia-like syndrome.
whyNot.C: Blocking mu receptors (naloxone) reverses opioid effects and causes no psychosis.

items.objective: Explain how NMDA receptor antagonists model the positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia that did not respond to two different antipsychotics was started on clozapine 10 weeks ago, and his hallucinations have improved. He now has a sore throat and a temperature of 38.9°C (102°F). Which of the following laboratory values should be obtained first to assess the most dangerous adverse effect of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Clozapine can cause severe neutropenia (agranulocytosis), most often in the first months. Fever or sore throat in a patient taking clozapine needs an urgent absolute neutrophil count; the drug is stopped if the count is severely low. The ANC is measured before starting and regularly during treatment.

Takeaway: fever on clozapine means an urgent absolute neutrophil count.

whyNot.E: Creatine kinase helps in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which he does not have.
whyNot.C: Clozapine does not characteristically cause thrombocytopenia.
whyNot.D: A level guides dosing and toxicity but does not explain fever with sore throat.
whyNot.B: Eosinophilia can accompany clozapine myocarditis, but fever with sore throat points to infection from neutropenia.

items.objective: Recognise clozapine-induced neutropenia and the need to measure the absolute neutrophil count.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has had auditory hallucinations, delusions of persecution, social withdrawal and declining self-care since age 20. MRI of the brain is part of a research study. Which of the following structural findings is most consistently reported in this disorder?
items.explanationHtml:
Chronic schizophrenia is associated with enlarged lateral and third ventricles, reduced grey matter volume (especially frontal and temporal cortex and hippocampus) and reduced neuropil. These changes are group findings and do not diagnose the disorder in an individual.

Takeaway: ventricular enlargement with reduced cortical volume is the classic structural finding in schizophrenia.

whyNot.A: Caudate atrophy is characteristic of Huntington disease.
whyNot.D: Mesial temporal sclerosis is the lesion of temporal lobe epilepsy.
whyNot.B: These point to small-vessel disease, demyelination or leukodystrophy.
whyNot.E: This is osmotic demyelination after rapid sodium correction.

items.objective: Recall the main structural brain findings in schizophrenia.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with schizophrenia has done well on risperidone but has developed amenorrhoea and a high serum prolactin level. She is switched to aripiprazole, and over the next 2 months her prolactin level returns to normal while her psychosis stays controlled. Which of the following properties of aripiprazole best explains this result?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of the vesicular monoamine transporter

options.label: C
options.html: Partial agonism at dopamine D2 receptors

options.label: D
options.html: Selective antagonism of dopamine D1 receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Aripiprazole is a D2 partial agonist. Where dopamine is scarce, such as at pituitary lactotrophs exposed to a full antagonist, it provides enough receptor stimulation to keep prolactin suppressed; where dopamine is excessive (mesolimbic pathway) it acts as a functional antagonist. It is often used to correct antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia. Its main movement side effect is akathisia.

Takeaway: D2 partial agonists lower rather than raise prolactin.

whyNot.E: 5-HT2A antagonism is shared by risperidone, which raised her prolactin.
whyNot.D: Lactotrophs are inhibited through D2, not D1, receptors.
whyNot.A: VMAT2 inhibition depletes dopamine and would tend to raise prolactin.
whyNot.B: Muscarinic agonism is the mechanism of a newer non-D2 antipsychotic, not of aripiprazole.

items.objective: Explain why D2 partial agonists do not raise prolactin.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with schizophrenia takes chlorpromazine. He has fallen twice after getting out of bed, and his blood pressure falls from 132/80 mm Hg supine to 104/66 mm Hg standing. Blockade of which of the following receptors best explains his falls?
items.explanationHtml:
Low-potency first-generation antipsychotics such as chlorpromazine strongly block alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on arterioles and veins, so standing does not trigger adequate vasoconstriction and orthostatic hypotension follows. Clozapine, quetiapine and iloperidone share this effect, which is why their doses are raised slowly.

Takeaway: orthostatic hypotension from antipsychotics reflects alpha-1 blockade, most with low-potency agents.

whyNot.C: D2 blockade causes parkinsonism, which can cause falls, but not the postural drop in blood pressure.
whyNot.D: H1 blockade causes sedation and weight gain.
whyNot.E: Muscarinic blockade causes dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention.
whyNot.B: Antipsychotics do not block beta-1 receptors; reflex tachycardia is usually preserved.

items.objective: Attribute antipsychotic orthostatic hypotension to alpha-1 receptor blockade.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old graduate student is brought in by her roommate. Six days ago, two days after her father died suddenly, she began hearing her father's voice telling her she is being watched and stopped sleeping. She is treated with a low dose of an antipsychotic.
