Three weeks after symptoms began, they have resolved completely and she is back at her studies. She has no history of mood episodes or substance use. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Psychotic symptoms lasting more than 1 day but less than 1 month, with full return to previous functioning, is brief psychotic disorder. A marked stressor beforehand is common. Follow-up is still needed, because some patients go on to develop a longer-lasting psychotic or mood disorder.

Takeaway: psychosis for under a month with full recovery is brief psychotic disorder.

whyNot.E: Schizophreniform disorder lasts at least 1 month.
whyNot.D: Schizophrenia needs at least 6 months of illness with functional decline.
whyNot.A: Adjustment disorder does not include psychotic symptoms.
whyNot.C: Prolonged grief needs at least 12 months since the death in adults and does not explain psychosis.

items.objective: Diagnose brief psychotic disorder from its duration and full recovery.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old man has been seen for 10 weeks because he believes his neighbours are broadcasting his thoughts. He hears voices commenting on his actions and has stopped attending college. Before this he was a good student with friends. Urine drug screen, thyroid function and MRI of the brain are normal. He has no mood symptoms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
He meets the symptom criteria for schizophrenia, but the illness has lasted between 1 and 6 months: schizophreniform disorder. About two-thirds of people with this diagnosis later meet criteria for schizophrenia. Treatment is the same as for a first episode of schizophrenia.

Takeaway: a schizophrenia-like illness lasting 1 to 6 months is schizophreniform disorder.

whyNot.A: Symptoms have lasted longer than 1 month.
whyNot.B: He has prominent hallucinations and a major fall in function, which do not fit delusional disorder.
whyNot.D: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of continuous signs of illness.
whyNot.C: There are no mood episodes.

items.objective: Distinguish schizophreniform disorder from schizophrenia by duration.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has had three admissions for mania over 8 years, each with grandiose and persecutory delusions. Her family says that between episodes she still hears voices and believes the government monitors her phone, even when her mood is normal; during the last admission these beliefs continued for 2 months after her mood stabilised. Mood episodes have been present for most of her illness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features

items.explanationHtml:
Schizoaffective disorder requires mood episodes for the majority of the illness plus at least 2 weeks of delusions or hallucinations without a mood episode. Her psychosis persisting for months after mood recovery separates this from bipolar I disorder with psychotic features. Treatment combines an antipsychotic with a mood stabiliser for the bipolar type.

Takeaway: psychosis that persists 2 weeks or more without mood symptoms, in an illness dominated by mood episodes, is schizoaffective disorder.

whyNot.A: In bipolar disorder with psychotic features, psychosis occurs only during mood episodes.
whyNot.E: Mood episodes have been present for most of her illness, which argues against schizophrenia.
whyNot.C: She has hallucinations and recurrent manic episodes.
whyNot.B: Cyclothymia does not include manic episodes or psychosis.

items.objective: Differentiate schizoaffective disorder from a mood disorder with psychotic features.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old accountant is referred by his employer's lawyer. For 18 months he has been convinced that a famous news presenter is secretly in love with him and sends him coded messages during broadcasts. He has written her many letters. He works effectively, pays his bills and has no hallucinations, disorganised speech or mood symptoms. Physical examination, cognition and laboratory tests are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A fixed, non-bizarre erotomanic belief for at least 1 month, with otherwise preserved behaviour and no other psychotic symptoms, is delusional disorder. Building a trusting relationship without colluding with or directly challenging the delusion is key; an antipsychotic may help but adherence is often poor.

Takeaway: an isolated delusion with intact function is delusional disorder.

whyNot.D: He has no hallucinations, disorganisation or negative symptoms, and his function is preserved.
whyNot.E: Schizotypal traits involve odd beliefs and eccentricity, not a fixed delusion held for over a year.
whyNot.C: Obsessions are unwanted and recognised as intrusive; his belief is held with conviction.
whyNot.B: Cognition is normal, and a dementia would not explain an isolated, well-organised belief.

items.objective: Diagnose delusional disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his parents because for 3 weeks he has been convinced that his phone is implanting thoughts in his head. He has not slept for 2 nights. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 104/min and blood pressure is 138/86 mm Hg. Pupils are 6 mm and reactive. He is oriented but suspicious. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in evaluation?

options.label: E
options.html: Urine drug screen with basic blood tests

items.explanationHtml:
A first episode of psychosis needs a search for substance-induced and medical causes. His tachycardia, mild hypertension and dilated pupils raise the possibility of stimulant use. Start with a urine drug screen and basic blood tests (blood count, electrolytes, glucose, kidney and liver function, TSH), plus HIV and syphilis testing; image the brain if there are neurological signs or atypical features.

Takeaway: every first episode of psychosis begins with a drug screen and basic medical tests.

whyNot.C: Lumbar puncture is for suspected infection or encephalitis, which his presentation does not suggest yet.
whyNot.A: EEG is for suspected seizures or encephalopathy.
whyNot.B: Genetic testing is guided by dysmorphic or developmental features.
whyNot.D: Formal testing does not help in the acute assessment.

items.objective: Plan the initial evaluation of first-episode psychosis.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with no psychiatric history has developed suspicious beliefs over 2 months: she thinks her husband is poisoning her food. Her husband says she has become apathetic and disinhibited, and she has had morning headaches. She takes no medicines and does not drink alcohol. On examination, she has mild word-finding difficulty. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Psychosis that begins late in life, with personality change, headaches and a focal sign (word-finding difficulty), suggests a structural brain lesion such as a frontal or temporal tumour. MRI is needed before attributing the symptoms to a primary psychiatric disorder.

Takeaway: late-onset psychosis with neurological features needs brain imaging first.

whyNot.D: Treating the psychosis before excluding a structural cause risks missing a treatable lesion.
whyNot.B: Psychotherapy does not address a possible brain lesion.
whyNot.C: Wilson disease presents much earlier in life.
whyNot.E: There is no depressive syndrome to treat.

items.objective: Identify features of psychosis that require neuroimaging.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia continues to have persecutory delusions and command hallucinations. He took risperidone at a full dose for 8 weeks and then olanzapine at a full dose for 10 weeks; pharmacy records and drug levels confirm adherence. He attempted suicide 4 months ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.label: C
options.html: Switch to a long-acting injectable of olanzapine

items.explanationHtml:
Failure of two adequate antipsychotic trials defines treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Clozapine is the only drug with proven superiority in this setting and it also reduces suicidal behaviour, which matters after his recent attempt. Baseline blood count, regular absolute neutrophil counts and monitoring for myocarditis, constipation and seizures are required.

Takeaway: after two failed adequate antipsychotic trials, use clozapine.

whyNot.A: His symptoms are psychotic, and there is no depressive syndrome described.
whyNot.E: A third standard antipsychotic is unlikely to succeed after two adequate trials.
whyNot.B: Lithium augmentation has weak evidence in schizophrenia and does not target resistance.
whyNot.C: Adherence is confirmed, so the problem is drug response, not adherence.

items.objective: Choose clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia.

items.stemHtml:
A 33-year-old man with schizophrenia was admitted 4 days ago with agitation and was given haloperidol, with dose increases each day. Today he is confused and sweating, with rigid limbs. Temperature is 40.1°C (104.2°F), pulse is 128/min and blood pressure fluctuates between 98/60 and 176/104 mm Hg. Results:

TestResultReference range
Creatine kinase22,400 U/Lbelow 200 U/L
Leukocytes15,600/mm³4,500–11,000/mm³
Creatinine1.8 mg/dL0.6–1.2 mg/dL
Potassium5.1 mEq/L3.5–5.0 mEq/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Give intravenous antibiotics and await cultures

options.label: E
options.html: Stop haloperidol and begin cooling and IV fluids

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion and a very high creatine kinase after rising doses of a D2 antagonist are neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Stop the antipsychotic, cool the patient and give IV fluids to protect the kidneys from rhabdomyolysis, in an intensive care setting. Benzodiazepines help; dantrolene or bromocriptine are added in severe cases. Antipsychotics can be restarted cautiously after about 2 weeks, preferably a lower-potency agent.

Takeaway: in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, stop the drug and give supportive care first.

whyNot.C: More dopamine blockade would worsen the syndrome.
whyNot.A: Cyproheptadine is for serotonin syndrome, which causes clonus rather than rigidity.
whyNot.B: Infection should be excluded, but the drug must be stopped first; this picture is NMS until proved otherwise.
whyNot.D: Anticholinergics treat dystonia, not this life-threatening syndrome, and impair heat loss.

items.objective: Manage neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable on olanzapine for a year. Over this time he has gained 11 kg (24 lb). BMI is now 31 kg/m². Fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL (reference range 70–100 mg/dL), HbA1c is 6.1% and triglycerides are 260 mg/dL (below 150 mg/dL). He wants to keep taking medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his antipsychotic treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Olanzapine and clozapine cause the most weight gain, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. In a stable patient with emerging metabolic syndrome, switching to an agent with a lower metabolic burden (aripiprazole, lurasidone or ziprasidone) is appropriate, with lifestyle support. Metformin is an evidence-based add-on if switching is not possible.

Takeaway: antipsychotic-induced metabolic syndrome is managed by switching to a metabolically lighter drug and lifestyle measures.

whyNot.E: Clozapine causes as much or more metabolic harm and is reserved for treatment resistance.
whyNot.A: Adding a second antipsychotic adds metabolic risk.
whyNot.B: Stopping carries a high risk of relapse in a stable patient.
whyNot.D: Low-potency first-generation agents also cause weight gain and have many other adverse effects.

items.objective: Manage metabolic adverse effects of second-generation antipsychotics.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia has been admitted four times in 2 years. Each time, he responds well to oral paliperidone within weeks, then stops taking it a few months after discharge because he "forgets" or feels he no longer needs it, and he relapses. He tolerates the drug well. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to his treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Stop medication and rely on psychotherapy

options.label: E
options.html: Twice-daily oral dosing of a different antipsychotic

items.explanationHtml:
Repeated relapse after stopping an effective drug is the main indication for a long-acting injectable antipsychotic. Injections given every few weeks or months guarantee delivery, show missed doses at once, and reduce rehospitalisation. Using the same drug he already responds to keeps efficacy and tolerability known.

Takeaway: relapse from non-adherence is an indication for a long-acting injectable antipsychotic.

whyNot.D: He responds to medication; the problem is adherence, not resistance.
whyNot.A: There is no mood disorder to treat.
whyNot.C: Without medication his relapse risk is very high.
whyNot.E: More frequent oral dosing worsens adherence.

items.objective: Use long-acting injectable antipsychotics for relapse due to non-adherence.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman with schizophrenia was switched from haloperidol to aripiprazole 2 weeks ago. She now feels an unbearable inner restlessness, cannot sit through a meal and paces the ward. She has no tremor, rigidity or abnormal postures. Her psychosis remains controlled. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Subjective restlessness with an urge to move, starting days to weeks after a dopamine-blocking drug, is akathisia; aripiprazole commonly causes it. Options are to lower the dose or switch, or to add a low dose of propranolol; benzodiazepines and mirtazapine are alternatives. Akathisia matters because it is distressing and has been linked to agitation, non-adherence and suicidal thinking.

Takeaway: akathisia responds to dose reduction or propranolol rather than anticholinergics.

whyNot.B: Anticholinergics work for dystonia and parkinsonism but are of little help for akathisia.
whyNot.E: VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia, a late syndrome of involuntary movements.
whyNot.A: More dopamine blockade would worsen akathisia.
whyNot.C: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia or severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

items.objective: Treat antipsychotic-induced akathisia.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man began clozapine 3 weeks ago for treatment-resistant schizophrenia; the dose has been increased steadily. He now has fever of 38.4°C (101.1°F), fatigue and chest discomfort. Pulse is 124/min and blood pressure is 102/68 mm Hg. Troponin I is 1.8 ng/mL (0.04 ng/mL or less) and C-reactive protein is raised. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with nonspecific ST changes. The absolute neutrophil count is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Reduce the clozapine dose by half

options.label: E
options.html: Stop clozapine and obtain an echocardiogram

items.explanationHtml:
Clozapine-induced myocarditis typically appears in the first 4 to 8 weeks with fever, tachycardia, chest pain or dyspnoea, a raised troponin and C-reactive protein, sometimes with eosinophilia. Stop clozapine, assess ventricular function with an echocardiogram and involve cardiology. Rechallenge is usually avoided.

Takeaway: fever, tachycardia and a raised troponin early in clozapine treatment mean myocarditis: stop the drug.

whyNot.B: Fever with a raised troponin in the first weeks is not benign clozapine fever.
whyNot.C: Myocarditis requires stopping the drug, not reducing it.
whyNot.D: This is an acute coronary syndrome regimen; the picture fits drug myocarditis in a young man.
whyNot.A: Beta-blockade treats benign tachycardia, not myocarditis.

items.objective: Recognise and manage clozapine-induced myocarditis.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man has taken haloperidol for 8 years. His daughter has noticed repeated chewing, lip pursing and tongue movements over several months, which embarrass him. He is psychiatrically stable. Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale scores are moderate. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy for these movements?
items.explanationHtml:
Late-onset involuntary orofacial movements after years of a D2 blocker are tardive dyskinesia. VMAT2 inhibitors (deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) are first-line. Review the antipsychotic too: lowering the dose or switching to a lower-risk agent such as clozapine or quetiapine can help, but stopping abruptly may transiently worsen the movements.

Takeaway: treat bothersome tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor.

whyNot.A: Anticholinergics can worsen tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.D: This may mask movements briefly but deepens the underlying problem.
whyNot.C: Diphenhydramine treats acute dystonia.
whyNot.E: Dopaminergic drugs would risk psychotic relapse and are not a treatment for tardive dyskinesia.

items.objective: Treat tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with schizophrenia has stopped speaking and eating for 3 days. She stands in one position for hours, resists being moved, and her arm stays where the examiner places it. Temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 96/min and blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg. Creatine kinase and blood tests are normal. She has not received an antipsychotic recently. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Mutism, stupor, posturing, negativism and waxy flexibility are catatonia. A benzodiazepine (lorazepam) is both a diagnostic challenge and first-line treatment. ECT is used if lorazepam fails or the patient is medically endangered (for example, not eating, autonomic instability). Antipsychotics are best avoided until catatonia resolves.

Takeaway: treat catatonia with lorazepam, then ECT if needed.

whyNot.A: High-potency antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and raise the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
whyNot.D: An antidepressant acts too slowly and does not treat catatonia directly.
whyNot.C: Feeding is supportive, but catatonia needs active treatment.
whyNot.E: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity.

items.objective: Treat catatonia with benzodiazepines.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with panic disorder is given lorazepam for a short period while an SSRI takes effect. At the GABA-A receptor, which of the following best describes how this drug enhances inhibitory transmission?

options.label: A
options.html: It directly opens the chloride channel in the absence of GABA

options.label: B
options.html: It increases the duration of chloride channel opening

options.label: C
options.html: It increases the frequency of chloride channel opening

options.label: D
options.html: It inhibits GABA reuptake into presynaptic terminals

items.explanationHtml:
Benzodiazepines bind at the interface of the alpha and gamma subunits of the GABA-A receptor and make GABA more effective, so the chloride channel opens more often. Without GABA they do nothing, which gives them a ceiling effect and makes them safer in overdose than barbiturates, unless combined with alcohol or opioids.

Takeaway: benzodiazepines raise the frequency of GABA-A channel opening; barbiturates raise its duration.

whyNot.B: Prolonged opening is the barbiturate effect.
whyNot.A: Benzodiazepines need GABA present; direct opening at high doses is a barbiturate property.
whyNot.D: Reuptake inhibition is the action of tiagabine.
whyNot.E: GABA transaminase inhibition is the action of vigabatrin.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of benzodiazepines at the GABA-A receptor.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with generalized anxiety disorder is brought to the emergency department after taking about 40 alprazolam tablets. She is drowsy but rousable, with a respiratory rate of 14/min. She takes no other medicines. A drug is considered that would reverse the sedation. By which mechanism would this drug act?

options.label: B
options.html: Agonism at the GABA binding site

options.label: D
options.html: Competitive antagonism at the benzodiazepine binding site

items.explanationHtml:
Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. It reverses sedation but can precipitate seizures in long-term benzodiazepine users or after co-ingestion of proconvulsant drugs such as tricyclics, so most isolated benzodiazepine overdoses are managed with supportive care alone.

Takeaway: flumazenil competitively blocks the benzodiazepine site but risks seizures in dependent patients.

whyNot.A: Opioid agonists would deepen sedation.
whyNot.C: NMDA blockade does not reverse benzodiazepine effects.
whyNot.E: Cholinesterase inhibition (physostigmine) is used for anticholinergic toxicity.
whyNot.B: This would increase, not reverse, inhibition.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism and risks of flumazenil.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had excessive worry about money, his health and his children for over a year, with muscle tension and poor sleep. He is in recovery from alcohol use disorder and asks for a medicine that is not habit-forming and will not make him drowsy at work. He is prescribed a drug that takes several weeks to work. Which of the following is the primary mechanism of this drug?

options.label: C
options.html: Binding of the alpha-2-delta subunit of calcium channels

options.label: E
options.html: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist used for generalized anxiety. It does not act on GABA-A receptors, so it causes little sedation, no dependence or withdrawal, and no cross-tolerance with alcohol. Its effect builds over 2 to 4 weeks, and it does not help acute panic.

Takeaway: buspirone is a non-sedating, non-addictive 5-HT1A partial agonist with a delayed onset.

whyNot.E: This is the mechanism of benzodiazepines, which are habit-forming and sedating.
whyNot.B: H1 blockade (hydroxyzine) causes drowsiness.
whyNot.A: Beta-blockers act within hours on physical symptoms of performance anxiety.
whyNot.C: This is the gabapentinoid mechanism; these drugs sedate and can be misused.

items.objective: State the mechanism and features of buspirone.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman has a sudden episode of pounding heart, chest tightness and fear of dying while shopping. She breathes rapidly and develops tingling around her mouth and painful flexion spasms of her wrists and fingers. Which of the following best explains the tingling and spasms?

options.label: A
options.html: A fall in total serum calcium from parathyroid suppression

options.label: E
options.html: More calcium bound to albumin as blood becomes alkaline

items.explanationHtml:
Hyperventilation during a panic attack blows off carbon dioxide and causes acute respiratory alkalosis. In alkaline blood, albumin releases hydrogen ions and binds more calcium, so ionised calcium falls while total calcium is unchanged. Low ionised calcium raises neuronal excitability, causing perioral paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm.

Takeaway: hyperventilation lowers ionised calcium through alkalosis, causing tingling and carpopedal spasm.

whyNot.A: Parathyroid function does not change in minutes; total calcium is unchanged.
whyNot.B: Catecholamines shift potassium into cells and lower it.
whyNot.C: Adrenergic surges raise, not lower, blood glucose.
whyNot.D: Acidosis would raise ionised calcium, not lower it.

items.objective: Explain the physiology of paraesthesia and carpopedal spasm in hyperventilation.

items.stemHtml: In an experiment, a tone is repeatedly paired with a mild electric shock until the tone alone produces freezing, a rise in heart rate and stress-hormone release. Exaggeration of this kind of learning is thought to contribute to phobias and posttraumatic stress disorder. Which of the following brain structures is most essential for acquiring this conditioned fear response?
items.explanationHtml:
Classical fear conditioning depends on the amygdala, especially the basolateral nucleus, which links the cue to the threat. The central nucleus then drives the freezing, autonomic and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal responses. Exposure therapy builds new extinction learning, which relies on the medial prefrontal cortex inhibiting amygdala output.

Takeaway: the amygdala acquires conditioned fear; exposure therapy builds prefrontal extinction learning.

whyNot.B: The cerebellum supports motor learning such as eyeblink conditioning, not fear associations.
whyNot.C: The mammillary bodies support episodic memory and are damaged in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
whyNot.D: Auditory cortex relays the tone but does not form the fear association.
whyNot.E: This nucleus sets circadian rhythm.

items.objective: Identify the amygdala as the core structure for conditioned fear.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man spends 4 hours a day checking that doors are locked and repeating prayers until they feel right; he recognises that the fears are excessive. Functional imaging studies of patients with this disorder most consistently show increased activity in which of the following circuits?

options.label: C
options.html: Mesolimbic projection to the nucleus accumbens

items.explanationHtml:
In obsessive-compulsive disorder, imaging shows hyperactivity in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops linking the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex with the caudate and thalamus. Successful treatment with SSRIs or exposure and response prevention reduces this activity.

Takeaway: OCD is linked to overactive orbitofrontal-caudate-thalamic circuits.

whyNot.A: These coordinate balance and eye movement.
whyNot.B: These are involved in memory and are affected early in Alzheimer disease.
whyNot.D: This region processes visual information.
whyNot.C: This reward pathway is implicated in addiction and psychosis.

items.objective: Recall the neural circuit implicated in OCD.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old violinist has a racing heart, sweaty palms and a shaking bow arm before concerts, but no anxiety at other times. Taking propranolol an hour before performances controls these symptoms. Which of the following best explains how propranolol helps?

options.label: A
options.html: It blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum

options.label: D
options.html: It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling in the cortex

options.label: E
options.html: It stimulates central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Performance anxiety produces a sympathetic surge. Propranolol blocks beta-1 and beta-2 receptors, reducing tachycardia, palpitations and tremor, which also interrupts the cycle of noticing symptoms and worrying more. It does not treat generalized social anxiety and is avoided in asthma.

Takeaway: propranolol relieves the peripheral adrenergic symptoms of performance anxiety.

whyNot.D: Propranolol has no GABA-ergic action.
whyNot.C: Serotonin reuptake inhibition takes weeks and is not the action of propranolol.
whyNot.E: Central alpha-2 agonism describes clonidine and guanfacine.
whyNot.A: D2 blockade describes antipsychotics.

items.objective: Explain the use of beta-blockers in performance anxiety.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder has had only a partial response to two SSRIs at high doses. Her psychiatrist prescribes a tricyclic antidepressant that differs from most others in its class by being a particularly potent inhibitor of serotonin reuptake. Which of the following drugs was most likely prescribed?
items.explanationHtml:
Clomipramine is the most serotonergic tricyclic and has proven efficacy in OCD, which responds selectively to drugs with strong serotonin reuptake inhibition. It carries typical tricyclic risks: anticholinergic effects, orthostasis, weight gain, seizures at high doses and cardiotoxicity in overdose.

Takeaway: clomipramine is the serotonergic tricyclic used for OCD.

whyNot.E: Nortriptyline is relatively selective for noradrenaline reuptake.
whyNot.C: Desipramine is the most noradrenaline-selective tricyclic.
whyNot.D: Doxepin is a strongly antihistaminic tricyclic used mainly for sleep or itch.
whyNot.A: Amoxapine has dopamine-blocking properties and is not used for OCD.

items.objective: Identify clomipramine as the tricyclic effective in OCD.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has worried constantly for the past year about her job, finances and her children's safety, though there is no particular threat. She has trouble falling asleep, tires easily, has tense shoulders and is irritable. She does not drink alcohol or use drugs. TSH is normal. She wants medication along with therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Excessive, uncontrollable worry about many things for at least 6 months with physical symptoms is generalized anxiety disorder. First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy plus or instead of an SSRI or SNRI such as escitalopram, sertraline, venlafaxine or duloxetine. Buspirone is an alternative or adjunct.

Takeaway: start an SSRI or SNRI for generalized anxiety disorder.

whyNot.A: Long-term benzodiazepines risk dependence and are not first-line.
whyNot.D: Antipsychotics carry metabolic risks and are not first-line for anxiety.
whyNot.C: Propranolol helps performance anxiety, not pervasive worry.
whyNot.E: A hypnotic treats sleep only and carries its own risks.

items.objective: Choose first-line pharmacotherapy for generalized anxiety disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has had five episodes in 2 months of sudden pounding heart, shortness of breath, trembling and a fear that he is dying, each peaking within minutes. They come without warning, including once while he was relaxing at home. He now avoids going far from home in case another happens. ECG, TSH, glucose and a urine drug screen are normal. He drinks one cup of coffee a day. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Clonazepam as the only long-term treatment

options.label: C
options.html: Exposure therapy for a specific phobia

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent unexpected panic attacks followed by worry and behaviour change is panic disorder. After excluding medical causes, treat with CBT and/or an SSRI or SNRI, starting at a low dose because early jitteriness can mimic panic. A benzodiazepine may bridge the first weeks in selected patients.

Takeaway: panic disorder is treated with an SSRI and/or CBT, not long-term benzodiazepines.

whyNot.B: Benzodiazepine monotherapy risks dependence; at most it bridges the first weeks.
whyNot.D: Beta-blockers do not prevent panic attacks.
whyNot.A: Bupropion is activating and not effective for panic disorder.
whyNot.C: His attacks are unexpected, not triggered by one object or situation.

items.objective: Treat panic disorder with an SSRI and CBT.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man comes to the emergency department 40 minutes after sudden chest tightness, palpitations, sweating and a sense that he was about to die. He has had "anxiety attacks" before and thinks this is another. He has hypertension and smokes. Pulse is 102/min and blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg. He is anxious but the examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give oral lorazepam and observe for 1 hour

options.label: B
options.html: Have him breathe into a paper bag

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain an ECG and serial troponin measurements

options.label: D
options.html: Refer for outpatient cognitive behavioural therapy

items.explanationHtml:
Panic symptoms overlap with acute coronary syndrome, arrhythmia and pulmonary embolism. A middle-aged smoker with hypertension and new chest tightness needs an ECG and serial troponin measurements before the episode is attributed to anxiety, even with a history of panic.

Takeaway: exclude cardiac causes before diagnosing a panic attack in someone at cardiovascular risk.

whyNot.A: Treating as panic first could miss a myocardial infarction.
whyNot.D: Psychiatric follow-up comes only after cardiac causes are excluded.
whyNot.E: Medical causes must be excluded before any panic diagnosis.
whyNot.B: Rebreathing is unhelpful and can be dangerous if hypoxia is the cause.

items.objective: Exclude medical emergencies before attributing chest symptoms to panic.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old engineer has been offered a promotion that requires frequent flights. Since a turbulent flight 8 years ago he has refused to fly; even booking a ticket makes him sweaty and nauseated. He has no other fears and no depressive symptoms. Which of the following is the most effective treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent fear and avoidance of one situation for at least 6 months is a specific phobia (situational type). Exposure therapy, graded or intensive and increasingly using virtual reality, is the most effective treatment and often works in a few sessions.

Takeaway: specific phobia is treated with exposure therapy.

whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines may blunt fear for a single flight but interfere with learning and do not cure the phobia.
whyNot.E: Insight-oriented therapy is less effective than exposure for phobias.
whyNot.A: Medication has little role in specific phobia.
whyNot.C: Hypnosis is not an evidence-based first-line treatment.

items.objective: Treat a specific phobia with exposure therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has avoided taking the bus, going to the supermarket and standing in queues for a year, because she fears she could not get away or get help if she felt faint. She now leaves home only when her partner goes with her. She has never had an unexpected panic attack. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Fear and avoidance of two or more situations (public transport, open or enclosed spaces, queues or crowds, being outside alone) because escape or help might be hard is agoraphobia, which can be diagnosed with or without panic disorder. Treatment is CBT with exposure, with or without an SSRI.

Takeaway: fear of several situations where escape would be hard is agoraphobia.

whyNot.C: Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected panic attacks.
whyNot.D: Her fear is of being trapped or helpless, not of being judged by others.
whyNot.B: Her fear is tied to specific situations, not diffuse worry.
whyNot.E: Specific phobia involves one kind of situation; she fears several for the same reason.

items.objective: Diagnose agoraphobia.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old singer has severe palpitations and tremor before auditions and concerts, enough to cancel two shows. She is comfortable at parties, at work meetings and with strangers. She has no asthma. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Anxiety limited to performing is the performance-only form of social anxiety disorder. Propranolol taken shortly before the event reduces adrenergic symptoms without sedation. CBT also helps. Daily SSRIs or SNRIs are reserved for generalized social anxiety.

Takeaway: use as-needed propranolol for performance-only anxiety.

whyNot.C: Daily SSRIs are for generalized social anxiety, not anxiety limited to performance.
whyNot.B: Benzodiazepines impair performance and risk dependence.
whyNot.A: Buspirone is for generalized anxiety.
whyNot.D: Hydroxyzine sedates and does not target performance symptoms.

items.objective: Manage performance-only social anxiety.

items.stemHtml: A 21-year-old college student washes her hands up to 60 times a day because of fears of contamination, and her skin is cracked and bleeding. She knows the fears are exaggerated but feels unbearable distress if she does not wash. This takes over 3 hours a day and she has missed classes. Which of the following is the most appropriate psychotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Intrusive contamination fears with compulsive washing that she recognises as excessive is obsessive-compulsive disorder with good insight. The most effective psychotherapy is exposure and response prevention: gradual exposure to feared contamination while resisting the urge to wash. An SSRI, often at a higher dose than for depression, can be combined with it.

Takeaway: the psychotherapy of choice for OCD is exposure and response prevention.

whyNot.D: Insight-oriented therapy has little evidence in OCD.
whyNot.E: Support alone does not reduce compulsions.
whyNot.A: DBT targets emotional dysregulation and self-harm.
whyNot.C: Interpersonal therapy is used mainly for depression.

items.objective: Select exposure and response prevention for OCD.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man asks a plastic surgeon for a third rhinoplasty. He says his nose is "grotesquely crooked" and spends hours a day checking it in mirrors and comparing it with others'. He has stopped dating and dropped out of university. The surgeon sees a normal, symmetrical nose after two earlier operations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Reassure him that his nose looks normal and discharge

options.label: D
options.html: Refer for CBT and consider an SSRI

items.explanationHtml:
Preoccupation with a perceived flaw that others cannot see, with repetitive checking and impairment, is body dysmorphic disorder. Effective treatments are CBT (with exposure and response prevention) and SSRIs, often at high doses. Suicidal thinking is common and should be assessed.

Takeaway: body dysmorphic disorder needs CBT and an SSRI, not cosmetic surgery.

whyNot.A: Cosmetic procedures rarely relieve the preoccupation and often lead to further requests.
whyNot.E: An antipsychotic is considered only as an add-on when insight is absent and first-line treatment fails.
whyNot.B: Reassurance alone does not help and can increase checking.
whyNot.C: There is no skin disease.

items.objective: Recognise body dysmorphic disorder and avoid cosmetic intervention.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old military veteran returned from deployment 5 months ago, where a roadside explosion killed a friend. He has nightmares, flashbacks when he hears loud noises, avoids driving on highways, feels detached from his family and is constantly on guard. He has no suicidal thoughts and does not drink heavily. He is willing to engage in treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Intrusions, avoidance, negative changes in mood and thinking, and hyperarousal lasting more than 1 month after a trauma is posttraumatic stress disorder. Trauma-focused psychotherapy (cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure or EMDR) is the preferred first treatment. An SSRI (sertraline, paroxetine) or venlafaxine is used when therapy is unavailable, declined or not enough.

Takeaway: trauma-focused psychotherapy is first-line for PTSD; avoid benzodiazepines.

whyNot.B: Benzodiazepines do not treat PTSD and may worsen outcomes.
whyNot.D: Antipsychotics are not first-line for PTSD.
whyNot.A: Single-session debriefing does not prevent or treat PTSD.
whyNot.E: Trauma-focused therapies are more effective than general support.

items.objective: Choose first-line treatment for PTSD.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman was assaulted on her way home 12 days ago. Since then she has had intrusive memories, nightmares, a sense of being in a daze, avoidance of the street where it happened, and trouble sleeping and concentrating. She is not using alcohol or drugs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Trauma-related intrusion, dissociation, avoidance and arousal lasting 3 days to 1 month after the event is acute stress disorder. Offer support and trauma-focused CBT; many patients recover, but some progress to PTSD, which is diagnosed if symptoms persist beyond 1 month.

Takeaway: the same trauma-response picture is acute stress disorder before 1 month and PTSD after.

whyNot.E: PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than 1 month.
whyNot.B: Her symptoms follow a traumatic event and meet the full trauma-response pattern.
whyNot.D: GAD requires 6 months of diffuse worry.
whyNot.C: She has no hallucinations or delusions.

items.objective: Distinguish acute stress disorder from PTSD by timing.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man lost his job 6 weeks ago. Since then he has felt low, worried and irritable, sleeps poorly and struggles to look for work. He still enjoys time with his children, his appetite is normal and he has no thoughts of death. He has no history of psychiatric illness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Emotional or behavioural symptoms that begin within 3 months of an identifiable stressor, cause distress or impairment, and do not meet criteria for another disorder are adjustment disorder. Symptoms should resolve within 6 months after the stressor or its consequences end. Treatment is psychotherapy focused on coping and problem solving.

Takeaway: distress after a stressor that falls short of other disorders is adjustment disorder.

whyNot.C: He has too few symptoms and preserved enjoyment.
whyNot.B: GAD needs 6 months of diffuse worry.
whyNot.D: This requires 2 years of symptoms.
whyNot.E: Job loss is a stressor, not a traumatic event of the PTSD type.

items.objective: Diagnose adjustment disorder.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl has refused to go to school for 6 weeks. In the morning she complains of stomach aches and cries that something bad will happen to her mother while she is away. She will not sleep unless a parent is in the room and calls her mother repeatedly from friends' houses. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Developmentally excessive fear of separation from attachment figures, with worry about harm befalling them, school refusal, physical complaints and reluctance to sleep alone for at least 4 weeks, is separation anxiety disorder. Treatment is CBT with parents involved and a prompt, supported return to school; an SSRI is added for moderate to severe cases.

Takeaway: school refusal driven by fear for a parent's safety is separation anxiety disorder.

whyNot.E: Her fear centres on separation from her mother, not on school itself.
whyNot.A: Her worry is focused on separation, not on many topics.
whyNot.B: No depressed mood or anhedonia is described.
whyNot.C: Her refusal is driven by fear, not defiance.

items.objective: Diagnose separation anxiety disorder in a child.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has taken lorazepam 2 mg nightly for anxiety and sleep for 12 years. She has fallen twice in 3 months and her daughter notices forgetfulness. Her anxiety is mild and she has started sertraline. She agrees she would like to stop lorazepam. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

options.label: D
options.html: Switch to an equivalent dose of diazepam indefinitely

options.label: E
options.html: Taper lorazepam gradually over weeks to months

items.explanationHtml:
Long-term benzodiazepine use in older adults raises the risk of falls, fractures and cognitive impairment. After years of use, dependence is likely, so gradual tapering, often by small steps every 2 to 4 weeks and slower near the end, with CBT for insomnia, prevents withdrawal and improves success.

Takeaway: taper long-term benzodiazepines slowly, especially in older adults.

whyNot.B: Abrupt cessation after years of use risks withdrawal, including seizures.
whyNot.C: Z-drugs carry similar risks of falls and confusion in older adults.
whyNot.A: Continuing exposes her to ongoing falls and cognitive risk.
whyNot.D: Long-acting benzodiazepines accumulate in older adults; switching is only a step towards tapering.

items.objective: Plan a benzodiazepine taper in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl is brought by her mother because of patchy hair loss. For a year she has pulled out scalp hair while studying, feeling tension beforehand and relief afterwards. She has tried to stop many times. Examination shows irregular areas of broken hairs of different lengths without scarring; a skin scraping is negative for fungus. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent hair pulling with tension and relief, repeated attempts to stop, and broken hairs of varying length is trichotillomania, an obsessive-compulsive related disorder. Habit reversal training (awareness training, a competing response and social support) is the most effective treatment.

Takeaway: trichotillomania is treated with habit reversal training.

whyNot.E: Minoxidil treats androgenetic alopecia, not hair pulling.
whyNot.D: Fungal infection has been excluded.
whyNot.C: Steroid injection treats alopecia areata.
whyNot.B: Antipsychotics have no first-line role.

items.objective: Treat trichotillomania with habit reversal training.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman reports 8 months of near-constant tension, poor sleep and worry about her health and work. She also has heat intolerance, a fine tremor, 4 kg (9 lb) of unintended weight loss and frequent bowel movements. Pulse is 108/min and irregular. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Measure TSH and free thyroxine and obtain an ECG

options.label: D
options.html: Start propranolol and review in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Anxiety with heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, frequent stools and an irregular tachycardia suggests hyperthyroidism, possibly with atrial fibrillation. Thyroid function tests and an ECG come first; treating the thyroid disease will often relieve the anxiety.

Takeaway: look for hyperthyroidism and arrhythmia before diagnosing an anxiety disorder.

whyNot.E: Treating anxiety before excluding a medical cause would miss her likely diagnosis.
whyNot.B: Psychotherapy alone would leave a medical cause untreated.
whyNot.D: Propranolol helps symptoms but the cause must be identified.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines are not first-line and do not address the cause.

items.objective: Identify medical causes of anxiety symptoms.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium for 10 years with a stable level. She passes about 5 L of urine a day and is always thirsty. Urine osmolality stays low after water deprivation and does not rise after desmopressin. Her psychiatrist wants to continue lithium. Which of the following drugs would most directly reduce lithium entry into the cells responsible for this problem?
items.explanationHtml:
Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by entering collecting-duct principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), where it impairs vasopressin signalling and aquaporin-2 expression. Amiloride blocks ENaC, reducing lithium uptake into these cells. Thiazides also reduce polyuria, but they raise lithium levels.

Takeaway: amiloride blocks lithium entry through ENaC and treats lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

whyNot.D: The kidney is already unresponsive to vasopressin.
whyNot.E: Loop diuretics do not block the collecting-duct lithium channel and worsen volume loss.
whyNot.C: Demeclocycline itself causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
whyNot.A: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition acts in the proximal tubule, not on principal cells.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism and treatment of lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with bipolar disorder has had a stable lithium level for 3 years. His primary care physician starts hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. Three weeks later his lithium level has risen by half. Which of the following best explains the rise?

options.label: A
options.html: Decreased glomerular filtration from afferent arteriole constriction

options.label: B
options.html: Displacement of lithium from plasma proteins

options.label: D
options.html: Increased proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and lithium

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of hepatic metabolism of lithium

items.explanationHtml:
Lithium is filtered and then reabsorbed mostly in the proximal tubule alongside sodium. Thiazides cause mild volume and sodium depletion, and the proximal tubule responds by reabsorbing more sodium, and lithium with it. Dehydration and low-salt diets work the same way. NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors raise lithium mainly by lowering glomerular filtration.

Takeaway: thiazides raise lithium by increasing proximal sodium and lithium reabsorption.

whyNot.E: Lithium is not metabolised by the liver.
whyNot.B: Lithium is not protein bound.
whyNot.C: Thiazides do not change lithium absorption.
whyNot.A: This is the main mechanism of the NSAID interaction, not the thiazide one.

items.objective: Explain the thiazide-lithium interaction.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man taking phenelzine for depression attends a wine-tasting party with aged cheeses. An hour later he has a pounding occipital headache, sweating and a blood pressure of 228/124 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

options.label: B
options.html: Direct agonism of vascular alpha-1 receptors by phenelzine

options.label: C
options.html: Excess serotonin from inhibited serotonin reuptake

options.label: E
options.html: Release of stored noradrenaline by unmetabolised dietary tyramine

items.explanationHtml:
Tyramine in aged cheese, cured meats and some wines is normally destroyed by MAO-A in the gut and liver. With MAO inhibited, it reaches sympathetic nerve terminals, is taken up and displaces stored noradrenaline, causing a hypertensive crisis.

Takeaway: MAO inhibitors plus tyramine release noradrenaline and cause a hypertensive crisis.

whyNot.B: Phenelzine is not a direct adrenergic agonist.
whyNot.C: Excess serotonin causes serotonin syndrome, with clonus and hyperthermia rather than an isolated hypertensive crisis.
whyNot.D: Histamine release causes flushing and hypotension.
whyNot.A: This is the action of mirtazapine.

items.objective: Explain the tyramine reaction with MAO inhibitors.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman with depression also has bulimia nervosa, with frequent purging. She asks for an antidepressant that will not cause weight gain or sexual side effects. Her physician avoids one such drug because of an increased risk of a serious adverse effect in her situation. Which of the following adverse effects is the concern?
items.explanationHtml:
Bupropion (noradrenaline and dopamine reuptake inhibitor) avoids sexual dysfunction and weight gain but lowers the seizure threshold. The risk is higher in bulimia and anorexia nervosa, where electrolyte disturbances add to it, so it is contraindicated there.

Takeaway: avoid bupropion in eating disorders because of seizure risk.

whyNot.B: Hypertensive crisis is the risk of MAO inhibitors with tyramine.
whyNot.C: Priapism is linked to trazodone.
whyNot.A: Agranulocytosis is linked to clozapine and carbamazepine, not antidepressants used here.
whyNot.D: QT prolongation is linked to citalopram at higher doses and tricyclics.

items.objective: Recall the seizure risk of bupropion and its contraindications.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman has been depressed since her husband died a year ago. She has lost 7 kg (15 lb), wakes at 3 AM and cannot get back to sleep. Her physician chooses an antidepressant that will help her sleep and appetite. The drug increases noradrenaline and serotonin release by blocking presynaptic inhibitory autoreceptors and heteroreceptors. Which of the following receptors does it block?
items.explanationHtml:
Mirtazapine blocks presynaptic alpha-2 receptors, removing the brake on noradrenaline and serotonin release. It also strongly blocks H1 receptors, causing sedation and increased appetite, which is useful in an older adult with insomnia and weight loss. It causes little sexual dysfunction.

Takeaway: mirtazapine is an alpha-2 antagonist that helps sleep and appetite.

whyNot.E: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist.
whyNot.B: Beta-2 receptors are not presynaptic brakes on monoamine release here.
whyNot.D: Muscarinic blockade causes anticholinergic effects, not increased release.
whyNot.C: D2 blockade is the action of antipsychotics.

items.objective: State the mechanism and clinical niche of mirtazapine.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after taking a large amount of amitriptyline. She is drowsy with dry, flushed skin and dilated pupils. Pulse is 128/min and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. ECG shows a QRS duration of 140 ms. Blockade of which of the following explains the QRS widening and guides the most important antidote?

options.label: D
options.html: Fast sodium channels in ventricular myocytes

options.label: E
options.html: Muscarinic receptors in the sinoatrial node

items.explanationHtml:
Tricyclics block fast sodium channels, slowing ventricular depolarisation and widening the QRS, which predicts arrhythmias and seizures. Sodium bicarbonate counters this by raising extracellular sodium and pH, which reduces drug binding to the channel.

Takeaway: tricyclic overdose widens the QRS through sodium channel blockade; give sodium bicarbonate.

whyNot.C: Potassium channel blockade prolongs the QT interval rather than the QRS.
whyNot.E: Muscarinic blockade explains the tachycardia, not the wide QRS.
whyNot.A: Alpha-1 blockade explains the hypotension.
whyNot.B: Calcium channel blockade causes bradycardia and AV block.

items.objective: Explain QRS widening in tricyclic overdose and its treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man with a major depressive episode takes part in a sleep study. Compared with healthy controls, which of the following findings is most likely on his polysomnogram?

options.label: C
options.html: Longer total sleep time with fewer awakenings

items.explanationHtml:
Depression typically shows shortened REM latency, more REM in the first part of the night, less slow-wave sleep, fragmented sleep and early-morning waking. Many antidepressants suppress REM sleep.

Takeaway: depression shortens REM latency and reduces slow-wave sleep.

whyNot.B: Slow-wave sleep is reduced in depression.
whyNot.A: REM sleep is present and often increased early in the night.
whyNot.C: Depression usually causes fragmented sleep and early waking, though some patients oversleep.
whyNot.E: Sleep-onset REM periods in naps are a feature of narcolepsy.

items.objective: Recall sleep architecture changes in depression.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with major depression has not improved after adequate trials of two antidepressants and psychotherapy. She starts a nasal spray given in the clinic, after which she is observed for 2 hours because she may feel detached from her surroundings and her blood pressure may rise. Which of the following is the mechanism of this drug?

options.label: D
options.html: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Esketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist given intranasally for treatment-resistant depression and for depression with acute suicidal thinking, alongside an oral antidepressant. Dissociation, sedation and raised blood pressure mean it is given under supervision with a period of observation.

Takeaway: esketamine is an NMDA antagonist used for treatment-resistant depression under observation.

whyNot.E: SNRIs are oral and do not cause acute dissociation.
whyNot.D: This describes zuranolone and brexanolone.
whyNot.B: MAO inhibitors are oral or transdermal and do not need post-dose observation for dissociation.
whyNot.A: Melatonin agonists help sleep and have no rapid antidepressant effect.

items.objective: State the mechanism and monitoring of esketamine.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has been stable on lithium for 5 years. She is planning a pregnancy and asks about risks to the baby. First-trimester exposure to lithium is associated with a small increase in the risk of which of the following?

options.label: B
options.html: Craniofacial and CNS defects with absent ears

items.explanationHtml:
First-trimester lithium is associated with cardiac malformations, classically Ebstein anomaly (apical displacement of the tricuspid valve leaflets). The absolute risk is lower than once thought. Many patients continue lithium with fetal echocardiography and close monitoring because relapse carries serious risks.

Takeaway: lithium in early pregnancy slightly raises the risk of Ebstein anomaly.

whyNot.E: Neural tube defects are linked to valproate and carbamazepine.
whyNot.A: Cleft lip and palate are linked to several antiseizure drugs and corticosteroids.
whyNot.D: Limb defects are linked to thalidomide.
whyNot.B: This describes isotretinoin embryopathy.

items.objective: Recall the teratogenic risk of lithium.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman develops severe depression 3 weeks after delivering her first child. She is prescribed a 14-day oral course of a drug related to an endogenous neurosteroid that falls sharply after delivery. Which of the following best describes this drug's mechanism of action?

options.label: E
options.html: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Brexanolone (an IV formulation of allopregnanolone) and zuranolone (an oral analogue) mimic allopregnanolone, a progesterone metabolite whose levels fall abruptly after delivery. They are positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A receptors, at both synaptic and extrasynaptic sites. Sedation is the main adverse effect, so driving is avoided during treatment.

Takeaway: neuroactive steroids for postpartum depression enhance GABA-A signalling.

whyNot.C: This is the mechanism of esketamine.
whyNot.A: Oxytocin agonism is not an approved antidepressant mechanism.
whyNot.D: SSRIs take weeks and are not neurosteroids.
whyNot.B: Neuroactive steroids act on membrane GABA-A receptors, not as progestins.

items.objective: State the mechanism of neuroactive steroid treatments for postpartum depression.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman has had depressed mood and loss of interest for 3 months, sleeps poorly, has trouble concentrating and feels worthless. PHQ-9 score is 18. She has never had periods of elevated mood and has no thoughts of suicide. She started sertraline 4 weeks ago and has taken it daily at the starting dose. She feels slightly better and has no side effects. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Stop sertraline and start psychotherapy alone

items.explanationHtml:
Partial improvement at 4 weeks on a starting dose calls for increasing the dose towards the effective range before switching or augmenting. Reassess after another 4 to 6 weeks. Adding psychotherapy improves outcomes in moderate to severe depression.

Takeaway: optimise the antidepressant dose before switching or augmenting.

whyNot.E: Switching is premature when she is improving and the dose has not been optimised.
whyNot.A: Augmentation is for partial response after an adequate dose and duration.
whyNot.C: ECT is not indicated for moderate depression without psychosis or high risk.
whyNot.D: She is improving on medication.

items.objective: Optimise the antidepressant dose in partial response.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has responded well to paroxetine for depression over 4 months but has had erectile dysfunction and delayed ejaculation since starting it, and he is thinking of stopping treatment. He has no seizure or eating disorder history. Which of the following is the most appropriate change?
items.explanationHtml:
SSRIs and SNRIs commonly cause sexual dysfunction, a frequent reason for stopping treatment. Bupropion, which acts on noradrenaline and dopamine, rarely does. Mirtazapine is another option. Cross-tapering avoids discontinuation symptoms from paroxetine.

Takeaway: for SSRI sexual dysfunction, switch to bupropion or mirtazapine.

whyNot.D: Another SSRI is likely to cause the same sexual side effects.
whyNot.E: SNRIs cause sexual dysfunction at similar rates.
whyNot.A: Abrupt stopping of paroxetine causes discontinuation symptoms and risks relapse.
whyNot.C: Clomipramine is strongly serotonergic and causes sexual dysfunction.

items.objective: Manage SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man has had severe depression for 2 months. For the past week he has eaten and drunk very little, believes his bowels have rotted and that he deserves to die for imagined crimes. He has lost 9 kg (20 lb). Creatinine has risen to 1.9 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL). He refuses medication. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Start sertraline and review in 4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Severe depression with psychotic features (nihilistic and guilty delusions) and refusal to eat or drink is a medical emergency. ECT works fastest and best in this setting, after capacity assessment and appropriate consent or legal authorisation. Its main adverse effect is temporary memory loss.

Takeaway: psychotic depression with refusal to eat or drink is an indication for ECT.

whyNot.E: An antidepressant acts too slowly for life-threatening refusal to eat and drink.
whyNot.C: Lithium is unsafe with his kidney injury and acts too slowly.
whyNot.D: Psychotherapy cannot help in time and he has psychotic depression.
whyNot.B: Esketamine is not established for psychotic depression.

items.objective: Identify indications for ECT.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had low mood, hypersomnia, low energy and hopelessness for 6 weeks. Two years ago she was admitted for 10 days of no sleep, grandiosity and spending her savings. She is not taking any medicine and has no suicidal thoughts. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
A past manic episode makes this bipolar I depression. Evidence-based treatments include quetiapine, lurasidone, lumateperone, cariprazine, the olanzapine-fluoxetine combination and lithium. Antidepressants alone can trigger mania or rapid cycling.

Takeaway: treat bipolar depression with drugs such as quetiapine or lurasidone, not an antidepressant alone.

whyNot.D: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder risks triggering mania.
whyNot.A: Bupropion monotherapy carries the same switching risk.
whyNot.E: Venlafaxine has a particularly high switching risk.
whyNot.B: Haloperidol has no antidepressant efficacy in bipolar depression.

items.objective: Choose treatment for bipolar depression.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man started sertraline 3 weeks ago for depression. For 5 days he has slept 2 hours a night, talks rapidly, has started three businesses and says he has a special mission. He is irritable but not violent, and he has no medical illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue sertraline and add a benzodiazepine for sleep

options.label: D
options.html: Stop sertraline and start a mood-stabilising treatment

items.explanationHtml:
A full manic episode emerging on an antidepressant that persists beyond the drug's physiological effect is diagnosed as bipolar I disorder. Stop the antidepressant and start an antimanic treatment (lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic). Long-term mood stabilisation follows.

Takeaway: antidepressant-emergent mania requires stopping the antidepressant and treating mania.

whyNot.A: Continuing the antidepressant sustains the manic switch.
whyNot.C: A higher antidepressant dose would drive the mania further.
whyNot.E: Any antidepressant can maintain mania.
whyNot.B: Psychotherapy alone does not treat mania.

items.objective: Manage mania emerging during antidepressant treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had two episodes of major depression lasting several months. Her husband describes periods of 5 to 6 days, a few times a year, when she sleeps 4 hours a night, is unusually talkative and productive, and redecorates the house; she has never been hospitalised, has never been psychotic and functions well during these times. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Episodes of elevated mood lasting at least 4 days without marked impairment or psychosis are hypomanic. Hypomania plus major depressive episodes, without mania, is bipolar II disorder. Patients often present only with depression, so ask about hypomania and get collateral history.

Takeaway: hypomania plus major depression, never mania, is bipolar II.

whyNot.A: Bipolar I requires a manic episode with marked impairment or psychosis.
whyNot.C: She has had full major depressive episodes, which exclude cyclothymia.
whyNot.D: Hypomanic episodes rule out unipolar depression.
whyNot.E: Her depressive episodes are discrete, with hypomania in between.

items.objective: Diagnose bipolar II disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man says he has felt "down" most days for as long as he can remember, at least the past 5 years. He has low energy, poor self-esteem and trouble making decisions, but he works and has never had 2 weeks with enough symptoms for a major depressive episode. He has never had elevated mood. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Depressed mood most days for at least 2 years (1 year in young people) with symptoms such as low energy and low self-esteem is persistent depressive disorder. Treatment combines psychotherapy and an antidepressant.

Takeaway: chronic depressed mood for 2 years or more is persistent depressive disorder.

whyNot.C: Cyclothymia requires hypomanic symptoms as well.
whyNot.D: He has never met criteria for a major depressive episode.
whyNot.A: There is no identifiable stressor and the course is years long.
whyNot.B: Avoidant personality centres on fear of rejection, not chronic depressed mood.

items.objective: Diagnose persistent depressive disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has had irritability, tearfulness, bloating and food cravings in the 7 days before every period for 2 years, causing arguments at work. Symptoms resolve within 3 days of the start of menstruation. Daily symptom diaries over two cycles confirm the pattern. She does not want to become pregnant in the near future and has no contraindication to oestrogen. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Mood symptoms confined to the luteal phase and confirmed by prospective ratings are premenstrual dysphoric disorder. SSRIs are first-line and work quickly, so they can be taken throughout the cycle or only in the luteal phase. A drospirenone-containing combined oral contraceptive is an alternative.

Takeaway: SSRIs are first-line for PMDD.

whyNot.B: Danazol has androgenic side effects and is not used.
whyNot.A: Benzodiazepines risk dependence and are not first-line.
whyNot.D: Progesterone has not been shown to help.
whyNot.E: Spironolactone may reduce bloating but does not treat mood symptoms.

items.objective: Treat premenstrual dysphoric disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman delivered a healthy baby 4 days ago. She has been crying easily, feels overwhelmed and anxious, and has mood swings, but she sleeps when the baby sleeps, enjoys holding her daughter and has no thoughts of harming herself or the baby. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Reassure her and arrange follow-up within 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Tearfulness and mood lability in the first days after birth, with preserved function and bonding, are postpartum blues, which affect most new mothers and resolve within 2 weeks. Reassure, encourage support and rest, and review; persistence beyond 2 weeks or more severe symptoms suggest postpartum depression.

Takeaway: postpartum blues are self-limited; reassure and follow up.

whyNot.D: Medication is not needed for this self-limited condition.
whyNot.E: Zuranolone is for postpartum depression, not blues.
whyNot.A: There are no psychotic features or risk to warrant admission.
whyNot.B: Stopping breastfeeding is not necessary.

items.objective: Distinguish postpartum blues from postpartum depression.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman 6 days after delivery is brought in by her husband. For 2 days she has barely slept, is confused about the time, and believes the baby has been swapped for an impostor. She has a history of a manic episode at age 22. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit her to hospital and ensure the infant's safety

options.label: B
options.html: Reassure the family and review in 1 week

options.label: C
options.html: Refer for outpatient cognitive behavioural therapy

items.explanationHtml:
Postpartum psychosis (rapid onset of confusion, delusions, insomnia) is a psychiatric emergency, strongly linked to bipolar disorder. It carries risks of suicide and infanticide. Admit (ideally to a mother-and-baby unit), ensure the infant is safe, exclude medical causes such as infection or thyroid disease, and treat with an antipsychotic and mood stabiliser, or ECT.

Takeaway: postpartum psychosis needs urgent admission and protection of the infant.

whyNot.B: This is an emergency, not a self-limited condition.
whyNot.E: An antidepressant alone could worsen a bipolar-related psychosis.
whyNot.D: Zuranolone treats postpartum depression, not psychosis.
whyNot.C: Psychosis with risk to the baby cannot be managed this way.

items.objective: Manage postpartum psychosis.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with depression tells you he plans to shoot himself this weekend with the rifle he keeps at home, and has written a note to his wife. He drinks heavily and lives alone. He refuses voluntary admission and wants to go home. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Ask his wife to remove the rifle and discharge

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge with a written safety plan

options.label: E
options.html: Start an antidepressant and see him in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
A specific plan, access to lethal means, a note and risk factors (older male, alcohol use, living alone) mean imminent suicide risk. When he refuses voluntary admission, involuntary hospitalisation is justified to keep him safe while he is assessed and treated.

Takeaway: imminent suicide risk with refusal of admission justifies involuntary hospitalisation.

whyNot.C: A safety plan is insufficient with a specific, imminent plan and access to a firearm.
whyNot.E: This leaves him at high immediate risk.
whyNot.B: Means restriction helps, but his risk remains imminent.
whyNot.A: Outpatient care is not safe now.

items.objective: Manage a patient at imminent risk of suicide.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy has had depressed mood for 2 months after a breakup. He has passive thoughts that "everyone would be better off without me" but no plan or intent and no past attempts. His father keeps an unlocked handgun at home. He agrees to outpatient care with an antidepressant and therapy. In addition, which of the following is the most important intervention to reduce his risk of suicide?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask him to sign a no-suicide contract

options.label: B
options.html: Avoid asking further about suicide to prevent suggestion

options.label: C
options.html: Counsel the family on removing or locking up the gun

items.explanationHtml:
Firearms are the most lethal suicide method, and access to them strongly raises the chance that an attempt is fatal. Lethal means counselling, removing the gun from the home or locking it unloaded with ammunition stored separately, is one of the most effective prevention measures, together with a safety plan and close follow-up after starting an antidepressant in a young person.

Takeaway: restricting access to firearms is a key suicide prevention step.

whyNot.A: No-suicide contracts have no proven protective effect.
whyNot.E: Benzodiazepines can disinhibit and are not protective.
whyNot.D: Close early follow-up is needed after starting an antidepressant in a teenager.
whyNot.B: Asking about suicide does not increase risk.

items.objective: Apply lethal means counselling in suicide prevention.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl has had low mood, irritability, poor sleep and falling grades for 3 months. PHQ-A score indicates moderate to severe depression. She has no suicidal plan and no past manic symptoms. She has started cognitive behavioural therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to add?
items.explanationHtml:
For moderate to severe adolescent depression, combining CBT with an SSRI is most effective. Fluoxetine (and escitalopram) have the best evidence and approval for this age group. Because of the boxed warning for suicidal thinking in people under 25, review closely in the first weeks.

Takeaway: fluoxetine plus CBT, with close follow-up, for moderate to severe adolescent depression.

whyNot.A: Tricyclics are not effective in adolescent depression and are dangerous in overdose.
whyNot.E: Paroxetine has not shown benefit in adolescents and has worse discontinuation effects.
whyNot.D: Lithium is not a first-line antidepressant.
whyNot.B: Bupropion lacks evidence as first-line treatment in adolescents.

items.objective: Choose pharmacotherapy for adolescent depression.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman taking fluoxetine for depression was prescribed tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. She is now agitated, sweating and has diarrhoea. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F) and pulse is 118/min. Reflexes are brisk with sustained clonus at both ankles and horizontal ocular clonus. Muscle tone is increased in the legs more than the arms. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: E
options.html: Stop both drugs and give a benzodiazepine

items.explanationHtml:
Agitation, diarrhoea, sweating, fever and clonus with hyperreflexia (worse in the legs) within a day or two of adding tramadol to an SSRI is serotonin syndrome. Stop all serotonergic drugs, give supportive care and a benzodiazepine for agitation, and add cyproheptadine if symptoms persist. Severe hyperthermia needs sedation, paralysis and intubation.

Takeaway: serotonin syndrome is treated by stopping serotonergic drugs and giving benzodiazepines, then cyproheptadine.

whyNot.B: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia; it is not first-line here.
whyNot.C: Antipsychotics can worsen hyperthermia and cause NMS-like problems.
whyNot.A: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist used in NMS and could worsen serotonin toxicity.
whyNot.D: Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dry skin and reduced bowel sounds.

items.objective: Recognise and treat serotonin syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is admitted with her second manic episode. She has not responded to quetiapine in the past and agrees to start lithium for acute treatment and long-term prevention. She takes no other medicines. Which of the following tests are most important before starting lithium?

options.label: B
options.html: Creatinine, TSH, calcium and a pregnancy test

items.explanationHtml:
Lithium is cleared by the kidney and can cause kidney impairment, hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia, and it is teratogenic in early pregnancy. Baseline creatinine (eGFR), TSH, calcium and a pregnancy test, with an ECG in older patients or those with heart disease, are needed. Levels are checked about 12 hours after a dose, 5 days after each change.

Takeaway: before lithium, check kidney function, thyroid, calcium and pregnancy status.

whyNot.D: These are monitored with valproate.
whyNot.C: This is screened before carbamazepine in people of Asian ancestry.
whyNot.A: This is the key test for clozapine.
whyNot.E: These are relevant to valproate.

items.objective: List baseline tests before starting lithium.

items.stemHtml:
The patient was discharged on lithium, and her levels were stable at 0.8 mEq/L for 9 months. A week ago she started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. She now has nausea, diarrhoea and a coarse hand tremor. She is alert and oriented with no confusion, ataxia or seizures. Results:

TestResultReference range
Lithium1.9 mEq/L0.6–1.2 mEq/L
Sodium137 mEq/L136–145 mEq/L
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL0.6–1.2 mg/dL

ECG shows sinus rhythm with normal intervals. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Continue lithium at half the dose with the thiazide

options.label: D
options.html: Stop both drugs and give IV saline

items.explanationHtml:
She has mild to moderate lithium toxicity caused by the thiazide. Hold lithium, stop the thiazide, and give IV isotonic saline to restore volume and lithium excretion, with repeat levels. Kidney function is normal and there are no severe neurological signs, so dialysis is not needed now.

Takeaway: moderate lithium toxicity without severe neurological signs: stop lithium and the interacting drug and give IV saline.

whyNot.E: Dialysis is reserved for severe neurological toxicity or very high levels, especially with poor kidney function.
whyNot.A: Charcoal does not bind lithium.
whyNot.C: The interacting drug and toxic level must both be addressed.
whyNot.B: Amiloride treats nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, not toxicity.

items.objective: Manage moderate lithium toxicity caused by a drug interaction.

items.stemHtml: The patient's lithium level returns to the therapeutic range and she restarts lithium at a lower dose. Over the next year she develops polyuria of about 5 L a day and constant thirst. Serum sodium is 146 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L) and urine osmolality is 140 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 155 mOsm/kg. Her mood has been stable for the first time in years. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Polyuria with dilute urine that barely responds to desmopressin is lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Amiloride blocks ENaC, reducing lithium entry into principal cells and improving concentrating ability. Use the lowest effective lithium level and keep monitoring kidney function.

Takeaway: treat lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with amiloride when lithium must continue.

whyNot.B: Her kidneys did not respond to desmopressin.
whyNot.C: Fluid restriction in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus risks hypernatraemia.
whyNot.D: Thiazides reduce polyuria but caused her lithium toxicity before.
whyNot.E: Her mood is finally stable on lithium; manageable polyuria does not require stopping it.

items.objective: Treat lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is brought in by her sister. For 8 days she has slept 2 to 3 hours a night, talked continuously, spent $20,000 on jewellery and believes she has been chosen to save the world. She is not taking any medicine. She has no medical illness and is not pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate acute pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
