She has severe mania with psychotic features. First-line treatment is lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic; in severe mania, combining an antipsychotic with lithium or valproate works faster and better than either alone. Admission is usually needed.

Takeaway: severe mania is treated with an antipsychotic plus lithium or valproate.

whyNot.D: Sertraline given alone in mania can drive the episode further instead of treating it.
whyNot.B: Lamotrigine needs slow titration and does not treat acute mania.
whyNot.A: Buspirone has no antimanic effect.
whyNot.E: Topiramate has not shown efficacy in mania.

items.objective: Choose acute treatment for severe mania.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is well on valproate. She is starting a new relationship and plans to become pregnant within a year. She has had three manic episodes, one with psychosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue valproate and add folic acid 4 mg daily

options.label: B
options.html: Continue valproate until pregnancy is confirmed, then switch

options.label: C
options.html: Stop valproate and give no maintenance treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Switch to lithium or a suitable antipsychotic before conception

items.explanationHtml:
Valproate carries a high risk of neural tube defects and of lower IQ and neurodevelopmental disorders in exposed children, so it is avoided in people who can become pregnant. With a history of severe episodes, she needs maintenance treatment: switch before conception to lithium (with fetal echocardiography and level monitoring) or an antipsychotic with reassuring pregnancy data, under specialist care.

Takeaway: switch from valproate before conception; do not stop maintenance treatment in severe bipolar disorder.

whyNot.A: High-dose folic acid does not remove the neural tube and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate.
whyNot.C: Stopping all treatment risks relapse, which is especially dangerous postpartum.
whyNot.D: Carbamazepine is also teratogenic and interacts with contraceptives.
whyNot.B: Neural tube closure happens before most pregnancies are recognised.

items.objective: Plan bipolar maintenance treatment before pregnancy.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she could not move her right leg after an argument with her partner 4 hours ago. She drags the leg behind her when she walks. Hip extension on the right is weak when tested directly. When she flexes her left hip against resistance, the examiner's hand under her right heel is pressed down firmly. Reflexes and plantar responses are normal, and MRI of the brain and spine is normal. She is distressed by the weakness and wants to return to work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Weakness that disappears during an automatic movement is a positive Hoover sign: hip extension is weak on request but strong when it happens automatically during opposite hip flexion. Together with a dragging gait and normal investigations, this establishes functional neurological symptom disorder. The symptoms are real and not produced on purpose.

Takeaway: functional neurological symptom disorder is diagnosed from positive signs such as the Hoover sign, not only by excluding disease.

whyNot.C: Malingering requires deliberate feigning for an external reward; she has none and wants to go back to work.
whyNot.A: Factitious disorder involves deliberate falsification; nothing suggests she is producing the weakness on purpose.
whyNot.E: Somatic symptom disorder centres on excessive thoughts and worry about symptoms; an acute motor deficit with positive functional signs fits functional neurological symptom disorder.
whyNot.D: A normal MRI, normal reflexes and a positive Hoover sign argue against a demyelinating lesion.

items.objective: Recognise functional weakness from a positive Hoover sign.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old accountant has seen four physicians in the past year because he is convinced that he has colon cancer. He has no bowel symptoms, weight loss or bleeding. Colonoscopy 8 months ago was normal. He checks his stools daily and reads about cancer each night, and each normal test reassures him for only a few days. Physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Preoccupation with having a serious illness, with no or mild bodily symptoms, lasting 6 months or more and leading to repeated checking and medical visits, is illness anxiety disorder. Reassurance helps only briefly.

Takeaway: fear of disease without significant symptoms is illness anxiety disorder; prominent distressing symptoms point to somatic symptom disorder.

whyNot.E: Somatic symptom disorder needs distressing bodily symptoms; he has none, only fear of disease.
whyNot.A: His belief responds briefly to reassurance and he can consider other explanations, so it is not a fixed delusion.
whyNot.C: He has no motor or sensory symptoms.
whyNot.B: He does not falsify symptoms or signs.

items.objective: Distinguish illness anxiety disorder from somatic symptom disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has well-controlled joint inflammation on methotrexate; her ESR and C-reactive protein have been normal for a year. She still reports constant, severe pain in her hands and spends several hours each day searching online about her illness. She has visited the emergency department nine times in 6 months and says she is sure the arthritis is destroying her joints despite normal imaging. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

items.explanationHtml:
Somatic symptom disorder requires distressing bodily symptoms with disproportionate thoughts, anxiety or time devoted to them, usually for 6 months or more. The symptoms do not have to be medically unexplained: a real, controlled disease with an excessive response qualifies.

Takeaway: a medical diagnosis does not exclude somatic symptom disorder; judge the response to the symptom.

whyNot.B: Illness anxiety disorder applies when bodily symptoms are absent or mild; her pain is prominent and distressing.
whyNot.D: That diagnosis applies when behaviour or emotion worsens the medical disease itself; her arthritis is controlled, and the problem is her excessive response to the symptom.
whyNot.A: She has no motor or sensory symptom that is inconsistent with neurological disease.
whyNot.C: There is no external reward, and she is not feigning symptoms.

items.objective: Diagnose somatic symptom disorder in a patient who also has a confirmed medical disease.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with known coronary artery disease has had three episodes of chest pressure on exertion this month. He has not told anyone and has stopped taking his prescribed nitroglycerin because, he says, "if I don't think about it, it isn't real." He has no other psychiatric symptoms. His wife brings him in after he nearly fainted while shovelling snow. Which of the following best describes the psychiatric contribution to his presentation?

options.label: D
options.html: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

options.label: E
options.html: Somatic symptom disorder with predominant pain

items.explanationHtml:
When a psychological or behavioural factor, here denial with nonadherence, adversely affects the course or treatment of a real medical condition, the diagnosis is psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.

Takeaway: denial or nonadherence that worsens a known disease is coded as a psychological factor affecting that condition.

whyNot.E: He minimises rather than dwells on his symptoms, the opposite of somatic symptom disorder.
whyNot.C: He is avoiding the illness, not preoccupied by fear of having one.
whyNot.A: Adjustment disorder is distress or impaired function after a stressor; his problem is denial that worsens a medical disease.
whyNot.B: He is not falsifying or inducing symptoms.

items.objective: Identify psychological factors affecting a medical condition.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman has had frequent episodes of generalized shaking despite two antiseizure drugs. Her roommate filmed an event that lasted 9 minutes. Which of the following features of the event most strongly suggests a functional (non-epileptic) attack rather than an epileptic seizure?

options.label: A
options.html: A bite on the side of the tongue

options.label: C
options.html: Eyes tightly closed and resisting opening

options.label: E
options.html: The same sequence of movements in every event

items.explanationHtml:
Eyes closed during the event, with resistance to eye opening, strongly favours a functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) attack. So do side-to-side head movements, asynchronous limb movements, a long duration and quick recovery. Video-EEG of a typical event confirms the diagnosis.

Takeaway: closed eyes during a convulsive event point to a functional attack.

whyNot.A: A lateral tongue bite favours an epileptic generalized seizure.
whyNot.D: Events arising from sleep favour epileptic seizures.
whyNot.B: Prolonged postictal confusion favours an epileptic seizure; functional attacks usually end with rapid recovery.
whyNot.E: Stereotyped events favour epilepsy; functional attacks vary.

items.objective: Identify clinical features that distinguish functional non-epileptic attacks from epileptic seizures.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has had loss of vision in both eyes for 2 days, beginning the morning after he witnessed a serious road accident. He walks around furniture without bumping into it. Pupillary light reflexes are normal, and a rotating striped drum produces normal optokinetic nystagmus. He is not seeking compensation or time off and is frightened by the symptom. Refer to the figure. Which lettered end point corresponds to the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Normal pupils and preserved optokinetic nystagmus show that the visual pathway works, so the blindness is inconsistent with structural disease. He is not producing it on purpose and gains nothing from it. On the tree: not on purpose, not mainly fear of disease, neurological and inconsistent, which leads to end point B, functional neurological symptom disorder.

Takeaway: intact optokinetic nystagmus in a patient reporting blindness points to functional visual loss.

whyNot.A: End point A is reached when the main problem is fear of having a disease with mild symptoms; he has a striking symptom.
whyNot.C: End point C is reached when the symptom is not neurological; his symptom is visual loss inconsistent with disease.
whyNot.D: End point D requires deliberate production with an external reward; he has neither.
whyNot.E: End point E requires deliberate production of symptoms; nothing suggests this.

items.objective: Classify a presentation as functional neurological symptom disorder using intentionality and the nature of the symptom.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman notices her heartbeat after climbing stairs and becomes certain that she is about to have a heart attack. Echocardiography, ECG and Holter monitoring are normal. Her physician explains that she interprets normal bodily sensations as signs of a dangerous disease, and recommends a treatment that teaches her to test and replace these interpretations. Which of the following treatments is being described?
items.explanationHtml:
Cognitive behavioural therapy targets catastrophic misinterpretation of normal bodily sensations, together with checking and reassurance-seeking. It has the best evidence in illness anxiety and somatic symptom disorders.

Takeaway: CBT changes the catastrophic interpretation of bodily sensations that drives health anxiety.

whyNot.D: Psychodynamic therapy explores unconscious conflicts rather than directly testing catastrophic interpretations.
whyNot.A: Biofeedback trains control of physiological signals such as muscle tension; it does not target beliefs about illness.
whyNot.C: Interpersonal therapy addresses relationships and role transitions.
whyNot.E: Reassurance relieves anxiety only briefly and does not change the interpretation.

items.objective: Match cognitive behavioural therapy to the misinterpretation of bodily sensations in health anxiety.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old nurse is found confused at work with a capillary glucose of 32 mg/dL. She has had three similar episodes. She has no history of diabetes. A blood sample taken during the episode shows an insulin concentration well above the reference range and a C-peptide concentration below the reference range. A screen for sulfonylureas is negative. Which of the following best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Beta cells cleave proinsulin into insulin and C-peptide in equal amounts. Pharmaceutical insulin contains no C-peptide, and the hypoglycemia it causes suppresses the patient's own secretion, so high insulin with low C-peptide means exogenous insulin.

Takeaway: hypoglycemia with high insulin and low C-peptide means injected insulin.

whyNot.D: An insulinoma secretes insulin and C-peptide together, so C-peptide would be high.
whyNot.B: A sulfonylurea makes beta cells secrete, so C-peptide would be high, and the screen would be positive.
whyNot.A: Hypoglycemia from cortisol deficiency comes with low, not high, insulin.
whyNot.E: She has had no gastric surgery, and late dumping raises both insulin and C-peptide.

items.objective: Use insulin and C-peptide levels to identify surreptitious insulin injection.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old pharmacy technician has recurrent fasting hypoglycemia. During an episode, serum insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin are all raised. Pancreatic imaging is normal. A drug screen detects an agent that she has access to at work. This agent most likely causes hypoglycemia by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: B
options.html: Activating the insulin receptor tyrosine kinase

options.label: C
options.html: Closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels on beta cells

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis via AMP kinase

items.explanationHtml:
High insulin and C-peptide with a positive drug screen points to a sulfonylurea (or meglitinide). These drugs bind the SUR1 subunit and close ATP-sensitive potassium channels. Beta cells depolarise, calcium enters and insulin is secreted with C-peptide.

Takeaway: sulfonylureas cause endogenous insulin release, so C-peptide rises.

whyNot.B: That is how insulin itself acts, and injected insulin would lower C-peptide.
whyNot.D: DPP-4 inhibitors enhance glucose-dependent secretion and rarely cause hypoglycemia on their own.
whyNot.A: Thiazolidinediones improve insulin sensitivity and do not cause hypoglycemia alone.
whyNot.E: Metformin reduces hepatic glucose output and does not raise insulin or C-peptide.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism by which sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia with high C-peptide.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman who works in a hospital pharmacy has palpitations, tremor and a 6-kg weight loss. Her thyroid is not enlarged or tender. TSH is suppressed and free thyroxine is high. Radioactive iodine uptake in the neck is very low, and serum thyroglobulin is undetectable. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses TSH, so the gland takes up little iodine and releases little thyroglobulin. Low uptake with a low thyroglobulin points to ingested thyroid hormone. In thyroiditis, uptake is also low, but thyroglobulin is high.

Takeaway: low radioiodine uptake with low thyroglobulin means exogenous thyroid hormone.

whyNot.C: Thyroiditis also lowers uptake, but injured follicles leak thyroglobulin, so it would be raised.
whyNot.A: Graves disease causes diffusely increased radioiodine uptake.
whyNot.D: Ovarian thyroid tissue makes thyroglobulin and takes up iodine in the pelvis, so thyroglobulin is not low.
whyNot.E: A toxic goiter shows increased uptake in nodules and usually a palpable gland.

items.objective: Use thyroglobulin to distinguish factitious thyrotoxicosis from thyroiditis.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old laboratory worker has gum bleeding and large bruises. She takes no prescribed drugs. Prothrombin time and INR are markedly prolonged; aPTT is mildly prolonged. Both correct when her plasma is mixed with normal plasma. Factors II, VII, IX and X are low, while factor V and fibrinogen are normal. A toxicology screen detects an anticoagulant used as a rodent poison. The substance most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: D
options.html: Formation of an inhibitor antibody against factor VIII

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase

items.explanationHtml:
Low factors II, VII, IX and X with a normal factor V is the signature of a vitamin K antagonist. Warfarin and the long-acting rodenticide anticoagulants (superwarfarins) inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase, so these factors are not gamma-carboxylated.

Takeaway: low II, VII, IX and X with normal factor V means a vitamin K antagonist.

whyNot.B: Direct factor Xa inhibitors are not used as rodent poisons, and they do not impair the synthesis of the vitamin K-dependent factors.
whyNot.A: Heparins act through antithrombin, prolong the aPTT most and do not lower factor levels.
whyNot.C: Direct thrombin inhibitors do not impair synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X and are not rodent poisons.
whyNot.D: An acquired inhibitor does not correct on mixing and would leave factor VIII low, not II, VII, IX and X.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of warfarin-type anticoagulants from the factor pattern.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man in jail reports severe headaches and "seeing spirits" the week before his trial. He asks to be moved to the hospital wing. He describes the visions vaguely, and his account changes between interviews. When observed without his knowledge, he chats calmly with other inmates. Which of the following best describes his behaviour?
items.explanationHtml:
Feigned symptoms that are inconsistent, disappear when unobserved and serve a clear external goal (avoiding trial, a transfer) are malingering. It is a behaviour, not a mental disorder.

Takeaway: on-purpose symptoms with an external reward are malingering.

whyNot.B: Factitious disorder lacks an obvious external reward; avoiding trial and gaining a transfer are external goals.
whyNot.A: His symptoms are vague, changeable and absent when he is unobserved.
whyNot.E: Symptoms are produced on purpose here, which excludes somatic symptom disorder.
whyNot.D: There is no history of psychosis or functional decline, and the timing fits a goal.

items.objective: Recognise malingering from an external incentive and inconsistent symptoms.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has had nine admissions for vomiting and diarrhea. A laxative is found in his stool, and he improves whenever his mother is not allowed to visit. His mother, a former medical assistant, is attentive and asks for more endoscopies. Which of the following is the correct diagnostic attribution?

options.label: A
options.html: Child: factitious disorder imposed on self

options.label: C
options.html: Mother: factitious disorder imposed on another

items.explanationHtml:
When a caregiver deliberately falsifies or causes illness in another person without an external reward, the caregiver receives the diagnosis factitious disorder imposed on another. The child is a victim of maltreatment, and the case must be reported.

Takeaway: in factitious disorder imposed on another, the diagnosis belongs to the caregiver.

whyNot.A: The child is the victim; he is not producing his own illness.
whyNot.D: There is no external reward such as money; her motive is the role of caring for a sick child.
whyNot.E: Somatic symptom disorder concerns the patient's own symptoms and is not deliberate.
whyNot.B: A laxative in the stool and recovery away from the mother show an external cause.

items.objective: Attribute factitious disorder imposed on another to the caregiver.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman, a respiratory therapist, has had 14 admissions for recurrent skin abscesses that grow mixed bowel organisms. The lesions occur only on her thighs and forearms. A nurse finds a syringe of murky fluid in her bag. She has no disability claim, is employed, and repeatedly asks for further surgery. Refer to the figure. Which lettered end point corresponds to the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Abscesses with mixed bowel organisms in reachable sites, a syringe of contaminated fluid and a wish for surgery indicate deliberate self-induced illness. With no external reward, the motive is the sick role. The tree leads to end point E, factitious disorder imposed on self.

Takeaway: deliberate self-induced illness without an external reward is factitious disorder.

whyNot.A: End point A is reached only when symptoms are not produced on purpose; she is injecting material.
whyNot.B: End point B is for symptoms not produced on purpose; her abscesses are self-induced.
whyNot.C: End point C is for symptoms not produced on purpose.
whyNot.D: End point D needs an obvious external reward; she has no claim, money or other gain.

items.objective: Classify self-induced illness without external reward as factitious disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student has swelling at both angles of the jaw and erosion of the inner surfaces of her upper incisors. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². She admits to binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting several times a week. Which of the following sets of laboratory findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: High chloride, high potassium, high bicarbonate

options.label: B
options.html: High chloride, low potassium, low bicarbonate

options.label: C
options.html: Low chloride, high potassium, low bicarbonate

options.label: D
options.html: Low chloride, low potassium, high bicarbonate

options.label: E
options.html: Normal chloride, normal potassium, normal bicarbonate

items.explanationHtml:
Vomiting removes hydrochloric acid, so chloride falls and bicarbonate rises. Volume depletion activates aldosterone, which increases potassium and hydrogen ion secretion in the collecting duct. The result is a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

Takeaway: self-induced vomiting gives a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.

whyNot.B: A hyperchloremic acidosis fits stool bicarbonate loss, as with laxatives, not vomiting.
whyNot.C: Vomiting causes renal potassium loss, not hyperkalemia, and raises bicarbonate.
whyNot.E: Several episodes a week usually disturb the electrolytes.
whyNot.A: Vomiting loses chloride, and the alkalosis and aldosterone drive potassium loss.

items.objective: Predict the electrolyte and acid-base pattern of recurrent vomiting.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with a BMI of 18 kg/m² has fatigue. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L) and bicarbonate is 34 mEq/L (22–28 mEq/L). Blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. She denies vomiting and says she takes no medications. Which of the following findings would most strongly indicate surreptitious vomiting rather than diuretic misuse?
items.explanationHtml:
After vomiting, the kidney conserves chloride, so urine chloride is low. While a diuretic is acting, chloride is lost in the urine. Urine sodium is unreliable in vomiting because filtered bicarbonate drags sodium into the urine.

Takeaway: metabolic alkalosis with low urine chloride points to vomiting rather than diuretics.

whyNot.B: A high urine chloride with alkalosis fits active diuretic use or a tubular disorder.
whyNot.A: Renin is raised by volume depletion from either vomiting or diuretics.
whyNot.D: Magnesium can fall with either cause, so it does not separate them.
whyNot.C: Urine sodium can be high in vomiting (bicarbonaturia) and with diuretics, so it does not separate them.

items.objective: Use urine chloride to separate vomiting from diuretic misuse in metabolic alkalosis.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa and a BMI of 13.9 kg/m² is admitted. Her serum phosphate is normal on admission. Three days after nutrition is started she has leg weakness, shortness of breath and ankle edema, and her serum phosphate is 1.0 mg/dL (3.0–4.5 mg/dL). Which of the following best explains the fall in phosphate?

options.label: A
options.html: Dilution by the volume of the feeds

options.label: B
options.html: Increased urinary phosphate loss caused by parathyroid hormone

options.label: C
options.html: Insulin-driven uptake of phosphate into cells

options.label: D
options.html: Phosphate binding by calcium in the feed

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced intestinal absorption due to vitamin D deficiency

items.explanationHtml:
Feeding releases insulin, which drives glucose into cells, where glycolysis and ATP synthesis use phosphate. Insulin also shifts potassium and magnesium inward. Total-body phosphate is already depleted after starvation, so the serum level falls sharply in the first days.

Takeaway: refeeding hypophosphatemia comes from an insulin-driven shift of phosphate into cells.

whyNot.B: PTH is not the driver; the fall follows the insulin response to carbohydrate.
whyNot.E: Malabsorption would not cause an abrupt fall within days of feeding.
whyNot.A: Dilution cannot explain a fall of this size.
whyNot.D: Binding in the gut would reduce absorption but not cause this rapid intracellular shift.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of hypophosphatemia in refeeding syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa has had no menstrual periods for 8 months. Her BMI is 15.5 kg/m². Pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following sets of hormone levels is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: High LH, high FSH, low estradiol

options.label: B
options.html: High LH, normal FSH, high testosterone

options.label: C
options.html: Low LH, high FSH, normal estradiol

options.label: D
options.html: Low LH, low FSH, low estradiol

options.label: E
options.html: Normal LH, normal FSH, high prolactin

items.explanationHtml:
Energy deficit and low leptin slow hypothalamic GnRH pulses, so LH, FSH and estradiol are all low: functional hypothalamic amenorrhea. The low estrogen contributes to bone loss.

Takeaway: anorexia nervosa causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

whyNot.A: High gonadotropins with low estradiol indicate primary ovarian insufficiency.
whyNot.B: This pattern suggests polycystic ovary syndrome.
whyNot.E: A prolactinoma is not suggested, and starvation does not raise prolactin markedly.
whyNot.C: This mixed pattern does not fit hypothalamic suppression.

items.objective: Predict the reproductive hormone pattern in anorexia nervosa.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa also has depressed mood and wants to stop smoking. She asks for a medication that might help both. Her physician advises against a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor that is often used for these two problems. Which of the following adverse effects is the main reason for avoiding it in her?
items.explanationHtml:
Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold, and the risk was higher in people with bulimia nervosa, whose electrolyte disturbances add to it. It is contraindicated in bulimia and anorexia nervosa. Fluoxetine is the drug of choice for bulimia nervosa.

Takeaway: avoid bupropion in eating disorders because of the seizure risk.

whyNot.D: The drug has little serotonergic action, and the concern in bulimia is seizures.
whyNot.E: This drug tends to cause weight loss, not gain.
whyNot.B: QT prolongation is not the labelled concern; seizure risk is.
whyNot.A: Agranulocytosis is linked to clozapine and some other drugs, not this one.

items.objective: Explain why bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia nervosa.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with Parkinson disease started a new medication 9 months ago and his tremor improved. His wife reports that he has since lost a large sum of money betting online, which is unlike him. The medication most likely responsible acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: C
options.html: Direct stimulation of D2 and D3 dopamine receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole stimulate D2 and D3 receptors, including in the mesolimbic reward pathway. They are the drugs most strongly linked to impulse-control disorders such as gambling, shopping and hypersexuality.

Takeaway: new compulsive gambling on Parkinson treatment points to a dopamine agonist.

whyNot.E: MAO-B inhibitors are much less often linked to compulsive behaviours.
whyNot.D: COMT inhibitors extend levodopa action and are not the usual cause.
whyNot.A: Anticholinergics cause confusion and dry mouth, not compulsive gambling.
whyNot.B: Amantadine is not the classic cause of new pathological gambling.

items.objective: Link dopamine agonists to drug-induced impulse-control disorders.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old boy living in a house built in the 1930s has been seen eating flakes of peeling paint from the windowsills. He is irritable and has abdominal pain. Blood count shows a microcytic anemia, and a smear shows coarse blue granules in many red cells. Inhibition of which of the following enzymes contributes most directly to his anemia?
items.explanationHtml:
Pica for paint chips in an old house suggests lead poisoning. Lead inhibits ferrochelatase, which inserts iron into protoporphyrin, and ALA dehydratase. Heme synthesis fails, causing a microcytic anemia, and impaired RNA breakdown leaves basophilic stippling.

Takeaway: pica for old paint causes lead poisoning, which blocks ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase.

whyNot.A: ALA synthase is the rate-limiting step but is not the main target of lead.
whyNot.E: Deficiency of this enzyme causes porphyria cutanea tarda, not lead poisoning.
whyNot.D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolysis with normocytic cells, not microcytosis with stippling.
whyNot.C: G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis, not microcytosis with stippling.

items.objective: Explain the heme synthesis defect in lead poisoning presenting with pica.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman has had abdominal pain, headaches and fatigue for 2 years. She has seen eight specialists. Upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, CT of the abdomen, MRI of the brain and extensive blood tests have been normal. She calls the office several times a week, worries constantly that something has been missed, and has stopped working. She asks for another CT scan. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?

options.label: B
options.html: Referral to a ninth specialist for a fresh opinion

options.label: C
options.html: Regular scheduled visits with one primary care physician

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat CT of the abdomen every 6 months

options.label: E
options.html: Visits only when new symptoms arise

items.explanationHtml:
This is somatic symptom disorder. Care works best with one coordinating physician, regularly scheduled brief visits with a focused examination each time, avoidance of unnecessary tests, attention to function, and CBT.

Takeaway: manage somatic symptom disorder with scheduled visits to one physician and minimal unnecessary testing.

whyNot.B: Further referrals reinforce the cycle of testing and bring only brief relief.
whyNot.D: Unindicated imaging adds cost and radiation and does not reduce worry.
whyNot.A: Invasive procedures without an indication can cause harm and are avoided.
whyNot.E: Visits on demand reward new symptoms; scheduled visits work better.

items.objective: Choose the evidence-based care model for somatic symptom disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man has been convinced for a year that he has HIV infection, although he has had no sexual or other exposure for 3 years. He has had seven negative HIV tests, the latest 2 weeks ago, and checks his lymph nodes several times a day. He has no physical symptoms. He feels relieved after each negative test, but the worry returns within days. He has no psychotic symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Refer to an infectious diseases specialist

items.explanationHtml:
Persistent fear of a serious illness without significant symptoms, with excessive checking, is illness anxiety disorder. Cognitive behavioural therapy has the best evidence, and an SSRI can be added. Repeated testing and reassurance maintain the cycle.

Takeaway: treat illness anxiety disorder with CBT, not repeated tests.

whyNot.C: Repeated tests give only short relief and reinforce checking.
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines carry dependence risk and do not treat the underlying health anxiety.
whyNot.E: He is not psychotic; his belief is not fixed.
whyNot.B: A further specialist opinion is not indicated and reinforces the cycle.

items.objective: Choose CBT for illness anxiety disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman has had weakness of the left leg for 3 weeks, after a minor car accident in which she was not injured. She walks by dragging the left foot. Her left hip extension, weak on direct testing, becomes strong during resisted flexion of the right hip. Reflexes, tone, plantar responses and sensation are normal. MRI of the brain and spine is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain the diagnosis and refer for specialist physiotherapy

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat MRI of the spine in 6 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Tell her that no medical problem was found

items.explanationHtml:
A positive Hoover sign with otherwise normal findings establishes functional neurological symptom disorder. Explain the diagnosis, showing her the sign, and stress that the symptoms are real and can improve. Then refer for specialist physiotherapy, with psychological therapy as needed.

Takeaway: functional weakness is treated with a clear explanation and specialist physiotherapy.

whyNot.E: A purely negative message leaves her without a diagnosis or plan.
whyNot.C: The imaging is normal and the diagnosis rests on positive signs; repeat imaging is not indicated.
whyNot.D: There is no inflammatory lesion to treat.
whyNot.B: There is no clinical or imaging evidence of demyelination.

items.objective: Manage functional weakness with explanation and physiotherapy.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had episodes of generalized shaking twice a week for 6 months despite levetiracetam and lamotrigine. The events last 5 to 15 minutes, with side-to-side head movements, pelvic thrusting and eyes closed. She recovers quickly and can recall parts of each event. Routine EEG and MRI of the brain are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Serum prolactin after the next event

options.label: E
options.html: Video-EEG monitoring to record a typical event

items.explanationHtml:
Closed eyes, side-to-side head shaking, pelvic thrusting, long duration and preserved recall suggest functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) attacks. Video-EEG monitoring that captures a typical event without epileptiform activity confirms the diagnosis and allows antiseizure drugs to be tapered.

Takeaway: video-EEG of a typical event is the diagnostic test for non-epileptic attacks.

whyNot.A: The features strongly suggest non-epileptic events; adding drugs adds harm without benefit.
whyNot.C: Prolactin is an unreliable test and cannot replace recording the event.
whyNot.D: Device therapy is for confirmed drug-resistant epilepsy.
whyNot.B: A routine EEG between events is often normal in both conditions.

items.objective: Use video-EEG to diagnose suspected non-epileptic attacks.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl has been unable to walk for 5 days, beginning after she was bullied at school. Examination shows inconsistent weakness of both legs, a positive Hoover sign on both sides, and normal reflexes and sensation. Spine MRI is normal. Her mother asks whether her daughter is "making it up." Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: "Her tests are normal, so there is nothing physically wrong."

options.label: B
options.html: "It is caused by stress, so she needs a psychiatrist only."

options.label: C
options.html: "It is probably a phase; she should return to school tomorrow."

options.label: D
options.html: "No. The brain is not sending signals properly; it is real and can improve."

options.label: E
options.html: "We cannot be sure until more tests are done."

items.explanationHtml:
In functional neurological symptom disorder the symptoms are not produced on purpose. A good explanation says the symptoms are real, names the problem as one of nervous system function rather than damage, and gives hope of recovery. It is the first step of treatment.

Takeaway: explain functional symptoms as real, common and treatable.

whyNot.A: This dismisses real symptoms and offers no diagnosis or plan.
whyNot.C: This dismisses the symptoms and gives no treatment.
whyNot.E: The diagnosis rests on positive signs; more tests are not needed and add uncertainty.
whyNot.B: Blaming stress alone is unhelpful; treatment includes physiotherapy and an explanation of the disorder.

items.objective: Communicate a diagnosis of functional neurological symptom disorder to a family.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man with somatic symptom disorder attends his scheduled 4-weekly visit. He describes the same back pain and asks for another MRI of the spine; one 3 months ago was normal. His examination is unchanged and he has no red-flag features. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Acknowledge the pain and explain why a scan will not help

options.label: B
options.html: Order the MRI again so that he is reassured

options.label: C
options.html: Refer him to a spine surgeon for an opinion

options.label: D
options.html: Start an opioid for the pain between visits

options.label: E
options.html: Tell him the pain is imaginary and discharge him

items.explanationHtml:
In somatic symptom disorder, acknowledge the symptom, examine briefly, avoid tests without an indication, and keep the focus on function and coping. Continuing scheduled visits and offering CBT help more than another scan.

Takeaway: validate the symptom but decline unindicated tests in somatic symptom disorder.

whyNot.B: Repeat imaging without an indication gives only short relief and reinforces testing.
whyNot.E: His pain is real; dismissing it damages the relationship.
whyNot.C: There is no surgical indication.
whyNot.D: Opioids are avoided in somatic symptom disorder because of dependence and little benefit.

items.objective: Respond to a request for unnecessary testing in somatic symptom disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old woman with long-standing somatic symptom disorder has had low mood, early waking, poor concentration and loss of interest in her grandchildren for 2 months. She has no suicidal thoughts. She is already seeing her primary care physician monthly and has started CBT. Which of the following medications is most appropriate?
items.explanationHtml:
She has coexisting major depression. An SSRI such as sertraline (or an SNRI) treats the depression and may ease bodily symptoms, alongside CBT and scheduled visits.

Takeaway: treat coexisting depression in somatic symptom disorder with an SSRI or SNRI, not opioids or benzodiazepines.

whyNot.B: Opioids are avoided in somatic symptom disorder and do not treat depression.
whyNot.A: Benzodiazepines carry dependence risk and do not treat depression.
whyNot.D: An antipsychotic is not first-line for depression without psychosis.
whyNot.C: An MAO inhibitor is not first-line because of dietary and drug interactions.

items.objective: Choose an SSRI for depression coexisting with somatic symptom disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes has had three admissions for diabetic ketoacidosis this year. He says he skips insulin doses because he fears having a low blood sugar during soccer games, after one episode in front of his team. He has no low mood, no weight or shape concerns, and no other psychiatric symptoms. Which of the following best describes this problem?

options.label: D
options.html: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

items.explanationHtml:
Fear of hypoglycemia leads to insulin omission that worsens a real disease. This is psychological factors affecting other medical conditions. Address the fear directly, for example with education, a plan for glucose checks around sport and psychological support, while treating the diabetes.

Takeaway: an emotion or behaviour that worsens a known disease is a psychological factor affecting that condition.

whyNot.C: He is not preoccupied with having an undiagnosed disease.
whyNot.B: He omits insulin out of fear, not to be seen as ill.
whyNot.A: He has no weight or shape concerns; insulin omission for weight control would raise this question.
whyNot.E: He is not preoccupied with bodily symptoms.

items.objective: Diagnose psychological factors affecting a medical condition in an adolescent with diabetes.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has had right arm weakness for 2 weeks, beginning after a stressful job interview. Strength varies with distraction, and the arm drifts down without pronation. Her physician suspects a functional disorder. Which of the following findings would most strongly argue against this diagnosis and require further investigation?

options.label: B
options.html: An extensor plantar response on the right

options.label: C
options.html: Drift of the arm without pronation

options.label: D
options.html: Give-way weakness of the right grip

options.label: E
options.html: Weakness that improves when she is distracted

items.explanationHtml:
An extensor plantar response is an objective sign of upper motor neuron disease and is not produced by functional weakness. Its presence needs imaging and further assessment. Functional and structural disorders can also coexist.

Takeaway: objective neurological signs mean structural disease must be looked for, even when functional signs are present.

whyNot.D: Give-way weakness is typical of functional weakness.
whyNot.C: Drift without pronation is a feature of functional weakness.
whyNot.A: Coexisting anxiety is common and does not argue against the diagnosis.
whyNot.E: Variability with distraction supports functional weakness.

items.objective: Recognise objective signs that argue against a purely functional diagnosis.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old teacher reports that her vision has narrowed to a small central area over 3 weeks, since the death of her brother. Visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye. On tangent-screen testing her visual field measures the same width at 1 metre and at 2 metres. Pupils, fundi and optical coherence tomography are normal, and she has no financial or legal claims. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Bilateral occipital infarction with macular sparing

items.explanationHtml:
A real field defect gets wider as the test distance increases. A field of the same width at 1 and 2 metres (a tubular field) is optically impossible. With normal eye findings and no external gain, this is functional neurological symptom disorder.

Takeaway: a non-expanding tubular visual field indicates functional visual loss.

whyNot.A: Glaucoma shows optic disc cupping and nerve fibre loss on OCT.
whyNot.E: Retinitis pigmentosa causes night blindness and visible pigmentary change in the retina.
whyNot.D: She has no external incentive, and she is distressed by the symptom.
whyNot.B: An organic field defect widens as the test distance increases, and a stroke would begin suddenly.

items.objective: Recognise a tubular visual field as a sign of functional visual loss.

items.stemHtml: A neurologist sees several patients with functional neurological symptom disorder. Which of the following features in a patient is most strongly associated with a good outcome?

options.label: B
options.html: An ongoing lawsuit about the precipitating event

options.label: C
options.html: Belief that the cause is an undiscovered disease

options.label: D
options.html: Sudden onset, short duration and early acceptance of the diagnosis

options.label: E
options.html: Symptoms present for more than 5 years

items.explanationHtml:
Better outcomes in functional neurological symptom disorder are associated with acute onset, short duration, early diagnosis and acceptance of it, and younger age. Long duration, compensation claims, rejection of the diagnosis and personality disorder predict worse outcomes.

Takeaway: early diagnosis and acceptance predict recovery from functional symptoms.

whyNot.E: Long duration predicts a poorer outcome.
whyNot.B: Pending claims or compensation predict a poorer outcome.
whyNot.A: Personality disorder is associated with a poorer outcome.
whyNot.C: Rejecting the diagnosis predicts a poorer outcome.

items.objective: Identify favourable prognostic factors in functional neurological symptom disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man has had palpitations and chest tightness for 9 months. Cardiac evaluation, including stress testing and Holter monitoring, is normal. He thinks about the symptoms most of the day, has stopped exercising for fear of collapsing, and has visited the emergency department many times. He does not fake symptoms and wants them gone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Distressing bodily symptoms for over 6 months with excessive thoughts, anxiety and behaviour around them is somatic symptom disorder.

Takeaway: prominent symptoms plus a disproportionate response equals somatic symptom disorder.

whyNot.C: His bodily symptoms are prominent, not mild or absent.
whyNot.A: He does not falsify symptoms.
whyNot.D: He has no external reward and does not feign symptoms.
whyNot.B: His symptoms are not neurological.

items.objective: Diagnose somatic symptom disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old nurse is admitted for her fifth episode of severe hypoglycemia. Blood drawn during the episode shows a high insulin and an undetectable C-peptide. A sulfonylurea screen is negative. She asks when she can have the pancreatic surgery she read about. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrange endoscopic ultrasound of the pancreas

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge her immediately and inform her employer

options.label: C
options.html: Discuss the findings supportively, with psychiatry

options.label: E
options.html: Start diazoxide to suppress insulin release

items.explanationHtml:
High insulin with low C-peptide proves exogenous insulin, so this is factitious disorder. Discuss the findings in a supportive, nonpunitive way, involve psychiatry, avoid unnecessary procedures and offer ongoing care. Hostile confrontation usually leads the patient to leave and seek care elsewhere.

Takeaway: once factitious illness is proven, present the findings supportively and involve psychiatry.

whyNot.A: The pattern shows exogenous insulin; imaging for an insulinoma is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Surgery would be harmful; there is no tumour.
whyNot.B: Abrupt punitive action causes harm and is not the first step.
whyNot.E: Diazoxide suppresses endogenous insulin release and does not address exogenous insulin.

items.objective: Manage proven factitious hypoglycemia with a supportive discussion and psychiatric involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man comes to the emergency department at 2 AM with severe low back pain. He says only one opioid works and that he is allergic to all NSAIDs and to tramadol. He winces when his back is touched but bends easily to pick up his phone from the floor. When told he will be offered physiotherapy and acetaminophen, he leaves. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
items.explanationHtml:
Inconsistent findings, a request for a specific drug and leaving when it is refused indicate feigned symptoms for an external reward: malingering.

Takeaway: feigned symptoms to obtain drugs are malingering.

whyNot.E: In somatic symptom disorder symptoms are not feigned and there is no specific external goal.
whyNot.B: Factitious disorder lacks an obvious external reward; obtaining a drug is one.
whyNot.C: His free bending is inconsistent with severe pain, and he leaves when the drug is refused.
whyNot.A: Conversion disorder involves motor or sensory deficits, not pain feigned for a goal.

items.objective: Recognise drug-seeking malingering.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old girl has had six episodes of bloodstream infection with mixed gut organisms through her central venous catheter. Each episode starts during her mother's visits, and none has occurred during two weeks when only her father visited. Her immunological work-up is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Confront the mother privately before involving others

options.label: C
options.html: Refer the child to a child psychiatrist

items.explanationHtml:
Repeated unexplained illness tied to one caregiver suggests factitious disorder imposed on another, which is child maltreatment. The physician must protect the child and report to child protective services. Reasonable suspicion is enough; proof is not required.

Takeaway: suspected factitious illness in a child must be reported to child protective services.

whyNot.D: Replacing the line does not protect the child from deliberate contamination.
whyNot.B: The work-up is normal and the pattern points to a person, not an immune defect.
whyNot.A: Confrontation can put the child at risk and is not the first step.
whyNot.C: The child is the victim; the priority is her safety.

items.objective: Report suspected factitious disorder imposed on another.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old medical student has been admitted with daily fevers of 40.3°C (104.5°F) measured on the ward thermometer when she is alone. During each fever her pulse is 72/min and she looks well. Blood counts, inflammatory markers, blood cultures, echocardiography and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A high fever with a normal pulse, a well appearance and normal markers suggests factitious fever. Confirm it by observed temperature measurement, or by checking the temperature of freshly voided urine, before any more tests.

Takeaway: confirm a suspicious fever under observation before further work-up.

whyNot.E: Further imaging is not indicated until the fever itself is confirmed.
whyNot.B: There is no evidence of infection, and the readings are unconfirmed.
whyNot.A: A marrow biopsy is invasive and not justified while the fever itself is unproven.
whyNot.D: A liver biopsy carries bleeding risk and should not precede confirming that fever exists.

items.objective: Confirm suspected factitious fever by observed measurement.

items.stemHtml: A 37-year-old operating room technician has had non-healing ulcers on her left forearm and both thighs for a year. The ulcers have straight edges and angular shapes and appear only on skin she can reach with her right hand. Biopsies show nonspecific injury, and cultures grow skin organisms. She is eager for skin grafting and has no claims or work absences. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Wounds with geometric shapes, only in reachable sites, in a health care worker eager for procedures and without external reward suggest self-inflicted injury: factitious disorder imposed on self (dermatitis artefacta).

Takeaway: geometric wounds in reachable sites, without external gain, suggest factitious disorder.

whyNot.C: She has no external reward such as money or time off.
whyNot.D: Pyoderma ulcers have undermined violaceous borders and typical histology, not geometric edges in reachable sites.
whyNot.E: The lesions are being produced, not only worried about.
whyNot.A: Biopsies show no vasculitis, and the distribution follows reach, not vessels.

items.objective: Recognise self-inflicted skin lesions as factitious disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman has palpitations, heat intolerance and weight loss. Her thyroid is not palpable and not tender. TSH is suppressed, and free T4 and total T3 are high. Radioactive iodine uptake at 24 hours is 2% (reference range, 10–30%). ESR is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?

options.label: B
options.html: Repeat radioactive iodine uptake in 6 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Thyrotoxicosis with low iodine uptake leaves two main causes: thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone. Thyroglobulin separates them. It is high in thyroiditis and low when hormone is taken, because the suppressed gland releases little.

Takeaway: in low-uptake thyrotoxicosis, a low thyroglobulin points to ingested thyroid hormone.

whyNot.E: Graves disease is excluded by the very low uptake.
whyNot.D: Ultrasound is not the most specific test here; thyroglobulin directly separates the two remaining causes.
whyNot.A: There is no nodule to biopsy.
whyNot.B: Repeating the uptake does not separate thyroiditis from exogenous hormone.

items.objective: Order thyroglobulin to detect factitious thyrotoxicosis.

items.stemHtml: A 42-year-old woman who works for a pest control company has hematuria and bruising. INR is 9.6. She takes no prescribed drugs. She is treated with intravenous vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate, and her INR falls to 1.3. Two days later it is 6.5 again. A blood test detects brodifacoum. Which of the following is the most appropriate ongoing treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: A single further dose of intravenous vitamin K

options.label: C
options.html: Daily fresh frozen plasma for one week

options.label: D
options.html: High-dose oral vitamin K for months, with INR checks

items.explanationHtml:
Brodifacoum is a long-acting superwarfarin that persists for weeks to months. After bleeding is controlled, give high-dose oral vitamin K for a prolonged period, often months, guided by INR checks. Assess for deliberate ingestion, including factitious disorder or self-harm, and involve psychiatry.

Takeaway: superwarfarin poisoning needs prolonged high-dose oral vitamin K.

whyNot.A: The poison lasts weeks to months, so a single dose will not hold the INR.
whyNot.C: Plasma is a temporary measure for bleeding and cannot cover months of effect.
whyNot.E: Protamine reverses heparin, not vitamin K antagonists.
whyNot.B: Andexanet reverses factor Xa inhibitors, not vitamin K antagonists.

items.objective: Treat long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide poisoning.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old warehouse worker reports constant neck pain and inability to lift his arms since a minor workplace fall 4 months ago. He has a pending workers' compensation claim. During the visit he cannot raise his arms above shoulder height, but in the parking lot he is seen lifting heavy boxes into his car. Imaging is normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
items.explanationHtml:
Symptoms that disappear when the patient believes he is unobserved, with a clear financial incentive, indicate malingering. Document objective findings carefully.

Takeaway: inconsistent symptoms with a pending claim suggest malingering.

whyNot.C: Functional symptoms are not under voluntary control and do not vanish when the patient thinks he is unobserved.
whyNot.B: Factitious disorder lacks an external reward; a compensation claim is one.
whyNot.E: The inconsistency and the clear financial incentive point to feigning.
whyNot.A: Normal imaging and full strength when unobserved argue against a structural cause.

items.objective: Recognise malingering related to a compensation claim.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman is admitted to a psychiatric unit after reporting that her husband and two children died in a fire last month and that she is suicidal. Staff are moved by her story. Records from another hospital show the same story given there 6 months earlier; her family is in fact alive and well. She has no legal, financial or housing problems and asks to stay longer. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Fabricated psychological symptoms to gain the patient role, with no external reward, are factitious disorder imposed on self. The disorder can involve psychological as well as physical symptoms.

Takeaway: factitious disorder can present with feigned psychiatric symptoms.

whyNot.D: There is no external gain such as housing, money or avoidance of legal trouble.
whyNot.C: Her symptoms are built on a fabricated loss.
whyNot.E: The loss she describes never happened, so there is no bereavement to grieve.
whyNot.A: She knows the story is false, as shown by the repeated identical account.

items.objective: Recognise factitious disorder with psychological symptoms.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman whose husband has type 2 diabetes has had three episodes of confusion with sweating. During a monitored episode, plasma glucose is 38 mg/dL with high insulin, high C-peptide and high proinsulin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Screen blood for sulfonylureas and meglitinides

items.explanationHtml:
High insulin, C-peptide and proinsulin occur both in an insulinoma and in sulfonylurea or meglitinide ingestion. A drug screen must come before imaging, especially when the patient has access to these drugs.

Takeaway: screen for oral hypoglycemic agents before imaging for an insulinoma.

whyNot.A: Imaging should wait until oral hypoglycemic agents are excluded.
whyNot.E: Treatment should not start before the cause is known.
whyNot.B: Antibodies are considered after drug screening when the picture fits.
whyNot.C: Surgery without a localised tumour or drug screen is not justified.

items.objective: Screen for oral hypoglycemic agents in endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with factitious disorder imposed on self has had 30 hospital admissions in 5 years at four hospitals. She has agreed to see a psychiatrist. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term care strategy?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit at every presentation for observation

options.label: C
options.html: One primary physician coordinating care with psychiatry

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer care to a new hospital every year

items.explanationHtml:
Long-term management of factitious disorder rests on one coordinating physician who works with psychiatry, shares information appropriately between services, avoids unnecessary procedures and keeps offering care.

Takeaway: coordinated care through one physician with psychiatric input reduces harm in factitious disorder.

whyNot.D: Refusing emergency care is unsafe and unethical; she may also have real illness.
whyNot.A: Routine admission reinforces the sick role and exposes her to harm.
whyNot.B: Investigating every new symptom leads to harmful tests and procedures.
whyNot.E: Fragmented care is how the pattern continues.

items.objective: Plan coordinated long-term care for factitious disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old pharmacy assistant has had watery diarrhea for 8 months, with potassium of 2.9 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L). She has had two colonoscopies with normal biopsies and asks for a capsule endoscopy. Her BMI is 23 kg/m², and she has no concerns about her weight or shape. A stool screen detects bisacodyl. She is not seeking compensation or time off. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Secret laxative use to create illness, with eagerness for tests and no external gain or weight motive, is factitious disorder imposed on self. When laxatives are used for weight control, consider an eating disorder instead.

Takeaway: secret laxative use without a weight motive or external gain suggests factitious disorder.

whyNot.A: She has no binge eating or concern about weight or shape.
whyNot.C: A laxative in the stool explains the diarrhea.
whyNot.E: A stimulant laxative in the stool explains the watery diarrhea and hypokalemia.
whyNot.D: She has no external reward.

items.objective: Separate factitious diarrhea from an eating disorder.

items.stemHtml: A mother brings her 6-year-old son for the fourth opinion about "seizures" that she describes in detail. No one else has ever seen one, including school staff and nurses during a 5-day hospital stay with video-EEG, which showed no events. She asks for a gastrostomy tube because he "chokes during seizures." The boy is well and growing normally. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

options.label: C
options.html: Functional non-epileptic attacks in the child

options.label: D
options.html: Illness anxiety disorder in the mother

items.explanationHtml:
A caregiver reporting events nobody else sees and pushing for invasive procedures in a well child suggests factitious disorder imposed on another. Report to child protective services, and do not perform unnecessary procedures.

Takeaway: caregiver-reported events that no one else witnesses, plus requests for invasive care, suggest factitious disorder imposed on another.

whyNot.A: Prolonged monitoring, school observation and normal growth do not support the reported frequency.
whyNot.D: Pushing for invasive procedures and fabricating events goes beyond health anxiety.
whyNot.C: No events, functional or epileptic, have been seen by anyone else.
whyNot.E: No external reward is evident; the motive is the role of caring for a sick child.

items.objective: Recognise fabricated illness reported by a caregiver.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl is brought by her parents because she has lost 11 kg in 5 months. She eats only vegetables and runs daily. She says she is "still too big." Her BMI is 14.6 kg/m² (about 70% of the median BMI for her age). Pulse is 42/min lying and 68/min standing, blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg, and temperature is 35.4°C (95.7°F). Potassium is 3.1 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L) and phosphate is 3.2 mg/dL (3.0–4.5 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit to hospital for medical stabilisation and refeeding

options.label: D
options.html: Start olanzapine and review in 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Weekly weight checks with a dietitian

items.explanationHtml:
She has anorexia nervosa with marked bradycardia, orthostatic changes, hypotension, hypothermia, hypokalemia and a weight about 70% of median. Each is a reason for admission for medical stabilisation and supervised nutritional rehabilitation.

Takeaway: medical instability in anorexia nervosa needs hospital admission.

whyNot.B: Family-based treatment is the long-term therapy, but she is medically unstable now.
whyNot.C: Antidepressants do not restore weight or correct her instability.
whyNot.D: Medication does not address the immediate medical risks.
whyNot.E: Her bradycardia, orthostasis, hypothermia and hypokalemia need inpatient care.

items.objective: Recognise criteria for admission in adolescent anorexia nervosa.

items.stemHtml: The patient was admitted, given thiamine, and started on nutrition. On day 3 she reports weakness and mild ankle swelling. Pulse is 58/min and regular. Serum phosphate is 1.4 mg/dL (3.0–4.5 mg/dL), potassium is 3.3 mEq/L, and magnesium is 1.4 mEq/L (1.5–2.0 mEq/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give a bolus of intravenous dextrose

options.label: C
options.html: Replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and keep feeding

options.label: D
options.html: Start insulin to improve glucose uptake

items.explanationHtml:
This is refeeding syndrome: phosphate, potassium and magnesium fall as insulin drives them into cells. Replace the electrolytes, continue nutrition (adjusting the rate if needed), and monitor closely with daily electrolytes and cardiac monitoring.

Takeaway: in refeeding syndrome, replace electrolytes and continue monitored feeding.

whyNot.E: Stopping feeds prolongs starvation; correct the electrolytes and continue with monitoring.
whyNot.B: Diuretics worsen hypokalemia and do not treat the cause.
whyNot.A: A carbohydrate load worsens the intracellular shift of phosphate.
whyNot.D: Insulin drives phosphate further into cells.

items.objective: Manage refeeding hypophosphatemia.

items.stemHtml: After 3 weeks the patient is medically stable and has gained 3 kg. She lives with both parents, who are keen to help. Which of the following is the most appropriate ongoing treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Dietary advice from her primary care physician alone

items.explanationHtml:
For adolescents with anorexia nervosa, family-based treatment, in which parents take charge of refeeding at first, has the strongest evidence for weight restoration and recovery.

Takeaway: family-based treatment is first line for adolescent anorexia nervosa.

whyNot.C: No medication reliably restores weight or prevents relapse in anorexia nervosa.
whyNot.E: Medication alone is not adequate treatment.
whyNot.D: Family-based treatment has the strongest evidence in adolescents.
whyNot.A: She needs specialised psychological treatment, not advice alone.

items.objective: Choose family-based treatment for adolescent anorexia nervosa.

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman binges and then vomits about four times a week. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². She has enlarged parotid glands, calluses on the back of her right hand, and erosion of her upper incisors. Potassium is 3.6 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L). She agrees to start cognitive behavioural therapy. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to add?
items.explanationHtml:
Bulimia nervosa is treated with CBT for eating disorders plus fluoxetine, the best-studied drug, used at a higher dose (60 mg daily) than for depression.

Takeaway: fluoxetine plus CBT for bulimia nervosa; never bupropion.

whyNot.A: Bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia nervosa because of the seizure risk.
whyNot.C: Lisdexamfetamine is approved for binge-eating disorder, not bulimia nervosa.
whyNot.E: An antipsychotic is not indicated for bulimia nervosa.
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines do not treat bulimia nervosa and carry dependence risk.

items.objective: Choose fluoxetine for bulimia nervosa.

items.stemHtml:
A 23-year-old woman with a BMI of 20 kg/m² has fatigue and palpitations. She is preoccupied with her weight. Results:

TestResultReference range
Sodium137 mEq/L136–145 mEq/L
Potassium2.7 mEq/L3.5–5.0 mEq/L
Chloride88 mEq/L95–105 mEq/L
Bicarbonate36 mEq/L22–28 mEq/L
Amylase210 U/L25–125 U/L
Urine chloride8 mEq/L—

Which of the following behaviours most likely explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
A hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with a low urine chloride and a raised amylase (salivary, from parotid swelling) indicates self-induced vomiting. Her potassium needs urgent replacement and an ECG.

Takeaway: low urine chloride with alkalosis and a raised amylase points to vomiting.

whyNot.E: Laxatives cause stool bicarbonate loss and more often a normal anion gap acidosis, and do not raise amylase.
whyNot.B: Active diuretic use raises urine chloride.
whyNot.C: Fasting alone does not cause this degree of hypochloremic alkalosis or raise amylase.
whyNot.A: Exercise does not produce this electrolyte pattern.

items.objective: Interpret electrolytes and urine chloride to identify purging by vomiting.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m² eats very large amounts of food rapidly, alone and until uncomfortably full, about twice a week for a year. She feels disgusted afterward but does not vomit, fast or exercise to compensate. She has started cognitive behavioural therapy and asks about medication. Which of the following is approved for this condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent binges with loss of control and distress, without regular compensation, is binge-eating disorder. CBT is first line. Lisdexamfetamine is approved for moderate to severe binge-eating disorder in adults; screen for cardiovascular disease and misuse risk.

Takeaway: lisdexamfetamine is the approved drug for binge-eating disorder.

whyNot.E: Phentermine is a short-term weight-loss drug, not a treatment for binge-eating disorder.
whyNot.D: Orlistat reduces fat absorption and does not treat bingeing.
whyNot.A: Bupropion is not approved for binge-eating disorder.
whyNot.C: Methylphenidate is not approved for binge-eating disorder.

items.objective: Choose lisdexamfetamine for binge-eating disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder eats only white bread, plain pasta and one brand of crackers. He gags at other textures. He has dropped from the 40th to the 5th percentile for weight over 2 years. He has no worries about his body shape and wants to be bigger. Celiac serology and a blood count are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Restriction driven by sensory aversion, causing weight loss, without body-image concerns, is avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder. It is common in autism and is treated with CBT with graded food exposure and dietitian support.

Takeaway: restrictive eating without body-image disturbance suggests ARFID.

whyNot.A: He has no fear of weight gain and no body-image disturbance.
whyNot.D: Pica is eating non-food substances.
whyNot.E: Rumination is repeated regurgitation of food, not restricted choice.
whyNot.C: He gags at textures rather than having dysphagia or food impaction.

items.objective: Diagnose avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation says she has been chewing several cups of ice every day and feels very tired. Hemoglobin is 9.6 g/dL (12.0–16.0 g/dL) and MCV is 74 fL (80–100 fL). Which of the following tests is most likely to explain her craving?
items.explanationHtml:
Ice craving (pagophagia), a form of pica, is closely tied to iron deficiency, which is common in pregnancy. A low ferritin confirms it, and the craving usually resolves with iron replacement.

Takeaway: ice craving with microcytic anemia means check ferritin.

whyNot.A: Ice is not a source of lead; ice craving points to iron deficiency.
whyNot.E: Thyroid disease does not cause ice craving with microcytosis.
whyNot.B: Thalassemia trait is possible, but ice craving strongly suggests iron deficiency.
whyNot.D: B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis, not microcytosis.

items.objective: Investigate pica for ice with iron studies.

items.stemHtml: A 30-month-old boy whose family rents an apartment in a 1925 building is often seen putting paint flakes and soil in his mouth. He has had poor appetite, constipation and fewer words than before. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test?
items.explanationHtml:
A young child with pica in an old house, with constipation, poor appetite and developmental regression, may have lead poisoning. Measure a venous blood lead level (a capillary result needs venous confirmation), check iron studies, and find and remove the source.

Takeaway: pica in an old house means check a venous blood lead level.

whyNot.C: Iron deficiency often coexists, but his exposure and symptoms require a lead level first.
whyNot.A: A radiograph can show paint flakes but does not measure exposure.
whyNot.B: His regression needs assessment, but lead poisoning must be confirmed first.
whyNot.D: Urine porphyrins are not the screening test for lead poisoning.

items.objective: Investigate pica for lead poisoning in a young child.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has had two or three outbursts a week for 3 years in which he shouts and swears, and twice this year he has broken furniture, each after a minor frustration. Each lasts a few minutes, is not planned, and is followed by remorse. Between outbursts his mood is normal. He has no substance use, head injury, or periods of decreased need for sleep. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent, impulsive, disproportionate aggressive outbursts followed by remorse, without another explanation, is intermittent explosive disorder. CBT and an SSRI such as fluoxetine are used.

Takeaway: impulsive, disproportionate outbursts with remorse suggest intermittent explosive disorder.

whyNot.A: Antisocial aggression is usually planned or used for gain, without remorse.
whyNot.B: He has no manic episodes.
whyNot.C: He has no identity disturbance, fear of abandonment or self-harm.
whyNot.D: Conduct disorder is diagnosed in those under 18 and involves a wider pattern of rule violation.

items.objective: Diagnose intermittent explosive disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old financially comfortable woman has been arrested twice for shoplifting. She takes cheap items she does not need, such as hair clips, and later throws them away or gives them away. She describes rising tension before each theft and relief afterward, and feels ashamed. She has no manic episodes, and she does not steal from anger. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Repeated failure to resist stealing items not needed for use or value, with tension before and relief during the act, is kleptomania. CBT is the main treatment, and naltrexone has some evidence.

Takeaway: stealing unneeded items for tension relief is kleptomania.

whyNot.A: She steals items without value or need and feels shame, unlike theft for gain.
whyNot.B: She has no manic episodes.
whyNot.E: There are no obsessions; the act brings pleasure or relief rather than neutralising a feared outcome.
whyNot.D: There is no feigned illness.

items.objective: Diagnose kleptomania.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman with restless legs syndrome has taken ropinirole for 2 years. Her husband reports that she now gambles online for hours each night and has run up large debts. She has no history of mood episodes or gambling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Refer to a gambling support group only

items.explanationHtml:
New compulsive gambling on a dopamine agonist is a drug-induced impulse-control disorder. Taper and stop the agonist, and switch restless legs treatment to an alpha-2-delta ligand after checking iron. A slow taper avoids dopamine agonist withdrawal.

Takeaway: dopamine agonist-induced gambling is treated by tapering off the agonist.

whyNot.A: Adding an antipsychotic does not remove the cause.
whyNot.B: A higher dose would worsen the behaviour.
whyNot.C: Support helps, but the drug causing the behaviour must be withdrawn.
whyNot.D: There is no bipolar disorder.

items.objective: Manage a dopamine agonist-induced impulse-control disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa has not menstruated for a year. Her BMI is 16.4 kg/m². DXA scan shows a lumbar spine Z-score of −2.4. Calcium and vitamin D levels are normal. Which of the following is most likely to improve her bone density?

options.label: E
options.html: Weight restoration with return of menses

items.explanationHtml:
Bone loss in anorexia nervosa comes from low estrogen, high cortisol and low IGF-1 caused by starvation. Weight restoration with return of menses is the most effective treatment. Combined oral contraceptives do not help bone.

Takeaway: weight restoration is the treatment for bone loss in anorexia nervosa.

whyNot.B: Oral contraceptives do not improve bone density in anorexia nervosa and can mask recovery of menses.
whyNot.C: Bisphosphonates are not first line in young women and persist in bone for years.
whyNot.A: Her levels are normal, and calcium alone does not reverse the deficit.
whyNot.D: Teriparatide is not a first-line treatment for young women with anorexia nervosa.

items.objective: Choose weight restoration for bone loss in anorexia nervosa.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has trouble finishing schoolwork, often leaves his seat in class and interrupts others. His parents and teacher report the same problems at home and at school for the past 2 years. He begins treatment with methylphenidate, and his attention improves within days. Which of the following best describes how this drug acts?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocks reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline by their transporters

options.label: B
options.html: Irreversibly inhibits monoamine oxidase type B

options.label: C
options.html: Reverses monoamine transporters and displaces dopamine from vesicles

options.label: D
options.html: Selectively inhibits the noradrenaline transporter alone

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulates presynaptic alpha-2A adrenergic receptors in the cortex

items.explanationHtml:
Methylphenidate binds the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters and blocks reuptake, so both transmitters stay longer in the synapse, especially in prefrontal-striatal circuits that support attention and inhibition.

Takeaway: methylphenidate is a dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor; amphetamines are releasers.

whyNot.C: Reversing transporters and emptying vesicles is how amphetamines act, not methylphenidate.
whyNot.E: Alpha-2A agonism is the mechanism of guanfacine and clonidine, nonstimulant ADHD drugs.
whyNot.B: MAO-B inhibitors such as selegiline are used in Parkinson disease, not ADHD.
whyNot.D: Selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibition describes atomoxetine and viloxazine; methylphenidate also blocks dopamine reuptake.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of methylphenidate in ADHD and contrast it with amphetamines and nonstimulants.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is evaluated for learning difficulties. He has moderate intellectual disability, avoids eye contact and flaps his hands when excited. Examination shows a long, narrow face, prominent jaw, large protruding ears, flat feet, hyperextensible finger joints and enlarged testes. His maternal uncle has similar features. Which of the following molecular changes is most likely responsible?

options.label: A
options.html: Deletion of the paternally inherited 15q11–q13 region

options.label: B
options.html: Expansion of a CAG repeat in the coding region of HTT

options.label: C
options.html: Expansion of a CGG repeat that leads to methylation and silencing of FMR1

options.label: D
options.html: Expansion of a CTG repeat in the 3′ untranslated region of DMPK

options.label: E
options.html: Expansion of a GAA repeat in an intron of the frataxin gene

items.explanationHtml:
This is fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and a frequent genetic cause of autistic features. A full mutation (more than about 200 CGG repeats) in the 5′ untranslated region of FMR1 on the X chromosome triggers promoter hypermethylation, so the FMRP protein, which regulates synaptic protein translation, is not made. Expansion occurs through female carriers, which fits an affected maternal uncle.

Takeaway: fragile X: CGG expansion, FMR1 silencing, long face, large ears, macro-orchidism, X-linked through carrier mothers.
