whyNot.D: A CTG expansion in DMPK causes myotonic dystrophy type 1, with myotonia, distal weakness and cataracts.
whyNot.B: A CAG expansion in HTT causes Huntington disease, an adult-onset movement and cognitive disorder.
whyNot.E: A GAA expansion in the frataxin gene causes Friedreich ataxia, with ataxia, areflexia and cardiomyopathy.
whyNot.A: Loss of the paternal 15q11–q13 region causes Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonia, hyperphagia and obesity.

items.objective: Recognise fragile X syndrome and its CGG-repeat mechanism as a cause of intellectual disability.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old girl with ADHD also has frequent eye blinking, shoulder shrugging and throat clearing that began 2 years ago. A stimulant improved her attention but caused marked insomnia. She is switched to an extended-release drug that improves attention and lessens her tics. Her parents are told it can lower her blood pressure and must not be stopped abruptly. This drug most likely acts at which of the following receptors?

options.label: A
options.html: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor, as an antagonist

options.label: B
options.html: Alpha-2A adrenergic receptor, as an agonist

options.label: C
options.html: Beta-1 adrenergic receptor, as an antagonist

options.label: D
options.html: Dopamine D2 receptor, as an antagonist

options.label: E
options.html: Serotonin 5-HT1A receptor, as a partial agonist

items.explanationHtml:
Extended-release guanfacine (or clonidine) stimulates postsynaptic alpha-2A receptors on prefrontal pyramidal neurons, strengthening working-memory networks, and reduces central sympathetic outflow. It helps ADHD with coexisting tics or insomnia. Lower blood pressure, bradycardia and sedation are expected; abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound hypertension.

Takeaway: alpha-2A agonists (guanfacine, clonidine) treat ADHD and tics; taper them to avoid rebound hypertension.

whyNot.A: Alpha-1 antagonists such as prazosin lower blood pressure but are not ADHD or tic treatments.
whyNot.C: Beta-blockers do not improve attention and are not used for ADHD.
whyNot.D: D2 antagonists reduce tics but do not treat ADHD and are not linked to rebound hypertension.
whyNot.E: 5-HT1A partial agonism describes buspirone, an anxiolytic without benefit in ADHD.

items.objective: Identify alpha-2A agonists as nonstimulant ADHD treatment suited to coexisting tics, and their withdrawal risk.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has had severe temper outbursts about four times a week since he was 6 years old, both at home and at school. He screams, throws objects and hits his siblings over minor frustrations. Between outbursts he is irritable and angry most of the day, nearly every day. He has never had a period of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep or grandiosity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Frequent severe outbursts (three or more per week) with a persistently irritable mood between them, lasting more than a year, beginning before 10 and diagnosed between 6 and 18, define disruptive mood dysregulation disorder. It is a depressive-spectrum condition; these children are at risk of later depression and anxiety, not mania.

Takeaway: chronic irritability plus frequent severe outbursts in a child aged 6–18 = DMDD, not bipolar disorder.

whyNot.E: ODD involves defiance and anger at authority, but when DMDD criteria are met, DMDD is diagnosed instead.
whyNot.A: Bipolar I needs a discrete manic episode; he has never had elevated mood, grandiosity or reduced need for sleep.
whyNot.D: Intermittent explosive disorder has normal mood between outbursts, and it is not diagnosed when DMDD criteria are met.
whyNot.B: Conduct disorder centres on violating others' rights (theft, cruelty, destruction), not on chronic irritability.

items.objective: Distinguish disruptive mood dysregulation disorder from bipolar disorder and ODD.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old girl with ADHD has an older brother who misused his prescribed amphetamine. Her parents prefer a medication with no misuse potential, and she starts a drug that selectively blocks noradrenaline reuptake. Which of the following adverse effects requires specific monitoring during the first months of treatment?

options.label: D
options.html: Prolongation of the QT interval with torsades de pointes

items.explanationHtml:
Atomoxetine is a selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor without abuse potential. Like antidepressants, it carries a boxed warning for suicidal thinking in children and adolescents, so families are told to watch for mood change and suicidality, especially early in treatment. Rare liver injury and modest rises in heart rate and blood pressure also occur.

Takeaway: atomoxetine: no misuse potential, but monitor young people for suicidal thinking.

whyNot.A: Agranulocytosis is a concern with clozapine and some antithyroid drugs, not atomoxetine.
whyNot.D: QT prolongation is not its boxed warning and is rarely a clinical problem at usual doses.
whyNot.E: Severe skin reactions are linked to drugs such as lamotrigine and carbamazepine.
whyNot.B: Hypothyroidism is a lithium adverse effect, not an atomoxetine one.

items.objective: Recall the boxed warning for suicidal thinking with atomoxetine.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for learning and behaviour problems. He has mild intellectual disability and hyperactivity. He is small for his age, with a small head circumference, short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum and a thin upper lip. Exposure to which of the following during pregnancy is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Growth deficiency, microcephaly and the facial triad of short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum and thin upper lip point to fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability. Alcohol disrupts neuronal migration and causes apoptosis in the developing brain and midline face.

Takeaway: fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability.

whyNot.B: Isotretinoin causes ear, cardiac, thymic and central nervous system malformations, not this facial pattern.
whyNot.D: Fetal hydantoin effects include distal phalanx and nail hypoplasia and a broad nasal bridge.
whyNot.C: Lithium exposure is associated with Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve.
whyNot.E: Warfarin embryopathy causes nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses.

items.objective: Recognise fetal alcohol spectrum disorder as a preventable cause of intellectual disability.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy has had repetitive blinking, head jerking, sniffing and occasional barking sounds for 3 years. They wax and wane, worsen with stress, and he can hold them back briefly at school at the cost of a rising inner urge. Drugs that block one class of receptor in the striatum reduce these symptoms. Excess activity of which neurotransmitter is most strongly implicated?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic for more than a year, beginning in childhood, is Tourette disorder. Cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits are involved, and increased dopaminergic signalling in the striatum is implicated: D2-blocking antipsychotics and the dopamine-depleting VMAT2 inhibitors suppress tics, while stimulants can occasionally worsen them.

Takeaway: Tourette disorder: dopaminergic excess in basal ganglia circuits; D2 blockade suppresses tics.

whyNot.A: Cholinergic excess relative to dopamine underlies parkinsonism, not tics.
whyNot.C: Glutamate is the main cortical excitatory transmitter but is not the target of tic-suppressing drugs.
whyNot.E: Serotonin is targeted in co-occurring OCD; serotonergic drugs do not reliably suppress tics.
whyNot.D: Glycine is an inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem, unrelated to tics.

items.objective: Link Tourette disorder to striatal dopamine signalling and its pharmacological suppression.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl wets the bed about four nights a week and has never been dry at night. Daytime voiding, physical examination and urinalysis are normal. Before a school camp, she is prescribed a drug taken at bedtime, and her parents are told to stop her drinking from 1 hour before the dose until morning. Which of the following best describes how this drug reduces bed-wetting?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocks muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle

options.label: B
options.html: Constricts afferent arterioles through V1a receptors

options.label: C
options.html: Contracts the internal urethral sphincter through alpha-1 receptors

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

options.label: E
options.html: Inserts aquaporin-2 channels in collecting duct cells through V2 receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Desmopressin is a synthetic vasopressin analogue selective for V2 receptors. It raises cAMP in principal cells of the collecting duct, which inserts aquaporin-2 water channels, so less dilute urine is produced overnight. Because free water is retained, drinking after the dose risks hyponatraemia and seizures.

Takeaway: desmopressin reduces nocturnal urine volume via V2-aquaporin-2; restrict evening fluids to avoid hyponatraemia.

whyNot.C: Alpha-1 agonists tighten the bladder neck but are not used for enuresis.
whyNot.A: Antimuscarinics such as oxybutynin treat an overactive bladder, not nocturnal polyuria, and have no fluid-restriction rule.
whyNot.D: Loop diuretics block Na-K-2Cl and would increase urine output.
whyNot.B: Desmopressin has little V1a activity; vasoconstriction is not how it reduces urine volume.

items.objective: Explain the V2-receptor mechanism of desmopressin and why fluid restriction is required.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman admitted after cutting her forearms tells the resident on the first day that he is the only doctor who has ever understood her. Three days later, after he declines to increase her medication, she calls him cold and useless. She describes one nurse as an angel and the others as cruel. Which of the following defence mechanisms is she most clearly using?
items.explanationHtml:
Seeing people as wholly good or wholly bad, and switching abruptly between idealisation and devaluation, is splitting. It is the characteristic defence of borderline personality disorder and can divide a care team unless staff share one consistent plan.

Takeaway: all-good or all-bad views of others, with sudden switches, is splitting, typical of borderline personality disorder.

whyNot.B: Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else, as in paranoid personality disorder.
whyNot.A: Displacement redirects feelings from their real target to a safer one, such as shouting at a pet after a bad day.
whyNot.C: Reaction formation is acting opposite to an unacceptable impulse, such as being overly sweet to a disliked person.
whyNot.E: Sublimation channels an unacceptable impulse into a socially valued activity; it is a mature defence.

items.objective: Identify splitting as the defence characteristic of borderline personality disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man is brought by his sister, who worries that he is isolated. He lives alone, wears mismatched layers of clothing in summer and says he can often tell what strangers are thinking. He believes that number patterns on licence plates carry messages meant for him, though he admits this may be coincidence. He feels uneasy with people, even coworkers he has known for years. He has never heard voices. These features have been present since his late teens. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Odd beliefs (magical thinking, sensing others' thoughts), ideas of reference held with some doubt, eccentric appearance, and social anxiety that does not ease with familiarity, present since early adulthood without sustained psychosis, define schizotypal personality disorder, a cluster A disorder.

Takeaway: eccentric beliefs and ideas of reference without fixed delusions or hallucinations = schizotypal personality disorder.

whyNot.C: Schizoid personality disorder involves detachment without eccentric beliefs or perceptual oddities.
whyNot.B: Paranoid personality disorder centres on distrust and suspicion of others' motives, not magical thinking.
whyNot.A: Avoidant personality disorder involves fear of rejection but no odd beliefs or eccentric behaviour.
whyNot.D: Schizophrenia needs psychotic symptoms such as fixed delusions or hallucinations for at least a month; his beliefs are held with doubt.

items.objective: Distinguish schizotypal personality disorder from schizoid personality disorder and schizophrenia.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has believed since adolescence that he has a 'sixth sense' for future events. He interprets songs on the radio as hints meant for him, dresses unusually and has no close friends apart from his mother. He has never had hallucinations or fixed delusions. Compared with the general population, his first-degree relatives are most likely to have an increased risk of which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
His features fit schizotypal personality disorder, which lies on a genetic spectrum with schizophrenia. It is more common among relatives of people with schizophrenia, and schizophrenia is more common among relatives of people with schizotypal personality disorder. A minority of patients later develop schizophrenia.

Takeaway: schizotypal personality disorder belongs to the schizophrenia spectrum and shares familial risk with it.

whyNot.B: Bipolar disorder runs in families of patients with mood disorders, not specifically with schizotypal traits.
whyNot.C: OCD is linked to tic disorders and OCD-related conditions, not to cluster A traits.
whyNot.A: Antisocial personality disorder clusters with conduct disorder and substance use in families.
whyNot.D: Panic disorder clusters with other anxiety and depressive disorders.

items.objective: Recognise the familial link between schizotypal personality disorder and schizophrenia.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman says she wishes she had friends and a partner but always assumes others will find her boring and laugh at her. She turned down a promotion because it required presenting at meetings, and she joins social events only if she is sure she will be liked. She has felt inferior to others since adolescence. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A lifelong pattern of feeling inadequate and avoiding people and jobs because of fear of criticism or rejection, despite wanting connection, is avoidant personality disorder (cluster C).

Takeaway: avoidant patients want relationships but fear rejection; schizoid patients do not want them.

whyNot.E: Schizoid patients are indifferent to relationships and do not long for friends.
whyNot.B: Dependent patients cling to others and seek reassurance rather than avoiding contact.
whyNot.C: OCPD is preoccupation with order, rules and perfection, not fear of rejection.
whyNot.D: Paranoid patients avoid others because they distrust their motives, not because they feel inferior.

items.objective: Distinguish avoidant from schizoid and dependent personality disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is assessed in prison after convictions for fraud and assault. He lies easily, has been fired from several jobs for aggression and shows no remorse for injuring a stranger. A psychiatrist considers antisocial personality disorder. Which of the following findings from his history is required for this diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: A conviction for a violent crime

options.label: C
options.html: Evidence of conduct disorder beginning before age 15

items.explanationHtml:
Antisocial personality disorder is diagnosed only in adults (age 18 or older) who have a pervasive disregard for others' rights and evidence of conduct disorder with onset before age 15. Without the childhood conduct disorder, adult antisocial behaviour alone does not meet criteria.

Takeaway: antisocial personality disorder needs age 18 or older plus conduct disorder that began before 15.

whyNot.E: ADHD is a common comorbidity but is not a criterion.
whyNot.B: A criminal record is common but not required; the criteria describe behaviour, not convictions.
whyNot.A: Substance use often coexists but is not required, and antisocial acts must not occur only during intoxication.
whyNot.D: ODD can precede conduct disorder, but the required childhood history is conduct disorder before 15.

items.objective: State the age and childhood conduct disorder requirements for antisocial personality disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old accountant is referred by his employer because his reports are always late. He rechecks every figure several times and rewrites reports that already meet the firm's standards. He refuses to delegate because others 'do it wrong', keeps detailed lists for household chores and will not throw away old manuals. He believes his standards are correct and that his colleagues are careless. Which of the following features most clearly separates his condition from obsessive-compulsive disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: He has recurrent intrusive images that he tries to suppress

options.label: B
options.html: He performs checking rituals to neutralise an unwanted fear

options.label: C
options.html: He recognises that his thoughts are excessive and unwanted

options.label: D
options.html: He views his habits as reasonable and consistent with who he is

options.label: E
options.html: His symptoms began after a major work deadline was missed

items.explanationHtml:
His perfectionism, rigidity, list-making, reluctance to delegate and hoarding of worthless objects describe obsessive-compulsive personality disorder. The traits are ego-syntonic: he endorses them. OCD, by contrast, involves true obsessions and compulsions experienced as intrusive and unwanted (ego-dystonic).

Takeaway: OCPD traits feel right to the patient; OCD symptoms feel intrusive and unwanted.

whyNot.A: Intrusive, resisted images are obsessions, the hallmark of OCD rather than OCPD.
whyNot.B: Rituals performed to neutralise anxiety are compulsions, which define OCD.
whyNot.E: A personality disorder is lifelong, not triggered by a single recent event.
whyNot.C: Insight that thoughts are excessive and unwanted describes OCD; OCPD patients defend their behaviour.

items.objective: Differentiate obsessive-compulsive personality disorder from OCD by the ego-syntonic nature of the traits.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old surgeon is admitted for elective knee surgery. He demands that only the department chair operate on him, refers to the residents as 'interns who should be grateful to watch' and becomes enraged when a nurse asks him to wait his turn. He describes himself as the best surgeon in the region and shows no interest in other patients' needs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Grandiosity, entitlement, a need for admiration, lack of empathy and rage at perceived slights define narcissistic personality disorder. Beneath the grandiose surface, self-esteem is fragile, which explains the strong reaction to criticism.

Takeaway: grandiosity, entitlement and lack of empathy point to narcissistic personality disorder.

whyNot.C: Histrionic patients seek attention through emotional display and seductiveness rather than claims of superiority.
whyNot.A: Antisocial patients violate others' rights through deceit or aggression; entitlement alone does not meet criteria.
whyNot.E: Paranoid patients distrust others' motives; he is contemptuous, not suspicious.
whyNot.B: Borderline patients have unstable relationships, self-harm and fear of abandonment, not stable grandiosity.

items.objective: Recognise narcissistic personality disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman cannot decide what to wear or what to order in a restaurant without asking her mother or partner. She agrees with her partner even when she thinks he is wrong, for fear he will leave. When a previous relationship ended, she began dating someone new within a week because she could not bear being alone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A pervasive need to be cared for, difficulty making everyday decisions without excessive advice, reluctance to disagree for fear of losing support, and urgently seeking a new relationship when one ends define dependent personality disorder (cluster C).

Takeaway: dependent personality disorder: needs others to make decisions and quickly replaces lost relationships.

whyNot.B: Borderline patients fear abandonment too, but with unstable intense relationships, self-harm and mood reactivity.
whyNot.A: Avoidant patients avoid relationships because they fear rejection; they do not cling to others for decisions.
whyNot.E: Histrionic patients seek attention through dramatic display, not reliance on others for decisions.
whyNot.D: Generalized anxiety disorder is excessive worry across many topics, not a pattern of submissive reliance.

items.objective: Recognise dependent personality disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy has been asked to leave two preschools because he cannot sit for circle time, runs out of the classroom and hits other children when he has to wait. His parents report the same behaviour at home for more than a year. Hearing and vision screening and development are otherwise normal. Rating scales from his parents and teacher support ADHD. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Atomoxetine, because stimulants are unsafe before age 6

options.label: C
options.html: No intervention until he is 6 years old

items.explanationHtml:
For preschool children (4–5 years) with ADHD, evidence-based parent training in behaviour management, plus behavioural support in the preschool, is first-line. Methylphenidate is added if behavioural treatment does not bring significant improvement and moderate to severe impairment continues.

Takeaway: preschool ADHD: behavioural parent training first; methylphenidate only if that is not enough.

whyNot.B: Methylphenidate is second-line in preschoolers, after an adequate trial of behavioural treatment.
whyNot.A: Stimulants are not contraindicated before age 6, and atomoxetine is not the preferred first step.
whyNot.E: Antipsychotics are not ADHD treatments and carry metabolic and movement risks.
whyNot.C: Waiting would leave a significantly impaired child untreated; treatment is recommended from age 4.

items.objective: Manage ADHD in a preschool child with behavioural parent training first.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because her teacher says she daydreams, loses her belongings and does not finish classwork, although she is not disruptive. Her parents note similar problems with homework and chores. Her growth and examination are normal, and recent hearing and vision screens were normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the brain with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
ADHD is a clinical diagnosis based on DSM criteria. Validated rating scales completed by parents and teachers document symptoms and impairment in more than one setting and screen for coexisting conditions. Routine EEG, imaging and laboratory tests are not needed without specific clinical features.

Takeaway: diagnose ADHD with information from at least two settings, usually parent and teacher rating scales.

whyNot.B: EEG is indicated only if staring spells suggest absence seizures (brief, frequent, with eyelid flutter), not for routine ADHD evaluation.
whyNot.C: Brain imaging has no role in diagnosing ADHD without focal neurological signs.
whyNot.A: Response to a stimulant does not confirm ADHD; stimulants improve attention in most children.
whyNot.E: Thyroid tests are needed only if there are clinical signs of thyroid disease.

items.objective: Use parent and teacher rating scales to diagnose ADHD rather than routine tests.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy with newly diagnosed ADHD is about to start a stimulant. He plays soccer without symptoms. His paternal uncle died suddenly at age 23 while running, and no cause was found. The boy's blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg and pulse 82/min, and his cardiac examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain an ECG and cardiology evaluation before starting a stimulant

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain an echocardiogram for every child starting a stimulant

options.label: D
options.html: Start guanfacine, which carries no cardiac concern

options.label: E
options.html: Start methylphenidate and recheck his blood pressure in 1 month

items.explanationHtml:
Before a stimulant, screen for fainting or chest pain with exertion, palpitations, known heart disease and unexplained sudden death in young relatives. A positive family history, as here, warrants an ECG and cardiology review to look for inherited arrhythmia syndromes or cardiomyopathy. Without such findings, routine ECG is not required.

Takeaway: a family history of unexplained sudden death in a young relative calls for an ECG and cardiology review before a stimulant.

whyNot.E: Starting without cardiac assessment ignores a red-flag family history.
whyNot.D: Alpha-2 agonists slow the heart and lower blood pressure, and the inherited cardiac risk still needs assessment.
whyNot.A: Most children with this history can be treated safely after evaluation; a permanent ban is not warranted.
whyNot.C: Routine echocardiography for all children starting stimulants is not recommended.

items.objective: Screen for cardiac risk before stimulant therapy and refer when the family history is positive.

items.stemHtml:
A 10-year-old boy with ADHD has taken extended-release methylphenidate each morning for 6 months, with good control of his symptoms at school. His mother says he barely eats lunch but is hungry in the evening. He has no chest pain or palpitations.

MeasureAt startToday
Weight-for-age percentile50th25th
Height-for-age percentile50th45th
Blood pressure104/66 mm Hg108/68 mm Hg
Pulse84/min90/min

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Add megestrol acetate to stimulate appetite

options.label: B
options.html: Dose after breakfast plus calorie-dense evening snacks

items.explanationHtml:
Appetite suppression with some weight loss is the most common stimulant adverse effect. First steps are nutritional strategies: give the dose with or after a good breakfast and offer calorie-dense meals and snacks in the evening when the drug has worn off, then recheck growth. If weight keeps falling, consider a lower dose, an alternative drug or a nonstimulant. His small rise in pulse and blood pressure is expected and acceptable.

Takeaway: manage stimulant-related appetite loss first with meal timing and evening calories, and keep monitoring growth.

whyNot.D: Stopping effective treatment is premature; simple nutritional measures usually suffice.
whyNot.C: His height has barely changed; growth hormone testing is not indicated for stimulant-related weight loss.
whyNot.A: Megestrol is not used for this purpose in children and has endocrine adverse effects.
whyNot.E: Amphetamines suppress appetite at least as much, so switching would not help.

items.objective: Manage stimulant-related appetite suppression with meal timing and calorie strategies.

items.stemHtml: An 18-month-old boy is seen for a well-child visit. He does not point to show his parents things, rarely looks at them when called by name and says no words. He lines up toy cars and becomes very upset if the order is changed. A validated autism screening questionnaire completed by his mother is positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Reassure the parents that boys often speak later

options.label: C
options.html: Refer for speech therapy alone and review in 6 months

options.label: D
options.html: Refer now for diagnostic assessment and early intervention

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat the screening questionnaire at the 24-month visit

items.explanationHtml:
A positive screen with red flags (no pointing, no words by 16 months, poor response to name, repetitive play) needs immediate referral for a diagnostic evaluation and to early intervention services at the same time, plus formal audiology to exclude hearing loss. Starting intervention early improves outcomes, so it should not wait for the formal diagnosis.

Takeaway: a positive autism screen means parallel referral for diagnosis and early intervention, plus a hearing test.

whyNot.E: Waiting 6 months for another screen delays effective early intervention.
whyNot.B: Reassurance is wrong in the face of multiple red flags and a positive screen.
whyNot.C: Speech therapy alone does not address his social and behavioural needs, and he still needs a diagnostic assessment.
whyNot.A: Brain MRI is not part of routine autism evaluation without focal signs, seizures or regression.

items.objective: Refer a toddler with a positive autism screen for diagnostic evaluation and early intervention without delay.

items.stemHtml: The boy is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder at 22 months. His hearing is normal. He has no dysmorphic features, his head circumference is normal and the skin examination is normal. His parents ask whether any further testing is recommended. Which of the following is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: Chromosomal microarray and fragile X DNA testing

options.label: D
options.html: No further testing, because autism is a behavioural diagnosis

options.label: E
options.html: Serum lead, ferritin and thyroid tests for all children with autism

items.explanationHtml:
Every child with autism should be offered genetic testing. Chromosomal microarray detects copy-number variants and fragile X testing detects FMR1 expansion (it can be missed clinically in young boys). Exome sequencing is increasingly used as a first-tier test where available. Results inform recurrence risk, surveillance and family testing.

Takeaway: offer chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing to every child diagnosed with autism.

whyNot.D: Genetic testing has a meaningful yield and affects counselling, so it is recommended even without dysmorphic features.
whyNot.C: A standard karyotype detects far fewer abnormalities than microarray and is not first-line.
whyNot.E: Lead and iron studies are targeted to risk factors such as pica; they are not universal tests for autism.
whyNot.B: EEG is reserved for suspected seizures or regression, not done routinely.

items.objective: Order first-tier genetic testing after a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder.

items.stemHtml: At age 7, the boy attends a specialist school and receives applied behaviour analysis and speech therapy. Over the past 4 months he has had daily episodes of severe aggression and head-banging when routines change, despite a well-delivered behavioural plan. Medical causes of pain, including dental problems and constipation, have been excluded. Which of the following medications is most appropriate?
items.explanationHtml:
Risperidone (or aripiprazole) is the evidence-based choice for severe irritability, aggression and self-injury in autism when behavioural treatment alone is not enough. Weight, glucose and lipids must be monitored, along with prolactin-related effects and movement disorders.

Takeaway: risperidone or aripiprazole treat severe irritability in autism; monitor metabolic effects.

whyNot.B: Benzodiazepines can cause paradoxical disinhibition in children and do not treat chronic irritability.
whyNot.C: Methylphenidate treats co-occurring ADHD symptoms, not severe aggression and self-injury.
whyNot.A: Carbamazepine is not an evidence-based treatment for irritability in autism.
whyNot.E: SSRIs have not shown benefit for irritability or repetitive behaviour in children with autism.

items.objective: Select an atypical antipsychotic for severe irritability in autism after behavioural treatment.

items.stemHtml: An 11-year-old girl has had eye blinking, facial grimacing, neck jerks and repeated sniffing and humming for 2 years. Classmates now tease her, and she avoids speaking in class. She has no attention or learning problems and no obsessive thoughts. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Botulinum toxin injections to the neck

items.explanationHtml:
Her tics are causing social harm, so treatment is reasonable. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, built around habit-reversal training (awareness and a competing response), is first-line. Medication (alpha-2 agonists, then antipsychotics such as aripiprazole) is added for severe or refractory tics.

Takeaway: impairing tics: start with behavioural therapy (habit reversal); reserve antipsychotics for severe cases.

whyNot.D: Haloperidol reduces tics but has substantial adverse effects and is not first-line.
whyNot.C: Clonazepam is not a recommended initial treatment and causes sedation and dependence.
whyNot.B: Botulinum toxin is an option for a single troublesome focal motor tic in older patients, not first-line here.
whyNot.E: Deep brain stimulation is reserved for severe, treatment-refractory adults.

items.objective: Start behavioural therapy for impairing tics in Tourette disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl who had been dry at night for 2 years has wet the bed most nights for the past 3 weeks. Her mother says she drinks large amounts of water and has lost weight. She has no fever or dysuria. Examination is normal apart from dry lips. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Secondary enuresis with polydipsia and weight loss strongly suggests new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus. A urinalysis for glucose and ketones (with a fingerstick glucose) is the quick, essential first test.

Takeaway: secondary enuresis with thirst and weight loss: check the urine (and blood) for glucose first.

whyNot.B: An alarm treats primary nocturnal enuresis and would miss a medical cause.
whyNot.A: Desmopressin is inappropriate before excluding diabetes, and could cause dangerous hyponatraemia with polydipsia.
whyNot.C: Imaging is not a first step; the history points to a metabolic cause.
whyNot.E: VCUG evaluates reflux after febrile urinary infections, which she has not had.

items.objective: Evaluate secondary enuresis with urinalysis to detect diabetes or infection.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has never been dry at night and wets the bed five nights a week. He has no daytime symptoms or constipation, and his examination and urinalysis are normal. His father wet the bed until age 10. The family wants the treatment most likely to give lasting dryness and is willing to work on it for several weeks. In addition to voiding before bed and limiting evening drinks, which of the following is most appropriate?
items.explanationHtml:
For monosymptomatic primary nocturnal enuresis in a motivated family, the enuresis alarm gives the highest long-term cure rate and the lowest relapse rate, by conditioning arousal to bladder fullness. It takes several weeks to work.

Takeaway: the enuresis alarm is the best long-term treatment for primary nocturnal enuresis.

whyNot.A: Desmopressin works quickly but relapse is common when it is stopped.
whyNot.C: Imipramine is effective but its cardiotoxicity, especially in overdose, makes it a last resort.
whyNot.D: Antimuscarinics are for daytime overactive bladder symptoms, which he does not have.
whyNot.E: Frequent waking disrupts sleep and does not teach the child to wake to a full bladder.

items.objective: Choose the enuresis alarm for durable control of primary nocturnal enuresis.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy soils his underwear several times a day. His mother says he passes large, hard stools every 5–6 days that sometimes block the toilet, and he hides when he needs to go. Abdominal examination shows a firm mass in the left lower quadrant, and rectal examination shows a dilated rectum full of hard stool. Growth and neurological examination are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: A low-fibre diet to reduce stool volume

options.label: B
options.html: A reward chart for clean underwear, without medication

options.label: D
options.html: Oral polyethylene glycol disimpaction, then maintenance therapy

items.explanationHtml:
This is retentive encopresis: chronic constipation with overflow leakage around retained stool. Treatment is disimpaction (high-dose oral polyethylene glycol, or enemas), then months of maintenance laxative to keep stools soft, scheduled toilet sitting after meals and positive reinforcement, with education that removes blame.

Takeaway: most encopresis is constipation with overflow: disimpact, then maintain soft stools with a toileting routine.

whyNot.B: Rewards help, but without clearing the impaction and softening stool the overflow continues.
whyNot.E: This is a bowel problem first; psychotherapy alone will not relieve the impaction.
whyNot.C: A barium enema is not needed when the history and examination clearly show functional constipation.
whyNot.A: Low fibre would worsen constipation; adequate fibre and fluid help.

items.objective: Treat retentive encopresis with disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has severe temper outbursts four or five times a week, with irritability between them, which began at age 7. He has no history of manic episodes, substance use or developmental problems, and his attention and learning are normal. A diagnosis of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder is made. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Admission to an inpatient psychiatric unit

options.label: B
options.html: Lithium titrated to a therapeutic level

options.label: C
options.html: Parent training and cognitive behavioural therapy

options.label: E
options.html: Valproate titrated to a therapeutic level

items.explanationHtml:
Psychosocial treatment comes first: parent management training and cognitive behavioural approaches that target irritability and frustration tolerance. Medication (a stimulant when ADHD coexists, an SSRI for irritability, or an antipsychotic for severe aggression) is added if needed. DMDD is not a bipolar disorder, so mood stabilisers are not first-line.

Takeaway: DMDD: start with parent training and CBT; it is not treated as bipolar disorder.

whyNot.B: Lithium is a bipolar treatment and has not shown benefit for DMDD.
whyNot.E: Valproate is not a first-line treatment for DMDD and has significant adverse effects.
whyNot.D: Antipsychotics are reserved for severe aggression unresponsive to other treatment because of metabolic risk.
whyNot.A: He is not described as dangerous; outpatient care is appropriate.

items.objective: Initiate psychosocial treatment for disruptive mood dysregulation disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother after he was caught breaking into a neighbour's garage. Over the past year he has stolen from shops, set fire to a trash bin at school, threatened classmates with a knife and skipped school most weeks. He shows little concern for those affected. He has no history of inattention or hyperactivity, and drug screening is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: D
options.html: Lithium titrated to a therapeutic level

items.explanationHtml:
This is conduct disorder. The most effective treatments are intensive family- and community-based programmes such as multisystemic therapy, which work with the family, school and peer group, plus parent management training. Medication only treats specific comorbidities or severe aggression.

Takeaway: treat conduct disorder with intensive family and community-based therapy, not medication alone.

whyNot.B: Stimulants help when ADHD coexists; he has no ADHD symptoms.
whyNot.A: Antipsychotics are reserved for severe aggression after psychosocial measures, and haloperidol is not preferred.
whyNot.C: Individual insight-oriented therapy has little evidence in conduct disorder.
whyNot.D: Lithium has a limited role in aggression and is not first-line treatment for conduct disorder.

items.objective: Choose multisystemic, family-based treatment for conduct disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 5-year-old girl started kindergarten 4 months ago and has not spoken a word to her teacher or classmates, although she joins activities and nods or points. At home she chats normally with her parents and sister. Her hearing and language development were normal at a recent evaluation. She becomes visibly tense when strangers speak to her. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Referral for autism spectrum disorder assessment

options.label: D
options.html: Requiring her to speak before she may join activities

options.label: E
options.html: Speech and language therapy for an expressive language disorder

items.explanationHtml:
Consistent failure to speak in specific social settings for more than a month (beyond the first month of school) while speaking normally elsewhere is selective mutism, an anxiety disorder closely tied to social anxiety. First-line treatment is cognitive behavioural therapy with gradual, rewarded steps toward speaking, involving the school. An SSRI is added for severe or persistent cases.

Takeaway: selective mutism is an anxiety disorder; treat it with graded-exposure CBT involving the school.

whyNot.E: Her language is normal at home and on testing, so she does not have a language disorder.
whyNot.A: Medication is reserved for children who do not respond to psychological treatment.
whyNot.D: Pressuring her to speak increases anxiety and reinforces avoidance.
whyNot.C: She has normal social interaction at home and joins activities, so autism is not suggested.

items.objective: Treat selective mutism with cognitive behavioural therapy and school involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 3-year-old girl was adopted 6 months ago from an orphanage where she had lived since birth with frequently changing caregivers. Her adoptive parents are worried because she runs up to strangers in the park, climbs into their laps and would leave with them without looking back. She does not check on her parents in unfamiliar places. Her language and play skills are close to age level, and she makes good eye contact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
After severe early neglect, disinhibited social engagement disorder presents with overly familiar behaviour toward unfamiliar adults and a lack of checking back with the caregiver. Reactive attachment disorder, the other neglect-related disorder, is the opposite pattern: withdrawal and failure to seek comfort. Treatment centres on a stable, nurturing caregiving relationship.

Takeaway: after neglect: indiscriminate friendliness = disinhibited social engagement; withdrawal = reactive attachment disorder.

whyNot.D: Reactive attachment disorder causes inhibited, emotionally withdrawn behaviour, not indiscriminate approach to strangers.
whyNot.B: Her eye contact, play and language are near normal, which argues against autism.
whyNot.A: Impulsivity may overlap, but the core problem is social disinhibition rooted in neglect, and ADHD is rarely diagnosed at 3.
whyNot.E: Separation anxiety causes distress on leaving the caregiver, the opposite of her behaviour.

items.objective: Distinguish disinhibited social engagement disorder from reactive attachment disorder after early neglect.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has cut her thighs when distressed since age 15. She describes intense, short-lived anger and despair after arguments, a constant sense of emptiness, a string of brief intense relationships and panic when her partner is late home. She has no psychotic symptoms and is not currently suicidal. Which of the following is the most effective treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is borderline personality disorder. Dialectical behaviour therapy teaches distress tolerance, emotion regulation, mindfulness and interpersonal effectiveness and has the best evidence for reducing self-harm and suicide attempts. Medications only target comorbid conditions or symptoms.

Takeaway: borderline personality disorder is treated mainly with psychotherapy, especially DBT.

whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines can worsen impulsivity and disinhibition and carry dependence and overdose risk.
whyNot.C: Lithium is not a treatment for borderline personality disorder and is dangerous in overdose.
whyNot.E: Antipsychotics are at most short-term adjuncts for specific symptoms, not primary treatment.
whyNot.B: ECT treats severe depression and catatonia, not personality disorders.

items.objective: Choose dialectical behaviour therapy for borderline personality disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder comes to the emergency department 5 hours after swallowing about 20 tablets of 500-mg acetaminophen after an argument with her boyfriend. She now regrets it and asks to go home. She is alert, and vital signs are normal. She has no abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge with a safety plan and an outpatient DBT appointment

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer directly to the inpatient psychiatric unit

items.explanationHtml:
A potentially toxic ingestion (about 10 g) needs medical assessment first. Measure serum acetaminophen (from 4 hours after ingestion) and liver tests, and start acetylcysteine according to the treatment nomogram. Early symptoms are often absent despite a toxic dose. After medical stabilisation she needs a full psychiatric and suicide risk assessment.

Takeaway: after a self-harm overdose, treat the poisoning first: acetaminophen level and acetylcysteine as indicated, then psychiatric assessment.

whyNot.A: She may have taken a hepatotoxic dose, and her suicide risk has not yet been assessed.
whyNot.E: Psychiatric transfer must wait until the overdose is assessed and treated.
whyNot.B: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures; it has no role in acetaminophen poisoning.
whyNot.C: Ipecac is no longer used for poisoning.

items.objective: Prioritise medical evaluation of an acetaminophen overdose in a patient who self-harms.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder is admitted to a medical ward with pyelonephritis. On day 2 she tells the attending physician that the night nurses are cruel and that he is the only person she trusts. Several nurses are angry and want her to receive a different nurse each shift, while two others defend her. Which of the following is the most appropriate action by the attending physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Arrange a team meeting to agree on one consistent care plan and clear limits

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge her early to oral antibiotics to reduce ward conflict

options.label: C
options.html: Order a psychiatric consultation to initiate antipsychotic treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Reassign her care to the nurses she likes best

options.label: E
options.html: Tell her that the nurses are excellent and her complaints are unfounded

items.explanationHtml:
She is splitting the team into all-good and all-bad camps. The response is a team meeting so that all staff give consistent messages, with predictable routines and clear, nonpunitive limits, while acknowledging her distress without taking sides.

Takeaway: when a patient splits the team, align the team on one consistent plan and boundaries.

whyNot.D: Giving her only the favoured staff reinforces splitting and deepens the conflict.
whyNot.E: Arguing about the nurses invalidates her and escalates the conflict; acknowledge feelings and restate the plan.
whyNot.B: Discharge decisions must rest on medical readiness, not on staff conflict.
whyNot.C: Splitting is not a psychotic symptom, and antipsychotics are not the answer to team conflict.

items.objective: Manage splitting by a patient with borderline personality disorder through consistent team communication.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old business owner with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is seen in clinic. He says he has 'read everything' about diabetes, that only a specialist of his calibre should treat him and that the clinic's dietitian is 'not worth his time'. He refuses insulin because 'that is for people who cannot manage themselves'. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Acknowledge his expertise and frame insulin around his own goals

options.label: B
options.html: Agree to continue his current regimen to avoid conflict

options.label: C
options.html: Insist that he see the dietitian before any further discussion

options.label: D
options.html: Refer him to a different physician immediately

options.label: E
options.html: Tell him firmly that his attitude is harming his care

items.explanationHtml:
His grandiosity and entitlement suggest narcissistic traits. Confrontation threatens his fragile self-esteem and provokes resistance. It works better to acknowledge his expertise and concerns and frame the recommendation around his goals and sense of control, for example by emphasising self-titration and mastery of insulin.

Takeaway: with narcissistic patients, acknowledge their competence and frame advice around their own goals rather than confronting them.

whyNot.E: Confrontation tends to provoke anger and disengagement in narcissistic patients.
whyNot.D: Transferring care avoids rather than addresses the problem, and he would carry the same pattern elsewhere.
whyNot.B: Accepting poorly controlled diabetes to avoid conflict harms the patient.
whyNot.C: An ultimatum invites a power struggle and is unlikely to change his behaviour.

items.objective: Communicate effectively with a patient who has narcissistic traits.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with lifelong suspiciousness of others needs a colonoscopy after a positive fecal immunochemical test. He asks why the hospital wants 'so much information' about him and suspects the test is an excuse to experiment on him. He has no hallucinations, and his beliefs are not fixed when discussed. Which of the following approaches is most likely to gain his cooperation?

options.label: A
options.html: A clear, matter-of-fact explanation of each step

options.label: B
options.html: Ask a family member to sign the consent form for him

options.label: C
options.html: Proceed without discussion, since detailed information increases suspicion

options.label: D
options.html: Start a low-dose antipsychotic before discussing the procedure

options.label: E
options.html: Use a warm, very friendly manner and reassure him that everyone is on his side

items.explanationHtml:
He has paranoid personality traits. Patients with paranoid traits respond best to honest, clear and matter-of-fact explanations of what will happen and why, with time for questions and no hidden agenda. Excessive warmth can itself arouse suspicion.

Takeaway: with paranoid patients, be clear, honest and businesslike; explain each step.

whyNot.E: Excessive friendliness often increases suspicion about hidden motives.
whyNot.D: He is not psychotic; antipsychotics are not indicated to obtain consent.
whyNot.C: He has decision-making capacity and must give informed consent; withholding information would deepen mistrust.
whyNot.B: A capable adult consents for himself; a relative cannot sign in his place.

items.objective: Communicate effectively with a patient who has paranoid personality traits.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man has avoided friendships, dating and team projects at work since his teens because he expects to be ridiculed. He wants to change and agrees to treatment. He has no depressive symptoms, substance use or medical illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: CBT with graded exposure to social situations

options.label: D
options.html: No treatment, because personality disorders do not respond to therapy

items.explanationHtml:
This is avoidant personality disorder. It overlaps heavily with social anxiety disorder and responds to cognitive behavioural therapy that challenges beliefs about rejection and uses graded exposure and social skills practice. An SSRI may be added if social anxiety disorder coexists.

Takeaway: avoidant personality disorder responds to CBT with graded exposure, as social anxiety does.

whyNot.A: Daily benzodiazepines risk dependence and do not change the underlying avoidance.
whyNot.E: Propranolol is used for performance anxiety on specific occasions, not pervasive avoidance.
whyNot.C: Antipsychotics have no role; he has no psychotic features.
whyNot.D: Avoidant personality disorder improves with psychotherapy.

items.objective: Treat avoidant personality disorder with cognitive behavioural therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old college student is brought by his roommate, who finds him strange. Since high school he has worn a cape to class, believed that he can influence the weather by concentrating, and felt that classmates' conversations often refer to him, although he accepts this may not be true. He has no close friends. He has never heard voices, his speech is vague but coherent and he functions well enough to pass his courses. Urine drug screen is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing eccentric dress, magical thinking, ideas of reference held with doubt, odd speech and a lack of close friends, without hallucinations or fixed delusions, is schizotypal personality disorder. Management is supportive psychotherapy, with monitoring for a later psychotic disorder.

Takeaway: eccentricity and magical thinking without frank psychosis since adolescence = schizotypal personality disorder.

whyNot.D: Schizophrenia needs clear psychotic symptoms such as fixed delusions or hallucinations, and usually a decline in functioning.
whyNot.A: Brief psychotic disorder is an acute psychotic episode lasting less than a month, not a lifelong trait pattern.
whyNot.C: Schizoid personality disorder lacks the eccentric beliefs and perceptual oddities he shows.
whyNot.B: Delusional disorder needs a fixed false belief for at least a month; his ideas are held with doubt.

items.objective: Diagnose schizotypal personality disorder and separate it from psychotic disorders.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old accountant has changed over the past 8 months. Previously reserved, he now makes crude jokes to clients, has spent thousands of dollars on impulse purchases and eats sweets compulsively. He shows no concern when his wife expresses alarm. He has no history of psychiatric illness or substance use, and he denies low mood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Diagnose antisocial personality disorder and refer for psychotherapy

options.label: B
options.html: Diagnose narcissistic personality disorder and advise couples therapy

options.label: C
options.html: Neurological examination, cognitive testing and MRI of the brain

options.label: D
options.html: Reassure his wife that this is a normal midlife change

options.label: E
options.html: Start lithium for a presumed manic episode

items.explanationHtml:
Personality disorders begin by early adulthood. A new personality change in midlife, with disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and hyperorality, suggests a neurological cause, especially behavioural-variant frontotemporal dementia or a frontal lesion. He needs neurological and cognitive assessment and brain MRI.

Takeaway: a new personality change in middle age is a medical or neurological problem until proved otherwise.

whyNot.A: Antisocial personality disorder needs a lifelong pattern beginning with conduct disorder before 15.
whyNot.B: A personality disorder cannot begin at 52; this is a change from his usual self.
whyNot.E: There is no elevated mood, decreased sleep or other manic features, and a neurological cause must be excluded first.
whyNot.D: Disinhibition, hyperorality and loss of empathy are not normal ageing.

items.objective: Recognise that new-onset personality change in midlife requires neurological evaluation.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a sore throat. She is dressed in an eye-catching outfit, compliments the male physician's appearance, describes her week as 'absolutely devastating' with little detail, and touches his arm while talking. Her mood shifts quickly from tearful to laughing. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach by the physician?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask her to see a female colleague in future

options.label: B
options.html: Point out her flirtatious behaviour and tell her it is inappropriate

options.label: C
options.html: Professional manner, firm boundaries and a chaperone

options.label: E
options.html: Respond in kind to build rapport

items.explanationHtml:
Attention-seeking, seductive behaviour, shallow and labile emotion and vague, impressionistic speech suggest histrionic personality traits. The physician should stay courteous and professional, keep clear boundaries, focus on the clinical problem and use a chaperone for examinations.

Takeaway: with histrionic patients, be professional and keep firm boundaries, with a chaperone for examinations.

whyNot.A: Transferring her care is unnecessary; professional boundaries manage the behaviour.
whyNot.B: Direct confrontation is likely to humiliate her and damage the relationship.
whyNot.E: Reciprocating breaches professional boundaries.
whyNot.D: Refusing care is not justified; she needs evaluation of her sore throat.

items.objective: Maintain professional boundaries with a patient who has histrionic traits.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with dependent personality disorder and well-controlled hypertension calls the clinic several times a week asking whether she should take a walk, change her breakfast or skip a dose when she feels well. Each call is reassured, and the calls keep increasing. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask her family to make her health decisions

options.label: B
options.html: Brief scheduled visits with limits on unscheduled calls

options.label: C
options.html: Prescribe a daily benzodiazepine to reduce her anxiety

options.label: D
options.html: Tell her to stop calling and only attend when ill

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer her care to another practice

items.explanationHtml:
Patients with dependent traits do better with predictable, regularly scheduled visits that meet their need for support, combined with clear limits on unscheduled contact and gentle encouragement to make decisions themselves. Psychotherapy can build autonomy.

Takeaway: dependent patients: regular scheduled visits, firm limits and encouragement of self-reliance.

whyNot.D: Abrupt rejection heightens her fear of abandonment and may increase crisis contacts.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines risk dependence and do not address the pattern.
whyNot.E: Ending the relationship is not justified and will not help.
whyNot.A: Handing decisions to others reinforces dependence and undermines her autonomy.

items.objective: Manage patients with dependent personality traits with scheduled visits and clear limits.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman says her mood 'changes a hundred times a day'. After a perceived slight from a friend she becomes enraged or despairing within minutes, and the feeling settles within hours, often after she cuts herself. She describes feeling empty most of the time and fears being abandoned by her partner. She has never had several consecutive days of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep or increased goal-directed activity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: E
options.html: Major depressive disorder with mixed features

items.explanationHtml:
Mood shifts lasting hours, triggered by interpersonal events, with chronic emptiness, fear of abandonment and self-harm, fit borderline personality disorder. Bipolar disorders need discrete episodes lasting days (at least 4 days for hypomania) that are not simply reactions to interpersonal stress.

Takeaway: minutes-to-hours reactive mood shifts with emptiness and self-harm = borderline personality disorder, not bipolar disorder.

whyNot.A: Bipolar II needs at least one hypomanic episode lasting 4 or more days, which she has never had.
whyNot.C: Cyclothymia involves at least 2 years of recurrent hypomanic and depressive symptom periods, not mood shifts within hours triggered by interpersonal events.
whyNot.E: Major depression with mixed features needs a depressive episode of at least 2 weeks with concurrent hypomanic symptoms.
whyNot.D: Histrionic patients show shallow, dramatic emotion and attention-seeking, without self-harm or chronic emptiness as core features.

items.objective: Differentiate borderline personality disorder from bipolar spectrum disorders by the duration and triggers of mood shifts.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder attends weekly DBT. She has developed a major depressive episode with early-morning waking and poor appetite. She has two previous overdoses, the most recent 8 months ago, and denies current suicidal intent. Which of the following prescribing plans is most appropriate?

options.label: B
options.html: An SSRI dispensed in small quantities, with close follow-up

options.label: C
options.html: Lithium, titrated to a therapeutic level

options.label: D
options.html: Lorazepam as needed for acute distress

options.label: E
options.html: No antidepressant, because depression in borderline personality disorder never responds

items.explanationHtml:
A coexisting major depressive episode should be treated. Choose a drug that is relatively safe in overdose, such as an SSRI, prescribe limited quantities and review frequently, while continuing DBT and safety planning.

Takeaway: for patients who have overdosed, choose antidepressants safe in overdose and dispense small amounts.

whyNot.A: Tricyclics are highly toxic in overdose, and a large supply is dangerous for someone with prior overdoses.
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines can increase impulsivity and are risky in overdose combinations.
whyNot.C: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is dangerous in overdose; it is not first-line for unipolar depression.
whyNot.E: Comorbid major depression does respond to treatment and should not be left untreated.

items.objective: Prescribe safely for comorbid depression in a patient with borderline personality disorder and prior overdoses.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman comes to her physician 3 months after her husband died of a heart attack. She cries when she finds his belongings and some evenings feels a wave of sadness when she sets the table. Twice, while falling asleep, she briefly heard him call her name. She has returned to part-time work, enjoys visits from her grandchildren and is sleeping 6 to 7 hours a night. She has no thoughts of harming herself. Which of the following best describes her condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Sadness in waves triggered by reminders, preserved enjoyment, returning function and no thoughts of self-harm describe ordinary grief. Briefly hearing or seeing the dead person, especially at sleep onset, is common and is not psychosis.

Takeaway: brief perceptions of the dead person with intact function and self-worth are part of normal grief.

whyNot.D: Prolonged grief disorder needs at least 12 months since the death in adults, with persistent yearning and impairment.
whyNot.C: She lacks pervasive low mood, anhedonia, worthlessness and the neurovegetative change of a depressive episode.
whyNot.A: Adjustment disorder is not diagnosed when the reaction is ordinary bereavement.
whyNot.B: Brief, hypnagogic perceptions of the deceased are culturally ordinary and do not indicate psychosis.

items.objective: Distinguish ordinary grief, including brief perceptions of the deceased, from psychiatric disorders.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old woman is evaluated 18 months after her 22-year-old son died of leukemia. Every day she spends hours thinking about him, keeps his room unchanged and avoids the hospital where he was treated. She says that part of her died with him and that life has no meaning without him. She has not returned to work. She still enjoys time with her sister and has no feelings of worthlessness, and her sleep and appetite are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
More than 12 months after a death, daily yearning and preoccupation with the dead person, a sense that part of oneself has died, avoidance of reminders, a feeling that life is meaningless and impaired function meet the criteria for prolonged grief disorder.

Takeaway: intense yearning with identity disruption and impairment beyond 12 months is prolonged grief disorder.

whyNot.A: Her distress is centred on the loss; she keeps pleasure elsewhere and has no worthlessness or neurovegetative change.
whyNot.C: Her son died of illness; she has no intrusive trauma memories, nightmares or hyperarousal.
whyNot.B: Persistent depressive disorder is a chronic low mood across most areas of life for at least 2 years.
whyNot.E: The duration and degree of impairment exceed ordinary grief.

items.objective: Recognise the duration and core features of prolonged grief disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with major depressive disorder is seen in clinic. A resident reviews his history to estimate his long-term risk of dying by suicide. Which of the following features of his history most increases that risk?

options.label: A
options.html: A drug overdose 2 years ago that required intensive care

options.label: B
options.html: A sister who has major depression

options.label: D
options.html: Marriage and two children at home

items.explanationHtml:
A previous suicide attempt is the strongest single predictor of eventual death by suicide, and an attempt serious enough to need intensive care carries particular weight.

Takeaway: ask every patient with suicidal thoughts about past attempts; a prior attempt is the strongest predictor.

whyNot.B: A family history of mood disorder raises risk, but far less than a personal history of an attempt.
whyNot.E: Light weekend drinking adds little risk; heavy use and intoxication matter.
whyNot.C: Controlled hypertension is not a meaningful suicide risk factor.
whyNot.D: Being married with children at home is protective.

items.objective: Identify a previous suicide attempt as the strongest predictor of suicide.

items.stemHtml: A public health team in the United States is planning a programme to reduce suicide deaths among men aged 45 to 64. They first review which method accounts for the largest share of suicide deaths nationally. Which of the following methods is it?
items.explanationHtml:
Firearms account for about half of all US suicide deaths. Attempts with a gun are far more often fatal than attempts by other methods, which is a main reason men, who use firearms more, die by suicide more often than women.

Takeaway: firearm access is a major, modifiable determinant of whether a suicide attempt is fatal.

whyNot.D: Hanging and suffocation are the second most common method, not the first.
whyNot.B: Poisoning is the most common method of nonfatal attempts, especially in women, but causes fewer deaths.
whyNot.E: Jumping causes a small share of suicide deaths.
whyNot.A: Cutting is common in self-injury but rarely fatal.

items.objective: State that firearms cause the largest share of US suicide deaths.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old girl has made shallow cuts on her forearms several times a month for a year. She says that when she feels overwhelmed after arguments, cutting makes the tension disappear within minutes, and she has never wanted to die. Each episode has been followed by more frequent cutting. Which of the following learning principles best explains why the behaviour persists?
items.explanationHtml:
Cutting removes an unpleasant emotional state, and the removal of something aversive makes the behaviour more likely: negative reinforcement. This is the usual function of nonsuicidal self-injury.

Takeaway: a behaviour that is strengthened because it takes away distress is maintained by negative reinforcement.

whyNot.E: Positive punishment adds an aversive consequence and decreases a behaviour.
whyNot.B: Extinction is the fading of a behaviour when its reinforcement stops.
whyNot.A: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with a reflexive response; this is an operant, voluntary behaviour.
whyNot.C: Negative punishment removes something pleasant and decreases a behaviour.

items.objective: Apply operant conditioning to explain the persistence of nonsuicidal self-injury.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day says, "I know smoking is wrecking my lungs and I've been thinking for a few months that I should stop, but I'm not ready to pick a date. I'd miss my cigarette breaks with my coworkers." According to the stages-of-change model, which stage is he in?
items.explanationHtml:
He recognises the problem and is weighing the pros and cons but has no plan or date: contemplation. The clinician's task in this stage is to explore his ambivalence.

Takeaway: awareness and ambivalence without a plan defines contemplation.

whyNot.D: In precontemplation the person does not see a problem or intend to change.
whyNot.E: Preparation means intending to act soon with concrete steps such as a quit date.
whyNot.A: Action means he has already changed the behaviour.
whyNot.C: Maintenance follows at least several months of sustained change.

items.objective: Identify the contemplation stage of change.

items.stemHtml: An 83-year-old woman with moderate Alzheimer disease lives with her daughter, who is her paid caregiver. She is brought to the emergency department by a neighbour. She has lost 7 kg (15 lb) in 4 months, her clothes are soiled, and she has a deep pressure injury over the sacrum. Her pill organiser holds medication that was dispensed 2 months ago. There are no bruises or fractures. Which of the following best describes this situation?
items.explanationHtml:
A dependent person whose responsible caregiver does not provide food, hygiene, medicines or pressure care is a victim of caregiver neglect.

Takeaway: when a responsible caregiver fails to meet a dependent adult's basic needs, it is neglect, which is reportable.

whyNot.C: There are no injuries from force such as bruises, burns or fractures.
whyNot.B: Nothing in the history suggests misuse of her money or property.
whyNot.E: Self-neglect applies to an older adult without a responsible caregiver who fails to meet their own needs.
whyNot.D: No threats, humiliation or isolation are described.

items.objective: Recognise caregiver neglect as a form of elder abuse.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man is confused on the second day after repair of a hip fracture. He was independent and managed his own finances before admission. He cannot keep count of the days of the week backward, drifts off mid-sentence and at night pulls at his intravenous line; in the morning he is calmer. An EEG is obtained. Which of the following findings is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Acute, fluctuating inattention and disorganized thinking after surgery is delirium. Delirium of most causes produces generalized slowing of the EEG background; the exception is sedative or alcohol withdrawal, which produces fast activity.

Takeaway: delirium usually shows diffuse EEG slowing, which helps separate it from primary psychiatric illness.

whyNot.D: A normal EEG would argue against delirium and favour a primary psychiatric cause.
whyNot.C: Three-per-second spike-and-wave discharges are typical of absence seizures in children.
whyNot.E: Periodic sharp-wave complexes suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, which progresses over weeks to months.
whyNot.B: Focal temporal spikes indicate a focal epileptic focus, not a global confusional state.

items.objective: Link delirium to diffuse EEG slowing and distinguish it from dementia.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic because of 2 months of low mood, poor sleep and trouble concentrating at work. He says, "Lately I think everyone would be better off without me." He has no history of psychiatric treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Ask him directly whether he has thought about ending his life

options.label: E
options.html: Start sertraline and review him in 4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
His remark is a possible expression of suicidal thinking. The next step is to ask directly about thoughts of suicide, then about plan, intent, means and past attempts. That assessment decides whether he needs admission or outpatient care.

Takeaway: when a patient hints at suicide, ask directly; asking does not increase risk.

whyNot.A: Admission depends on the risk assessment, which has not been done.
whyNot.E: Treatment can start after his safety has been assessed.
whyNot.D: Referral without first assessing suicide risk could miss an emergency.
whyNot.C: Checking thyroid function is reasonable later but is not the priority.

items.objective: Ask directly about suicidal ideation when a patient hints at it.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his brother. He separated from his wife a month ago, has been drinking heavily and has lost his job. He says he has decided to shoot himself this weekend with the rifle in his garage and has written letters to his children. He is not intoxicated, is oriented and refuses to stay in hospital. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask his brother to remove the rifle and then discharge him

options.label: B
options.html: Discharge him with a safety plan and a clinic visit tomorrow

options.label: C
options.html: Have him sign an agreement not to harm himself

options.label: D
options.html: Place him on an emergency involuntary psychiatric hold

options.label: E
options.html: Start an antidepressant and arrange review in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
He has a specific plan, a lethal method, preparatory acts (letters) and stated intent, with several risk factors. His risk is imminent, and because he refuses admission, an emergency involuntary hold is required to keep him safe.

Takeaway: imminent suicide risk with refusal of admission justifies an involuntary emergency hold.

whyNot.B: A safety plan is suitable for lower-risk patients, not for someone with intent and preparation.
whyNot.A: Removing one firearm does not make it safe to discharge someone with intent.
whyNot.E: An antidepressant takes weeks to work and does nothing for the immediate danger.
whyNot.C: Agreements not to self-harm have no proven protective value.

items.objective: Use an involuntary hold for imminent suicide risk when admission is refused.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy is seen in clinic with his parents after a breakup. For a week he has sometimes wished he would not wake up, but he has no plan or intent and no past attempts. He is engaged at school and agrees to follow-up. His father keeps an unlocked handgun in the bedroom, and there is a large supply of his mother's oxycodone in the kitchen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Admit him to an inpatient psychiatric unit

options.label: B
options.html: Arrange a follow-up visit in 3 months

options.label: C
options.html: Ask him to sign a no-suicide contract

options.label: D
options.html: Counsel the parents to remove or lock up the gun and opioids

items.explanationHtml:
Passive thoughts of death without plan or intent, good engagement and supportive parents make outpatient care appropriate, with a safety plan and early follow-up. The most effective single step is lethal-means counselling: removing or locking up the firearm and the opioids, because access to lethal means makes impulsive attempts more likely to be fatal.

Takeaway: counsel families to remove or secure firearms and medicines when a young person has suicidal thoughts.

whyNot.A: His risk is low to moderate with strong supports, so admission is not required.
whyNot.C: No-suicide contracts are not protective and do not replace assessment and safety planning.
whyNot.E: An antidepressant is not indicated for a week of passive ideation after a breakup without a depressive episode.
whyNot.B: Follow-up should be within days, not months.

items.objective: Apply lethal-means counselling for an adolescent at lower suicide risk.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old woman has cut her thighs about twice a week for 3 years, usually after conflicts with friends. She has intense, quickly changing moods, chronic emptiness and stormy relationships. She has never attempted suicide. She asks for treatment to help her stop. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Repeated self-injury driven by emotional dysregulation, with features of borderline personality disorder, is best treated with dialectical behavior therapy. It teaches distress tolerance and emotion regulation and reduces self-harm.

Takeaway: dialectical behavior therapy is the treatment of choice for recurrent self-injury with emotion dysregulation.

whyNot.E: Benzodiazepines can disinhibit and are not a treatment for self-injury.
whyNot.B: No medication reliably reduces self-injury; an SSRI treats coexisting depression.
whyNot.D: Unstructured psychodynamic therapy has weaker evidence than dialectical behavior therapy here.
whyNot.C: She has no acute suicide risk; admission is not needed and can reinforce crisis-driven care.

items.objective: Choose dialectical behavior therapy for recurrent nonsuicidal self-injury.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man comes to the clinic 14 months after his wife's death. He thinks about her nearly all day, visits her grave daily, feels he no longer knows who he is and has withdrawn from his friends. He has not resumed volunteer work he loved. He sleeps 7 hours, eats well and has no suicidal thoughts. Thyroid function and a basic metabolic panel are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Daily preoccupation, identity disruption and withdrawal 14 months after the death meet the criteria for prolonged grief disorder. Psychotherapy designed for it (grief-focused, often with cognitive behavioural elements) is the most effective treatment.

Takeaway: prolonged grief disorder responds best to grief-focused psychotherapy.

whyNot.E: Reassurance alone is not enough once the disorder is established and impairing.
whyNot.A: Benzodiazepines do not treat grief and carry dependence and fall risks in older adults.
whyNot.D: An antipsychotic has no role; he has no psychosis.
