whyNot.B: Electroconvulsive therapy is for severe or psychotic depression, which he does not have.

items.objective: Treat prolonged grief disorder with grief-focused psychotherapy.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman is seen 2 months after her mother's death. For 6 weeks she has felt depressed most of the day, has lost interest in everything, wakes at 4 AM, has lost 5 kg (11 lb) and feels she is a worthless person who failed everyone. She has had passing thoughts that she would be better off dead but no plan or intent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Begin an SSRI and arrange psychotherapy

options.label: B
options.html: Explain that these feelings are normal in the first year of grief

options.label: D
options.html: Refer her to a bereavement support group only

options.label: E
options.html: Wait until 12 months after the death to reassess

items.explanationHtml:
She meets criteria for a major depressive episode: pervasive low mood and anhedonia, early waking, weight loss, worthlessness and thoughts of death. A recent loss does not exclude the diagnosis, and the episode should be treated with an antidepressant and psychotherapy, with safety planning.

Takeaway: treat a major depressive episode even when it follows a bereavement.

whyNot.B: Pervasive worthlessness, anhedonia and neurovegetative change go beyond normal grief.
whyNot.E: Twelve months is the duration rule for prolonged grief disorder, not for depression.
whyNot.C: A hypnotic treats only one symptom and leaves the depression untreated.
whyNot.D: A support group can help, but on its own it is not adequate treatment for a depressive episode.

items.objective: Diagnose and treat major depression that arises after a bereavement.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a swollen left cheek and a bruised wrist. She says she walked into a door. Her partner stays at her side, answers most questions for her and says she is clumsy. The bruises on her wrist are of different colours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the partner how the injuries happened

options.label: B
options.html: Call the police to report an assault

options.label: C
options.html: Confront the partner about the injuries

options.label: E
options.html: Speak with the patient alone, without her partner

items.explanationHtml:
Injuries that do not match the story, bruises of different ages and a controlling partner who answers for her suggest intimate partner violence. She must be asked about it in private, where she can speak safely.

Takeaway: always interview a patient alone when partner violence is possible.

whyNot.A: The partner's account adds nothing and may put her at risk.
whyNot.B: A competent adult decides about reporting; first she needs a safe, private conversation.
whyNot.C: Confronting the partner can escalate the danger to her.
whyNot.D: A skeletal survey is used for suspected child abuse, not for an adult with localised injuries.

items.objective: Interview a patient privately when intimate partner violence is suspected.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman tells her physician, in private, that her husband has hit her several times in the past year. She has bruises on her upper arm. She has no children. He has never used a weapon or tried to strangle her. She does not want the police involved and is not ready to leave. She is alert and fully understands her situation. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Assess her safety and make a safety plan with her

options.label: C
options.html: Recommend couples counselling with her husband

options.label: D
options.html: Report the assault to the police despite her objection

options.label: E
options.html: Say you will not treat her unless she leaves him

items.explanationHtml:
A competent adult has the right to decide whether to report or leave. The clinician assesses danger, makes a safety plan, offers advocacy and hotline resources, documents the injuries and arranges follow-up. Her decisions may change over time.

Takeaway: for a competent adult experiencing partner violence, assess danger, safety-plan and respect autonomy.

whyNot.D: Reporting against a competent adult's wishes is not required here and may increase danger.
whyNot.C: Couples counselling is not recommended while abuse is ongoing; it can provoke retaliation.
whyNot.E: Conditioning care on leaving is coercive and abandons the patient.
whyNot.B: Adult protective services serve elderly or dependent adults, not competent younger adults.

items.objective: Respond to disclosed partner violence with risk assessment and safety planning.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman with dementia is brought to the clinic by her son, who is her only caregiver. She has oval bruises on both upper arms in a pattern of fingertip marks. The son says she bruises easily. Platelet count and coagulation tests are normal. She cannot give a reliable account and lacks decision-making capacity. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask the patient's permission before taking any action

options.label: E
options.html: Report the findings to adult protective services

items.explanationHtml:
Grip-pattern bruises on a dependent adult with normal coagulation strongly suggest physical abuse. Suspected elder abuse is reportable to adult protective services in nearly every state; proof is not needed. The clinician should also ensure she is safe today.

Takeaway: suspected elder abuse is reported to adult protective services; certainty is not required.

whyNot.D: Waiting leaves a dependent adult exposed to further harm.
whyNot.A: She lacks capacity, and reporting suspected abuse of a dependent adult does not require consent.
whyNot.B: Confrontation can increase the risk to her and is not the clinician's role.
whyNot.C: Normal blood counts and coagulation make a marrow cause very unlikely.

items.objective: Report suspected elder abuse to adult protective services.

items.stemHtml: A 50-year-old man with fatty liver drinks about 5 beers a night. He says, "I love winding down with a beer, but my liver numbers scare me." The physician wants to respond in keeping with motivational interviewing. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.html: "If you were my brother, I would insist that you quit."

options.label: B
options.html: "Most people who drink like you end up in hospital."

options.label: C
options.html: "So a beer helps you unwind, and you're also worried about your liver."

options.label: D
options.html: "Why haven't you cut down since our last visit?"

options.label: E
options.html: "You must stop drinking now, or you will develop cirrhosis."

items.explanationHtml:
A double-sided reflection states both sides of the patient's ambivalence without judgement. It lets him hear his own reasons for change and invites him to explore them. Warnings, confrontation and "why" questions provoke resistance.

Takeaway: motivational interviewing uses reflections that draw out the patient's own reasons for change.

whyNot.E: A directive warning tends to provoke defensiveness rather than change.
whyNot.D: "Why" questions about failure sound accusatory and increase resistance.
whyNot.A: Imposing the clinician's personal view ignores the patient's autonomy.
whyNot.B: Scare tactics based on generalisation are confrontational and ineffective.

items.objective: Use a double-sided reflection in motivational interviewing.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman is restless and confused on the third day after hip fracture surgery. She mistakes the nurse for her daughter, is worse at night and pulls at her urinary catheter but has not hurt anyone. She usually wears glasses and hearing aids, which are at home. Urinalysis and electrolytes are normal; her only new drugs are scheduled acetaminophen and low-dose oxycodone. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Apply wrist restraints to protect the catheter

options.label: B
options.html: Give diphenhydramine at bedtime for sleep

options.label: C
options.html: Give lorazepam at night to help her sleep

options.label: D
options.html: Restore her glasses and hearing aids and reorient her

items.explanationHtml:
She has postoperative delirium without dangerous agitation. First-line care is non-drug: restore glasses and hearing aids, remove tethers such as the catheter, reorient, mobilise, keep a day-night routine and involve family, while reviewing drugs and pain control.

Takeaway: manage delirium with non-drug measures first and treat its causes; drugs are for dangerous agitation.

whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium except in alcohol or sedative withdrawal.
whyNot.A: Restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium duration.
whyNot.B: Anticholinergic drugs such as diphenhydramine worsen delirium in older adults.
whyNot.E: Antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation that endangers the patient or others.

items.objective: Apply non-pharmacologic delirium management in an older inpatient.

items.stemHtml: A 73-year-old man is brought by his wife because his memory has worsened over 3 months. He has lost interest in golf, sleeps poorly and says he feels slowed down. On cognitive testing he often answers "I don't know" and gives up quickly, but when encouraged he recalls 3 of 3 words. He manages his own medicines. Complete blood count, vitamin B12, TSH and MRI of the brain are normal for age. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Subacute onset, prominent loss of interest, low effort on testing and preserved recall when encouraged point to depression presenting with cognitive complaints. Reversible causes have been excluded. Treat the depression and reassess cognition; follow him over time, because late-life depression can precede a neurodegenerative disease.

Takeaway: in an older adult with memory complaints and depressive features, treat the depression and reassess.

whyNot.C: Cholinesterase inhibitors are for dementia, which is not supported here.
whyNot.D: Memantine is for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease.
whyNot.A: Amyloid imaging does not change management in a likely depressive presentation.
whyNot.B: An EEG is not needed; there is no suspicion of seizures or delirium.

items.objective: Recognise and treat depression that presents with cognitive complaints in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man has been unable to achieve an erection since radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer 6 months ago. Before surgery his erections were normal. Injury to which of the following is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.html: Parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves

options.label: B
options.html: Somatic motor fibres of the pudendal nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Sympathetic fibres from the hypogastric plexus

items.explanationHtml:
Erection is parasympathetic: fibres from S2 to S4 travel in the pelvic splanchnic nerves and then the cavernous nerves, which run along the posterolateral prostate and are easily injured at prostatectomy. Their nitric oxide release relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle.

Takeaway: erection depends on parasympathetic cavernous nerves that run beside the prostate.

whyNot.C: Sympathetic hypogastric fibres mediate emission, not erection.
whyNot.B: The pudendal nerve gives sensation and drives the muscles of ejaculation.
whyNot.D: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and anterior scrotal skin.
whyNot.E: The ilioinguinal nerve is sensory to the groin and anterior scrotum.

items.objective: Identify the autonomic innervation of erection and why prostatectomy causes erectile dysfunction.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man with erectile dysfunction is prescribed sildenafil, taken an hour before sexual activity. Which of the following is the direct effect of the drug in the corpus cavernosum?

options.label: B
options.html: It blocks alpha-1 receptors on arterial smooth muscle

options.label: C
options.html: It increases cAMP through beta-2 receptors

options.label: D
options.html: It releases nitric oxide from endothelial cells

options.label: E
options.html: It slows the breakdown of cGMP

items.explanationHtml:
Sildenafil inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, the enzyme that breaks down cGMP. cGMP made in response to nitric oxide therefore persists and relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle. Sexual stimulation is still needed to start nitric oxide release.

Takeaway: PDE5 inhibitors prolong the cGMP signal; they do not start it.

whyNot.A: Activating soluble guanylyl cyclase describes riociguat and nitric oxide itself.
whyNot.C: Beta-2 agonism and cAMP do not underlie sildenafil's action.
whyNot.B: Alpha-1 blockade describes drugs such as tamsulosin.
whyNot.D: Nitric oxide comes from nerves and endothelium during arousal; sildenafil does not release it.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of PDE5 inhibitors.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man takes tadalafil for erectile dysfunction. He develops chest pain and is about to be given a medication that would put him at risk of a dangerous fall in blood pressure because both drugs raise the same intracellular messenger in vascular smooth muscle. Which of the following is that medication?
items.explanationHtml:
Nitrates donate nitric oxide and raise cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors stop cGMP breakdown. Together they cause profound vasodilation and hypotension. Nitrates are avoided for about 48 hours after tadalafil, which is long-acting, and for about 24 hours after sildenafil or vardenafil.

Takeaway: never combine a nitrate with a PDE5 inhibitor.

whyNot.D: Metoprolol lowers heart rate through beta-1 blockade and does not act through cGMP.
whyNot.A: Aspirin inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase and does not raise cGMP.
whyNot.B: Atorvastatin lowers cholesterol and does not interact in this way.
whyNot.C: Clopidogrel blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor and does not cause this interaction.

items.objective: Recognise the nitrate and PDE5 inhibitor interaction.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man whose depression responded to paroxetine has developed delayed ejaculation and low desire. His psychiatrist wants an antidepressant with little effect on sexual function because it does not increase serotonin signalling. Which of the following drugs best fits?
items.explanationHtml:
Bupropion inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine and has almost no serotonergic action, so it rarely causes sexual dysfunction. It lowers the seizure threshold.

Takeaway: bupropion is the antidepressant least likely to cause sexual side effects.

whyNot.D: Sertraline is an SSRI with the same serotonergic sexual effects.
whyNot.E: Venlafaxine inhibits serotonin reuptake as well as norepinephrine reuptake.
whyNot.C: Clomipramine is a strongly serotonergic tricyclic with high rates of sexual dysfunction.
whyNot.B: Citalopram is an SSRI and causes the same serotonergic sexual side effects.

items.objective: Choose an antidepressant with low risk of sexual dysfunction based on mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia has taken risperidone for 8 months. He reports low sexual desire and tender breast enlargement. Serum prolactin is elevated, and LH and testosterone are low. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his symptoms?

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in the pituitary

items.explanationHtml:
Dopamine from the tuberoinfundibular pathway inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary. Blocking D2 receptors there raises prolactin, which suppresses hypothalamic GnRH; LH and testosterone fall, causing low desire, and prolactin with altered sex steroid balance causes gynecomastia.

Takeaway: antipsychotic hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH and causes sexual dysfunction and gynecomastia.

whyNot.D: Muscarinic blockade causes dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention.
whyNot.A: Alpha-1 blockade causes orthostatic hypotension and ejaculatory problems, not hyperprolactinemia.
whyNot.C: H1 blockade causes sedation and weight gain.
whyNot.E: 5-HT2A blockade tends to lessen, not cause, extrapyramidal and prolactin effects.

items.objective: Explain antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia and hypogonadism.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man is referred by a court after being arrested on a crowded subway. For more than a year he has been intensely aroused by pressing his body against strangers in crowds, and he has done so many times. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent, intense arousal from touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person, acted on, for at least 6 months is frotteuristic disorder.

Takeaway: frotteuristic disorder involves touching or rubbing against non-consenting people.

whyNot.A: Exhibitionism is exposing the genitals to an unsuspecting person.
whyNot.E: Voyeurism is watching an unsuspecting person undress or have sex.
whyNot.B: Fetishism involves non-living objects or non-genital body parts.
whyNot.D: Sexual sadism is arousal from another person's suffering.

items.objective: Classify paraphilic disorders by their focus of arousal.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man has for many years become sexually aroused when he wears women's lingerie in private. He identifies as a man, is content with his body and gender, and his wife is accepting. He has no distress about the interest, and his work and relationships are unaffected. Which of the following best describes his condition?
items.explanationHtml:
An atypical but consensual sexual interest that causes no distress or impairment and harms no one is a paraphilia, not a paraphilic disorder. A disorder requires distress, impairment, or acting on the urges with a non-consenting person.

Takeaway: a paraphilia becomes a disorder only with distress, impairment or harm to others.

whyNot.E: Transvestic disorder requires clinically significant distress or impairment, which he does not have.
whyNot.B: He identifies as a man and has no gender incongruence.
whyNot.A: Fetishistic disorder also requires distress or impairment, and cross-dressing is classed as transvestic.
whyNot.D: The behaviour is pleasurable and wanted, not an anxiety-driven compulsion.

items.objective: Distinguish a paraphilia from a paraphilic disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 15-year-old who was assigned female at birth has said for 2 years that he is a boy, uses a male name with friends and is markedly distressed by breast development and menstruation. He has missed many school days because of the distress. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A marked incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex for more than 6 months, with clinically significant distress and impaired functioning, is gender dysphoria. The diagnosis rests on the distress, not on being transgender.

Takeaway: gender dysphoria requires incongruence of at least 6 months with distress or impairment.

whyNot.B: Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with a perceived physical flaw, not gender incongruence.
whyNot.E: Transvestic disorder is arousal from cross-dressing with distress.
whyNot.C: A stable gender identity is not a delusion; there is no fixed false belief.
whyNot.A: Nothing suggests restriction of food intake, low weight or fear of weight gain.

items.objective: Recognise the diagnostic features of gender dysphoria.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old transgender man has used testosterone injections for 2 years. He does not smoke and has no symptoms of sleep apnea. His hematocrit has risen from 40% to 54% (reference range for men, 41–53%). Which of the following best explains the rise?
items.explanationHtml:
Androgens raise renal erythropoietin production and suppress hepcidin, which increases iron availability for red cell production. Erythrocytosis is the most important laboratory risk of testosterone therapy.

Takeaway: testosterone causes erythrocytosis by raising erythropoietin and lowering hepcidin; monitor hematocrit.

whyNot.A: A JAK2 mutation causes polycythemia vera, which is unlikely given the clear drug cause.
whyNot.E: Hemochromatosis causes iron overload, not erythrocytosis.
whyNot.C: He has no smoking, lung disease or sleep apnea to cause hypoxemia.
whyNot.D: Dehydration would raise hematocrit transiently, not steadily over months of therapy.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of testosterone-induced erythrocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had gradually worsening erectile dysfunction for a year. He no longer has morning erections. He smokes a pack a day and has hypertension. He has not had blood tests in 5 years. Examination, including the genitals, is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Fasting lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c

items.explanationHtml:
Gradual erectile dysfunction with loss of morning erections in a smoker with hypertension is most likely vascular. It is a marker of coronary risk, so the next step is cardiovascular risk assessment: lipids, glucose or HbA1c and blood pressure, plus advice to stop smoking.

Takeaway: erectile dysfunction is a sentinel for vascular disease; check cardiovascular risk factors.

whyNot.C: Duplex ultrasound is a specialist test for selected patients, not part of the initial work-up.
whyNot.B: Loss of morning erections already points to an organic cause.
whyNot.E: Prolactin is checked when desire is low or hypogonadism is suspected, not first here.
whyNot.D: The history suggests a vascular cause rather than a psychological one.

items.objective: Evaluate erectile dysfunction as a marker of cardiovascular risk.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with stable angina takes isosorbide mononitrate daily and sublingual nitroglycerin as needed. He asks for treatment of erectile dysfunction. Which of the following is the most appropriate option?
items.explanationHtml:
All PDE5 inhibitors are contraindicated in a patient who uses nitrates, because the combination causes severe hypotension. A vacuum device, intracavernosal or intraurethral alprostadil, or a prosthesis are the alternatives.

Takeaway: patients taking nitrates must not receive PDE5 inhibitors; use a non-PDE5 option.

whyNot.C: Sildenafil with a nitrate can cause life-threatening hypotension.
whyNot.B: Daily tadalafil keeps him permanently at risk of the interaction.
whyNot.D: Testosterone does not treat erectile dysfunction unless he is hypogonadal, which is not shown.
whyNot.E: Vardenafil is a PDE5 inhibitor with the same contraindication.

items.objective: Select erectile dysfunction treatment for a patient taking nitrates.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has taken sertraline for 5 months for major depressive disorder, which is now in remission after two earlier episodes. She has been unable to reach orgasm since starting it, and this has not improved over 4 months. She wants to keep the benefit for her mood. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent SSRI-induced anorgasmia in a patient whose recurrent depression is in remission is best managed by adding bupropion, which can relieve sexual side effects while preserving the response. Switching to bupropion is an alternative but risks relapse.

Takeaway: for persistent SSRI sexual dysfunction with a good mood response, adding bupropion is a common strategy.

whyNot.C: Stopping risks relapse of recurrent depression and discontinuation symptoms.
whyNot.B: A higher dose would worsen serotonergic sexual effects.
whyNot.D: Paroxetine causes the most sexual dysfunction of the SSRIs.
whyNot.E: Venlafaxine is serotonergic and causes similar sexual side effects.

items.objective: Manage SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction while preserving antidepressant response.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man says that for 2 years he has ejaculated within about a minute of penetration on almost every occasion, which distresses him and his partner. Erections are normal. Behavioural techniques practised for 3 months have not helped. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Lifelong premature ejaculation that does not respond to behavioural methods is treated with an SSRI, which delays ejaculation; daily paroxetine is among the most effective (off-label in the United States). Topical anaesthetic sprays or creams are another option.

Takeaway: SSRIs, used for their ejaculation-delaying effect, treat premature ejaculation.

whyNot.D: PDE5 inhibitors help when premature ejaculation coexists with erectile dysfunction; his erections are normal.
whyNot.E: Testosterone has no role without hypogonadism.
whyNot.A: Bupropion lacks the serotonergic effect that delays ejaculation.
whyNot.C: Finasteride can impair sexual function and does not treat premature ejaculation.

items.objective: Treat premature ejaculation with an SSRI after failed behavioural therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has been unable to have vaginal intercourse since her marriage a year ago because of pain and an involuntary tightening when penetration is attempted. She also cannot insert tampons. Pelvic examination with a single finger shows marked tightness of the pelvic floor muscles; the vulva, vagina and cervix are otherwise normal, and there is no discharge. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Pain and involuntary pelvic floor contraction with any attempt at penetration, with an otherwise normal examination, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder. Pelvic floor physical therapy with graded dilators, often combined with cognitive behavioural therapy, is the treatment.

Takeaway: genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder responds to pelvic floor therapy, dilators and CBT.

whyNot.E: Vaginal estrogen treats atrophy in postmenopausal women; her tissues are normal.
whyNot.B: There is no sign of candidal infection.
whyNot.D: The hymen and vulva are normal; surgery is not indicated.
whyNot.A: Nothing suggests that her contraceptive is the cause.

items.objective: Manage genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had little interest in sex for 8 months, which distresses her. Over the same time her periods have stopped and she has noticed a milky discharge from both nipples. She takes no medications. A pregnancy test is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Low desire with amenorrhea and galactorrhea after a negative pregnancy test suggests hyperprolactinemia, which suppresses GnRH. Measure serum prolactin (and TSH); if high, look for a pituitary adenoma.

Takeaway: look for medical causes such as hyperprolactinemia before treating low desire as primary.

whyNot.B: The endocrine symptoms must be evaluated before treating this as a relationship problem.
whyNot.A: Drug treatment for low desire is considered only after medical causes are excluded.
whyNot.E: Vaginal estrogen treats atrophy-related pain, not low desire with galactorrhea.
whyNot.D: Testosterone measurement does not explain amenorrhea with galactorrhea.

items.objective: Investigate medical causes of low sexual desire.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man seeks help because for years he has had urges to expose his genitals to strangers in parks. He has acted on them several times, feels ashamed and wants to stop. He has never had physical contact with a victim and has no other psychiatric disorder. He has started cognitive behavioural therapy. Which of the following medications is most appropriate to add?
items.explanationHtml:
For exhibitionistic disorder, cognitive behavioural therapy is the core treatment, and an SSRI is the usual first medication because it can reduce the intensity of sexual urges and compulsive features.

Takeaway: add an SSRI to CBT for paraphilic disorders; keep anti-androgens for high-risk cases.

whyNot.C: A GnRH agonist is reserved for severe paraphilic disorders with high risk of contact offending.
whyNot.B: Antipsychotics have no role without psychosis.
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines do not reduce paraphilic urges and may disinhibit.
whyNot.E: A stimulant would not reduce urges and could increase impulsivity.

items.objective: Choose first-line pharmacotherapy for a paraphilic disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old transgender woman comes to the clinic for a sore throat. Her insurance record still lists her legal name from birth. At check-in she tells the receptionist her name is Maya and that she uses she and her pronouns. Which of the following is the most appropriate way for the physician to address her?

options.label: A
options.html: Ask her to bring legal documents before the visit continues

options.label: B
options.html: Avoid using any name during the visit

options.label: C
options.html: Refer her to a gender clinic before treating her sore throat

options.label: D
options.html: Use her legal name to match the insurance record

options.label: E
options.html: Use the name Maya and she/her pronouns

items.explanationHtml:
Using the name and pronouns a patient asks for is basic respect and builds trust. The record should note them alongside the legal name needed for billing.

Takeaway: use and record the patient's chosen name and pronouns.

whyNot.D: Billing needs do not justify addressing her by a name she does not use.
whyNot.B: Avoiding her name is awkward and conveys discomfort.
whyNot.A: Her gender identity does not need documentary proof.
whyNot.C: Her sore throat should be treated today; gender-related referral is unrelated to the visit.

items.objective: Use a patient's chosen name and pronouns.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old transgender man has used testosterone for 3 years and has not had genital surgery. His last cervical cytology, 4 years ago, was normal. He has had sex with both men and women. He feels uncomfortable with pelvic examinations. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation about cervical cancer screening?

options.label: B
options.html: Pelvic ultrasonography can replace cervical screening

options.label: C
options.html: Screen now on the usual schedule for people with a cervix

options.label: D
options.html: Screening is needed only if he has sex with men

options.label: E
options.html: Screening is no longer needed while he takes testosterone

items.explanationHtml:
Screening follows the organs a person has. He has a cervix and is due, so he should have cervical cancer screening (for example, HPV-based testing) on the same schedule as anyone else. Steps such as a smaller speculum, explanation and self-collection where available can reduce discomfort.

Takeaway: transgender men with a cervix need cervical cancer screening on the usual schedule.

whyNot.E: Testosterone does not remove the cervix or prevent HPV-related cancer.
whyNot.D: HPV is transmitted through any genital contact; sexual history does not remove the need.
whyNot.B: Ultrasound does not detect cervical precancer.
whyNot.A: CA-125 is not a screening test for cervical cancer.

items.objective: Apply organ-based cancer screening in transgender patients.

items.stemHtml:
A 26-year-old transgender man has used weekly testosterone injections for 18 months. He feels well, does not smoke and has no snoring. Results of routine monitoring are shown.

TestResultReference range (men)
Hemoglobin18.6 g/dL13.5–17.5 g/dL
Hematocrit56%41–53%
Leukocytes7,200/mm34,500–11,000/mm3
Platelets260,000/mm3150,000–400,000/mm3

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue the current dose and recheck in 1 year

options.label: B
options.html: Reduce or hold the testosterone dose

items.explanationHtml:
A hematocrit above 54% on testosterone raises the risk of thrombosis and calls for reducing or holding the dose, or changing the formulation, and then rechecking. Isolated erythrocytosis with normal white cells and platelets on testosterone does not suggest a myeloproliferative neoplasm.

Takeaway: on testosterone, a hematocrit above 54% means reduce or pause the dose and recheck.

whyNot.A: Continuing unchanged leaves him with a raised thrombotic risk.
whyNot.D: Hydroxyurea is for myeloproliferative neoplasms, not drug-induced erythrocytosis.
whyNot.E: Aspirin does not correct the hematocrit and is not the response here.
whyNot.C: Isolated erythrocytosis with an obvious cause does not first need JAK2 testing.

items.objective: Respond to testosterone-induced erythrocytosis.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old transgender man started testosterone 12 months ago, and his menses have since stopped. He has sex with a cisgender male partner and uses no contraception, because he understood that testosterone would prevent pregnancy. Pregnancy test today is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate counselling?

options.label: A
options.html: Amenorrhea shows that he can no longer conceive

options.label: B
options.html: Pregnancy remains possible, so he should use contraception

options.label: C
options.html: Raise the testosterone dose to ensure he cannot ovulate

options.label: D
options.html: Recommend tubal ligation as the only option

options.label: E
options.html: Stop testosterone and recheck in 3 months

items.explanationHtml:
Testosterone often stops menses but does not reliably prevent ovulation, and it is teratogenic. Anyone who can become pregnant and has sex that could cause pregnancy needs contraception; an IUD or progestin-only method is often preferred.

Takeaway: testosterone is not a contraceptive; offer contraception.

whyNot.A: Amenorrhea on testosterone does not mean infertility.
whyNot.C: Higher doses do not provide contraception and add risks.
whyNot.E: Stopping his gender-affirming therapy is unnecessary; contraception solves the problem.
whyNot.D: Many reversible options exist; permanent sterilisation is only one choice.

items.objective: Counsel transgender men on testosterone about contraception.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old transgender woman takes oral estradiol and spironolactone. Last month lisinopril was started for hypertension and diabetic kidney disease. Today serum potassium is 5.9 mEq/L (3.5–5.0 mEq/L) and creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL). ECG shows no changes of hyperkalemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate change to her medications?
items.explanationHtml:
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing anti-androgen. Combined with an ACE inhibitor and kidney disease it has caused hyperkalemia, so it should be stopped and potassium rechecked. Other ways to suppress androgens can be discussed, and estradiol can continue.

Takeaway: spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor or kidney disease can cause hyperkalemia; monitor potassium.

whyNot.C: Estradiol does not cause hyperkalemia and is central to her care.
whyNot.B: A higher dose would worsen the hyperkalemia.
whyNot.E: Ethinyl estradiol carries the highest thrombosis risk and is not used in gender-affirming care.
whyNot.A: Adding potassium would be dangerous.

items.objective: Recognise spironolactone-induced hyperkalemia in gender-affirming hormone therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with chest pain an hour after snorting a white powder at a party. He is agitated and diaphoretic, with dilated pupils, pulse 124/min and blood pressure 178/104 mm Hg. The drug he used acts mainly through which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: E
options.html: Release of monoamines by reversing vesicular transport

items.explanationHtml:
Snorted powder with sympathomimetic toxicity and chest pain suggests cocaine. Cocaine blocks the reuptake transporters for dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin, so these transmitters accumulate in the synapse; it also blocks sodium channels, which makes it a local anaesthetic.

Takeaway: cocaine blocks reuptake; amphetamines release monoamines.

whyNot.E: Reversal of vesicular and membrane transporters to release monoamines is how amphetamines act.
whyNot.D: MAO inhibitors are antidepressants and are not snorted recreationally.
whyNot.B: NMDA antagonists (PCP, ketamine) cause nystagmus and dissociation more than chest pain.
whyNot.A: Mu agonists cause miosis and respiratory depression, not sympathetic overdrive.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of cocaine.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man is found confused after drinking heavily for 2 days without eating. Fingerstick glucose is 38 mg/dL (2.1 mmol/L), and venous lactate is mildly raised. Which of the following best explains his hypoglycemia?

options.label: A
options.html: A raised NADH/NAD+ ratio that blocks gluconeogenesis

options.label: B
options.html: Excess glycogen stored in the liver

options.label: C
options.html: Increased insulin secretion stimulated by ethanol

options.label: D
options.html: Increased peripheral glucose uptake by muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Oxidation of ethanol by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases generates NADH. A high NADH/NAD+ ratio drives pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, removing gluconeogenic substrates. After 2 days without food, glycogen is exhausted, so the liver cannot maintain blood glucose.

Takeaway: fasting plus alcohol causes hypoglycemia because excess NADH shuts down gluconeogenesis.

whyNot.C: Ethanol does not meaningfully stimulate insulin secretion.
whyNot.B: After 2 days of fasting, hepatic glycogen is depleted, not in excess.
whyNot.E: Glucose-6-phosphatase is not the step that ethanol metabolism blocks.
whyNot.D: Muscle glucose uptake is not increased by alcohol.

items.objective: Explain alcohol-induced fasting hypoglycemia through the NADH/NAD+ ratio.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman being treated for alcohol use disorder drinks wine at a wedding. Within 20 minutes she has facial flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting and palpitations. The drug she takes inhibits which of the following enzymes?
items.explanationHtml:
Disulfiram inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase. After a drink, acetaldehyde accumulates and causes flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension, which is meant to deter drinking.

Takeaway: disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up after alcohol.

whyNot.A: Alcohol dehydrogenase is inhibited by fomepizole, used for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.
whyNot.D: CYP2E1 is induced by chronic drinking and is not the target of disulfiram.
whyNot.C: Catalase is a minor pathway of ethanol oxidation and not a drug target here.
whyNot.E: Xanthine oxidase is inhibited by allopurinol.

items.objective: Identify the target enzyme of disulfiram.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old man who has drunk a fifth of vodka daily for 10 years is admitted for elective surgery and has no alcohol in hospital. Thirty hours later he has tremor, sweating, tachycardia and a generalized seizure. Which of the following neural adaptations to chronic alcohol best explains this?

options.label: A
options.html: Depletion of serotonin in the raphe nuclei

options.label: B
options.html: Excess dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway

options.label: C
options.html: Less glutamate release from cortical neurons

options.label: D
options.html: More GABA-A receptors with greater sensitivity to GABA

options.label: E
options.html: Reduced GABA-A responsiveness with up-regulated NMDA receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Alcohol enhances GABA-A inhibition and blocks NMDA excitation. Long-term exposure leads to compensatory down-regulation of GABA-A function and up-regulation of NMDA receptors. When alcohol stops, inhibition is weak and excitation strong: tremor, autonomic overactivity, seizures and delirium.

Takeaway: alcohol withdrawal is a hyperexcitable state from weak GABA-A and strong NMDA signalling.

whyNot.D: Greater GABA-A function would protect against, not cause, withdrawal hyperexcitability.
whyNot.C: Glutamatergic excitation rises in withdrawal; it does not fall.
whyNot.B: Nigrostriatal dopamine changes relate to movement disorders, not withdrawal seizures.
whyNot.A: Serotonin depletion does not explain the autonomic and convulsive picture.

items.objective: Explain the neurochemical basis of alcohol withdrawal.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man who smokes illicit fentanyl daily is given his first dose of sublingual buprenorphine in clinic, 3 hours after his last use. Within 30 minutes he has vomiting, abdominal cramps, yawning, rhinorrhea, dilated pupils and gooseflesh. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: A high-affinity partial agonist displaced a full agonist

options.label: B
options.html: An allergic reaction to the sublingual tablet

options.label: C
options.html: Buprenorphine is a pure mu-opioid antagonist

items.explanationHtml:
Buprenorphine binds the mu receptor more tightly than most opioids but activates it only partly. Given while fentanyl still occupies the receptors, it displaces the full agonist and abruptly lowers mu activation: precipitated withdrawal.

Takeaway: start buprenorphine once withdrawal has begun, or use a low-dose start, to avoid precipitated withdrawal.

whyNot.C: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist, not an antagonist; naloxone and naltrexone are antagonists.
whyNot.D: Buprenorphine is a kappa antagonist, and kappa effects do not explain mu withdrawal signs.
whyNot.B: Allergy would cause urticaria, angioedema or hypotension, not opioid withdrawal signs.
whyNot.E: Serotonin syndrome causes clonus, hyperthermia and agitation, not yawning and rhinorrhea.

items.objective: Explain buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is found confused, with nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus weakness and a wide-based gait. Before anyone gives thiamine, he receives a large bolus of intravenous dextrose, and his confusion worsens. Impaired activity of which of the following enzymes most directly explains why glucose made him worse?
items.explanationHtml:
Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase (and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase). With thiamine deficiency, a glucose load increases glycolytic flux to pyruvate that cannot enter the citric acid cycle, so neurons in vulnerable regions such as the mammillary bodies lose aerobic energy production. Thiamine is therefore given before or with glucose.

Takeaway: thiamine-dependent pyruvate dehydrogenase links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle; give thiamine with glucose.

whyNot.C: Lactate dehydrogenase does not require thiamine.
whyNot.D: Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin, not thiamine.
whyNot.A: Glucose-6-phosphatase is a gluconeogenic enzyme without a thiamine cofactor.
whyNot.B: Hexokinase does not depend on thiamine.

items.objective: Link thiamine deficiency to impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase in Wernicke encephalopathy.

items.stemHtml:
The figure shows the usual time course of four syndromes that can follow abrupt cessation of heavy, long-term drinking, in hours after the last drink.

Which of the following findings is most characteristic of the syndrome whose time course is shown by bar D?

options.label: B
options.html: Fluctuating confusion with fever and tachycardia

options.label: C
options.html: Hallucinations with intact orientation and normal vital signs

items.explanationHtml:
Bar D begins about 48 hours after the last drink and lasts to about 96 hours, sometimes later: the window of delirium tremens. It combines fluctuating confusion with autonomic hyperactivity (fever, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating) and can be fatal without treatment.

Takeaway: delirium tremens usually begins 2 to 4 days after the last drink and combines delirium with autonomic instability.

whyNot.C: Hallucinations with a clear sensorium are alcoholic hallucinosis, which occurs earlier (about 12 to 48 hours).
whyNot.A: Withdrawal seizures usually occur within the first 48 hours.
whyNot.E: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia is Wernicke encephalopathy, a thiamine deficiency state not tied to this timeline.
whyNot.D: Mild tremor with intact orientation is minor withdrawal, the earliest syndrome.

items.objective: Relate the alcohol withdrawal timeline to delirium tremens.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman who smokes 25 cigarettes a day starts a drug that reduces her craving and makes smoking less satisfying. It binds the same receptor as nicotine in the reward pathway but activates it less strongly. Which of the following describes its mechanism?

options.label: C
options.html: Antagonism at nicotinic receptors of the neuromuscular junction

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake

options.label: E
options.html: Partial agonism at alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptors

items.explanationHtml:
Varenicline is a partial agonist at alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic receptors. Its partial activation releases some dopamine to ease craving and withdrawal, while its occupancy blunts the reward from smoking.

Takeaway: varenicline is an alpha-4 beta-2 nicotinic partial agonist.

whyNot.D: Reuptake inhibition of norepinephrine and dopamine describes bupropion.
whyNot.B: Mu antagonism describes naltrexone.
whyNot.C: Neuromuscular nicotinic antagonists are paralytic agents.
whyNot.A: GABA-B agonism describes baclofen.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of varenicline.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man is brought in by police after attacking a stranger. He is agitated, does not seem to feel pain from a deep cut on his hand, and has horizontal and vertical nystagmus. Blood pressure is 168/100 mm Hg. The drug he most likely used acts by which of the following mechanisms?
items.explanationHtml:
Violence, analgesia, hypertension and nystagmus in several directions (including vertical) are typical of phencyclidine, an NMDA receptor antagonist. Ketamine acts the same way.

Takeaway: PCP and ketamine are NMDA antagonists; vertical nystagmus and violence suggest PCP.

whyNot.C: 5-HT2A agonists such as LSD cause perceptual changes, not violence with nystagmus.
whyNot.A: Cannabis causes conjunctival injection and increased appetite, not this picture.
whyNot.B: Opioids cause sedation and miosis.
whyNot.E: Cocaine causes sympathomimetic toxicity but not prominent vertical nystagmus or analgesia.

items.objective: Recognise PCP intoxication and its mechanism.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man is admitted with cellulitis of the leg. He drinks about 12 beers a day, and his last drink was 14 hours ago. He is anxious, sweating and tremulous. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 108/min and blood pressure is 154/94 mm Hg. He is fully oriented. His withdrawal score on the CIWA-Ar scale is 15. He has received intravenous thiamine. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his withdrawal?
items.explanationHtml:
He has moderate alcohol withdrawal. Benzodiazepines are the treatment, and symptom-triggered dosing guided by repeated CIWA-Ar scores controls withdrawal with less total drug than fixed schedules. Long-acting agents give a smoother course.

Takeaway: treat moderate alcohol withdrawal with a benzodiazepine dosed by CIWA-Ar.

whyNot.D: A score this high with autonomic signs needs treatment to prevent seizures and delirium.
whyNot.B: Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and does not treat withdrawal.
whyNot.A: Clonidine can blunt autonomic signs but does not prevent seizures or delirium.
whyNot.C: Naltrexone is for relapse prevention, not acute withdrawal.

items.objective: Treat alcohol withdrawal with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines.

items.stemHtml: On hospital day 3, the patient from the previous item becomes confused and disoriented to place and time, picks at the bed sheets and sees insects on the walls. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 134/min and blood pressure is 182/106 mm Hg. He is drenched in sweat. Fingerstick glucose is 104 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Stop benzodiazepines because of the confusion

options.label: E
options.html: Transfer to intensive care for escalating IV benzodiazepines

items.explanationHtml:
Fluctuating confusion with hallucinations and autonomic hyperactivity on day 3 is delirium tremens. It needs intensive care with rapidly escalating intravenous benzodiazepines, fluids, electrolytes and thiamine; phenobarbital or propofol is added if it is refractory.

Takeaway: delirium tremens is an ICU emergency treated with escalating IV benzodiazepines.

whyNot.B: Antipsychotics alone do not treat withdrawal and lower the seizure threshold.
whyNot.D: The confusion is due to undertreated withdrawal; stopping benzodiazepines would worsen it.
whyNot.A: Restraints increase injury and hyperthermia, and oral dosing is too slow here.
whyNot.C: The timing and setting explain the picture; treatment should not be delayed, though infection is considered.

items.objective: Manage delirium tremens.

items.stemHtml: The patient from the previous items recovers and is ready for discharge. He wants help to stay abstinent. He takes oxycodone every day for chronic back pain from a spinal fracture, prescribed by his pain specialist. AST is 96 U/L, ALT is 44 U/L, and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to prevent relapse?
items.explanationHtml:
Acamprosate is a first-line drug for maintaining abstinence. It is cleared by the kidneys, so it is safe with his liver enzymes, and it does not interact with opioids. Naltrexone in either form would block his prescribed oxycodone and precipitate withdrawal.

Takeaway: if a patient needs opioids, use acamprosate rather than naltrexone for alcohol use disorder.

whyNot.E: Naltrexone is contraindicated in a patient who takes opioids.
whyNot.D: The injectable form has the same opioid-blocking problem and lasts a month.
whyNot.C: Disulfiram is second line, needs a highly motivated patient, and carries hepatic risk.
whyNot.B: Long-term benzodiazepines carry dependence risk and are not relapse-prevention therapy.

items.objective: Choose acamprosate for alcohol use disorder in a patient who needs opioids.

items.stemHtml:
A 61-year-old woman with alcohol use disorder completed withdrawal treatment 5 days ago and wants medication to help her stay abstinent. She takes no opioids and has no heart disease. Laboratory results are shown.

TestResultReference range
Creatinine2.6 mg/dL (230 µmol/L)0.6–1.2 mg/dL
Estimated creatinine clearance22 mL/minabove 90 mL/min
AST34 U/L12–38 U/L
ALT28 U/L10–40 U/L
Bilirubin, total0.8 mg/dL0.1–1.0 mg/dL

Which of the following is the most appropriate medication?
items.explanationHtml:
Naltrexone is first line and is metabolised by the liver; her liver tests are normal and she takes no opioids. Acamprosate is excreted by the kidneys and is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is 30 mL/min or less.

Takeaway: match the alcohol use disorder drug to the patient: acamprosate needs kidney function, naltrexone needs no opioids.

whyNot.A: Acamprosate is contraindicated with creatinine clearance at or below 30 mL/min.
whyNot.B: Disulfiram is second line and depends on strict adherence and supervision.
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines have no role after withdrawal and risk dependence.
whyNot.C: Gabapentin is off-label and renally cleared, so it is a poor choice with her kidney function.

items.objective: Select naltrexone over acamprosate in severe kidney impairment.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man is found unresponsive in a public restroom with a syringe nearby. Respirations are 5/min and shallow, oxygen saturation is 82%, and his pupils are pinpoint. He has a pulse of 58/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Coma, slow breathing and miosis are the opioid toxidrome. Support ventilation with a bag-mask and give naloxone, repeating it as needed; fentanyl may need several doses. Observe him, because naloxone can wear off before the opioid does.

Takeaway: opioid overdose: ventilate and give naloxone, repeating as needed.

whyNot.B: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures; it does not reverse opioids.
whyNot.A: Activated charcoal is not used after injected drugs and is unsafe in a patient who cannot protect the airway.
whyNot.E: Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dilated pupils.
whyNot.C: Checking glucose is reasonable, but dextrose alone does not treat opioid respiratory depression.

items.objective: Treat opioid overdose with ventilation and naloxone.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman who injects illicit fentanyl is found with slow breathing and pinpoint pupils. After intranasal and then intravenous naloxone, her respiratory rate rises to 14/min, but she remains deeply sedated. Pulse is 48/min and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. Her forearms have several deep, necrotic ulcers away from injection sites. Glucose is normal. Which of the following adulterants best explains her persistent findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Xylazine, a veterinary alpha-2 agonist sedative, is widely mixed into illicit fentanyl. It causes sedation, bradycardia and hypotension that naloxone does not reverse, and chronic necrotic wounds. Naloxone is still given for the opioid component; the rest of care is supportive, with wound care.

Takeaway: sedation, bradycardia and necrotic wounds that persist after naloxone suggest xylazine.

whyNot.C: Levamisole is a cocaine adulterant that causes agranulocytosis and vasculitic skin lesions, not sedation with bradycardia.
whyNot.A: Carfentanil is a potent opioid whose effects respond to enough naloxone; it does not cause wounds.
whyNot.B: Nitazenes are potent opioids; their respiratory depression responds to naloxone, which here it did.
whyNot.D: Scopolamine causes anticholinergic toxicity with tachycardia and dilated pupils.

items.objective: Recognise xylazine adulteration of illicit fentanyl.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man with opioid use disorder who uses heroin daily asks to start buprenorphine today. His last use was 4 hours ago. He feels well, his pupils are mid-sized, and he has no yawning, sweating, rhinorrhea or gooseflesh; his withdrawal score is 2. His physician has a standard DEA registration. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Give buprenorphine once objective withdrawal signs appear

options.label: B
options.html: Give the full first dose of buprenorphine now

options.label: D
options.html: Refer him to a physician who holds a special buprenorphine waiver

items.explanationHtml:
Buprenorphine should be started once objective withdrawal is present (or with a low-dose start), so that it does not displace a full agonist and precipitate withdrawal. Any clinician with a standard DEA registration can now prescribe it; the separate waiver was eliminated in 2023.

Takeaway: start buprenorphine once withdrawal has begun; no special waiver is needed any longer.

whyNot.B: Dosing now, with opioid still on the receptors, risks precipitated withdrawal.
whyNot.E: Naltrexone needs 7 to 10 days without opioids and would precipitate severe withdrawal.
whyNot.C: Methadone for opioid use disorder is dispensed only through opioid treatment programmes.
whyNot.D: The buprenorphine waiver requirement no longer exists.

items.objective: Time buprenorphine initiation to avoid precipitated withdrawal.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman at 14 weeks of gestation tells her obstetrician that she has used heroin daily for 2 years and wants help. She has had two overdoses. She has no other medical problems. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
In pregnancy, opioid use disorder is treated with an opioid agonist, buprenorphine or methadone. It reduces overdose, relapse, obstetric complications and illicit use. Withdrawal management (detoxification) carries high relapse and overdose risk. The newborn is monitored for neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome.

Takeaway: treat opioid use disorder in pregnancy with buprenorphine or methadone, not withdrawal.

whyNot.E: Medically assisted withdrawal in pregnancy has high relapse and overdose rates.
whyNot.D: Naltrexone requires opioid abstinence first and has less evidence in pregnancy.
whyNot.A: Abstinence without medication carries a high risk of relapse and fatal overdose.
whyNot.C: Clonidine only eases withdrawal symptoms and does not treat the use disorder.

items.objective: Treat opioid use disorder in pregnancy with agonist therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has chest pain 1 hour after smoking crack cocaine. He is agitated and sweating. Pulse is 122/min, blood pressure is 176/108 mm Hg and temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevation; the first troponin is pending. Aspirin has been given. Which of the following is the most appropriate next drug?
items.explanationHtml:
In cocaine toxicity, benzodiazepines are first line: they reduce agitation and central sympathetic outflow, which lowers heart rate, blood pressure and temperature. Nitroglycerin or a calcium channel blocker can be added for persistent chest pain or hypertension.

Takeaway: treat cocaine-associated agitation and chest pain first with a benzodiazepine.

whyNot.D: A beta-blocker alone early in cocaine toxicity is avoided because unopposed alpha stimulation can worsen vasoconstriction.
whyNot.B: Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold and impairs heat loss.
whyNot.A: Thrombolysis is not indicated without ST elevation.
whyNot.E: A vasoconstrictor would worsen his hypertension and coronary spasm.

items.objective: Treat cocaine toxicity with chest pain using benzodiazepines first.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man has had five emergency visits in a year for bouts of severe vomiting and abdominal pain lasting several days. He takes long hot showers, which ease the symptoms. He has smoked cannabis several times a day for 4 years. Endoscopy and abdominal CT were normal. Which of the following is the most effective long-term treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent vomiting with relief from hot showers in a heavy, long-term cannabis user is cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. Acute episodes respond to fluids, haloperidol or topical capsaicin, but the only lasting cure is stopping cannabis.

Takeaway: cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome resolves only with cannabis cessation.

whyNot.C: Antiemetics give limited relief and do not prevent recurrence.
whyNot.B: There is no biliary disease; the imaging was normal.
whyNot.A: Acid suppression does not address the cause.
whyNot.D: A gastric emptying study is a test, not a treatment, and the diagnosis is already clear.

items.objective: Treat cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome with cessation.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman smokes 20 cigarettes a day and wants to quit. She has bulimia nervosa, now treated, with no binge-purge episodes for 6 months. She has no seizure history and no kidney disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Varenicline is among the most effective single smoking-cessation drugs and can be used here. Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with current or past bulimia or anorexia nervosa because of seizure risk. Combination nicotine replacement is another effective option.

Takeaway: avoid bupropion with an eating disorder or seizure history; varenicline is a strong choice.

whyNot.A: Bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia or anorexia nervosa because of seizure risk.
whyNot.D: Nortriptyline is a second-line option with more side effects.
whyNot.C: Naltrexone is not a smoking-cessation drug.
whyNot.B: Clonidine is second line with troublesome side effects.

items.objective: Choose smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy around bupropion contraindications.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is admitted for pneumonia. For 15 years she has taken alprazolam 1 mg three times daily, which was not continued on admission. On hospital day 2 she is anxious, tremulous and sweating, with pulse 112/min, and she says she cannot sleep. She is oriented. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: D
options.html: Restart a benzodiazepine and taper slowly

items.explanationHtml:
Abrupt cessation of a long-term benzodiazepine causes withdrawal that can progress to seizures and delirium. Restart a benzodiazepine at an equivalent dose (a longer-acting agent can be used) and plan a gradual taper over weeks to months.

Takeaway: never stop long-term benzodiazepines abruptly; restart and taper slowly.

whyNot.E: Antiseizure drugs such as phenytoin do not prevent benzodiazepine withdrawal seizures.
whyNot.B: Flumazenil would worsen withdrawal and can provoke seizures.
whyNot.A: Haloperidol does not treat withdrawal and lowers the seizure threshold.
whyNot.C: Untreated sedative withdrawal can progress to seizures.

items.objective: Manage benzodiazepine withdrawal by restarting and tapering.

items.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man has been stable on methadone 90 mg daily from an opioid treatment programme for 2 years. Ten days after starting treatment for active pulmonary tuberculosis, he reports yawning, runny nose, abdominal cramps, sweating and craving at the end of each day. He denies other drug use, and urine testing confirms this. Which of the following best explains his symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Covert use of a full opioid agonist

items.explanationHtml:
Rifampin strongly induces CYP3A4 and other enzymes that metabolise methadone. Methadone levels fall and he develops withdrawal later in each dosing interval. The methadone dose usually needs to be raised while rifampin is given, and lowered after it stops.

Takeaway: enzyme inducers such as rifampin cause methadone withdrawal; adjust the dose.

whyNot.C: Isoniazid neuropathy causes distal numbness and tingling, not opioid withdrawal signs.
whyNot.E: Serotonin syndrome causes agitation, clonus and hyperthermia, not yawning and rhinorrhea.
whyNot.B: Ethambutol affects vision, not opioid withdrawal.
whyNot.A: Additional opioid use would cause sedation, not withdrawal, and his urine testing is negative.

items.objective: Recognise rifampin-methadone interaction causing withdrawal.

items.stemHtml: At a routine visit, a 46-year-old man completes the AUDIT-C questionnaire, and his score is positive. He drinks about 4 drinks on most evenings and 7 on Saturdays. He has never had withdrawal symptoms, and he functions well at work. Liver tests are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: No action is needed while his liver tests are normal

items.explanationHtml:
A positive screen for unhealthy alcohol use is followed by a brief intervention: personalised feedback, advice and a goal agreed with the patient. Assess him for alcohol use disorder and arrange follow-up or referral if a disorder is present.

Takeaway: a positive alcohol screen leads to brief counselling and assessment.

whyNot.D: He has no withdrawal history; inpatient detoxification is unnecessary.
whyNot.B: Normal liver tests do not call for a biopsy.
whyNot.E: Disulfiram is not started after a screening result, and only with motivation for abstinence.
whyNot.C: Normal liver tests do not make heavy drinking safe; he needs counselling.

items.objective: Follow a positive alcohol screen with a brief intervention.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has had double vision since he struck his head in a bicycle crash 2 weeks ago. The images are one above the other and are worst when he walks down stairs or reads. He keeps his head tilted toward his left shoulder. On examination, his right eye sits higher than the left, and this vertical misalignment is greatest when he looks down and to the left. Tilting his head toward the right shoulder makes it worse. Injury to which of the following nerves best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
The superior oblique depresses the eye most effectively when the eye is adducted, and it also intorts the eye. When the right trochlear nerve is injured, the right eye drifts upward (right hypertropia). The drift is greatest on looking down and to the left, because that brings the right eye into adduction. Tilting the head toward the right shoulder demands intorsion of the right eye; the weak superior oblique cannot supply it, so the superior rectus intorts the eye and lifts it further. The patient therefore tilts the head away, toward the left. The trochlear nerve is thin and has a long intracranial course, so it is often injured by head trauma.

Takeaway: vertical diplopia worst looking down and in, with a head tilt away from the affected side, points to a trochlear nerve palsy on the side of the higher eye.

whyNot.B: A left trochlear palsy makes the left eye the higher one, worst on looking down and to the right, with a tilt toward the right shoulder.
whyNot.D: A right oculomotor palsy leaves the eye down and out with ptosis and often a dilated pupil, not a raised eye.
whyNot.C: A right abducens palsy causes horizontal diplopia, worst on looking to the right, with no vertical misalignment.
whyNot.A: A left oculomotor palsy would weaken elevation, depression and adduction of the left eye and cause left ptosis.

items.objective: Localise vertical diplopia with a compensatory head tilt to a trochlear nerve palsy on the side of the hypertropic eye.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old carpenter has had ringing in both ears for several years and now finds it hard to follow conversation in noisy rooms. He has used power saws and nail guns daily for 30 years, usually without hearing protection. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows a symmetric sensorineural hearing loss that is deepest at 4000 Hz, with better thresholds at 8000 Hz. Damage to which of the following structures is most likely the primary cause of his hearing loss?

options.label: A
options.html: Cochlear nerve fibres in the internal acoustic canal

items.explanationHtml:
Repeated loud noise injures the cochlea mechanically and metabolically. The outer hair cells, which amplify basilar membrane motion, are lost first, in the region of the cochlea tuned near 3000–6000 Hz. This gives the typical audiometric notch around 4000 Hz, with partial recovery at 8000 Hz. Hair cells do not regenerate in humans, so the loss is permanent. Prevention relies on hearing protection and limiting exposure.

Takeaway: a 4000 Hz notch after years of loud noise reflects loss of cochlear outer hair cells.

whyNot.C: Fixation of the stapes footplate (otosclerosis) causes a conductive loss with an air-bone gap, not a sensorineural notch.
whyNot.D: Atrophy of the stria vascularis causes a flat sensorineural loss across all frequencies, typically in older adults.
whyNot.E: A damaged tympanic membrane causes conductive loss and would be seen on otoscopy.
whyNot.A: A lesion of the cochlear nerve, such as a vestibular schwannoma, usually causes asymmetric loss with poor speech discrimination.

items.objective: Attribute noise-induced hearing loss with a 4000 Hz notch to outer hair cell damage.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has had weakness of her left leg for 3 weeks, which began after a minor fall at work. She drags the leg when she walks. When she tries to push her left heel down into the bed, there is almost no force. When she lifts her right leg against resistance, her left heel presses firmly down. Tone, reflexes and plantar responses are normal and symmetric, and sensation is normal. MRI of the brain and spine is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Explain the diagnosis openly and refer for functional-disorder physiotherapy

options.label: B
options.html: Order nerve conduction studies and electromyography of both legs

options.label: C
options.html: Repeat MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium contrast

options.label: D
options.html: Start a benzodiazepine for the anxiety that may underlie it

options.label: E
options.html: Tell her the examination is normal and that nothing is physically wrong

items.explanationHtml:
Involuntary hip extension of the 'weak' leg when the other leg flexes against resistance (Hoover sign) is a positive sign of functional neurological symptom disorder. The diagnosis rests on such positive signs, not only on normal tests. Outcomes are best when the clinician explains the diagnosis clearly, as a genuine and potentially reversible problem of nervous system function, and refers to physiotherapy designed for functional disorders, with psychological therapy where helpful.

Takeaway: make functional weakness a positive diagnosis, explain it openly and treat it with targeted physiotherapy.

whyNot.B: Normal tone, reflexes and sensation with a positive Hoover sign make a peripheral nerve or muscle cause unlikely, so more testing adds little.
whyNot.E: Saying 'nothing is wrong' invalidates real symptoms and worsens engagement and outcome.
whyNot.D: A benzodiazepine does not treat functional weakness and adds dependence risk.
whyNot.C: Normal imaging and positive functional signs do not justify repeating the scan.

items.objective: Manage functional limb weakness with an open explanation of the diagnosis and functional-disorder physiotherapy.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic convinced that she is 5 months pregnant. She and her partner have tried to conceive for 6 years. Her periods stopped 5 months ago, her abdomen has enlarged, her breasts are tender and she reports feeling movements. Serum β-hCG is negative, and pelvic ultrasonography shows a normal, non-pregnant uterus. She has no hallucinations or other unusual beliefs, and she becomes tearful but asks sensible questions when shown the results. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Pseudocyesis is a false belief of being pregnant accompanied by objective-seeming signs such as amenorrhea, abdominal enlargement, breast changes and perceived fetal movement. It is classed among the somatic symptom and related disorders and often follows infertility or pregnancy loss. Unlike a delusion, the belief usually yields to clear evidence, as it does here. Management is a compassionate explanation, attention to grief and mood, and psychotherapy.

Takeaway: believed pregnancy with physical signs, negative tests and no psychosis is pseudocyesis.

whyNot.A: A delusion would persist despite the negative tests, usually with other features of psychosis.
whyNot.B: She is not deliberately producing the signs to take on the sick role.
whyNot.C: Illness anxiety is preoccupation with having a serious disease, with few or no bodily signs.
whyNot.D: There is no intentional feigning and no external reward.

items.objective: Recognise pseudocyesis as a somatic symptom-related disorder distinct from a delusion of pregnancy.

items.stemHtml:
A 29-year-old nurse is brought to the emergency department after being found confused in the hospital locker room. Fingerstick glucose is 32 mg/dL, and she recovers after intravenous dextrose. She has had three similar episodes in 2 months. She has no diabetes and takes no prescribed medications. Blood drawn during the episode shows:

TestResultReference range
Glucose34 mg/dL70–100 mg/dL (fasting)
Insulinhigh
C-peptidelow
Sulfonylurea screennegative

Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypoglycemia?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypoglycemia with high insulin but low C-peptide means the insulin did not come from the pancreas, because the beta cell releases C-peptide in equal amounts with insulin. Injected insulin suppresses the patient's own secretion. In a health worker with access to insulin, this points to factitious disorder (or, if someone else gave it, harm by another person). The next steps are a careful, non-confrontational conversation and psychiatric involvement.

Takeaway: high insulin with low C-peptide during hypoglycemia means exogenous insulin.

whyNot.B: Insulin autoimmune syndrome gives very high insulin with raised, not low, C-peptide and is rare.
whyNot.C: An insulinoma secretes proinsulin, so C-peptide is high along with insulin.
whyNot.D: Endogenous beta-cell hyperfunction raises C-peptide, typically after meals.
whyNot.E: Sulfonylureas stimulate the beta cell, so C-peptide is high, and the screen is negative.

items.objective: Use insulin and C-peptide levels during hypoglycemia to identify exogenous insulin as a sign of factitious disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old accountant is referred by his employer after missing several deadlines. He insists every report be checked line by line and rewrites colleagues' work because their methods are 'sloppy'. He refuses to delegate, works most evenings and has few friends outside work. He sees nothing wrong with his standards and believes others should simply try harder. He has no intrusive thoughts and no rituals that he wishes he could stop. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A lifelong, inflexible preoccupation with order, perfection and control that costs efficiency and relationships, held as reasonable by the person (ego-syntonic), is obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (cluster C). In obsessive-compulsive disorder, unwanted intrusive thoughts and compulsions are experienced as distressing and excessive (ego-dystonic). Psychotherapy is the main treatment.

Takeaway: perfectionism the patient considers correct is OCPD; unwanted obsessions and rituals are OCD.

whyNot.A: Autism involves early-onset social communication deficits and restricted interests, not adult perfectionism alone.
whyNot.B: Avoidant personality disorder is driven by fear of rejection, not by insistence on standards and control.
whyNot.C: Generalized anxiety centres on pervasive worry across many areas rather than rigid control of tasks.
whyNot.D: OCD requires intrusive obsessions or compulsions that the person finds unwanted, which he denies.

items.objective: Distinguish ego-syntonic obsessive-compulsive personality disorder from ego-dystonic OCD.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman comes for her annual visit. She cares alone for her husband, who has moderate Alzheimer disease, wanders at night and needs help with bathing. She sleeps about 4 hours a night, feels worn out and irritable, and has stopped seeing friends. She still enjoys her grandchildren's visits, eats normally and has no thoughts of death. Her husband is safe at home and has not been harmed. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Advise moving her husband to a nursing home this week

options.label: B
options.html: Arrange respite care and caregiver support services

options.label: D
options.html: Reassure her that this is expected and review in a year

options.label: E
options.html: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor

items.explanationHtml:
She shows caregiver strain: exhaustion, poor sleep and social withdrawal from heavy, unrelieved care, without the criteria for a depressive disorder. Strain predicts depression in the carer and earlier institutional placement of the patient. The first step is practical relief: respite care, home help, adult day programmes, caregiver education and support groups, with follow-up for depression and for the safety of both.

Takeaway: treat caregiver strain first with respite and support services, and keep screening the carer for depression.

whyNot.A: Placement may come later, but it is a family decision and not the first step for manageable strain.
whyNot.C: Benzodiazepines add falls and confusion in older adults and leave the cause unchanged.
whyNot.D: Strain is common but treatable; waiting a year risks depression and a care breakdown.
whyNot.E: She does not meet criteria for a depressive disorder, so an antidepressant is not the first step.

items.objective: Recognise caregiver strain and manage it first with respite care and caregiver support.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman reports pain with vaginal intercourse for a year, which has led her to avoid sex. She also has vaginal dryness and burning. Her last menstrual period was 6 years ago. Over-the-counter lubricants and moisturizers helped only a little. Pelvic examination shows pale, thin vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae and no lesions. She has no history of breast or endometrial cancer or of venous thrombosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Dryness, burning and painful intercourse with thin, pale mucosa after menopause is the genitourinary syndrome of menopause, caused by estrogen deficiency. When lubricants and moisturizers are not enough, low-dose vaginal estrogen restores the epithelium and relieves pain, with minimal systemic absorption. Treating the cause often restores sexual function.

Takeaway: postmenopausal dyspareunia from atrophic mucosa is treated with low-dose vaginal estrogen once moisturizers fail.

whyNot.A: Flibanserin targets low sexual desire, not pain from atrophic tissue.
whyNot.C: PDE5 inhibitors have no established role in female sexual pain.
whyNot.D: Testosterone is considered only for low desire, and it does not treat atrophy.
whyNot.E: Topical anesthetic masks pain briefly but leaves the atrophy untreated.

items.objective: Treat genitourinary syndrome of menopause causing dyspareunia with low-dose vaginal estrogen.
